t1|1.c: When the industry was suddenly wiped out, people in it could only accept it or quietly push back.
t1|1.e: The episode opens by framing tutoring workers' situation as two choices: endure it quietly, or find ways around it in private. Jing Chen covered education for two years and now has to think about changing careers herself, which is where the discussion starts. The pivots, departures and illegal tutoring discussed later can all be seen as those two choices playing out in real life.
ex: Jing Chen covered education for two years and now must consider "switching careers" too

t1|1.c: After the crackdown, the tutoring industry's corners filled with bizarre, absurd stories.
t1|1.e: The episode isn't about the policy text but about the strange things hiding in the industry's corners after the crackdown. The show's outline points to at least three kinds: big companies' odd pivots, illegal tutoring that still goes on, and how education CEOs dealt with parents showing up to protest. The title's "home stacked with Moutai and cash" belongs here too.
ex: Related story: "Down Jackets, Moutai and the Parents' Committee"

t1|1.c: From the same policy shock, some who stayed or left ended up resigned, others pleased.
t1|1.e: The episode looks at two groups of workers: those who left and those who stayed. The show notes describe their fates as "some resigned, some pleased," showing the same shock landed differently on different people. At the end the episode returns to the starting question of whether children really need tutoring, but the show page doesn't give the answer.

t2|2.c: Big tech firms are a sea of people, which leaves individuals with nowhere to share their troubles.
t2|2.e: The episode opens with a rewritten comic poem: big companies are a sea of people where individuals easily disappear, worries have nowhere to go and they pile up year after year. That's the starting point: big-tech employees' mental struggles are often hidden by huge organizations and a hectic pace. The episode then asks whether depression really is an illness big-tech employees are prone to.

items.d: Stress is hard to talk about

t2|2.c: When it comes to depression at big companies, individuals, employers and coworkers each have a role.
t2|2.e: The episode breaks the topic into layers: what people who fear they may be depressed should do first, how those already diagnosed can cope, how companies should help employees and whether any do it well, and what coworkers can do when someone is struggling. The structure shows the show doesn't treat depression as purely personal. The show page doesn't list the specific advice.

root.d: Needs several parties to face it

items.d: Figure out what to do first
How to face it and cope

t2|2.c: People with depression aren't alone. Company and self-help can carry them until good things happen.
t2|2.e: Ren Youbing has lived with depression himself, and the episode starts from his own story. His message on the show page invites everyone to keep living together until the day good things happen. The two books the show recommends are titled around "you are not alone" and a "self-help guide." The attitude it conveys: depression can be talked about, kept company and handled with practical self-help.
ex: Recommended book: "You Are Not Alone in Depression"
Recommended book: "Your First Self-Help Guide to Depression"

result.d: Until the day good things happen

t3|3.c: Little reliable news leaves North Korea, so an insider's several perspectives beat scattered rumors.
t3|3.e: The episode begins by noting how little the outside world knows about North Korea, and how hard it is to tell true from false in the bits online. Terry lived in Pyongyang for work and is at once a trader, an observer who writes for a WeChat account and a tour guide. The show sees this mix as offering a fuller picture. The conversation starts with how he got into the business and moves on to the economy, sanctions and daily life in Pyongyang.
ex: Buying groceries and cooking for himself in Pyongyang is part of the daily life discussed

terms.d: Trades with North Korea from the northeast
His company runs North Korea tours

result.d: Instead of rumors of unknown truth

t3|3.c: Trading with North Korea has a terrible reputation, and it's full of traps.
t3|3.e: The episode spends a lot of time on how business with North Korea actually works: how a North Korean company is set up, how such companies relate to the state, which industries the trade centers on and how money is made. The show notes call the trade "notorious" outright, and the episode discusses why, along with common traps, including counterfeit North Korean money.
ex: Topics include North Korea's market economy and its current state
Counterfeit North Korean money is one risk of the trade

items.d: How North Korean firms are formed
How firms relate to the state

t3|3.c: After COVID, North Korea chose a long lockdown. Whether it opens up is the key to watch.
t3|3.e: The episode looks at North Korea under outside pressure: how much sanctions really hurt, and why it chose a long lockdown after the pandemic. It also asks whether North Korea resembles China in the past and whether it's more open than before, whether tourism reinforces or breaks stereotypes, and whether rumors of North Korean bitcoin mining are true, ending with thoughts on its future. The show page doesn't give the answers.

items.d: How much do they really hurt

t4|4.c: Every product category deserves to be reinvented, but not every brand gets a second chance.
t4|4.e: This is one clear judgment from the show notes: every consumer category has room to be reinvented, but only a few individual brands will get a chance to start over. It ties into the discussion of whether the new-consumer boom makes sense and why some brands never take hold. A category having an opportunity doesn't mean every brand in it does.

items: Not all get a second chance

d.verdict: A category's opportunity isn't a brand's opportunity

t4|4.c: The new-consumer boom deserves a rethink, including fake orders and the metrics brands chase.
t4|4.e: The episode first asks whether the boom in new consumer brands makes sense, and if so, why some brands still fail to take hold. It then discusses brushing, buying fake orders to inflate sales, and what "real brushing" means, and asks whether the new-consumer wave picked the wrong key metrics. The show page lists these as questions and doesn't state his conclusions.

t4|4.c: He praises Saturnbird, Alibaba and Freshippo, but has some regrets about Douyin.
t4|4.e: Zhiwei Wang praises Saturnbird, an instant coffee brand, "once again," and again marvels at what a great category coffee is, so this is a long-held view. He also singles out Alibaba and its grocery chain Freshippo for praise. On the other side, he expresses some regrets about Douyin and discusses the WeChat ecosystem. The show page doesn't spell out his reasons.
ex: He praises Saturnbird again and marvels at how good a category coffee is

t4|4.c: Chinese food needs new stories, and he approaches that task starting from content.
t4|4.e: The episode ends with Penguin Guide's next steps and his hopes for how Chinese food can be presented, using rice wine and sake as examples. Penguin Guide started as a WeChat content account and has also opened a flagship store on Tmall to sell products. The title notes that between searching for new stories he still fixes toilets himself, and the episode opens by asking whether a CEO needs to know how to fix a toilet.
ex: Rice wine and sake serve as examples of new stories for Chinese food
Related: Startup Insider Vol. 29 on content-driven e-commerce

items.d: Penguin Guide flagship store on Tmall
Rice wine and sake as examples

t6|5.c: Young people no longer read WeChat articles, and long video and long text have clearly split apart.
t6|5.e: The episode compares long videos with long articles, using "young people don't read WeChat accounts anymore" to mark a shift in audience habits. Lao Jiang makes long educational videos, and the show asks whether he still writes full scripts as a creator and what video does to in-depth discussion.

t6|5.c: Video unites an audience into a collective force more easily than text does.
t6|5.e: Another judgment in the show notes is that video rallies people more easily than text. Around this, the episode borrows Marshall McLuhan's idea of "hot" and "cool" media (hot media fill in the details for you, cool ones ask you to fill them in) to ask which one Bilibili is. It also covers public reach versus a loyal following, and how creators handle huge numbers of comments. The show page doesn't say which kind Bilibili turns out to be.
ex: Further reading: Marshall McLuhan's media theory

t6|5.c: The creators who define this era are also lonely ones.
t6|5.e: The second half covers how creators prove the value of their work, where Bilibili and its audience are headed, and what kind of creator belongs to this era, ending on "the lonely creator." The title calls this a look back and a reflection, and the episode is mostly Lao Jiang thinking about his own state as a creator.
ex: Related video: "Adding to Young People's Troubles"

items.d: Is being a creator still new
Showing what the work is worth
The future of Bilibili and viewers

t7|6.c: After many years running an in-depth content community, Lao Mai is still committed to Sspai.
t7|6.e: Sspai has run a community for in-depth content for many years. The episode asks Lao Mai why he keeps going, what he thinks of Zhihu, and how Sspai and Zhihu have worked together, talked and crossed paths. The show page doesn't list his specific answers.

t7|6.c: An internet that chases speed and good content that chases depth need to find a way to coexist.
t7|6.e: The episode places Zhihu's changes inside a bigger question. Are all knowledge platforms bound to fail or transform? How can an internet built for speed coexist with good content built for depth? What kind of future should we want for the Chinese internet? The three discuss these together, and the show page gives no conclusion.

d.verdict: The two need to find a way to coexist

t7|7.c: You can love Zhihu without pretending its changes never happened.
t7|7.e: Hanyang published a LatePost essay titled "I love Zhihu, but we can't pretend nothing has happened," and it unexpectedly went viral. On the show he explains why he wrote it, who the voices in the piece are and how Zhihu gets used, and why he got hooked on Zhihu and still uses it. The title's attitude: you can care about a platform without looking away from how it has changed.

t8|5.c: New creators don't have to rely on good looks. There are ways to get started.
t8|5.e: The episode takes a beginner creator's point of view: where the first money should go, whether a growth path simply can't be learned and what to make of all the tutorials, and how to start making videos without relying on looks. Lao Jiang also explains how his own style took shape. The phrase "besides relying on looks" suggests the show believes ordinary people have ways in, but the show page doesn't list the specific advice.

t8|5.c: Outsiders misread Bilibili. To understand its creators, look at how they earn and how the platform works.
t8|5.e: The second half focuses on Bilibili's creator ecosystem: the biggest outside misunderstanding about the platform, whether creators actually make money, what followers on different platforms are worth, running multiple accounts on Bilibili and whether to post elsewhere too, Bilibili's short videos, and where traffic comes from and how editors and site sections work. The show page lists only the questions, not Lao Jiang's answers.

items.d: How many accounts, where to post

t9|8.c: The outside view of Hegang as a resource-exhausted city is a misunderstanding.
t9|8.e: The first topic is the outside world's mistaken image of Hegang as a city whose resources have run out. The show notes say Hegang is a small city that gets little attention, yet its 890,000 people have their own stories. Through Beifang Li's local view, the episode covers Hegang's food, what makes it most unusual, and everyday life there.
ex: Hegang has a population of about 890,000

d.verdict: Hegang isn't bad at all

t9|8.c: Hegang isn't actually bad, but not many people want to move there.
t9|8.e: One premise of the episode is that Hegang itself isn't bad, which raises the question of why so few people come. Around that, the episode discusses whether Hegang suits outsiders who drift there, whether digital nomads who work remotely online could live there, what jobs exist locally, and why Beifang Li himself has been able to stay.

t9|8.c: Hegang's young people are a silent majority who are constantly urged to leave home.
t9|8.e: Later the episode turns to local young people, calling them "the silent majority" and noting that someone is always urging them to leave home. It also talks about the northeastern countryside and "Hegang's lucky ones," showing the pull between staying and leaving.

items.d: Those who stay and the lucky ones

t10|9.c: Background checks arose to catch fake degrees and identities, and are now a standard step at big companies.
t10|9.e: The show notes explain the origin of background checks: they emerged to counter scams like faked degrees and identities. Today they are a required part of hiring at big companies. They often look like a mere formality, but it's exactly in this routine that the two headhunters have run into plenty of scams.
ex: The episode covers the steps of a background check and which companies do them

t10|9.c: Background checks reveal how big companies define "talent."
t10|9.e: The show notes say the two headhunters have seen, through background checks, how big companies define talent. A check isn't just verifying facts. It also judges whether someone is worth recommending and who is obviously unreliable. The episode also discusses which kinds of people headhunters prefer to recommend, and what kind of talent is always in demand.

t10|9.c: Polishing a résumé has reasonable limits. Crossing into fakery gets exposed in background checks.
t10|9.e: The episode separates polishing from faking. There are proper ways to do the first, while the second gets caught by companies' background checks, and the two headhunters share many concrete cases. The show page doesn't spell out exactly where the line falls.

d.verdict: Polishing has limits, and faking gets caught

t10|9.c: Floods of capital and later crackdowns send talent rising and falling across industries.
t10|9.e: The two headhunters have also seen how outside forces shake the talent market. Waves of capital and the policy crackdowns that followed have pushed people from industry to industry, up and down. Using education as an example, the episode discusses how companies' hiring attitudes changed after that sector was hit.
ex: After the education crackdown, companies' hiring attitudes changed too

t11|10.c: Society's shared consensus is breaking down as each field develops its own worldview. That's postmodernity.
t11|10.e: The episode's central claim is that the consensus society once shared is coming apart. Each specialized field gradually forms its own basic picture of reality and drifts away from the others, and that is the postmodern condition. This is what the title's "age of vanishing consensus" means. Technology's "encapsulation," sealing its inner workings away so users can use it but not understand it, is discussed against this backdrop.
ex: Starting point: Hanyang's LatePost essay "A Sealed-Off Future"

t11|10.c: The future we chase becomes the past as soon as we grasp it, but moving forward is still worthwhile.
t11|10.e: Degang Kong describes a familiar experience: people treat something as the future and chase it with everything they have, and just as they master it, it quickly becomes the past. His attitude is that you can miss the good things of the past without stopping, because there are good things ahead. This echoes the episode's arc, from early-internet music software and download sites to today's "retro-futurism," imagining the future in a vintage style.

t11|10.c: Vaporwave's copyright problems expose a conflict between closed systems and contemporary art's demand for openness.
t11|10.e: The episode uses copyright problems in vaporwave, an online music style built from sampled old pop and commercial music, as a way in. It argues there is a built-in conflict between closed systems controlled by rights holders and contemporary art's demand for openness. Further reading attached to the episode also discusses the political aesthetics behind Steve Jobs and Apple's closed philosophy.
ex: Further reading: "Jobs and Apple's Closed-Source Philosophy"

d.verdict: The two are in built-in conflict

t11|10.c: The rules of the digital world should be set outside big companies and technical systems.
t11|10.e: He proposes the idea of "cyber-theology": the rules of the digital world shouldn't be set only by big companies and technology itself, but built separately, outside them. The episode closes with cyborg feminism, a theory that uses the human-machine hybrid to rethink gender and identity, and asks whether technology deserves optimism.

t12|7.c: He looks down on much of Web 3, but a world where nobody cares about it is scarier.
t12|7.e: This is the core attitude quoted on the episode page. Web 3 is a set of ideas for taking control of the internet back from big platforms and giving it to users. Hanyang disagrees with a lot of what Web 3 actually does today. Still, he finds a world where no one cares about it more frightening. Judging by the title, what matters to him is not Web 3 as it stands, but its link to whether the internet can get better.

d.verdict: So Web 3 is still worth caring about

t12|7.c: Whether the internet can get better is tied closely to the hacker spirit and to Web 3.
t12|7.e: The episode title sets the question "Can the internet still get better?" right next to the hacker spirit and Web 3. The hacker spirit here roughly means technologists building things out of curiosity and ideals. The suggested reading is "Why We Need Web 3.0" by Gavin Wood, an Ethereum co-founder. The episode is an audio version of the essay of the same name, mostly matching the text, plus extra notes and explanations the essay didn't include.
ex: Further reading: Ethereum co-founder Gavin Wood's "Why We Need Web 3.0"

items.d: Unimpressive, yet still worth caring about

t13|11.c: Problems caused by technology can't be solved by more technology, and newer generations may not realize it.
t13|11.e: This is one of the points listed for the episode. Trouble created by technology can't be fixed at the root by adding more technology. But that understanding doesn't pass automatically to people born later. Each generation has to learn it again. The episode's central question, whether you can live a non-technological life in modern society, starts from here.

t13|11.c: Goods must be packaged before they can travel, so packaging enables shipping and works against local living.
t13|11.e: The episode connects packaging with shipping and with staying local. A thing has to be wrapped and sealed before it can leave where it was made. So packaging is the opposite of a local life, where things are made and used in the same place. From there the talk moves to how packaging spread along with globalization, and to "world citizens who only skim the surface of the world." It opens by asking listeners: do you know where your drinking water comes from?
ex: Opening question: do you know where your home's drinking water comes from?

items: Know where your water comes from

t13|11.c: Once things stop being scarce, how we live depends on "should I," not "can I."
t13|11.e: Ruyi Li uses the Japanese idea of eating only what your local land produces as an example. Today you won't go hungry if you skip local food, yet some people still choose to live that way. When many things are no longer scarce, what we do is no longer limited by "can I?" It comes down to "should I?" and "do I want to?" That leaves room to choose a non-technological life on purpose.

items.d: Skip local food, still not hungry

t14|12.c: Lidar took ten years to reach cars, with misjudgments, comebacks and crashes along the way.
t14|12.e: Lidar is a sensor that scans its surroundings with lasers to measure how far away things are. Lichen has watched the industry grow in China almost from the beginning. In an earlier LatePost article, he summed up lidar's decade-long journey into cars in three words: misjudgment, comeback, crash. The episode starts from the US company Velodyne and the wider industry, and traces the ups and downs along that road.
ex: The story starts with US lidar maker Velodyne and its industry

t14|12.c: Lidar is expensive, and the core question is whether it's worth the extra cost to buyers.
t14|12.e: The episode title poses a what-if: if dropping lidar cut a car's price by 10%, would you take that deal? Around this question, the episode covers why lidar costs so much and when lidar on a car actually starts to help. It also covers how the 905nm and 1550nm laser wavelengths differ, and whether they are safe for human eyes. The episode page doesn't state his final answer.
ex: The Lotus Eletre, an electric SUV, carries four lidar units

root.d: Skip it, save 10% on the car

t14|12.c: Chinese carmakers are the most aggressive in putting lidar into their cars.
t14|12.e: The episode treats Chinese carmakers as the most aggressive players when it comes to fitting cars with lidar. It specifically asks why that is, and compares Chinese lidar companies with those abroad. The episode page, however, doesn't list the specific reasons.

t15|13.c: Of all the problems the pandemic brought, mental health is the one most easily overlooked.
t15|13.e: The episode opens by pointing out that people are busy worrying about when lockdown will end and how to get groceries, and forget to check on their own state of mind. Exhaustion, anxiety and anger are common during the pandemic, and people need to learn to live with them. The episode also covers how low your mood has to get before you should seek professional help, and where to find it.

t15|13.c: Teenagers may be the group least able to cope mentally during the pandemic.
t15|13.e: Kaiwen Xu believes teenagers may be the most psychologically vulnerable group under the strain of the pandemic. The episode also looks at two other groups. One is ordinary people who have been stuck at home for a long time and already feel terrible. The other is front-line workers such as journalists, doctors and local civil servants, and how they can protect their mental health in evidence-based ways.

t15|13.c: Workers with anxiety or depression should not face discrimination when looking for jobs.
t15|13.e: He firmly opposes discriminating against job seekers because they have anxiety or depression. The episode also recalls a saying popular around 2008: "Guard against fire, guard against theft, guard against therapy." From there it asks whether society's view of therapy has improved today.
ex: A saying around 2008: guard against fire, theft and therapy

items: Guard against fire, theft and therapy

t15|13.c: Therapists can't change society, but every person they help counts.
t15|13.e: Kaiwen Xu sees therapists as working to save people inside a particular social and cultural setting. One person can't change that whole setting, but each person helped is one more saved. He has taken part in mental health support after several public crises, including the Wenchuan earthquake and the Foxconn worker suicides. The episode ends by answering the doubt that therapy is just paying someone to chat, and by discussing what you can do when a loved one seems off.
ex: He helped with crisis support after the Wenchuan earthquake and Foxconn suicides

t16|14.c: People disagree on whether DAOs are the future of companies, and even on what a DAO is.
t16|14.e: A DAO is an organization run by rules written on a blockchain and by member votes, with no boss in the usual sense. The episode opens with two attitudes: some see DAOs as the future of how companies are organized, others dismiss them. The episode page also admits that there is still no agreed definition. So the episode starts with what a DAO is and how it runs, then compares it with a company. The page doesn't state the guests' conclusions.
ex: Question: why choose a DAO, and how does it actually work?

marks.d: Definition and future both still debated

t16|14.c: A group that studies how DAOs are governed can itself be organized as a DAO.
t16|14.e: Wendy was a core founder of DAOONE and later started DAOrayaki, which focuses on how DAOs are governed and make decisions. The episode's first topic is how DAOrayaki came about and why it chose to be a DAO. That makes her both a researcher of DAOs and someone running one. The episode page doesn't list her specific reasons for that choice.
ex: Her path: core founder of DAOONE, then founder of DAOrayaki

items.d: Founded a group studying DAO governance

t16|15.c: The best way to understand DAOs is to join a few and quietly watch many more.
t16|15.e: Chao Wang calls himself a learner in the DAO world. He is deeply involved in a few DAOs and quietly follows many others. The episode covers why he joined these DAOs and how an ordinary person can join one. The way the episode is set up treats hands-on participation as the starting point for understanding DAOs. The page doesn't spell out the steps for joining.
ex: His DAOs include BanklessDAO, fwb and Seed Club

items.d: Learn how to join a DAO
Keep contributing to a few DAOs

t16|15.c: Only by comparing DAOs with open-source projects can you tell if they're genuinely new.
t16|15.e: Host Hanyang works on open source himself, meaning software whose code is public and improved by anyone. So the episode asks how open-source projects differ from DAOs. Is a DAO just an old thing with a new name, or something truly new? The episode ends by asking how DAOs make money, a key question in telling them apart from loose online communities. The page lists only these questions, not the guests' answers.
ex: Question: how do DAOs make money?

items: Organized and governed on a blockchain
Must answer how they make money

t18|16.c: Putting a camera brand's logo on a phone doesn't automatically make its photos better.
t18|16.e: The episode starts from a photographer's first reaction to the Xiaomi and Leica partnership, and asks whether a camera brand's logo can really make a phone shoot better. It then turns to how much Leica itself has built up in digital imaging, to judge how much substance such deals carry. The page gives no conclusion. But the title's framing suggests a co-brand has to be tested against the whole process of making a photo.
ex: Starting point: Xiaomi's partnership with Leica

items: Makes the phone seem more professional
The glow of a camera brand
The brand's real digital imaging work

t18|16.c: The phone photo you see has already been processed by the manufacturer before you see it.
t18|16.e: The episode breaks down the many factors behind image quality, and the lens is only one of them. The bigger point is that a photo has already gone through a series of processing steps on the phone before you ever look at it. That is the "tampering" by manufacturers the title refers to. The episode page doesn't list the specific steps.

items.d: Several things shape image quality together

t18|16.c: Color and filters are ultimately about taste, and the trendy "film look" needs unpacking too.
t18|16.e: The second half of the episode asks how color, filters and taste relate, and what "amusing ourselves to death" looks like in photography. Only then does it turn to what the "film look" popular in phone apps really is, how to take better-looking photos, and whether to edit colors yourself. The episode page notes that the images for Tianxi's novel were shot on an iPhone 3GS and then processed. That suggests editing and taste, beyond the gear, deserve their own discussion.
ex: Images for Tianxi's novel were shot on an iPhone 3GS, then processed in a classical style

t19|7.c: Behind business wisdom we take for granted, there are often deeper beliefs.
t19|7.e: The episode opens by noting that many things seem obvious but turn out to be deep when you think about them. Why must companies innovate? Why do people in tech believe in progress? Rather than explaining these as business strategy, Hanyang traces both questions back to Thiel's convictions and religious faith. This was the topic he most wanted to discuss before starting the show.
ex: Two questions: why must companies innovate, and why believe in progress?

items.d: Can the future beat the present?

t19|7.c: Act as if you'll live forever: put what lasts ahead of what quickly fades.
t19|7.e: The episode page opens with a passage from writer David Perell about Thiel's faith. Roughly: great people trade today's temptations for tomorrow's rewards. They treat others as if they'll know them for ten thousand years. And they do work they'd be proud to tell their grandchildren about. This extremely long time horizon is a clue to why Thiel insists on progress and innovation.
ex: The opening passage comes from Perell's essay "Peter Thiel's Religion"

d.verdict: Live as if you'll live forever

t19|7.c: Thiel's view of innovation traces back to the ideas of René Girard and Saint Augustine.
t19|7.e: The suggested readings sketch where Thiel's thinking comes from. First, French thinker René Girard and his work on desire, which argues that we want things by imitating others. Second, Thiel's own book Zero to One. Third, Augustine's The City of God. The episode also quotes Thiel's advice to graduates: his early wish to be a lawyer was less a plan for the future than an excuse for the present. The page doesn't go into the detailed arguments.
ex: Thiel once worked at the law firm Sullivan & Cromwell
Further reading: Zero to One, a Girard collection on desire, The City of God

items.d: We learn desire by imitating others

t20|31.c: This isn't blockchain's first winter, so it should be seen as part of a repeating cycle.
t20|31.e: The episode was meant to explain recent blockchain changes to people outside the industry. But recording slipped from before Beijing's COVID outbreak to early July, just as the industry entered a new bear market, a long stretch of falling prices. So the hosts added an opening segment on blockchain's "Nth" winter: why prices fell so hard this time, and how it compares with earlier crashes. Calling it the "Nth" winter already says that winters keep coming back in this industry.
ex: Recording slipped from before Beijing's outbreak to early July 2022

items.d: Why the fall was so hard

t20|31.c: To explain blockchain to outsiders, start with DeFi, smart contracts and how to pick a blockchain.
t20|31.e: Most of the episode explains blockchain in the simplest terms. Smart contracts are programs on a blockchain that run automatically when conditions are met, and DeFi is financial services built from them. The episode covers what they can do, the main kinds of public blockchains, how an organization picks a chain when issuing tokens, and why launching a new chain is hard. It also asks whether you can judge Ethereum by how Web 2.0 companies measure profit. The page doesn't list the answers.
ex: Question: is it fair to judge Ethereum like a startup?

items.d: Programs that run on the chain

t20|31.c: Crypto is extremely noisy, so telling useful information apart is a must-have skill for anyone involved.
t20|31.e: Later on, the episode asks whether insiders actually made money, or whether, like the stock market, a few win and most lose. It also asks whether seed phrases, the strings of words used to recover a crypto wallet, are hostile to users. The last question is how to pick out useful information in such a noisy space. Many readers treat Yang Li's Prophet Weekly as a must-read, and filtering information is exactly what it does. The page doesn't describe his method.
ex: Many readers treat Prophet Weekly as their weekly must-read

t21|43.c: Building a hydropower plant itself needs electricity: to make power, you first need power.
t21|43.e: The title points to a counterintuitive fact. A hydropower plant exists to generate electricity, yet building one requires electricity in the first place. Through this chief engineer's work in China and Africa, the episode explains what a hydropower plant is, how it gets built, and its history in China. The episode page doesn't go into construction details.

items.d: To make power, you need power

t21|43.c: The Fengman plant is less China's "mother of hydropower" than a wailing wall.
t21|43.e: Hanyang asked whether the Fengman Hydropower Station is known as the mother of China's hydropower plants. His answer: it is a wailing wall for China and its hydropower. The episode cover shows the remains of Fengman's old dam with the new dam nearby, and the photos show cracks in the old dam. He has also explained in a Bilibili video why Fengman had to be blown up and rebuilt.
ex: His Bilibili video: why the dam on the banknote was blown up and rebuilt
Cover: remains of Fengman's old dam beside the new one

items: Cracked old dam, blown up and rebuilt

d.verdict: He'd rather call it a wailing wall

t21|43.c: Two hydropower plants, in Jilin and Zambia, reveal the parts of modern life we never see.
t21|43.e: The episode picks two plants: Fengman in Jilin province, and Kafue Gorge Lower in Zambia, built by a Chinese company. Power cuts made people suddenly notice where the electricity they take for granted comes from. Through these two stories, the episode tries to show the infrastructure that modern society keeps wrapped up and out of sight.
ex: Kafue Gorge Lower held its grid connection ceremony in July 2021

items.d: Jilin; old and new dams side by side
Zambian plant connects to the grid

t22|55.c: Games come down to experience, competition and addiction, and they can't do without addiction.
t22|55.e: The episode lists Zhongqing's three-part summary of what games are: experience, competition and addiction. He stresses that games need to be addictive. Related topics include the dopamine reward loop, where each small win makes you want another round, and how the joy of match-three puzzle games like Xiaoxiaole eventually wears thin. The episode page gives only these headings and doesn't spell out the argument.
ex: Related topic: the dopamine reward loop
Related topic: when match-three fun wears thin

t22|55.c: Big tech companies should make games that exist simply to make people happy.
t22|55.e: The episode starts with big internet companies' ambitions in gaming, using Dota and PUBG to show how they chase gaming trends. Its view is that these companies should make games that exist purely for fun. The most popular fun games may not be much to talk about, but they are part of people's daily lives. The episode also looks at companies building games like ordinary apps and churning out near-identical titles.
ex: Trend examples: Dota and PUBG

t22|55.c: In esports, being bad isn't the sin; making players realize they're bad is.
t22|55.e: The episode makes this point while discussing esports. Playing badly is not a problem in itself. What ruins the experience is making players clearly feel that they're no good. Alongside this, it touches on why "gamer" is a surprisingly heavy label, and how video game aesthetics shape the industry. Together these topics are all about how players feel. The episode page gives no specific examples.

d.verdict: Making players feel bad is the real sin

t22|55.c: Traditional game companies stubbornly assume a "simple" little mobile game is a sure hit.
t22|55.e: In a bonus segment after 1:03:30, the two talk as veteran gamers about who counts as a gaming giant, and whether fewer people play big traditional games. They think traditional game companies often refuse to change course until they hit a wall, believing a "simple" mobile game is bound to succeed. They also joke that Assassin's Creed has basically gone mad. Their conclusion: mobile games will develop an aesthetic of their own.
ex: Target of their jokes: the Assassin's Creed series

items.d: Who counts, and how they got there
Old studios think simple means success
Mobile games will find their own style

t22|55.c: Game makers love what they do, so someone is always making games that don't earn much.
t22|55.e: The episode admits that the most popular fun games are the biggest commercial successes. But it also stresses that gaming is an industry driven by love, so there are always people making works that don't make much money. The episode description sums it up: gamers spend their whole lives reconciling conflicting feelings about this industry. The closing wish: may everyone play something good.

t23|7.c: Everyone knows how Jobs's return ended; the details of those months are what's worth a look.
t23|7.e: The story of Steve Jobs going back to Apple has been told many times. Rather than retell the ending, the episode looks at what he was doing in the months around his return, and even in the days he decided to go back. That's the idea behind the Big Company Moments series: pull specific moments out of big companies' histories and look at them closely. One small detail from the episode page: he told the previous CEO's secretary he only used Pilot pens.
ex: He told the former CEO's secretary he only used Pilot pens

t23|7.c: Before Jobs came back, Apple went through one CEO after another.
t23|7.e: The people covered in the episode notes include John Sculley, Michael Spindler and Gil Amelio, plus Ellen Hancock and Oracle founder Larry Ellison. The first three ran Apple one after another before Jobs returned, and they form the backdrop to his comeback. The episode page doesn't give Hanyang's own verdict on this period.
ex: People covered: Sculley, Spindler, Amelio, Hancock and Ellison

t23|7.c: From interim CEO to dropping the "i," Jobs's return was made official step by step.
t23|7.e: The sources cited in the episode mark a few milestones after his return. In 1997, he defended his comeback in a CNBC interview. At Macworld in 2000, he announced he was dropping the "i" from iCEO, his interim title, and becoming the permanent CEO. The sources also include the "Think Different" ad and a Harvard Business Review article on how Apple is organized for innovation. The page doesn't go into detail on these milestones.
ex: Reference book: The Second Coming of Steve Jobs

t24|7.c: When a company grows fastest, hiring is only the start; the real test is managing everyone.
t24|7.e: The episode comes from a 2021 LatePost story whose title says hiring 60,000 people is only the beginning. When Meituan, the Chinese food delivery and local services giant, was growing explosively, the hard part wasn't just bringing people in. Office space, hiring standards and company culture all had to keep up. The episode pieces together that "Meituan moment" from these angles.
ex: Source: LatePost's 2021 Meituan story, by reporter Pei Wan and editor Wei Song

items.d: How it judges and picks people
Culture at a much larger size

t24|7.c: Stories about a company's past should be told using what was known at the time.
t24|7.e: The episode adds a note: Big Company Moments covers past events, and its account is based on what was known when they happened. For example, after the article was written, Meituan probably didn't end up hiring the full 60,000 people that year. The note reminds listeners to treat the story as a snapshot of that moment, not a final verdict made with hindsight.
ex: Added note: Meituan probably didn't reach 60,000 hires that year

items: Go by what was known then

t24|7.sc: If you could do one thing
t24|7.c: Every manager faces one question: if you could do only one thing, which would it be?
t24|7.e: The episode description poses a question: if you could do only one thing at your company today, what is the single thing you could get done? That question steers the talk toward how a company views talent and where it puts its energy. The episode also links to an interview with startup coach Savio Kwan, a former Alibaba COO. His view: however the economy changes, the problems in front of a CEO stay about the same.
ex: Related talk: Savio Kwan on why CEOs' problems stay the same

t25|7.c: A product earning over 30 billion yuan a year, and genuinely new, is the market's biggest opportunity.
t25|7.e: The episode draws a line for what counts as a breakout product. It must bring in more than 30 billion yuan a year in player spending, and it must be innovative. A product that meets both conditions is, in the episode's view, the biggest opportunity in the market. This line is also the yardstick the episode uses when discussing how big companies judge a game's value.

t25|7.c: Gaming had three big chances in the past decade; Tencent caught two and missed Genshin Impact.
t25|7.e: The episode sees three big opportunities in the games market over the past ten years: Honor of Kings, PUBG Mobile and Genshin Impact. The first two went to Tencent, the third to miHoYo. So the question becomes: when a chance like Genshin comes along, how should a big company seize it? And what will the fourth opportunity be?
ex: Source: LatePost's story on Tencent missing Genshin, by Honghao Gao

items.d: Went to miHoYo; Tencent missed it

t25|7.c: A chance as big as Genshin Impact can only be won by investing on a huge scale.
t25|7.e: The title's phrase, "betting big to win big," means making a huge investment to go after a huge opportunity. A source cited in the episode says miHoYo president Wei Liu revealed that Genshin's development had already cost $100 million. After Genshin launched, an employee at a big company's Hangzhou studio said looking at their own project left them feeling deflated. A meme saying "we can't beat miHoYo" also circulated inside that company.
ex: miHoYo president Wei Liu said Genshin's development had cost $100 million
A "we can't beat miHoYo" meme spread inside a big rival

items.d: Could it become a breakout hit?

t26|76.c: Gcores has been lucky, and others can't simply copy the path it took.
t26|76.e: The episode page uses two lines as its subtitle: "I feel Gcores is especially lucky" and "You can't learn to be Gcores." The talk starts there. Why does a community that has been running for more than ten years need to reintroduce itself? What did it expect at the start, and where did it exceed those hopes? And how did Xia Zhao's earlier years in the clothing industry help? The page doesn't record his answers.
ex: Gcores released a video called "Reintroducing Gcores"

items.d: Explaining to outsiders what Gcores is

t26|76.c: Not every game needs media coverage, so Gcores has to find the ground where it can grow.
t26|76.e: The discussion starts from the idea that game media serves players, but not every game is fertile ground for Gcores. Mass-market games like CrossFire and Honor of Kings don't need dedicated media coverage. That leads to how Gcores picks topics, how it has kept going, and how game media is surviving in general. The episode also asks whether he has ever thought that "selling out a little" would let Gcores live comfortably.
ex: Games that don't need dedicated media: CrossFire and Honor of Kings

marks.d: Content that needs telling and explaining

t26|76.c: A small team can do many things by finding what genuinely excites each person.
t26|76.e: Gcores runs content, expos, retail and more. With a fairly small team doing all this, the episode asks whether it was planned in advance or grew on its own. One answer the page lists: in content, you have to find what excites each person. That ties into how Gcores keeps staff turnover low, and how it makes sure contributors' work fits the Gcores style.
ex: Businesses: content, the Hejubian expo, Gcores Industry retail, BOOOM game jams

t26|76.c: The value of audio as a medium has long been underestimated.
t26|76.e: The last part of the episode compares media: whether China suits "video essays" that tackle deep topics on video, how paid content relates to reaching a wide audience, and how the same topic plays out in different formats. The episode page lists "audio is underrated" as a point of its own. Gcores has made radio shows for years, and it also produced an audiobook, Heshi Qitan.
ex: Gcores released Heshi Qitan as an audiobook and a printed book

items: Gcores has long made radio shows

t26|76.c: Gcores' biggest weakness is that its people are too obsessed with creating.
t26|76.e: After covering the funding round and how the business is divided up, the episode asks about Gcores' weak spots. The very next item is the line in the title: "We're too obsessed with creating." It contrasts with how Xia Zhao describes himself in the guest notes: someone who "wants to make the company money." A love of creating is at the core of Gcores, and it is also what the company must balance as it tries to make money.
ex: Xia Zhao on himself: he wants to make the company money

items.d: After funding, the company must earn

t27|78.c: When demand exploded, 24-hour shifts and machines at full speed still couldn't keep up with orders.
t27|78.e: The episode opens with the situation at this Changchun medicine-box printing plant. Workers rotated in shifts around the clock and the machines ran at top speed, yet they still couldn't meet demand. The title's 97.2 million medicine boxes and the ibuprofen nobody could buy tie one printing plant to a nationwide shortage of fever medicine. The episode then asks whether orders were overflowing and what the biggest challenge was.
ex: The number in the title: 97.2 million medicine boxes

items.d: Output can't catch up with demand

t27|78.c: Printing medicine boxes is a separate business within printing, with its own ins and outs.
t27|78.e: The episode first explains how to think about the printing industry, then asks why printing medicine boxes is a distinct kind of printing business. That question stretches a shortage that seems to be only about drugs back to an overlooked earlier step in the supply chain: packaging, which has to be ready before medicine can leave the factory. The episode page doesn't record Hongjian's explanation.

items.d: A distinct kind of printing business

t27|78.c: Many drugmakers are based in China's northeast, the backdrop to the Changchun plant's situation.
t27|78.e: The plant is in Changchun, and the episode specifically asks why drugmakers cluster in the northeast. It also looks back at how the printing plant's business went during the pandemic years. It asks whether the big drug companies saw this surge coming, when the pressure might ease, and whether everyone was hoping the pandemic would end. The page lists only the questions; for Hongjian's answers you have to listen.

items.d: Why so many in the northeast?

t28|80.c: Working in VC means facing human nature every day, then saying no.
t28|80.e: Venture capitalists put money into young startups in exchange for a share of the company. A line on the episode page sums up the job: face human nature every day, then say no. The episode starts with what early-stage investing is, then asks how investors analyze a startup, how they decide whether to invest, and what "investing is betting on people" really means. The page doesn't spell out his methods.
ex: Question: who is the most impressive person you've met?

t28|80.c: The growth-above-all era is over, so VC may no longer be a dream job.
t28|80.e: The episode argues that from 2010 to 2020, VC was a great career choice and many people's dream job. But the era when growth mattered more than anything has passed. That leads to how yuan funds and dollar funds, investment funds raised in Chinese yuan or US dollars, differ now compared with before, and whether VC actually makes money. The page gives only the questions, not Minghao Zhuang's conclusions.
ex: 2010 to 2020: many people saw VC as a dream job

items.d: Growth above all; VC a dream job
Yuan and dollar funds both change

t28|80.c: Leaving VC to run strategy at a company was his way of rethinking his career.
t28|80.e: Minghao Zhuang left Matrix Partners China to become head of strategy at an internet company. The episode covers why he chose VC in the first place, why he stopped, and what he used to tell new colleagues when training them. It ends by asking whether VC is a good first job for young people. The episode page doesn't give his answer.
ex: Suggested reading: "Confessions of a VC Deserter"

items.d: Strategy head at an internet company

t28|80.c: Investing in games differs from investing in other sectors and calls for specialized judgment.
t28|80.e: The episode suggests listeners who already know VC start at 29:00. The second half moves to more specialized topics: how game investors differ from other investors, what is special about investing in the games industry, and Web3, the blockchain-based vision for the internet, plus AI-generated content. The episode page doesn't go into his views on these questions.

t29|7.c: Instead of a year-end review, the episode tells stories, because some things can't be summarized.
t29|7.e: This year-end episode has no recap and no list of the year's highlights. The episode page says just one thing: this one can't be summarized, it's all in the stories. The stories follow three threads, a snake, a person and the internet, which together make "two and a half stories." To hear what they are, you have to listen.
ex: The cover photo was taken in Yichun, Heilongjiang

t29|7.c: Beyond the stories, the episode recommends Yoshimi Takeuchi's books and videos on America's rise and fall.
t29|7.e: The further reading includes two books by Japanese thinker Yoshimi Takeuchi, published in Chinese as Starting from Despair and Overcoming Modernity. There are also two videos, about the rise and fall of the United States and what victory in the Civil War meant. The episode page doesn't explain how these connect to the stories, so this only notes the direction they point in.
ex: Yoshimi Takeuchi: Starting from Despair and Overcoming Modernity
Video: painter Winslow Homer and the meaning of the Civil War victory

items.d: A snake, a person, the internet
Takeuchi's books and US history videos

t30|88.c: Blockchain claims to have no borders or races, yet national and racial conflicts still exist.
t30|88.e: The title states the point directly: conflicts over nationality and race still exist in blockchain. The episode notes that the industry often promotes itself as borderless and colorblind. But several incidents over the past year show these tensions are far from small. Two articles linked on the episode page, "White Boy" and "Speechless," point to the same issue. For the specific incidents, you have to listen.
ex: Related articles: "White Boy" and "Speechless"

d.verdict: The conflicts still exist

t30|88.c: Tokens could make it easier for people to cooperate, but in practice they're mostly used to speculate.
t30|88.e: Mable once said on her own show that tokens, digital units issued on a blockchain, can make cooperation easier. The episode presses her on this: today blockchain doesn't seem to be helping people cooperate better, and mostly seems to help people speculate. What does she make of that? The episode page doesn't record her answer.

t30|88.c: Stereotypes about the industry make insiders embarrassed to say they work in blockchain.
t30|88.e: One line in the episode's introduction of Mable describes her as someone too embarrassed by stereotypes to call herself a "blockchain professional." She also rejects being introduced as "one of the most important Chinese figures in the industry." So the episode skips the usual beginner explanations and goes straight to perspectives and insights that only people inside the industry would notice.
ex: Cover photo: taken by Mable at the Hanging Temple, Shanxi, August 2021

items.d: Reluctant to call herself an insider

t30|88.c: To understand the industry, follow the writing of a few front-line researchers and investors.
t30|88.e: The episode ends by asking whether there's anyone in the industry she especially respects. The episode page lists the people and firms she recommends reading: Matti, Kyle Samani of Multicoin Capital, and the investment firm Paradigm. She also names Arthur Hayes, who didn't come up in the episode but whose essays she calls excellent.
ex: Kyle Samani of Multicoin Capital, and Paradigm
Arthur Hayes: not mentioned on air, but she calls his writing excellent

t31|43.c: When it comes to building hydropower plants, China is basically at "alien technology" level, far ahead.
t31|43.e: The title borrows a Chinese internet joke about the Zentradi, aliens from a sci-fi anime whose technology far outstrips Earth's, to describe China's hydropower building: way ahead of everyone else. Following episode 21, the show returns to hydropower and asks specifically where China stands in the industry. The episode page doesn't give the specific evidence.
ex: Episode 21 was among the show's most-played episodes

t31|43.c: Not everything needs to be built yourself, and spreading technology to other places has its own challenges.
t31|43.e: One point the episode lists is that not everything has to be made yourself. Connected questions include what challenges come with passing technology on to other places, what makes projects in Africa hard, and whether the so-called "debt trap," where countries borrow for infrastructure and can't repay, really exists. The episode page doesn't record Engineer Cao's specific answers.
ex: Question: does the "debt trap" really exist?

items.d: Why you needn't build it all

t31|43.c: Don't lump Africa together: Africans differ from us, but as people we share far more.
t31|43.e: The episode's last two points are firm views: don't treat Africa as one thing, and while Africans differ from us, as human beings we have more in common. The episode also covers what it feels like to come back from Africa, what he ate there, and different ideas of what "progress" means. That brings the engineering talk back down to real individual people.
ex: Topics: what he ate in Africa; different views of "progress"

t32|122.c: Chinese carmakers now design their own chips, breaking the old split between carmakers and chipmakers.
t32|122.e: The episode starts from a new trend: more and more Chinese carmakers are designing their own chips. In the gasoline-car era, carmakers built cars and chip companies made chips. That line is now blurring. Carmakers come in from two directions. Some start with power semiconductors, the chips that manage electrical power, while others start with self-driving chips. Drawing on his years at a European auto-chip company, the episode asks how hard this is and whether it can work.
ex: BYD and Li Auto started with power semiconductors
NIO and XPeng started with self-driving chips

root.d: A break from the gasoline-era division of labor

items.d: Where BYD and Li Auto started

t32|122.c: Car chips are easier to design than phone chips; the hard part is meeting automotive safety standards.
t32|122.e: The episode counts this as a point in carmakers' favor. Compared with chips for phones and other consumer electronics, car chips are generally easier to design. The real work goes into passing automotive-grade requirements, the industry's strict rules for safety and reliability. That gives carmakers without a chip background a way in.

terms.d: Where most of the effort goes

result.d: Making their own chips becomes feasible

t32|122.c: Car chips are rougher but safer; phone chips are more precise but more fragile.
t32|122.e: The two kinds of chips aim for different things. Phone chips chase precision, and that makes them more fragile. Car chips are comparatively crude but safer. This fits the earlier point that the hard part is meeting automotive standards: for a car chip, being safe and reliable matters more than being cutting-edge.

t32|122.sc: A fab you can't breathe in
t32|122.c: Chip factories are so sensitive that one speck of dust can cut the share of good chips.
t32|122.e: He describes chip factories as suffocating places. A single sneeze can lower the yield, the share of chips that come out usable, and a speck of dust is like a bomb. Making chips demands extreme cleanliness. That is why the episode title calls chipmaking the industry most afraid of customers coming to visit.
ex: A single sneeze can lower the yield
He compares a speck of dust to a bomb

items.d: A tiny disturbance in the room

t33|11.c: The biggest gap between AI and people is judging unmeasurable things, even forming biases.
t33|11.e: In his view, ChatGPT speaking fluently does not erase the line between people and machines. The real dividing line is whether AI starts making judgments about things that can't be measured, and even develops biases of its own. He says he "still feels" this way, meaning that chatbots at the time had not crossed that line.

items.d: The line between people and AI

t33|11.c: People are also trained on huge amounts of language; the difference is that we make mistakes.
t33|11.e: He suggests AI may need to realize that humans, too, are shaped by vast amounts of language, and what sets us apart is that we get things wrong. So the episode spends more time on the value of human language and error. The title sums people up as imprecise parrots, and asks whether there is anything new under the sun.

terms.d: People are raised on words too

t33|11.c: Feeding data to a person or to ChatGPT is always a race against time.
t33|11.e: The episode compares training AI with human learning: both are limited by how much time there is to feed them information. That raises a question: is all human knowledge really online? Perhaps a great deal was left behind when the world went digital. The episode page doesn't say who made this point.

items.d: Both people and AI need it
Much may have been left behind

t33|11.c: Creative work is organic; it can't be cleanly split into grunt work and the important part.
t33|11.e: Discussing which jobs AI might take over, the episode asks whether work really divides neatly into "dirty, tiring tasks" and "what truly matters." The answer given is that creation is organic: it grows as one whole and can't be pulled apart. The episode page doesn't spell out the reasoning or say who said it.

d.verdict: Creation is organic

t33|55.c: Whenever people fail to say exactly what they mean, they are still expressing something.
t33|55.e: He came to this after using ChatGPT nonstop for a long time. The episode also notes that ChatGPT's writing is "flat" and feels different from something a person wrote. His point is about one side of human language: the ways we miss the mark carry meaning of their own.

t34|16.c: AI won't replace photography, because photography doesn't make money anyway.
t34|16.e: The episode opens with this joke. Which jobs AI replaces comes down to economics, and since photography doesn't pay, it isn't on the list. The reply is another joke: AI wants to replace not only your life but your hobbies too. The episode page doesn't say who said which line.

items.d: It goes after work that pays
So it isn't on the list

t34|16.c: AI's influence on images began well before today's wave of AI-generated pictures.
t34|16.e: The episode argues that AI was already shaping photos and images long before text-to-image tools took off. Text-to-image is just the newest step in AI-generated content, or AIGC. The episode page lists this as a discussion point but gives no concrete examples.

t34|16.c: What images you can get from AI depends directly on how much imagination you bring.
t34|16.e: One first-person line in the episode notes makes this point: what AI can generate is directly tied to the user's own imagination. The tool multiplies the idea, but the idea has to come from a person. The episode also discusses the randomness in generation and how photographers usually work.
ex: Tim helped make this episode's cover with the AI image tool Disco Diffusion

result.d: Its ceiling is set by imagination

t34|16.c: The definition of a photo keeps widening, and photography is becoming image-making in general.
t34|16.e: The episode places AI-generated pictures inside photography's own history. Since the American photographer Stephen Shore, photographers have kept testing the medium's limits, and the definition of a photo has kept growing. That raises questions: how does photography relate to images in general, and is photography only about capturing truth? The episode page poses these questions without answering them.
ex: The episode mentions Stephen Shore's photo book Uncommon Places

t34|136.c: Visual artists, who should be hit first, already accept AI image tools and create with them.
t34|136.e: You'd expect visual artists to be first in line if AI-generated content hits any field. Yet he and Tianxi have both embraced it and use it in their own work. That leads the episode to ask whether AI-generated content is just a "brick" or a new kind of "photography," and what its biggest limitation is right now.

d.verdict: Visual artists choose to pick up the new tool

t35|156.c: The most useful thing glasses-wearers can do is stop wasting money on their eyes.
t35|156.e: The episode's main message is to stop spending money you don't need to. The title states three conclusions up front: don't get laser eye surgery, dry eye can't be cured, and paying more for glasses doesn't help. The episode page lists the questions but not the reasons behind these conclusions.

t35|156.c: Spending more on glasses doesn't help; first separate useful features from gimmicks.
t35|156.e: Host Hanyang says eyewear is a very high-margin business, and sellers invent lots of gimmicks to sell more. He personally doubts blue-light blocking, though he isn't sure. The episode asks Xiao Tan which features and specs actually matter, which are a tax on the gullible, and how to get your prescription right. The title gives the answer: paying more for glasses doesn't help.
ex: Blue-light blocking is one selling point the host questions

d.verdict: Paying more for glasses doesn't help

t35|156.c: In the UK, optometrists don't just test eyes; they also do part of an eye doctor's job.
t35|156.e: The episode describes a UK optometrist as China's eye-test technician plus part of an ophthalmologist. It also asks why people in the profession dislike being called eye-test technicians, when they are liable for medical errors, and what he thinks of eye testing in China.

terms.d: Also handles some diagnosis and care

t36|160.c: ZEKU's shutdown was so sudden that even directors only learned of it that day.
t36|160.e: Right up to the end, work went on as normal. A new technical executive had joined two months earlier. ZEKU's first application processor, the phone's main chip, had been taped out, meaning the design was sent to the factory for trial production. The modem chip, which handles cellular connections, went out just two days before, and a campus recruiting event ran the day before. Directors heard the news on the day itself, before the modem results came back.
ex: The modem chip was taped out May 10; the shutdown came May 12

items.d: Goal: its own phone main chip

t36|160.c: OPPO's phone business faced pressure at home and abroad, but it wasn't short of cash.
t36|160.e: In China, OPPO failed to grab the market Huawei left behind when its phones were hit. In Europe, a patent fight with Nokia could cost it buyers more willing to pay for high-end phones. Yet it clearly had money in the short term: it set aside about 1 billion yuan for severance of one month's pay per year worked plus three months, known as N+3. Because it could afford to keep going, the closure fueled speculation, and the episode page offers no final answer.
ex: The N+3 severance package cost about 1 billion yuan

items.d: Not short; about 1 billion yuan in severance

t36|160.c: ZEKU was hugely ambitious but held back by too many product lines and bad timing.
t36|160.e: Over four years, ZEKU started with a grand goal: OPPO's own system-on-chip, the all-in-one main chip of a phone. Later its scale was cut back. Its tape-outs went unusually well, but it spread itself across too many product lines, and there were rumors of internal infighting. The episode also notes a paradox: the effort could not have started any earlier. Hence the title, an ambition born at the wrong time.
ex: Built a team of 3,500+ people in under four years
Released the MariSilicon X imaging chip and MariSilicon Y Bluetooth audio chip

t36|160.c: ZEKU's life, from founding to shutdown, tracked a whole chip talent boom.
t36|160.e: Around the time ZEKU was founded, chip industry salaries soared as companies fought for engineers. By the time it closed, pay was already falling. The episode treats ZEKU as the symbol of this chip boom: its start and end line up neatly with the boom's beginning and end.

items.d: A marker of the boom's end

t36|160.c: Chinese chip companies face expectations, and criticism, far beyond normal business.
t36|160.e: The episode ends with the wider industry. Chinese chip companies carry hopes that go beyond ordinary business logic, and they get matching resources. At the same time, the criticism they face also goes beyond business. ZEKU's shutdown has to be seen in that light.

items: Criticism that isn't just about business

d.verdict: Both hopes and blame go beyond business itself

t37|166.c: GPT-3.5 went mainstream because OpenAI turned it into ChatGPT, a product anyone could use.
t37|166.e: He thinks GPT-3.5 sparked the boom not just because the model was better. The key was that OpenAI packaged it as ChatGPT, something ordinary people could open and use right away. A consumer product turned a technical advance into something everyone could feel. That's why GPT-3 had limited impact while ChatGPT set off a nationwide craze.

t37|166.c: Investors look a lot but invest little: models are hot, apps underrated, the middle layer ignored.
t37|166.e: He sees a gap between buzz and actual deals, and it's uneven. Money favors companies building the models themselves. Companies building apps on top are underrated, and the middle layer of tools and services between the two gets little attention. He is bullish on apps because some app companies already have a self-sustaining business and are turning a profit, and advertising still works as a business model.
ex: Some app companies already run self-sustaining, profitable businesses
Advertising still works as a business model

t37|166.c: A great model doesn't guarantee a great app, and a great app can push the model forward.
t37|166.e: He sees building models and building apps as different skills. Being good at models doesn't mean you can make a good app. Going the other way, getting the app right can improve the model. His example is ByteDance in the recommendation-algorithm era: product skill was the core, and technology was the means.
ex: ByteDance in the recommendation era: product was the core, tech the means

items.d: The core of an app company

t37|166.c: AI-native apps may split into generating and analyzing, and chatbots may not be the best format.
t37|166.e: Mobile internet brought new abilities like location and snapping photos on the go, and AI apps need to find traits that are uniquely theirs. He notes that many apps are built as chatbots, but whether that's the most efficient form is debatable. He sees two directions. Generative apps create something from nothing and build it up. Analytical apps distill value from huge amounts of data, going from big to small.
ex: He expects more interesting apps to appear within two months

root.d: Still searching for their own form

t37|166.c: The AI bubble isn't big enough: fewer firms are actually making the earliest-stage bets.
t37|166.e: He compares today with the mobile internet boom a decade ago. Back then, crowds of firms fought to do angel rounds, a startup's very first outside funding. Now fewer firms really invest at the angel stage, and more money goes to slightly later pre-A rounds. This matches the episode title, lots of hype but little investment: the talk is hot, but early bets are scarce.

items: Fewer firms invest at angel stage

d.verdict: The AI bubble actually isn't big enough

t38|172.c: COVID was the turning point: most of the stores opened in a rush started losing money monthly.
t38|172.e: bosie was founded in 2018 by someone with no fashion or big-company experience. In its second year it opened its first physical store, and the largest store reached about 2,000 square meters. Sales went from zero to about 140 million yuan within a year and hit about 700 million yuan in year three. After COVID arrived in 2020, most stores couldn't cover their costs and lost money every month.
ex: The largest store was about 2,000 square meters
Raised about 500 million yuan in total, valued above 2 billion yuan

t38|172.c: He calculated the company could last six months at most without change, so he cut deep.
t38|172.e: The post-COVID losses kept coming, so he ran the numbers. If nothing changed, the company could survive six more months at most. bosie made deep layoffs, shrinking from four or five hundred staff to just over a hundred. The crisis also made him start asking how the company had ended up there.
ex: Staff cut from about 400 to 500 people to just over 100

t38|172.c: He decided he wasn't a capable CEO and should hand the job to someone better suited.
t38|172.e: In his public letter announcing the move, he admitted he wasn't up to the job. He chose to hand the CEO role to someone better suited and move to an internal content venture, aiming to become an online influencer himself. The title's guesses about infighting or investors forcing him out are left unanswered on the episode page.

items: CEO role goes to someone better

d.verdict: Hand the CEO job to someone better suited

t39|182.c: Whether the deal pays off depends on whether Meituan can keep the Light Years Beyond team.
t39|182.e: The guest broke down what Meituan paid. The 360 million yuan of debt it took on is convertible debt, loans that can turn into shares. In substance it was domestic yuan investment put into a VIE, an offshore structure Chinese firms use to list abroad. The $50 million Meituan co-founder Wang Huiwen put in himself was not among the money returned to investors. Public information shows no value for team stock options, so keeping people is what will make or break the deal.
ex: The 360 million yuan of debt assumed was convertible debt
Wang Huiwen's own $50 million wasn't part of the refunds

items.d: Decides whether the deal is worth it

t39|182.c: Selling a company is harder than raising money: few buyers, strict secrecy, weak competition, little room for error.
t39|182.e: Compared with raising money, there are very few potential buyers for a whole company. Information must stay tightly confidential, buyers rarely compete hard against each other, and a single misstep is hard to undo. The guest lists these as the biggest differences between M&A and fundraising, and the reason so many deals are hard to close.

d.verdict: M&A is harder than fundraising

t39|182.c: A sale isn't done when two CEOs agree; terms, taxes and people can all derail it.
t39|182.e: An acquisition doesn't happen just because two bosses nod. One founder was rude to a mid-level manager on the buyer's side during talks and caused real trouble. Other founders discovered only at the end that they and their teams would get little money, because they misread the exit terms or ignored tax planning. Investors have a weak spot too: the exit clauses they write often can't actually be enforced.
ex: One founder caused trouble by being rude to a buyer's mid-level manager

items.d: Their attitude can sway the deal

t39|182.c: Deals full of conflicting interests only close when everyone faces reality and compromises together.
t39|182.e: An acquisition involves founders, the team, investors and the buyer, so clashing interests are unavoidable. Asked how such deals get done, the guest's answer is to face reality and compromise together. Everyone accepts the situation as it is and gives a little, and only then does the deal land. That line is also the episode's tagline.

t39|183.c: Chinese tech M&A is still early, but tight money is driving strategic deals and mergers to go public.
t39|183.e: The episode page credits this to both guests. China's tech M&A market is still early, because private-company investing hasn't yet hit a true bottom and founders long fixated on going public. That is changing. Cash buyouts are fewer, while strategic acquisitions that fit a buyer's business are growing. After Shanghai's STAR Market, its exchange for tech companies, raised its listing bar, similar-sized companies merging to list together became an option, once they settle who will be boss.
ex: AppDynamics accepted Cisco's $3.7 billion offer the day before its IPO

items.d: "A listed chairman ranks like an official"
Fewer cash deals, more strategic ones

t40|190.c: Robots must first handle many kinds of tasks before they can spread widely, not the other way around.
t40|190.e: He compares robots to computers. Computers became general-purpose machines first, and only then entered every home. Robots are the same: they must handle many kinds of tasks before they can spread at scale. This wave of excitement was sparked directly by Elon Musk's investment and progress in large models. Older approaches such as learning from demonstration, where a person shows a task and the robot copies it, are getting fresh attention.
ex: Musk says Tesla's humanoid robots could one day number 10 billion

t40|190.c: Even a simple robot motion needs several abilities working together, mostly still hand-coded as rules.
t40|190.e: To do one simple motion, a robot has to combine perception, decision-making and motion planning. Today these mostly come from huge amounts of rule-based programming written by engineers. Deep learning, where machines learn patterns from lots of data, plays only a small part. The result is robots that are very inflexible, so a factory owner who buys one may not get much use out of it.
ex: A new product variant takes two days to reprogram, but the order finishes in two days

t40|190.sc: Go is easy, factory work isn't
t40|190.c: AI can beat Go champions but still can't replace a worker on a Foxconn assembly line.
t40|190.e: Go has fixed rules, and AI beat the best players long ago. Physical work on an assembly line, though, keeps changing. Every time a factory switches products, the robot has to be reprogrammed, so it can't switch tasks on the fly the way a worker can. Getting general ability in the physical world is far harder than winning at a board game.
ex: Reprogramming a robot for a new product variant takes two days

d.verdict: General ability in the physical world is much harder

t40|190.c: Large models can give robots common sense, but mechanical limbs are improving far more slowly.
t40|190.e: Large models can supply common sense and make a robot's "brain" much smarter. But the mechanical side is evolving far more slowly, and the limbs stay clumsy. More general AI could speed up design, iteration and trial and error in virtual worlds, and even approach industrial design differently from humans, which would accelerate mechanical engineering. Still, a big leap in hardware will need breakthroughs in core technology and new approaches.

items.d: Large models add common sense; fast progress
Waiting for breakthroughs and new approaches

t40|190.c: General-purpose robots should be humanoid, and no one will be able to monopolize the technology.
t40|190.e: The world is built for humans, so a general-purpose robot is best shaped like one. People and machines will train each other, the way ChatGPT has made people better communicators. Many jobs will be replaced, but more new ones will appear, as always in history. He doesn't believe anyone can monopolize general-purpose robots, since open-source efforts will compete. He hopes to see an early version within three years.

items.d: The world is built for humans
Old jobs go, new ones appear

t41|7.c: Writing Xiaohongshu up as a business story or a target for attacking consumerism are both clichés.
t41|7.e: They read dozens of articles about Xiaohongshu and found two kinds: ones using it as a prop for business stories and product analysis, and ones using it to criticize consumerism. The sameness made them a little angry, and that drove this episode: drop the clichés and look at the internet and internet companies with a wider lens.
ex: Written from August 2022 to June 2023, with many visits to Xiaohongshu's headquarters

t41|7.c: We live in a society of display: what you did matters less than how it looks.
t41|7.e: The episode's promo line places Xiaohongshu in a bigger social picture. People care less about what they actually do and more about how it appears. So the title asks: what has Xiaohongshu shaped, and who is shaping it? The episode page doesn't say who said this line.

t41|7.c: The slogan says record your good life, but heavy use may make people skip living it.
t41|7.e: A line quoted on the episode page captures the paradox. An app urges people to record a beautiful life, yet heavy users may end up skipping life itself, left with only the recording and the display. The episode page doesn't say who said it.

t42|203.sc: A decade of highs and lows
t42|203.c: Product managers were first overrated, then underrated, and the job deserves a fresh look.
t42|203.e: Around 2015, product managers were stars, and the book Everyone Is a Product Manager was nearly required reading for founders. When the startup wave receded, the role lost its shine. PMs came to be seen as cogs in big companies, and some said the internet had only small fixes left to make. The episode thinks both views are off balance, and now is a good time to take another look at the job.
ex: The book Everyone Is a Product Manager was once a must-read for founders

t42|203.c: The title "product manager" is the biggest con in the industry.
t42|203.e: This is the episode's tagline, and the page doesn't say who said it. Around this idea, the episode discusses common misconceptions about product managers, whether PM training courses are any use, and, if they aren't, how someone actually becomes a good product manager.

items.d: How to become a good PM

t42|204.c: As big tech companies slowed down, indie building showed product managers another path.
t42|204.e: The episode notes that indie development, where one person or a tiny team builds a product, has always existed. But only when big companies lost momentum did people start paying attention to these once "small" projects. Some also feel large models have brought back a golden age for product managers. Both guests now run their own products or businesses, and the episode asks why so many people are striking out on their own.
ex: Shaonan builds flomo and Xiaobaotong; Fei Liu does cold-brew tea and a podcast

items.d: Indie building gets a second look
Building your own product or business

t43|207.c: "U.S. person" is defined broadly; offshore entities set up by Chinese firms or citizens may be covered too.
t43|207.e: He points out that "U.S. person" in the order means not only individuals but also companies and green card holders. Entities set up abroad by Chinese companies or Chinese citizens could also get pulled in. The notice does carve out exceptions.
