Buying shares of such Chinese tech companies on the stock market, or being a purely financial limited partner who doesn't help run the fund, doesn't count as a covered deal.
ex: Public-market investing and purely passive LP stakes aren't covered transactions

items.d: Set up by Chinese firms or citizens

t43|207.c: The US approach is "small yard, high fence": a narrow scope, guarded very strictly.
t43|207.e: As he reads it, the US singles out only a few areas that affect national security, then guards them tightly. The rule notice sorts investments in semiconductors, quantum computing and AI into two groups: those that must be reported and those that are banned. But the definitions are fairly vague and subjective, leaving a lot of room for interpretation when the rules are enforced.
ex: Three areas: semiconductors and microelectronics, quantum computing, and AI

terms.d: Only national-security areas are fenced in

result.d: Either report it or it's banned

t43|207.c: There's little room to negotiate; the final rules won't stray from the intent, and reversal is very unlikely.
t43|207.e: The notice opened a 45-day comment period, and by custom the detailed rules might not take effect until the following year. Still, he thinks the final rules won't depart from what lawmakers intended. The earlier fiscal 2024 National Defense Authorization Act reached even wider in reviewing US investment in China. In theory the order could be struck down in court as unconstitutional, but that's not just a legal question, and he sees almost no chance of it.

items.d: Limits investment in key Chinese tech
Won't stray from the original intent

t43|207.c: AI limits are drawn by use, not technical specs, so judgments are subjective and AI is hit hardest.
t43|207.e: The rule notice doesn't draw the line for AI using technical specs. Instead it looks at what the AI is used for. Deciding what counts as a given use is highly subjective and open to wide interpretation. That's why he thinks AI is the area hit hardest by these restrictions.

items: Judged by what it's used for

d.verdict: Drawing lines by use hits AI hardest

t43|207.c: As both China and the US grew more cautious, Mita stumbled after a strong start and pivoted to legal AI.
t43|207.e: Mita translated IPO filings, cross-border investment documents and tenders for international law firms, and that demand fell sharply in the first half. Renewals with Chinese branches of US companies also ran into trouble, as self-censorship rose on both sides. So Mita paused promoting Xiezuocat, its consumer writing tool, and shifted to a legal large model for legal advice and lawyer assistants. It is also weighing going abroad and raising money outside the US, such as from the Middle East, though that's hard.
ex: First-half revenue already matched the whole previous year
US legal AI startup Harvey had 100-plus US law firms waiting to try it

t44|215.c: Packing finance-worker stereotypes into memes makes even insiders laugh in recognition.
t44|215.e: She has a sharp eye for finance workers in Beijing, Shanghai and Hong Kong, and she rolls all the stereotypes into memes. Insiders with a sense of humor laugh because they recognize themselves, and outsiders get to laugh along. Hanyang saw her memes in a group chat and reached out to invite her on the show.

t44|215.c: The elite résumé path, leveling up like a video game, is hard to repeat in today's climate.
t44|215.e: Going from Beijing's best high school to Wharton and then a top investment bank, collecting credentials step by step, used to work. In today's economy that path is hard to repeat. The episode's tagline lands on this: we always overrate ourselves and underrate the times we live in. The page doesn't say who said it.
ex: Top Beijing high school, then Wharton, then a top investment bank

t44|215.c: Humor and self-mockery are weapons for coping when a career is suddenly derailed.
t44|215.e: The episode treats humor and laughing at yourself as a way to handle a career that suddenly stops. Around her experience before and after being pushed out of her job, it covers finding calm, fighting anxiety, discovering new joys, and settling into life as opportunities get scarcer. The episode page doesn't describe what exactly she did.

t45|221.c: Ads in content communities aim for lasting value: they give "endorphins," not "dopamine."
t45|221.e: He contrasts ads in content communities with traditional internet ads. Community content keeps being found and works slowly over time, like the lasting satisfaction of endorphins. Traditional ads deliver a quick dopamine hit. Indigo Social was founded in 2017 after its team saw the marketing value of expert answers on Zhihu, a Q&A platform, and it later expanded to Bilibili and Xiaohongshu.
ex: Audi placed its brand in the Chinese animated series Ling Cage
Yiche teamed up with creator Handy Geng to build a quirky homemade car

t45|221.c: The platforms split the work: Xiaohongshu for user experience, Zhihu for analysis, Bilibili for setting the tone.
t45|221.e: In carmakers' content marketing, Xiaohongshu leans toward sharing real ownership experience, Zhihu toward breaking down the product, and Bilibili toward PR and setting the brand's tone. But Bilibili users push back against ads more noticeably. How much ad revenue each platform earns also depends on who its users are.
ex: Pugongying and Huahuo are Xiaohongshu's and Bilibili's sponsored-post marketplaces

items.d: Sets the tone; users resist ads more

t45|221.c: The bar for influencers keeps rising: first looks, then expertise, and now taste.
t45|221.e: The episode traces how content communities' expectations of product influencers have changed. At first it was about good looks. Then it was about knowing the product. Now it goes further, to having taste. The bar for influencers keeps going up.

items.d: Knows the product, explains it well

t45|221.c: Carmakers chase quick returns and brand directors job-hop, so no one does slow brand-building.
t45|221.e: When carmakers split up marketing budgets, they focus on immediate return on spend, and Douyin takes the biggest share. Brand directors also change jobs often, so they have little reason to invest in slow brand work. Legacy carmakers and EV newcomers each have strengths and envy each other, one admiring the other's content skills, the other its marketing focus.
ex: Douyin takes the largest share of carmakers' marketing budgets

result.d: No one invests for the long run

t45|221.c: After competing on product and on sales volume, carmakers will ultimately compete on brand.
t45|221.e: This is the episode's bottom line. Carmakers are fighting hard on products and sales right now, but the contest will end up being about brand. The episode also notes that marketing in content communities in a way that's expert, youthful and close to everyday life is now a must-have skill for car brands.

t46|225.c: You can't generalize about Africa: West and East Africa differ, and so does each country.
t46|225.e: He insists West Africa and East Africa shouldn't be lumped together, and walks through the countries he has worked in one by one. Tanzania feels a lot like East Asia. Zambia is a normal country that Chinese people would recognize. Lesotho is the poorest place he's seen, yet it snows. Eswatini will upend whatever you thought you knew.
ex: South Africa left a poor impression, with power output steadily falling
Mozambique's capital is small and pleasant

items.d: A normal country Chinese people get
Failed finances, but the economy isn't that bad

t46|225.c: DR Congo is a true resource curse: even its mining waste is richer in copper than China's good ore.
t46|225.e: Ordinary copper ore in DR Congo is about 4% to 5% copper. The waste left after mining still holds about 1%, and waste reprocessed once more still has about 0.4%. China's good copper mines run only about 0.4%. With resources this rich, the country still hasn't developed, which he calls a true resource curse, where natural wealth fails to make a country better off.

t46|225.c: DR Congo is a sovereign state on paper but more like a place name in practice.
t46|225.e: In DR Congo, regional powers each run their own patch, and a visa issued by one isn't recognized by another. In Lesotho, by contrast, you can legally work but not legally reside. He sees DR Congo's elections as close to civil war, and thinks disorganized violence is more dangerous than open fighting. Still, he says it shouldn't be judged harshly. It is struggling hard, and many problems are social, not simply a matter of "lazy Black people."
ex: Lesotho: you can work legally, but not live there legally

d.verdict: Don't judge harshly; many problems are social

t46|225.c: Once a country develops, birth rates are sure to fall, and Africa is no exception.
t46|225.e: He points to what he saw in Tanzania. People there are starting to feel they can't afford many children, so they have just two. To him this is a universal rule of development, and Africa won't escape it either.
ex: Tanzanians also feel they can't afford kids, so they have only two

t46|225.c: Africa is well suited to modern farming; the old Chinese joke about "Jinkela" fertilizer has a point.
t46|225.e: He thinks Africa is very well suited to modern agriculture. A Chinese internet joke from a parody fertilizer ad goes, "African farming is underdeveloped, so it needs Jinkela." He thinks the joke is partly right, since "Jinkela" stands for fertilizer and other modern farm inputs.

t47|80.c: Over the past several months, dollar funds and founders alike have run into plenty of trouble.
t47|80.e: The episode centers on what the past several months have been like for dollar funds (investment funds that raise US dollars, mostly to back Chinese companies) and for founders. Two days before taping, the well-known firm GGV announced it was splitting up, which added a lot to talk about. They discuss what made the split unusual, how markets and companies have changed, and what dollar funds should do next. The episode page doesn't give his actual views.
ex: Two days before taping, investment firm GGV announced it was splitting up

root.d: Tough for both funds and founders

t47|80.c: Telling a $500M founder from a $1B or $10B one may not matter much right now.
t47|80.e: This is the question in the episode's subtitle. He has said before that the way he judges people isn't suited to venture capital. From there the conversation asks whether founders must be one particular type of person, and whether, in today's climate, the skill of judging how big a founder can grow a company is still worth much. The episode page lists the questions but not his answers.

marks.d: The scale investors try to judge

t47|80.sc: Seeing it from the other side
t47|80.c: Moving from investor to company executive changed how he sees both investing and startups.
t47|80.e: He went from investing to an executive role at a company, then started a podcast. The episode asks what changed in his thinking after switching seats, what he would do differently if he invested again today, whether investors are suited to starting companies, and whether founders should listen to investors' critiques. The episode page only lists these questions.

items.d: Felt his read on people didn't suit VC
From funding the work to doing it

t48|234.c: Musk and his companies are still unfolding, so this biography only tells half the story.
t48|234.e: The episode notes argue that Musk takes far more risk than most people, and his businesses have come close to the edge several times. Yet at least "in this version of the universe" he didn't end up with nothing. He has delivered, one by one, goals that first looked impossible. Because he and his companies are still changing, the biography only gets halfway. What he says and does will keep inspiring, provoking, and even changing the world.
ex: CITIC Press published the Chinese edition about a month before this episode aired

items.d: His businesses often came near the edge
Goals that looked impossible came true
Neither he nor his companies are done

t48|234.c: Success alone doesn't make a hero; it also takes legend and a tragic struggle.
t48|234.e: The episode notes offer a way to look at famous people: success isn't enough to make someone a hero, or to give them depth. Legend comes from a person and drama drawing each other in, and classic heroes always hit moments of tragedy and struggle. This book shows the legendary side of Musk. Perhaps only with more distance will people see him and his era clearly.

terms.d: A person and drama drawn together
Every classic hero goes through it

result.d: And only then a deep one

t48|234.c: Twenty years of shifting business bestsellers mirror how China's business mood has changed.
t48|234.e: The episode treats two decades of Chinese business bestsellers as a thread to follow: as reading lists change, so does the business climate behind them. Mu Li's own publishing career is one marker. She has worked on several of Walter Isaacson's biographies, and eight years ago she brought another Musk book to China. The episode page only names the topic and gives no firm conclusions.
ex: Eight years ago she helped bring Ashlee Vance's Musk biography to China
She also worked on Isaacson's Steve Jobs and Leonardo da Vinci

root.d: A thread for tracking business books

items.d: Brought to China eight years ago

t49|239.c: "3nm" hasn't been a real measurement for years; it's just a name the industry kept using.
t49|239.e: Early on, a chip process number meant the smallest width of a transistor's "gate" (the part that switches it on and off). A 500nm process meant a gate 500nm wide. As manufacturing neared physical limits, transistor designs kept changing, and the number stopped matching any real dimension. It simply stayed as a label. So asking whether "3nm is really 3nm" misses the point: it was never measuring length.
ex: In early 500nm processes, the gate really was 500nm wide

items.d: The number no longer matches real size

t49|239.c: Apple's 3nm and Huawei's 7nm are roughly four years apart, but phone users feel much less difference.
t49|239.e: At about two years per generation, the two are roughly four years apart. But from 5nm on, chipmakers need EUV lithography (machines that print circuits with extremely short-wavelength light), so going from 7nm to 3nm actually took longer. Meanwhile each new process brings only modest gains. Chips are also held back by the "memory wall": processors compute faster than data can be fetched from memory. So the gap users feel is smaller than the gap on paper.
ex: Apple's 3nm chip is only about 10% faster than its 4nm one

items.d: Less than the chip spec gap

t49|239.c: Moore's Law isn't a law of physics but a target the industry chases and makes come true.
t49|239.e: What Moore's Law describes has been revised several times. It was never a law of nature, but a goal that pulls the industry along. Chip progress is driven not only by scientists and engineers but by plain profit-seeking. Expectations draw investment, investment brings returns, and returns fund the next round. That loop is why the "law" keeps coming true.

t49|239.c: CPUs and GPUs were both once written off; GPUs suit AI but can't replace CPUs.
t49|239.e: Intel nearly dropped its CPU (a computer's general-purpose processor) line at one point, and GPUs (graphics chips), first good only for games, were hard to sell. Both later reshaped the industry. CPUs can do almost anything, so they run all kinds of automatically controlled products. GPUs excel at running many simple calculations at once, which suits training and running AI. But doing many things in parallel isn't the same as doing anything, so GPUs can't replace CPUs.
ex: Andy Grove led Intel out of memory chips and into CPUs

items: Hard to sell when only for games

d.verdict: GPUs can't replace CPUs

t49|239.c: Governments paid for the early chip industry, but policy alone rarely produces real innovation.
t49|239.e: Early chips were extremely expensive, and governments were the main buyers. In 1965 the US Air Force alone bought about 20% of all chips made in America. Japan's VLSI program (a state-backed push into very large-scale chips) suggests innovation needs both government support and plenty of freedom. That leaves him with deep respect for how technology, markets and business cycles work, and he urges more patience with the industry.
ex: In 1965 the US Air Force bought about 20% of America's chips
Japan's state-backed VLSI (very large-scale integration) program

result.d: Plus respect for markets and cycles

t50|244.c: Xiaohongshu has shifted from a contest over looks to a much wider mix of content.
t50|244.e: She has posted on Xiaohongshu since 2017, and the episode's headings sum up the change as moving from "are you pretty" to ever more variety. Along that thread, the episode tests whether old labels, like fueling appearance anxiety and consumerism, still fit today. It also asks whether the move to video will make Xiaohongshu look more and more like other platforms.
ex: The period covered runs from 2017 to 2023

t50|244.c: Xiaohongshu feels upbeat overall, while Bilibili viewers don't want creators treating content as a job.
t50|244.e: She creates on both platforms. The episode headings draw two contrasts: Xiaohongshu's mood is generally positive and aspirational, Bilibili's isn't, and Bilibili viewers don't want creators to make content their profession. That leads to another question: what people actually mean when they say Xiaohongshu is easy to make money on. The episode page doesn't spell out her reasons.

t50|244.c: View counts matter less to a creator's income than outsiders tend to think.
t50|244.e: This is one of the episode's clearest claims. Around it, the episode covers the details of sponsorships: which kinds of ads are easy to promote, how brands should work with creators, how photo-and-text creators differ from video creators, and how to make people want a product. It also asks how Xiaohongshu creates new demand, and whether every cosmetic has already been invented. The page lists these topics without the answers.

items.d: Which ads are easy to promote

t50|244.c: Creating on a platform comes with rules, and breaking them has a price.
t50|244.e: "Breaking the rules comes at a cost" is one of the episode's headings. The closing rapid-fire round touches the same point from another angle: has the platform trained her habits, does she get anxious, has she ever broken down, does she delete comments. The episode page doesn't record her answers.

t52|266.c: Wealth management is still sales-driven, so firms chase rallies and dump in downturns, just like small investors.
t52|266.e: Sales pressure in the industry rises and falls with the market: heavy when markets are good, light when they're bad. So firms swing with the market too, behaving like amateur investors who buy as prices climb and sell as they fall. That is her basic read on how wealth management works today.

t52|266.c: The days when buying almost anything made money are over; clients now care most about safety.
t52|266.e: The episode notes that long stretches of fast growth are the exception: in rich countries, income per person mostly grows under 2% a year. In her view, easy money is gone, and more people are willing to pay for professional advice. China Merchants Bank's private banking clients, who need 10 million yuan to invest, grew from about 80,000 in 2019 to about 120,000 by late 2021. Safety is now clients' top concern, and spreading assets between China and abroad is one option.
ex: In the 8 richest countries, 1970–2010 income per person mostly grew 1.7%–1.9% a year
China Merchants Bank private banking requires 10 million yuan in investable assets

t52|266.sc: Match the approach to the amount
t52|266.c: If you have under one or two million yuan to invest, learn to manage it yourself.
t52|266.e: With modest savings, paying for professional help may not be worth it. She suggests learning to do it yourself and understanding what you're actually buying. For example, the bank products sold most often, those in risk class 2, are largely backed by local government bonds. Once you have more money, you can hire experts from different fields to get you up to speed. Whatever the amount, it pays to build good judgment about money early.
ex: Popular class-2 bank products are largely backed by local government bonds

marks.d: Bring in experts to teach you

t52|266.c: Volatile assets test human nature, so ordinary people shouldn't trade them on their own.
t52|266.e: She points out that most people's day jobs don't train them to handle wild emotional swings. Volatile assets amplify the urge to buy when prices climb and sell when they drop, so don't trade them yourself. Families investing together also need to agree first on what "good" looks like. Otherwise a big loss can turn relatives against each other.
ex: Some families have fallen out after losing a lot of money

t52|266.c: Wealth managers handle family matters as well as money, and their wider benefit is helping capital flow more efficiently.
t52|266.e: Beyond deciding where to invest, wealth managers also help with clients' everyday needs, such as children's schooling, family medical care and social life. In a public mood that cares a lot about fairness, she sees the industry's broader value as helping money move around more efficiently. That's her way of explaining a job that means helping the rich get richer.

items.d: Where to invest and how to spread risk

t53|271.c: A nursing home shouldn't be an island; besides safety, older people need belonging and a sense of purpose.
t53|271.e: After actually running a nursing home, she believes older people shouldn't be treated as a separate group cut off from everyone else. Keeping them safe is only the baseline. On top of that, they need to feel they belong to a community and that they still matter. From there she hopes to explore an "age-free" way of caring for the elderly.

items.d: Part of a community, not isolated

t53|271.c: Unable to find a good nursing home for her family, she opened a homelike one herself.
t53|271.e: After returning to China in 2016, she looked for a nursing home for her family and found none she liked. So she set out to build one that felt like home and gave residents a social life. A little over a year later, she and a partner opened the first one in Ya'an. Along the way they disagreed over the vision and survived the pandemic's blow to small operators. The episode also covers why she chose not to add medical care.
ex: She previously researched repairing organs with 3D-printed materials in Australia

items.d: Couldn't find a home for family
Turns to culture and branded content

t53|271.c: "Age-free" elder care uses cultural activities and branded content to connect older people with other generations.
t53|271.e: During the pandemic she rethought what her home did well and began producing cultural content and a brand of its own, to bring older people closer to younger ones. Daily life includes experiments like "flat-table meetings." After one Double Ninth Festival event (a traditional day honoring elders), some residents were deeply moved. For the second home she wants a neighborhood feel rather than a closed compound.
ex: Holding "flat-table meetings" at the home
Related article: redefining life at 80 with Gen Z trends

t53|271.c: Robots and other new technology could stretch limited elder care to reach far more people.
t53|271.e: Demand for elder care far outstrips supply. She thinks robots and similar technology could help close that gap, letting limited services cover more people. She also notes that older people aren't just recipients of care, since more and more of them still work. Crossing into other fields offers openings too, and she cites how she picked up a rehabilitation glove project again.
ex: She revived a rehabilitation glove project

t54|7.c: You've got to keep wandering: instead of a year-end review, he tells four everyday stories.
t54|7.e: This year-end episode skips the usual look back and wrap-up. Instead it tells four stories, and the episode page gives only their tags: wandering around, an office chair, hot-pot mutton, making art. Hanyang's motto for himself is "while you're alive, you've got to wander." The cover photo was taken that January on the road from Yichun to Heihe. To hear the stories themselves, you have to listen.
ex: The cover was shot on the road from Yichun to Heihe

t54|7.c: Beyond the stories, the episode points listeners to northeastern food, Hong Kong and a few books.
t54|7.e: The extras listed on the episode page are: Hanyang's article on food in Changchun, Yang Li's article on Hong Kong, episode 31 about hydropower with an engineer named Cao, and three books. One is a history of the US Republican Party; the others are The Sound of the Mountain and Deep River. The page doesn't say which story each item goes with, so this only records where it points readers.
ex: Books: a Republican Party history, The Sound of the Mountain, Deep River

items.d: Articles, an old episode, three books

t55|274.c: Chinese car exports have gone through three phases, and since 2022 smart EVs have taken the lead.
t55|274.e: He splits the history into three stretches. From 2005 to 2016, Chinese cars got off to an embarrassing start and then stalled below one million a year. From 2017 to 2021, exports rose to one or two million a year, mostly gasoline cars. Since 2022, smart electric cars have surged. The goal has shifted from padding domestic sales numbers to genuinely building a business overseas.
ex: About 4.7 million cars expected in 2023; over 480,000 in November alone

items.d: One to two million a year

t55|274.c: BYD once copied Toyota's Corolla; now it supplies electric-car technology to Toyota.
t55|274.e: BYD's first car under its own brand, the F3, was modeled on the Toyota Corolla. Today the two have a joint venture in which BYD supplies the electric-vehicle technology. At the Tokyo show, Akio Toyoda met BYD founder Wang Chuanfu. At the Munich show, 60 companies from China's auto supply chain exhibited. Chinese cars now get noticed not just within the industry but by the media and the public.
ex: BYD exports: about 50,000 in 2022, nearly 200,000 in 2023's first nine months
60 Chinese auto supply-chain companies exhibited in Munich

items.d: The F3 modeled on the Corolla

t55|274.c: Going abroad has moved from a sideline to a top priority, driven by industry patterns and brutal competition at home.
t55|274.e: This wave brings three new things: carmakers dare to enter Europe and Japan, they sell mid-range and premium models, and they build factories abroad. Companies differ on whether to target Southeast Asia or Europe, and whether to build plants overseas. He sees this as fitting how car industries usually develop, and also as a result of fierce competition at home. Even as globalization retreats, Chinese and European carmakers are working more closely together.

items.d: Willing to enter Europe and Japan

t55|274.c: Chinese cars have the hard strengths now, but brand and cultural appeal will take time to build.
t55|274.e: The products themselves haven't fully settled. New-energy cars still need to become truly green, and smart features remain a big unknown. Brand and culture are the clearer weak spots. He notes that if the dispute between Great Wall and BYD over hybrid fuel tanks had happened abroad, BYD would have faced more pressure. And the story of a "rising national industry" doesn't sell in global markets.
ex: The Great Wall vs. BYD dispute over hybrid fuel tanks

items: Entering Europe and Japan, going upmarket

d.verdict: The cars are strong; brand and culture need time

t55|274.c: Carmakers are rushing abroad together, but the window of opportunity won't close soon.
t55|274.e: In 2023 Chinese carmakers rushed overseas all at once. He believes this window of opportunity won't shut any time soon. That leaves CEOs and founders torn: eager to seize a rare chance, yet worried about outside conditions they can't control.

items.d: Outside forces are hard to control

t56|278.c: Explaining economic ideas to a broad audience is worthwhile, and the bee economics episode convinced her.
t56|278.e: Discussing "shows we wanted to make but didn't," they start from their episode on the economics of bees and talk about the fun and value of explaining economic ideas to ordinary listeners. On the question of which episodes changed the hosts themselves, the page records Yue Xiaoya's answer: that episode made her more committed to covering economic concepts.
ex: Episode 115 of "Business Is Like That": the economics of bees

t56|278.c: Making the show changes the hosts too: after covering IMAX, she chose her screen carefully.
t56|278.e: Under the same question, her second example is more everyday. After making an episode about IMAX (a giant-screen film format), she deliberately picked which screen to see Oppenheimer on. Covering business topics was shaping the hosts' own spending choices.
ex: She carefully chose a screen to watch Oppenheimer

t56|279.sc: A new respect for Chinese chains
t56|279.c: After the episode on Lao Xiang Ji, he gained new respect for Chinese restaurant chains.
t56|279.e: On the question of which episodes changed the hosts, the page records Wenjie Xiao's answer. After making an episode about Lao Xiang Ji, a Chinese fast-food chain, he came to respect Chinese restaurant chains more, and went out to try many new chain brands.
ex: Lao Xiang Ji, a Chinese fast-food chain

t56|279.c: Meeting listeners in person gave him energy.
t56|279.e: The other thing he says affected him was a listener meetup in Beijing: seeing listeners face to face recharged him. The page sums this up in one line and doesn't say which event it was or go into more detail.

t57|284.c: Going from consulting to farming felt like dropping from 30,000 feet straight into the fields.
t57|284.e: The episode's subtitle is "landing from 30,000 feet." She worked as a McKinsey consultant and now calls herself "the vegetable farmer who's best at PowerPoint." She once wrote that she gets bored easily, which is why she went into consulting to see many industries. Farming, by contrast, is slow and repetitive. The episode asks how the two jobs differ, how she knows she can stick with it, and which beliefs flipped after she moved to Africa. The page doesn't give her answers.
ex: She calls herself "the vegetable farmer who's best at PowerPoint"

t57|284.c: To see what African farming lacks, look at the concrete steps: getting land, local relations, selling produce.
t57|284.e: The title borrows a popular catchphrase: "African farming is underdeveloped, so what exactly is it missing?" Rather than stopping at big-picture claims, the episode follows how she built her farm, step by step: what farming in Africa actually means, how to start from nothing, how to build good relations with locals, who buys the harvest, what produce traders care about most, and whether exporting to Europe is possible. The page only lists these questions.
ex: Scale: about 1,000 mu, roughly 165 acres, in Kenya

t58|291.c: In 2016 he bet that models would grow so big they'd need entirely new systems, which set OneFlow apart.
t58|291.e: As a postdoc in 2008 he chose to work where machine learning meets brain science. Deep learning hadn't taken off yet, so he couldn't land a faculty job and joined Microsoft Research Asia, where he built LightLDA. In 2016 he began building a training framework (core software for training AI models) against rivals like Google's TensorFlow. What set him apart was a contrarian bet: models would one day be so large they'd need a brand-new kind of system.
ex: LightLDA became a core system for search, recommendations and ads, used by Kuaishou and others

t58|291.c: Demand for running large models will outgrow demand for training them, so his new company focuses on running them.
t58|291.e: OneFlow built training frameworks, software for making models. SiliconFlow instead focuses on inference, meaning running finished models so people can actually use them. He saw that demand for running models would overtake demand for training them. He also wanted to keep the team together. He felt it would be a shame if everyone went back to big-company jobs instead of building inference software as a startup.
ex: The team was about 40 people joining Light Year, about 35 leaving

d.verdict: Running models will outgrow training them

t58|291.c: Pure software is hard to sell in China, so bundle it with what customers already pay for, and go global.
t58|291.e: Getting Chinese customers to pay for software alone has long been a problem for the industry, and it's what he wants to crack this time. His plan is to go global and target overseas markets. In China, he can't just sell software. The product has to be tied to something customers already pay for, which takes creative strategy and new product forms.

root.d: Pure software is hard to charge for

t58|291.c: Clever algorithms don't stay an advantage for long; years of accumulated engineering skill do.
t58|291.e: A good algorithmic idea pays off handsomely once it's built, so everyone pursues it and it spreads fast. That makes it hard to hold onto. Engineering optimization is the opposite: each improvement pays off only a little, so it has to be built up over years. In the end very few teams do it really well, which makes the skill rare.

marks.d: High payoff, so everyone does them
Small gains that add up over years

t58|291.c: Super apps probably won't come from today's model makers, but leading infrastructure suppliers will earn big returns.
t58|291.e: He hopes large models will spawn super apps (products everyone uses daily, like WeChat), but thinks they probably won't come from today's model companies. Competition among software suppliers will keep intensifying, yet those who pull ahead can earn sizable returns. He once overheard people at the next table say OneFlow had good technology but still got acquired without making money. He hopes SiliconFlow will set a better example this time.
ex: The hosts also ask: what if super apps build their own infrastructure?

t59|263.c: 3D will follow text, images and video, going from big-studio work to something anyone can make.
t59|263.e: VAST's long-term vision: text, images and video each went from something only professionals produced to something anyone could create and enjoy, and 3D will too. Today 3D content is still like AAA games, the big-budget kind that take huge teams, time and money. Generative technology's job is to lower that barrier.
ex: Tripo launched in December 2023 and has generated over 300,000 3D models

t59|263.c: First 3D tools need their Midjourney moment; then a 3D platform can have its TikTok moment.
t59|263.e: Step one is a 3D generator ordinary people can use. When results match versions 4 and 5 of Midjourney, the AI image tool, the tools will have matured, which they estimate will happen between late 2024 and early 2025. Step two is a 3D content platform. It takes off once a new kind of user-made content appears that people can copy and riff on. That may come before VR headsets mature. Headsets would help, but aren't required.
ex: One idea: build a 3D haunted house and invite friends to get scared
VAST is privately testing a platform for hosting 3D content

t59|263.c: 3D generation still stitches several parts together, and nobody agrees on the best way to represent a 3D object.
t59|263.e: A large language model is one model that handles everything from start to finish. Tripo instead combines several building blocks, including diffusion (which builds images up from noise step by step) and transformers (the architecture behind most large models). Representation is the other big difference. 2D images have a standard grid-of-pixels format, but for 3D, whether meshes, NeRFs or something else works best is still being explored.
ex: 3D formats include meshes, point clouds, voxels, NeRFs and Gaussian splatting

t59|263.c: VAST builds tools for ordinary people rather than replacing pro software; its long-term edge is product, community and developers.
t59|263.e: Big and small companies alike are working on 3D generation. VAST stands apart by targeting everyday users rather than replacing mainstream professional 3D software. The team sees this as a new field where Chinese teams aren't behind American ones, and they even welcome users trying rivals, to grow the number of people using 3D generation. They hold lots of native 3D data. Long term, their defensible edge lies in product, community and developer relations.
ex: A developer built Tripo Go, where models from different people battle each other
The team contributed to the open-source project Wonder3D

t59|263.c: Seasoned founders dodge known pitfalls and young ones charge ahead, so VAST puts both together.
t59|263.e: Even in the mobile internet era, plenty of founders started companies between 25 and 30. VAST's founder is very young, yet its core team includes several people who have founded companies before. Their reasoning: people who've done it before can steer clear of known pitfalls, while young people are bold enough to charge ahead.
ex: Yachen Song, born in 1997, worked at SenseTime and MiniMax
Ding Liang previously led general-purpose models at SenseTime

t60|225.c: Many stereotypes about the Northeast don't hold up, though their answers include plenty of bold, subjective takes.
t60|225.e: Before recording, Hanyang gathered a pile of listener questions about the Northeast, and the three answer them one by one. According to the episode notes, they knock down many stereotypes but also offer lots of sweeping opinions based on gut feeling. Questions range from whether it's really that cold, to research on women and crime in the Northeast from 1900 to 1931, to what the Northeast even is and whether the recent "Northeast renaissance" in literature and music is real.
ex: Before taping, they drank "sauce-aroma" red wine at Zhalantun's Six Nations Hotel
Once you leave the Northeast, can you ever go back?

items.d: As the episode notes put it
The show calls itself very subjective

t60|225.c: Both are vast and sparsely populated, yet the Nordic countries seem gloomy while the Northeast seems upbeat.
t60|225.e: A central question in the episode: why do the sparsely populated Nordic countries come across as depressed while the equally empty Northeast seems cheerful? From that contrast, the three move on to whether people drifting apart into isolated individuals is necessarily bad, the "freedom to brawl" that comes with voluntary groups, and customs like bride prices, cash gifts and dowries. The page lists the questions but not their answers.
ex: Bride prices, cash gifts at weddings, and dowries

t60|225.c: The Northeast's reputation as a travel spot is recovering, and getting to know it starts with the food.
t60|225.e: The episode starts from Harbin's sudden popularity with tourists and asks why the region's travel reputation has recently improved. It suggests routes and food, and even explains the difference between Northeastern barbecue and skewers. The episode page adds a long list of restaurants across cities, from braised pork bones in Changchun to small skewers in Hegang. Related links include Hanyang's articles on food in Changchun and grilled meat in Qiqihar.
ex: Harbin: Art Nouveau buildings stand near Central Street
For "Chinese Baroque" buildings, try the area around Chunhua Hospital

items.d: An family barbecue, classic marinated meat

t61|305.c: Three years of pandemic left many people with lasting psychological damage, and it is hitting ever younger people.
t61|305.e: She believes that over three-plus years, many people worldwide developed what she calls a "social-psychological disability," and the effects didn't end with the pandemic. More worrying is how young those affected are getting: child suicide rates rose after the pandemic, and one 6-year-old said "living has no meaning." She also notes that parenting education is missing, so many parents don't know how to be good parents.
ex: Chinese Academy of Sciences report: 24.1% of 18–24-year-olds screened at risk of depression
A 6-year-old said "living has no meaning"

t61|305.c: Young people flocking to temples and lotteries are looking for another way out after losing control over their fate.
t61|305.e: Young people visiting temples reflects uncertainty about the future and a sense that they can't steer their own lives. Buying lottery tickets means seeking through luck what the normal system won't give them. She views "going crazy" fairly positively, as a form of self-expression. Society, she says, should give people places and chances to let loose.
ex: The popular MBTI personality test measures poorly and isn't very scientific

t61|305.c: Economic strain keeps lowering people's expectations; civil-service exams get more crowded, yet some who get in can't adjust.
t61|305.e: She uses the idea of "diminishing expectations" to describe how the overall economy weighs on people's minds: hopes for the future get scaled back step by step. That leads the episode to how someone should face possible job loss. In search of stability, competition for civil-service and other state jobs keeps getting fiercer. Yet she notes that some people who make it into the system find they don't fit.

t61|305.c: Burnout is coming earlier: it used to appear about three years into a job, now it can appear within months.
t61|305.e: This is the burnout in the episode's title. She has seen that people used to hit burnout, feeling drained and unable to care about work, around three years into a job. Now it can happen within a few months. The episode page also notes growing attention to workplaces that treat people as less than human, and a young teacher in Zhengzhou who felt his job was a "cage."
ex: Burnout used to come about three years in; now within months

d.verdict: Burnout is arriving earlier and earlier

t61|305.c: To live as a real person, never treat others as tools, and never let others treat you as one.
t61|305.e: The backlash against livestream seller Li Jiaqi's remarks shows, in her view, that many people no longer believe hard work alone guarantees success. Many also increasingly feel they aren't living as full human beings. She holds up her mentor, psychologist Zhang Houcan, as a model: she never treated others as tools and never let anyone treat her as one.
ex: She sees her mentor Zhang Houcan as a model of living as a real person

marks.d: Used no one, and was used by no one

t62|315.c: People misunderstand philosophy in much the same way they misunderstand video games.
t62|315.e: The episode opens by pairing philosophy with video games: the public easily gets both wrong. From there he explains, in plain terms, what philosophy is and isn't, and the right way for ordinary people to get into it. The episode page gives only the comparison and doesn't say exactly how the two misunderstandings are alike.
ex: He wrote a popular introduction to philosophy

t62|315.c: Understanding the "burnout society" isn't enough; people need a way out of the exhaustion.
t62|315.e: The episode starts from a common frustration: the philosopher Byung-Chul Han described a "burnout society," where people wear themselves out pushing themselves, but didn't say how to escape it. The episode page states this in the first person without naming the speaker. Following that thread, the episode asks whether the great thinkers of the past can still help us understand life in the digital age. The page doesn't record his answer.
ex: Byung-Chul Han's The Burnout Society

items: Ideas for making sense of digital life

t62|315.c: Philosophy offers ordinary people three strategies for living: transcendence, immanence and nihilism.
t62|315.e: In his view, one thing philosophy offers ordinary people is a few strategies for making peace with life: transcendence, immanence and nihilism. Here the episode also compares how Plato talked about ideals with how big tech companies talk about "mission" and "vision." The episode page doesn't define the three strategies, so they aren't spelled out here.
ex: How Plato differs from big tech companies talking about mission and vision

t62|315.c: The quick joy of scrolling and shopping leaves people emptier; practical wisdom can push back against meaninglessness.
t62|315.e: The episode asks why the pleasure of scrolling and shopping always leaves people feeling emptier afterward. It suggests using Aristotle's "practical wisdom" (the skill of judging how to act well in real situations) to counter the sense that life is meaningless. Both topics take up a good part of the episode, but the page lists only the headings, not the arguments.

t62|315.c: You can always say "no" to the world; real life starts with knowing yourself, a full life with knowing others.
t62|315.e: The later part of the episode lands on two claims. First, whatever the world is like, you can always say "no" to it. Second, a real life begins with wanting to understand yourself, and a complete life begins with wanting to understand others. This is his answer to the crisis of meaning, though the episode page doesn't lay out his reasoning.
ex: The episode page includes a note on the poet Tomas Tranströmer

items.d: Possible whatever the world is like

t63|198.c: People who come to Tiaohai all have some doubts about the whole idea of a job.
t63|198.e: The episode title uses this line to sum up Tiaohai's customers. From there the conversation turns to this generation of young people in China's biggest cities. If Tiaohai is a business built for them, what other businesses do they need? And what makes Beijing special? The episode page doesn't say who said the line or give their answers.
ex: Related article: not everyone can be a beer pourer at Tiaohai

items.d: How the title sums them up

t63|198.c: A line outside a bar is odd, since meals end but drinking doesn't, so Tiaohai must be doing something right.
t63|198.e: The episode's promo offers a piece of reasoning. A meal has an end: diners finish and leave, so waiting for a table is normal. Drinking has no end: people can sit as long as they like, so bars shouldn't have lines. If people queue outside Tiaohai, it must be doing something right. The episode then covers its philosophy and business model, advice for copying it, and what's wrong with the traditional craft beer scene. The promo doesn't name the speaker.
ex: Reading listed on the episode page: Paul Graham's "Do Things That Don't Scale"

d.verdict: A bar with a line must have something special

t64|322.c: Fearing Sora is pointless: video generation is far from solved, and startups still have room.
t64|322.e: Multimodal AI, which handles images, video and sound, has come a long way, from GANs to diffusion models to Sora, OpenAI's video model. He grants that Sora was a shock but says fear doesn't help. Video generation isn't fully solved, and there's no agreement on what a "world model" (a model that simulates how the real world works) is or how to build one. That leaves plenty to explore, so startups still have a shot. Whether big companies' data advantage still holds is listed only as an open question.
ex: EMO can make the Mona Lisa recite poetry and the woman from Sora's video speak

items.d: The next stop, with no consensus yet

t64|322.c: Using a large model, EMO makes portraits talk without per-person training, more simply and more vividly.
t64|322.e: The XR Lab's approach is "digital asset production plus skills," where skills cover facial expressions, movement and interaction. Making a portrait talk had been done before. EMO is different because it uses a large model: one audio clip is enough to drive it, with no motion sequence needed. It works zero-shot, meaning no training on a specific person, so the process is simple and light, yet the results are livelier, richer and more adaptable.
ex: EMO was released at the end of February 2024

items: Driven by a voice clip alone

t64|322.c: At this stage, making the product better mostly means making the model better.
t64|322.e: Animate Anyone, which makes a person or pet in a photo dance, went into the "Dance King" feature of Alibaba's Qwen app, where research meets real use. Users taught the team a lot. Pets dancing proved more popular than people dancing, since pets can only dance with the help of technology. More people uploaded dogs than cats because the original model recognized dogs more easily, and the team has since tuned it for both. The feature is free, because what matters is user engagement and feedback.
ex: More dogs than cats got uploaded because the original model recognized dogs more easily

items.d: Pets beat people; more dogs than cats
Accept more cat and dog photos

t64|322.c: AI in the physical world advances more slowly, and hardware was and will remain a major bottleneck.
t64|322.e: His career spans the years before and after deep learning took off. Around 2007, the joke was that deep learning scored only one point better while using far more parameters. Then it broke through first in speech recognition. At Amazon Go, Amazon's cashierless stores, he also tackled real-world computer vision problems. Working across fields taught him to value understanding earned through practice, and he believes hardware has been, and will stay, a big bottleneck for AI in the physical world.
ex: The joke around 2007: one point better, far more parameters

items.d: Mocked as only one point better

t64|322.c: The biggest unknown in multimodal AI is world models, which should simulate cause and effect, not just statistics.
t64|322.e: He sees the key variable in multimodal AI as how world models, systems that simulate how the world works, will actually get built. A world model should simulate cause and effect, not just capture statistical patterns. But how to build one, and whether it needs to be 3D, he considers still uncertain. The episode also discussed what data a world model should take in and what it would make possible, but the show notes don't record the answers.

root.d: The biggest unknown in multimodal AI

t65|325.c: A robot's motor "cerebellum" now lags behind its "brain," so motion control deserves more attention.
t65|325.e: He argues that large models have pushed a robot's "brain" (understanding and decisions) forward quickly, while the "cerebellum" that handles movement has fallen behind, so that's where attention belongs. Recent advances are indeed about generating motion. Diffusion Policy, used behind Figure AI and Aloha, applies diffusion models, the technique behind AI image generators, to produce robot actions. The key gain is generalization, coping with new situations: washing dishes no longer requires each plate to sit in a precise spot.
ex: Diffusion Policy uses diffusion models to generate robot movements
Better generalization: plates no longer need precise placement for dishwashing

items.d: Large models boost understanding and decisions
Motion control becomes the weak spot

t65|325.c: Walking on legs and handling objects are separate tracks, and legs are hard because they're underactuated.
t65|325.e: During his PhD he talked with Boston Dynamics scientists and found their methods much like his. He sees the two abilities Boston Dynamics shows off as separate tracks: legged locomotion and manipulation, meaning handling objects. Legged movement is hard to control because it is underactuated: there are fewer motors than things you need to control. In abstract terms, it is the optimal control of hybrid systems, which mix smooth motion with sudden events like footsteps, the problem he studied for his PhD.

t65|325.c: Reinforcement learning, plus a field-wide boost in belief, made data-driven robot control credible.
t65|325.e: LimX's point-foot biped, a two-legged robot without flat feet, now moves and balances better thanks to reinforcement learning (learning by trial and error against rewards), applied to robot control over the past two years. He stresses this has no direct link to Transformers, the architecture behind large language models. But the whole field's "faith recharge" convinced people that controlling robots with data-driven methods actually works.
ex: LimX's three products: humanoid CL-1, wheel-legged quadruped W1, point-foot biped P1

terms.d: Applied to robot control in recent years

t65|325.c: Companies that started too early are so invested in old technology that they adopt new methods slowly.
t65|325.e: He points to Boston Dynamics: more than 30 years old, it still uses hydraulic actuation, which makes a commercial product almost impossible. He sees a broader pattern: tech companies that start too early get held back by their old technology stack. By contrast, MIT's open-source hardware designs and planetary gearboxes borrowed from other industries, gear sets that let motors deliver more force, have given the whole field an important push.
ex: When a direction isn't fully ready, small companies can explore more flexibly

d.verdict: Deep roots in old tech slow adoption of new tech

t65|325.c: The humanoid-robot direction looks more certain, but hardware is progressing slower than expected.
t65|325.e: He thinks what's more certain is the humanoid direction itself, while hardware has lagged expectations. Robot data is also tied to hardware: how to capture and represent touch, for example, depends on the sensors available. He sees humanoid robots as a cross-disciplinary field where people strong in both software and hardware may come to lead. On robots turning against humans, he is cautiously optimistic.

t66|330.c: A haircut shouldn't be a gamble: choosing a style, explaining it and daily care all have tricks.
t66|330.e: The episode starts from the host's frustration: taking off glasses for a haircut always feels like a gamble. So Bao Ge answers customers' most common puzzles from the stylist's side. When a customer says "whatever you think looks good," how does the stylist decide? How do you find a style that suits you and explain what you want? And why can't you blow-dry it the way the salon does? The show notes don't spell out his methods.

items.d: How to describe it to your stylist

t66|330.c: To understand pricey perms and dyes, look at the chemicals, who does what, and tiered pricing.
t66|330.e: Price is a core set of questions in the episode. In China's biggest cities, a perm often starts at 1,000 to 2,000 yuan. How different are cheap and expensive perm solutions and hair dyes? Is splitting prices into three tiers a way to nudge customers to spend more? And why doesn't the senior stylist personally handle steps like putting in perm rods and mixing color? Those are left for owner Bao Ge to explain, and the show notes don't record his answers.
ex: In China's biggest cities, a perm often starts at 1,000–2,000 yuan

terms.d: How much do cheap and pricey differ?
Some steps skip the senior stylist

t66|330.c: Hair salons are mostly regional brands, and nationwide chains rarely emerge.
t66|330.e: The episode raises this as an industry pattern: hairdressing rarely produces big national chains, and most brands are regional. On running a salon, it also asks what the hardest part of opening one is, whether far fewer people get haircuts around Chinese New Year, how internet platforms like Xiaohongshu and Meituan have changed things, and whether stylists hate being called "Teacher Tony," a jokey online nickname for hairdressers.

items.d: Opening a shop; how stylists grow

t67|339.c: Real estate's golden age is over, so people with several homes should diversify their assets.
t67|339.e: Ning Zhu has long warned about property and asset bubbles. He believes real estate's golden age has passed. People who own several homes should consider spreading their wealth across different asset classes instead of keeping it all in one kind of asset. That is the core advice behind this episode's title: diversified investing is better.
ex: In 2021 developers defaulted; in 2022 homes went undelivered and buyers stopped paying mortgages

items.d: Wealth tied up in several homes
Spread across different kinds of assets

t67|339.c: Guaranteed payouts and implicit government backing inflate bubbles, and most risks in his book came true.
t67|339.e: His 2016 book Guaranteed Bubble examined two risks: guaranteed payouts, where investment products always return principal and interest, and implicit guarantees, the assumption that the government will step in. In the January 2024 expanded edition, he notes that many major events of the following years had already been discussed in the first edition. He says he had actually hoped he would be wrong.

items.d: Warns of guaranteed payouts and implicit backing
Ended guaranteed returns; a change the book discussed

t67|339.c: Investors are often driven by irrational forces, and many overrate their own skill.
t67|339.e: Since returning to China in 2010, he has championed behavioral finance, the study of why people invest irrationally. He believes investors are often swayed by irrational factors. One example from the episode: many people think the gap between them and Warren Buffett is small. He also owns up to his own mistakes, such as choosing Lehman Brothers out of several options in 2008, the year it collapsed.
ex: Joining Lehman Brothers in 2008 is one mistake he admits
His mentor was Nobel laureate Robert Shiller

d.verdict: Most people overrate their investing skill

t67|339.c: In his own portfolio he favors gold and US Treasuries but remains skeptical of Bitcoin.
t67|339.e: Asked about his own portfolio, Ning Zhu named specific preferences. He likes gold and US Treasuries but still has doubts about Bitcoin. In the context of this episode, that is his diversification advice put into practice: in an uncertain world, spread risk across different kinds of assets.

t67|339.c: Markets must reward investors over time, governments must provide a safety net, and individuals must invest in themselves.
t67|339.e: He argues that if a market can't create value for investors over the long run, investors won't want to stay in it. On a bigger scale, he wants the government to build a social safety net that catches people when times are hard. Individuals, meanwhile, should build their human capital, meaning their own skills and knowledge, to cope with uncertainty.

root.d: What it takes to protect wealth

t68|341.c: Modern Art Museum Shanghai was converted from an old coal dock.
t68|341.e: The conversation starts with the museum's origins. The site was once a coal dock and was later converted into an art museum. At the time of recording, two exhibitions, roughly "Proliferation" and "Walking in the Dark" in English, had just opened there together on March 23.
ex: Two exhibitions opened on the same day, March 23

items.d: What the site used to be
Industrial space turned into a gallery

t68|341.c: Running an art museum is far more than putting on shows: there's funding, visitors and artist relationships.
t68|341.e: The questions on the show page sketch a museum's daily life: where its income and funding come from, who its main visitors are, and what it does besides exhibitions. Another question is how museum-artist relationships differ in China and abroad. How to approach art you don't understand, and people visiting museums just for photos, are also up for discussion. The page doesn't record his specific answers.

root.d: Exhibitions are only part of it

t68|341.c: An exhibition takes several parties working together, and the artworks go different ways once it closes.
t68|341.e: The episode covers what an exhibition is for and the roles of the museum, the curator (who picks the works and shapes the theme) and the artist. It also covers the basic process and the mountain of small tasks involved. Where the works go after a show closes, and why some get destroyed, comes up too. So do how unknown artists can land a solo or group show, and whether museums help newcomers find sponsors.

items.d: Where works go; some are destroyed

t69|348.c: Almost everyone seems uncomfortable with life, so we should ask what has gone wrong with everyday living.
t69|348.e: The episode starts from a gut feeling: these days, it seems everyone is uncomfortable with life, and the way in is everyday life itself. Did modernization come too fast, leaving people no time to prepare? Has the internet kept its promises? How did everyday life disappear, and was society bound to end up this way? The page doesn't record his answers.

t69|348.c: The everyday consumer life we take for granted deserves a hard, critical look.
t69|348.e: Xiaowei Wang's book is titled The Depths of Everyday Life, and the episode specifically discusses why everyday consumer life deserves criticism. The show page links to his talk at YiXi, a Chinese lecture platform. Its title sketches a worker's day that feels like a fishbone stuck in the throat: a packed subway in the morning, takeout at noon, and phone scrolling at night.

items.d: A day that sticks in your throat

t69|348.c: Sayings like "as long as you're happy" and "hard work pays off" deserve some doubt.
t69|348.e: The episode questions several popular sayings. If being happy is all that matters, do things really turn out fine? If you just work hard, do things really get better? Does "emotional value," the worth of making someone feel good, count as real value? The discussion ends with what we should actually do. These are the topics listed on the show page; the answers are in the audio.

items: Work hard and it gets better

t70|353.c: The Middle East social market is big with little competition, but more culturally varied and fragmented than expected.
t70|353.e: She joined MICO in 2019 to run YoHo, convinced the Middle East social market was huge. The pluses she lists: a large population, similar cultures and little competition. The hurdles: big cultural differences, few internet professionals, and a market more fragmented than she expected. She chose MICO, which focuses on overseas markets with the Middle East as its priority, partly because the region demands deep localization, building products fully around local habits.

d.verdict: Huge market, but you must localize deeply

t70|353.c: Middle East voice apps are about socializing, while similar apps in China lean toward content.
t70|353.e: In Egypt she came to understand why people need to chat with strangers. On her birthday, users even sent her about $3,000 in virtual gifts. She thinks the region has fewer wealthy people than outsiders imagine, and their money isn't easy to earn. Luxury spending isn't widespread, but ordinary salaried workers are willing to spend on entertainment.
ex: Users sent her about $3,000 in tips on her birthday

t70|353.c: The Middle East must be run country by country, and even small countries can produce big customers.
t70|353.e: The Arab world has about 400 million people across West Asia, the Arabian Peninsula and North Africa, with countries and ethnic groups intertwined, so each country needs its own approach. She recalls being criticized by Yemeni users during Saudi Arabia's national day. TopTop's biggest customer for a long time came from Bahrain, proof that small countries can have big spenders.
ex: For a long time, TopTop's single biggest customer was from Bahrain

items.d: Criticized by Yemeni users on national day

t70|353.c: When going abroad, the most important thing is choosing the right local head and partners.
t70|353.e: Her top advice for Chinese companies going overseas is to pick the right local leader and partners. On hiring, MICO shifted from recruiting experienced people to hiring and training young ones. She also hasn't seen a "lying flat" culture, people opting out of hard work, in Egypt's workplaces. Because local venture capital is underdeveloped in the Middle East, she advises Chinese founders there to raise money from China where possible.
ex: MICO's Middle East team grew from a few dozen people to over 300

result.d: A foothold in the Middle East

t70|353.c: MICO competes with several small apps at once while watching for a chance at a big one.
t70|353.e: Facing changes such as TikTok's bigger push into the Middle East, MICO runs several small apps in parallel. At the same time, it keeps an eye out for a chance to build one big app. She believes the company got through its 2020 policy crisis by making better-quality decisions.
ex: Its apps include MICO, YoHo, TopTop and Sugo

t71|359.c: Scaling laws alone won't get us to AGI, and today's models score high without real ability.
t71|359.e: Yi Ma thinks today's large models rest on a method found by trial and error, and the gains from scaling it up are not real intelligence. Current methods mimic only part of what memory does, and they burn huge resources. GPT's math reasoning relies on memorization and statistics, not cause-and-effect reasoning or logic. So he says young people who believe scaling laws (bigger models, more data and compute, better results) alone will deliver AGI, or human-level general AI, might consider changing careers.

t71|359.c: Deep networks are essentially compressing data, and white-box research explains that compression mathematically.
t71|359.e: After returning to Berkeley in 2017, he reviewed existing results and proposed that all deep networks are doing compression: distilling simple patterns from huge amounts of data. White-box large models aim to explain that process mathematically, so it is no longer an opaque black box. Understanding the principle points to more efficient compression, which in practice means less trial and error and lower GPU costs. His guiding principles are parsimony and self-consistency.
ex: ReduNet (2022) laid out the framework; CRATE (2023) did the engineering

result.d: Less trial and error, fewer GPUs

t71|359.c: Knowing a lot isn't intelligence, and a baby is more intelligent than GPT-4.
t71|359.e: He defines the core of intelligence as the ability to fix gaps in what you already know and to add new knowledge. GPT-4 holds far more knowledge, but a baby has more of this ability. Intelligence emerges, he argues, because the world contains patterns that are worth learning and can actually be learned.

d.verdict: Intelligence means correcting errors and adding knowledge

t71|359.c: True intelligence needs three shifts: black box to white box, open loop to closed loop, human-fed to autonomous.
t71|359.e: He believes reaching intelligence takes three shifts. One benefit of a closed loop, where a system adjusts itself based on feedback, is that it eases "catastrophic forgetting," losing old skills when learning new ones. Part of what autonomous learning means is that humans learn by building models inside their brains, without constantly checking against outside signals. These ideas draw on neuroscience and other fields. He also notes that early researchers, starting with Norbert Wiener's cybernetics, didn't distinguish machines from living things.

t71|359.c: Useful but opaque tools turn into magic, so regulation should target AI's uses, not the technology itself.
t71|359.e: Yi Ma argues that throughout history, any useful black box, something that works but that no one can explain, risks turning into superstition and magic. Comparing AI to the atomic bomb strikes him as laughable. He wants governments to regulate how technology is applied rather than the technology itself, since overregulation can lead to monopolies and stifle innovation. That's why he feels more urgency about helping people understand what AI actually does.
ex: HKU is pushing AI literacy courses so every major learns some AI

items.d: Works, but no one knows why
Like comparing AI to the atomic bomb
Targets the technology, not its uses

t72|362.c: AI content keeps getting more realistic, but the interfaces holding it are still hand-built, layer by layer.
t72|362.e: The episode uses a wine-and-bottle analogy. Generative AI keeps making more realistic content: the wine. But the product interfaces that hold that content, the bottles, have barely changed. Designers building an interface still wrestle with piles of repetitive, inefficient layers, the stacked elements that make up a screen. So the question becomes whether AI can also help people make the bottles more efficiently.

items: AI makes it ever more realistic

d.verdict: AI should help designers build interfaces too

t72|362.c: Listen to over 100 designers' complaints first, then build a tool around their shared pain points.
t72|362.e: Early on, the team interviewed more than 100 designers and distilled the frustrations they had in common. They then designed an AI productivity tool around those findings: Motiff. The episode also covers how design software has evolved, how the WeChat team approaches design, and designers' biggest headaches and where AI can help.

t72|362.c: Motiff entered the seemingly niche design-tool market and aimed at global customers from day one.
t72|362.e: The episode asks why Motiff picked a seemingly niche market, and where the opportunity lies when the industry leader, Figma, is already so big. Motiff targeted the global market from the start, and the conversation compares how products are sold in China and abroad. The page lists only these topics, not the specific answers.

t72|362.c: AI is used in real work far less than outsiders expect.
t72|362.e: The episode raises this as a pattern and discusses the reasons behind it. It also asks whether designers will still be needed in the future, and whether AI could replace the profession. The page doesn't record the guest's specific views.

t73|368.c: Niche e-commerce struggles in China, but in Thailand it can still lead its category.
t73|368.e: The episode notes lay out the situation in China: e-commerce sites focused on one category pay more than general platforms to win customers, lack supply-chain advantages, struggle to keep prices low, and lose users easily. Jumei, Mia, Mogujie and Secoo are examples. Huang's Konvy started almost alongside Lazada, a leading Southeast Asian marketplace, and became Thailand's biggest beauty e-commerce platform.
ex: Konvy's annual revenue is $64 million

d.verdict: Niche e-commerce still has room abroad

t73|368.c: Short on cash and e-commerce infrastructure, he survived a decade on classmates' money and bank loans.
t73|368.e: In 2012 he ran a Taobao-native brand in Beijing's Zhongguancun tech district and ended up about a million yuan in debt, then went back to Thailand to start over. Thailand lacked e-commerce infrastructure back then, and he lacked money. Early on he relied mainly on investment from old classmates and bank loans, and he raised his first funding round only in his tenth year.
ex: Raised an $11 million Series A+ in 2024, with Alibaba investing

t73|368.c: Guaranteeing authentic products is one of the hardest problems for a beauty platform.
t73|368.e: He ranks guaranteeing authenticity among the hardest problems a beauty platform faces. The episode also discusses how niche platforms survive and grow amid Southeast Asia's e-commerce wars. The show notes don't detail his methods.

t73|368.c: Online channels account for only 10–20% of sales in Thailand, so Konvy must sell offline too.
t73|368.e: In Thailand, e-commerce accounts for only 10% to 20% of sales, and physical stores remain the main channel. The episode discusses how Konvy builds offline channels in that environment. It also covers how brands plan a global strategy.
ex: Online channels make up only 10–20% of sales in Thailand

t73|368.c: Southeast Asian employees won't grind, so raising efficiency takes a different approach.
t73|368.e: In Southeast Asia, employees generally don't want to grind, working punishing hours to outdo each other. That makes raising efficiency a real management challenge for him. The show page lists the topic but doesn't spell out his methods.

t74|7.c: The Rust Belt story popular in China may not hold up, and the trip revealed many counterintuitive things.
t74|7.e: A causal chain is often repeated in China: deindustrialization put American workers out of work, angry workers elected Trump, and he started a trade war. Hanyang toured the Rust Belt asking whether that's true. The episode opens by contrasting stereotypes about the US election with the counterintuitive things seen on the ground. It also goes back to Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal to rethink who the Democrats' traditional supporters were.
ex: Roosevelt's New Deal coalition won the 1932 and 1936 elections

t74|7.c: Most Rust Belt factories were still profitable when they closed, so deindustrialization had other causes.
t74|7.e: The episode traces how America rose on coal, oil and steel. It points out that most Rust Belt factories were still making money when they shut down. Deindustrialization is traced to labor-management conflict, major strategic mistakes and other factors, not simply to factories failing as businesses.

t74|7.c: Rust Belt cities have split into three groups: declining, fully collapsed and revived.
t74|7.e: They sort Rust Belt cities into three groups: still declining, fully collapsed, and revived. Decline also took different forms: the Bethlehem Steel plant, the No. 9 coal mine and the Atlas cement plant each represent a different path. The Kalamazoo train station went from a freight hub to a way station for homeless people.
ex: An abandoned Van de Graaff particle accelerator outside Pittsburgh

t74|7.c: After industry left, decent jobs became scarce, and the people left behind are real but rarely seen.
t74|7.e: The episode focuses on people in the "hood," the run-down neighborhoods left after industry departed. Decent jobs are harder and harder to find, yet outsiders rarely see them. Everyday details tell the story: whether you can borrow a bathroom, for instance, is one way to judge if a place is safe. The episode closes on one point: these people really exist.

t74|7.c: Deglobalization, pulling economies apart again, is nearly impossible in practice.
t74|7.e: The episode points to a repair shop in Ohio that fixes only DJI drones. It shows how hard deglobalization is in real life. Even in the Rust Belt, everyday business is bound up with Chinese products.
ex: A repair shop in Ohio that fixes only DJI drones

items: A shop that fixes only DJI drones

d.verdict: Deglobalization is nearly impossible in practice

t75|373.c: Because he shared a name and birthday with a scientist, his visa was canceled with a five-year ban.
t75|373.e: In March 2023 he flew from Brazil to Houston for a team meeting, and border officers took him into a holding room at the airport. More than ten hours later, he was told he would be deported, his visa canceled, and barred from applying for a US visa for five years. The reason: a scientist with the same name and birthday. He also says his timing was bad, coinciding with weather problems and a hearing.

t75|373.c: The border questioning felt like a mini hearing, so absurd that even the officer found it ridiculous.
t75|373.e: He had to hand over his phone and give the password, and officers went through his chat history. They knew Chinese social apps quite well. He was even asked whether he was a member of the Communist Youth League. The whole interrogation felt like a small hearing, and even the officer asking the questions found them absurd.

t75|373.c: Unable to visit a hospital before entry, he was held in a private prison awaiting his flight.
t75|373.e: He needed a COVID test before his flight home, but people not yet admitted to the country can't go to a hospital, so he was taken to a prison for it and ended up staying two days. The prison was run by GEO, one of three private prison operators. He noticed that the toothbrushes, toothpaste and clothes there were all labeled "Made in China."
ex: GEO's market value exceeds $2 billion
He lined up with a dozen-plus Latin Americans to be booked in

t75|373.c: Deportation cost him far more than one trip: he moved from overseas business back to China.
t75|373.e: The deportation also affected his travel to other countries and regions, and he hasn't left China since. His company hired a lawyer to help apply for a visa waiver, with no progress so far. He also moved from overseas business to domestic work, shut out of the hot field of taking Chinese companies global.

t75|373.c: At the border, never lie but don't volunteer everything, and give officers a reason to let you in.
t75|373.e: Looking back, he offers several tips. Enter through Democratic-leaning "blue states" if possible, and avoid sensitive periods like elections. High-risk travelers can bring a new phone. Under questioning, never lie, but you don't have to say everything. Cases involving a honeymooning couple and travelers from Taiwan show that you should give the officer a reason to admit you, not a reason to turn you away.

items.d: To admit you, not refuse you

t76|380.c: Fusion has scaling laws too: bigger machines and stronger magnetic fields deliver better results.
t76|380.e: Yi Tan believes fusion also follows scaling laws: results improve predictably as scale goes up. Bigger devices, stronger magnetic fields and more efficient use of those fields all improve performance, and money and incentives can speed the process. Startorus aims to finish a next-generation device by 2027 with a Q above 10, meaning it releases more than ten times the energy used to heat it. That confidence comes from these scaling laws.

result.d: Money and incentives speed it up

t76|380.c: Fusion's pace over past decades is no guide to how fast it will advance next.
t76|380.e: Fusion has been studied for more than 70 years without going commercial, and the joke that it's "always 50 years away" was true for its time. He thinks that in this new phase, "less than 10 years" may turn out to be just as true. A fusion breakthrough would pay off without limit, but no one knows exactly how to get there. So he believes it needs all-out, saturation-level support.
ex: An industry report says five companies plan to generate power before 2030

d.verdict: The old pace can't predict the future

t76|380.c: Run experiments, collect data, fit the patterns: advancing fusion looks a lot like training AI.
t76|380.e: He says the only thing everyone trusts right now is experiments. Teams in different countries run them on different machines, then fit patterns to the data. No one can fully explain why the patterns hold, but they're considered reliable. He also argues that prioritizing engineering over basic science is both the reality of pushing toward fusion power and the right approach.

t76|380.c: Choosing the spherical tokamak was path dependence: his team knows its strengths and weaknesses best.
t76|380.e: There's no consensus yet on which approach or device will be commercially competitive. Startorus chose the spherical tokamak, a squat, nearly ball-shaped version of the ring-shaped magnetic fusion device, mainly because the team has studied it for more than 20 years and knows its pros and cons. He also admits a tokamak works like a transformer in principle, so it isn't suited to long, steady operation. Today it's kept running with lots of auxiliary equipment, which is exhausting.

t76|380.c: Its next device costs over a billion yuan, with fusion power in ordinary homes targeted in a decade.
t76|380.e: The next-generation device needs more than 1 billion yuan, so raising money is part of his every day. The biggest uncertainty is the missing data between where they are now and the goal: the scaling laws for this stage are still blank. He feels starting a company has unlocked his potential.
