He also hopes investors will be bolder and back technical approaches that differ from those of American companies.
ex: Two years as a startup may have achieved more than the previous twenty

items.d: In ordinary homes in about ten years

t77|384.c: Driver-assistance now sells cars, so some carmakers turn to suppliers instead of waiting to build their own.
t77|384.e: A year and a half ago, his biggest worry was that L2+ driver-assistance, which handles some driving under supervision, couldn't really help carmakers sell cars. Better technology, plus the boost from Huawei-backed AITO, changed that. Some carmakers can't wait for in-house development and are more eager to use suppliers. Tesla's FSD improved dozens of times over in six months, but he isn't worried about it coming to China. He thinks it's good: companies will compete on value rather than price.

items.d: Carmakers can't wait to build their own

t77|384.c: His self-driving Moore's law: every two years, hardware costs halve and software performance improves tenfold.
t77|384.e: Borrowing from the chip industry's Moore's law, he proposes a version for driver-assistance: every two years, hardware parts costs fall by half and software performance rises tenfold. Prices will keep falling, so even 150,000-yuan cars will come with advanced driver-assistance as standard. He expects low-quality competition may end within two years. Partnering with Qualcomm isn't only about value for money. It also lets Momenta reach gasoline and hybrid models.
ex: Even 150,000-yuan cars will come with advanced driver-assistance as standard

t77|384.c: Self-driving has no differentiation, only good and better, so the leader may take 70% of the market.
t77|384.e: He argues that cars as a whole need differentiation, but driver-assistance doesn't: there's only good and better. The top player could eventually take about 70% of the market. He rates a supplier's position on three measures, user experience, customer quality and customer count, and uses them to compare Huawei with Momenta. The episode also covers why Momenta chose to be a Tier 1 supplier selling directly to carmakers, rather than a Tier 2 supplier selling to Tier 1s.
ex: Three measures for suppliers: experience, customer quality, customer count

d.verdict: The market will concentrate at the top

t77|384.c: Building end-to-end isn't hard, but raising the worst-case floor is, and that takes a whole system.
t77|384.e: He thinks there may be tens of thousands of routes under the broad end-to-end approach, where one model goes from seeing the road to making driving decisions. Momenta first used neural networks for perception, then for decisions, and finally merged them into one large model. Building end-to-end isn't hard; raising the floor, so even the worst cases hold up, is. Getting technical calls right takes cheap, fast trial and error, plus one main product line that never forks, so short-term firefighting doesn't wear the team down.
ex: End of 2021: should that year's deliveries use models or hand-written rules?

t77|384.c: Focus on high-leverage work: product and technology are the biggest lever, and the organization keeps hiring better people.
t77|384.e: He stresses doing things with leverage, where a little effort moves a lot, such as paying people more and raising output per person. Momenta went from needing 400 people to deliver one car model to needing just a few. He sees product and technology as the company's biggest lever today, and the organizational lever as continually hiring and promoting better people. Big decisions come from meetings small enough to fit in one car.
ex: From 400 people per car model to just a few

items.d: Keep hiring and promoting better people
Pay more; a few people per model
Meetings that fit in one car

t78|391.c: Southeast Asia isn't one market: its countries differ widely in how they work and in culture.
t78|391.e: Having worked in Southeast Asia for a long time, he stresses that the region is not one unified market. Each country has its own way of doing things, and the cultures differ a lot. Running teams there also brings surprises. A foreign employee might quit because of the boss's management style, or even because of who won a ball game.
ex: An employee might quit over the boss's style, or over who won a game

d.verdict: Understand the region one country at a time

t78|391.c: TikTok moves fast, Temu hits hard and Shopee hangs on: each is playing a different game.
t78|391.e: The episode title sums up the three companies as fast, ruthless and resilient. TikTok is moving quickly to merge with Indonesia's Tokopedia after buying it. Temu is bringing rock-bottom prices into Southeast Asia, a market where prices were already very low. Shopee, the established local player, has to hold off these newcomers. Li also talks about the clear differences in how TikTok and Temu run their organizations.

items.d: Low prices in an already cheap market

t78|391.c: Shopee's pressure comes from newer rivals that are more efficient and lean harder on algorithms.
t78|391.e: He believes Shopee's challenge is that its new rivals run more efficiently. They also rely more on algorithms, meaning software that automatically decides what to show each shopper. The episode also looks back at Lazada, another older platform, and why it never caught up with Shopee.

t78|391.c: The investment rush into Southeast Asia has faded, and its star companies have lost most of their value.
t78|391.e: Around 2017, many Chinese investors poured money into Southeast Asian ride-hailing, food delivery and e-commerce platforms, hoping to find the next Alibaba, Meituan or Didi. Since then the stars have fallen hard. Grab, the ride-hailing and delivery app, has lost about 76% of its market value since listing in 2020. Indonesia's GoTo has lost about 85% since 2022. The episode ends by asking who still invests in the region, and in what.

t79|400.c: Focus has shifted from tech milestones to real use, and generative AI's value is ending rote work.
t79|400.e: He notices that last year the industry mostly talked about technical milestones, while this year it talks about putting AI to work. In his view, the value of generative AI, which produces text, images and more, lies in freeing people from mechanical work. The episode also asks whether AI will cost people their jobs, and why an "anti-iFlytek alliance" among stenographers later disappeared.

t79|400.c: While new companies give products away, iFlytek keeps charging and won't burn cash to buy users.
t79|400.e: A wave of new companies uses free products to attract users, but iFlytek still charges. It does care about its consumer business, but its approach to spending on promotion is different from burning cash to win users. The episode notes that when iFlytek was founded in 1999, venture capital in China was still immature. So from day one the company had to balance making a profit with funding research.
ex: In 2010 iFlytek tried its first consumer product: a voice-typing app

t79|400.c: Large models alone can't crack the "cocktail party" problem in speech, which still takes years of engineering.
t79|400.e: He thinks the real test of speech-to-text comes in messy situations, like several languages mixed together or many people talking at once. This is known as the "cocktail party" problem: picking out who said what in a noisy room. Large models on their own aren't enough to solve it. It still takes engineering skill built up over many years. iFlytek is also exploring end-to-end speech technology, where a single model goes straight from sound to text.

t79|400.c: AI software-as-a-service has to bundle software, hardware and service together.
t79|400.e: From the start, iFlytek Tingjian served both businesses and individual users. For businesses, it had to run on Chinese-made operating systems, and iFlytek designed its own hardware workstations so companies could host the system on their own premises. Upgrading the offline version meant sending people on-site, so iFlytek had to build delivery teams and a partner network. He adds that SaaS always forces a choice between one general product and custom versions for specific industries.
ex: Case study: how iFlytek went deep on conferences and trade shows

t79|400.c: AI SaaS has to succeed in three ways at once: product, market and finances.
t79|400.e: He sums up the goal of AI SaaS as three kinds of success: a product that works, a market that accepts it, and finances that add up. On going overseas, he thinks Europe has the strictest data rules, so companies need to build up compliance experience there. One open question for the industry in the coming year, he says, is whether a new business model will emerge.

t80|291.c: o1's breakthrough is reasoning, overturning the belief that large language models reason poorly.
t80|291.e: He splits model ability into three layers: language, common sense and reasoning. The first two were already in good shape, and o1 improves the third. DeepMind's AlphaGeometry also used reinforcement learning, where a model improves through trial and reward, yet drew far less attention. His explanation: reinforcement learning isn't new, and the Alpha family, like Go-playing AlphaGo, had its wow moment long ago. o1 instead broke the expectation that language models are bad at reasoning.

t80|291.c: Reinforcement learning and chain-of-thought both make up for missing data, and o1 wins by combining them well.
t80|291.e: He sees reinforcement learning and chain-of-thought, where a model writes out its reasoning step by step before answering, as fixes for the same data problem. Reinforcement learning adds specialized data and works best where rules and feedback are clear. Chain-of-thought adds more abstract, higher-level data. The two don't overlap and can be stacked. None of these ideas is earth-shattering on its own, but OpenAI put them together very well.

t80|291.c: Test-time compute turns one pass of reasoning into N passes, like a person thinking hard.
t80|291.e: "Test-time compute" means a model spends more computing power while answering. It doesn't directly fix gaps in the data. Instead, it turns one pass of reasoning into N passes, much like a person mulling something over. The chart he calls the most important in AI since 2022 shows exactly this scaling law on the answering side: more compute at answer time, better results. o1 is slow now, but he thinks early on, quality matters most. Making it faster and cheaper later is almost certain.
ex: Possible fixes: run parts of the reasoning in parallel and cut unneeded steps

t80|291.c: Total demand for computing power will rise, but for now there are more GPUs than needed.
t80|291.e: Judging by API prices, an o1 answer may cost dozens of times more to produce than one from GPT-4o, so overall demand for computing power will grow. But GPU prices have been falling since last year. Demand for training models is shrinking, and the growing demand for running them, called inference, can't yet fill the gap. So in the short term there's a GPU surplus. o1 also won't reverse the trend of fewer Chinese companies training their own foundation models.

items: o1 may cost dozens of times 4o

d.verdict: A GPU surplus in the short term

t80|291.c: AI app development hasn't cooled down but has spread into projects too small for VCs to notice.
t80|291.e: Working with developers every day, he doesn't feel the field has stalled or cooled. More solo developers, small businesses and people in other industries are trying things, because you no longer need a full AI team. Apps not cooling and VCs seeing no app boom aren't in conflict, since this demand is still too small for VCs to see. DingTalk's experience is that users now pay for small features, not big complex apps.
ex: The most-used open models on the platform: Qwen, DeepSeek and Llama
Some customers process hundreds of millions to a billion tokens of text daily

t81|55.c: Early video games were sold like publications: players got news about them, but no community.
t81|55.e: The discussion starts from the era when video games were like "publications." They were released and sold the way books and magazines are, and what players got around them was mostly news, not a community. This is the starting point of the whole argument. At first, games were just products people bought, not part of their lives.

d.verdict: Games went from product to part of life

t81|55.c: Ongoing operation, more ways to engage and tools for player-made content brought games into everyday life.
t81|55.e: The episode treats "how games became part of life" as its key question and offers two threads. First, the business model shifted from one-time purchases to ongoing operation, so a game is no longer a one-off sale. Second, people engage with games in more ways than just playing them. On top of that, tools and platforms for user-made content spread, letting players make and share content around games. The episode page lists these threads without going into detail.
ex: Thread one: from one-time purchase to ongoing service
Thread two: more ways to enjoy games

t81|55.c: Community is far bigger than playing games, and has to be understood through how social life works.
t81|55.e: In its second half, the episode moves from games to a broader question. It first discusses how social life fundamentally works, then argues that community is far bigger than the act of playing, and finally asks what a community actually is. The hosts describe it as a chain of connected reasoning, not an attempt to define gaming communities. The episode page doesn't record the answer they reached.

t82|225.c: We need meaning like we need food, and the hard part is letting go, not figuring things out.
t82|225.e: The episode treats "what's the point of living" as a serious question. In their view, the need for meaning is as basic as the need for food and water, not self-indulgence. The episode notes that most problems aren't hard to figure out. What's hard is truly making peace with them and letting go.

items: Most problems aren't hard to understand
Meaning is as basic as food

d.verdict: The hard part is letting go, not understanding

t82|225.c: Many jobs exist mainly to keep people busy and paid, which has drained work of meaning.
t82|225.e: The episode argues that modern society is full of jobs that work like relief programs. The Chinese term for this originally meant giving people aid by giving them work. In that sense, many jobs exist mainly so people have something to do and an income, not because the work itself is very valuable. As a result, work can no longer serve as a path to meaning.

t82|225.c: A person's worth goes beyond work, and what's broken is how we measure it, not the person.
t82|225.e: Since work struggles to give people meaning, the episode argues against judging a person's worth by work alone. In their view, when someone feels their life is pointless or that they're worthless, the problem usually isn't the person. It's the standard society uses to measure people.

t83|415.c: Humanities scholars bring their own view of technology, and scientists may oversimplify how tech and society interact.
t83|415.e: Some ask whether Harari, trained in the humanities, has any standing to talk about AI. The episode says he brings his own perspective. His writing breaks out of the "drawers" that academic fields sort knowledge into, and he excels at telling history on a grand scale. Scientists, by contrast, may see the link between technology and society too simply. The episode also admits Harari is often accused of starting from conclusions, but his insights often hit the mark.

items.d: Can a humanist talk about AI?
Writing history on a grand scale

t83|415.c: More information doesn't make people wiser, and the "naive" and "populist" views are two sides of one coin.
t83|415.e: The episode applies the book's two views of information to everyday life. The "naive view" assumes more information is always better, but more information doesn't necessarily make people better at judging it. Not reflecting may be the norm, since mistakes and blind following come from human nature. The "populist view" looks like its opposite but is really the other side of the same coin.

items: Two faces of the same idea

d.verdict: Same coin; not reflecting is the norm

t83|415.c: Even if Harari overstates AI, new technology is already shaking up how information flows.
t83|415.e: The episode grants that Harari may overrate what AI can do. But that doesn't change his core concern: new technology is already reshaping the networks through which information flows, and the problem exists now, without waiting for AI to "wake up." The deepfake scandal in South Korea and what happened to a girl in a small Eastern European town both show how hard these problems are to handle.
ex: South Korea's deepfake scandal
What happened to a girl in a small Eastern European town

root.d: No need to wait for AI to wake up

items.d: Shows how hard it is to handle

t83|415.c: Fear of being replaced by AI really stems from how hard finding meaning became in modern times.
t83|415.e: The episode pushes the fear of being replaced one step further back: even without AI, modern people struggle to find meaning. Building meaning and identity around work is not the historical norm. So the panic over losing work has older roots, in the condition of modern life itself.

t83|415.c: Individuals can start by reconnecting with concrete things and not giving away their rights too easily.
t83|415.e: On a personal level, the episode asks whether hands-on work like growing coffee or rice can reconnect the body with the world. Yuan shares a teaching case in which a "mock funeral" helped students choose their jobs. The Miaoya incident, involving an AI portrait app, is a reminder not to sign away your rights lightly. They suggest social media addiction may be a passing phase, and talk about the "other alarm clock" people in Yunnan live by, and daily practices to keep as tech changes fast.
ex: A "mock funeral" exercise helped students choose their jobs
The Miaoya incident: be wary of giving up your rights

items.d: Don't give them away, as with Miaoya

t84|418.c: Musk's reality distortion field is weakening, and the industry's near-religious faith in him is fading.
t84|418.e: The event was vague on key details. The next day Tesla's stock fell about 9% while Uber's rose about 10%. He sees high-tech progress as having two sides: the objective laws of the technology, and public expectations, which Tesla is great at pumping up. But within the self-driving world, some people's near-religious faith in Musk is already wearing off.
ex: The day after the event, Tesla fell about 9% and Uber rose about 10%

t84|418.c: Driverless companies compete on cutting cost per mile safely, and Musk's $0.20 figure doesn't hold up.
t84|418.e: He sees L4, self-driving that needs no human within set conditions, as a systems problem built from many smaller ones. For now the guide should be CPM, the all-in operating cost per mile, and the key contest is lowering it without compromising safety. CPM should also be calculated one standard way, like an accounting rule. A quick calculation shows Musk's $0.20 per mile is unrealistic. Better tech and lower costs go together, but operations are hard in the details, like checking tire pressure.
ex: Cruise's CEO listed 15 points before the event, and Musk addressed none of them
Operational details: checking tire pressure

t84|418.c: End-to-end driving is the right direction, but neither it nor scaling laws should be treated as faith.
t84|418.e: Testing Tesla's FSD in Houston, he had to take over about every 10 minutes on a good day. He accepts the general direction of end-to-end, where one model goes straight from what the car sees to how it drives, but thinks it has become an ideology. The original scaling laws papers came with many caveats, and the problem is extrapolating without limits. End-to-end has costs too: it's hard to explain, which makes regulatory approval hard. He also notes that "world models" trace back to the academic idea of internal representations, meant to capture physics for specific tasks.
ex: FSD in Houston: a takeover about every 10 minutes on a good day

root.d: Right direction, but not a faith

t84|418.c: Go-anywhere L5 autonomy will never arrive, so L4 is the real product, and it must make money.
t84|418.e: He sees L5, self-driving with no human needed anywhere, as a horizon that can never be reached. L4 is the product, and a product has to make money. One bottleneck is the remote-operation ratio: today one remote operator handles 3 vehicles, and that needs to reach 10. Before Tesla's Cybercab is mass-produced, an "Airbnb model" where owners send their own Model 3 or Y out for rides is also hard. No one knows yet who is liable if an owner's car hits someone.
ex: The Airbnb model's problem: who's liable when an owner's car crashes

t84|418.c: Don't expand too early, value profit over revenue, and stay far from hype but close to the product.
t84|418.e: Bot Auto has raised $20 million, and he discusses who is still willing to invest in self-driving. Looking back on his previous company, TuSimple, he concludes that you shouldn't expand too early and that profit matters more than revenue. He picked Houston over Silicon Valley because it's farther from investors and hype, but closer to the product and operations.
ex: Bot Auto raised $20 million

d.verdict: L4 needs to stay close to product and operations

t85|225.c: A country's industrialization can be gamed out from scratch, starting with population, resources and birth rate.
t85|225.e: This episode uses an imaginary country, "Zeyangpolis," to work out how a nation is built from nothing. The starting conditions: about 50 million people, limited resources and a very high birth rate. The question is how, under these conditions, it could take power and rise step by step. The episode page doesn't record the actual steps or conclusions.
ex: The imaginary country is called "Zeyangpolis"
Starting population: about 50 million

t85|225.c: Building a country from nothing happens in stages, and industrialization is the thread running through them.
t85|225.e: The episode title asks how many steps it takes to build a country from scratch, and this is the opening episode of The Road to Industrialization series. In other words, they break down nation-building with industrialization as the main thread. The page links background material: earlier episodes on building hydropower stations, a documentary on the Fengman hydropower station, and a bonus episode on a steel mill. It doesn't say what the steps are.
ex: Background: interviews on building hydropower plants, and a steel mill bonus episode

items.d: How many steps to build a country
Bonus episode on a steel mill

t86|423.c: Remote-controlling robots has two uses: supplying labor from afar and collecting data for robots to learn from.
t86|423.e: Teleoperation, where a person controls a robot remotely, was hugely controversial at the Optimus event. He thinks it's useful in itself. It lets people provide labor from a distance, and it collects data that helps robots improve. There are three common methods: mapping human motion from video, VR headsets, and dedicated rigs built with the same structure as the robot. Getting from teleoperation to autonomy will take more data and better models.
ex: You can judge a robot by how many people are standing around it

t86|423.c: Embodied AI is being pushed forward by reinforcement learning, imitation learning and multimodal models.
t86|423.e: He recalls that Berkeley's AI lab, BAIR, took reinforcement learning seriously early on and had an open, collaborative culture. Reinforcement learning, where a machine improves by trial and reward, comes in value-based and policy-based flavors, and can train in simulation or in the real world. The three technologies play different roles. Robotics companies mostly build their own reinforcement learning and imitation learning, which copies human demonstrations, but tend to use outside multimodal models that handle images and text.
ex: ETH Zurich's robot dog learned to climb hills in simulation
His project had a robot dog learn on real soft mats

d.verdict: Three technologies, three different roles

t86|423.c: General-purpose robots will definitely need world models, but nobody agrees yet on how to build them.
t86|423.e: He thinks "world model" is still a loose idea: anything that can infer what happens next from the current state counts. He compares OpenAI's Sora with other video models, and uses a robot making dumplings to show where today's world models fall short. He is sure world models will be part of general-purpose robots, but how to build them is still unclear.
ex: Making dumplings is still beyond today's world models

t86|423.c: Touch is underrated and dexterous hands are too hard, so mobile two-armed robots deserve investment now.
t86|423.e: He sees touch as a neglected sense. Skin is the body's largest organ, and touch is not the same thing as force sensing. Robots come in many forms, and Galaxea has concluded that two-armed manipulation matters more. Dexterous, human-like hands are very hard to develop and don't belong inside a company at this stage. Galaxea's current focus is a mobile manipulation robot body, teleoperation and the intelligence to run it.
ex: Galaxea's focus: a mobile manipulation body, teleoperation and intelligence

t86|423.c: Data is the biggest bottleneck, and end-to-end models are the trend but may not suit deployment today.
t86|423.e: He recalls AI pioneer Marvin Minsky predicting in 1970 that general intelligent machines would arrive within three to eight years. A small survey of Tsinghua Yao Class undergraduates found people more pessimistic about AGI this year than last. He sees data as the main bottleneck, with no clear industry standard for what collecting it should cost. Galaxea gathers data three ways. End-to-end models like VLA, which go from vision and language straight to action, are the trend but may not suit deployment today. Today's large-model approach is flawed but can be fixed along the way.
ex: In 1970 Minsky predicted general intelligent machines within 3 to 8 years

t87|425.c: A new product category only survives if its innovation matches a real need.
t87|425.e: New categories keep appearing, from bone-conduction headphones and floor washers to vlog cameras and smart glasses, yet few of each year's new products actually catch on. The episode starts from why consumer drones succeeded and asks what a winning category needs. Failed examples show that when innovation and need don't line up, the category doesn't last. The episode describes product-market fit as the core idea in consumer electronics.
ex: A success story: consumer drones

t87|425.c: Product managers must separate real needs from fake ones and dig beneath what users say they want.
t87|425.e: He covers the key questions before green-lighting a product: how a product manager tells real needs from fake ones, how to rank them, and how to uncover the deeper need behind what users say. How Narwal's floor washer dealt with tangled hair is one example of going from a need to engineering. He also explains why he moved from R&D into product management himself.
ex: How Narwal's floor washer solved hair tangling

t87|425.c: Floor washers are replacing vacuum cleaners, not competing with robot vacuums.
t87|425.e: Floor washers began abroad, first used to clean carpeted floors in overseas homes, and smart cleaning gadgets took off during the pandemic. The floor washer grew in the gap between vacuums, traditional cleaning tools and robot vacuums. He thinks it replaces the vacuum cleaner and doesn't clash with robot vacuums. The chart shows the floor washer market growing from about 90 million in 2019 to about 10 billion in 2022.
ex: Floor washers were first used on carpeted floors abroad

t87|425.c: A latecomer that defines its product well can reach the top tier of a mature category within years.
t87|425.e: The episode notes that Narwal, a young company, broke into the mainstream robot vacuum market within a few years, a lesson worth sharing with the industry. Floor washers went the same way. Narwal started late: he joined in 2021 and incubated the product line. After two product generations, Narwal entered the top three in China's floor washer market share for the first time in September 2024. The episode also discusses why Narwal entered late.
ex: In September 2024 Narwal first reached the top three in China's floor washer market

t88|430.c: The fifth flight's big breakthrough was the launch tower's arms catching the booster, more perfectly than insiders expected.
t88|430.e: The fifth flight's goal was to bring the first stage, the Super Heavy booster, back to the launch site and splash the second stage, Starship, down at sea. He sees the biggest step as the launch tower's arms cleanly catching the returning booster, a result that surprised him as he watched live. Starship's soft landing was also smoother than on the fourth flight, with better heat shielding. He thinks Starship sits between a rocket and a space shuttle, beyond what a traditional rocket is.
ex: The fourth landing was bumpy, and the fifth had better heat shielding

items.d: First stage flies back to the pad

t88|430.c: Low cost plus frequent launches means fast iteration, breaking traditional spaceflight's testing rules.
t88|430.e: Every part of Starship can be recovered, which sharply cuts the time and money spent building and launching. Low cost makes frequent launches and fast iteration possible, and each supports the other. This breaks the traditional aerospace rule of "test like you fly, fly like you test." The keys to cutting costs are reuse, off-the-shelf commercial parts and engineers who can do many jobs.
ex: A SpaceX structural engineer may handle both rocket and satellite structures

t88|430.c: Startups shouldn't copy SpaceX, whose early Falcon failures nearly sank the company.
t88|430.e: He advises startups not to copy SpaceX, because the Falcon rocket's early failures nearly brought the company down. By contrast, Jeff Bezos's Blue Origin uses a tortoise as its emblem and believes that rushing only slows you down. NASA's SLS rocket has many problems, yet it's the only option that fits America's schedule for landing astronauts on the Moon. Doing R&D at SpaceX, he says, takes both brains and toughness, and no fear of heights.
ex: Blue Origin's emblem is a tortoise
SLS is the only rocket that fits the Moon landing schedule

items: Early Falcon failures nearly sank it

d.verdict: Startups shouldn't copy SpaceX's approach

t88|430.c: Mars may have no economic value, but ordinary people going to space will become a trend.
t88|430.e: Starship was designed for landing on Mars, and the current plan needs five refuelings in low Earth orbit. For a crewed Mars landing, Musk says five years, a pessimistic estimate is ten, and NASA's plan targets 2050. He thinks Mars may not be worth much economically, but space travel is cool, and ordinary people going to space will be the trend.
ex: The Mars plan needs five refuelings in low Earth orbit
NASA envisions a crewed Mars landing by 2050

t88|430.c: China's commercial space industry is moving fast, but it lacks money and tolerance for failure.
t88|430.e: Between 2010 and 2020, China launched several major space programs, producing a burst of results like its space station, the Chang'e 5 lunar mission and the Tianwen Mars mission. He thinks Chinese commercial companies reach milestones faster, helped by policy support, a strong space foundation and trained talent. But the talent pool is still limited, and the industry needs more money and more tolerance for failure. SpaceX hasn't published its designs but doesn't go after those who learn from it, and its reuse approach has inspired Chinese teams.
ex: Beihang's space school admits about 150 to 160 yearly, and 60 to 70% enter the field
Copying the landing legs Falcon uses for recovery

items.d: A strength, but talent is limited
A weakness that needs more support
A weakness that needs more patience

t89|436.c: Long before AI, filmmaking was already highly technical, with computers involved from pre-production to post.
t89|436.e: Using Nanhai Guixu, an effects-heavy series in the Candle in the Tomb franchise, the episode walks through how such shows are made. From concept art and effects shooting to post-production, computers have long cut costs and saved time at many stages. The episode also reviews how filming and production technology has changed since 2000. Shooting against LED screens has gone from expensive to widespread.
ex: Case study: the effects-heavy series Nanhai Guixu

t89|436.c: Producers worry less about whether technology is new than about finding people who can use it.
t89|436.e: From a producer's point of view, the bigger headache isn't whether a technology is new, but finding people skilled enough to use it. Xinpianchang also works with several Chinese AI companies. It supplies them with material to train their models, while testing and using those models itself.
ex: Xinpianchang supplies training material to Chinese AI firms and tests their models

items: Skilled people are hard to find

d.verdict: Adoption is held back by people, not technology

t89|436.c: Mobile internet made sharing easy, and generative AI is now making creating easy.
t89|436.e: The episode's core view: mobile internet made sharing content easy, and generative AI, which produces text, images and video, further shortens the path from idea to finished work. It may also give rise to new communities and platforms. Film and content form a trillion-scale global market, and AI's impact is just beginning. The discussion starts from the flood of AI-generated posters for short dramas on video platforms.
ex: Video platforms are full of AI-generated posters for short dramas

t89|437.c: GPUs make rendering more detailed, and online collaboration platforms make film production more efficient.
t89|437.e: In the remake of The Lion King, GPUs made the fine rendering of light, shadow and fur possible. NVIDIA Omniverse, an online platform where teams collaborate on digital assets, can make film production more efficient. There's also room for Chinese alternatives in rendering software, and the Chinese renderer D5 is already used by many Chinese teams.
ex: Light, shadow and fur rendering in the Lion King remake
Chinese renderer D5 is used by many Chinese teams

t89|437.c: GANs, NeRF and digital humans are making their way into film and remote communication.
t89|437.e: He describes how technologies such as GANs, an AI method for generating realistic images, NeRF, which rebuilds 3D scenes from photos, and ACE digital humans are entering the film industry. He recalls how Jensen Huang's "digital double" was made for NVIDIA's GTC conference in 2021. Maxine can correct eye contact and adjust the picture in video calls, making remote conversations feel more natural. He also mentions two teams Huang sees as core even though they don't sell directly: developer relations and developer technology.
ex: Jensen Huang's digital double at GTC 2021
Maxine: eye-contact correction and picture adjustment in video calls

t89|437.c: AI makes creating easier, but human intent and emotion remain the heart of creative work.
t89|437.e: NVIDIA's Omniverse creator contest turned up many excellent creators who aren't professionals. The episode's third part concludes that AI makes it easier for ordinary people to express ideas, but some kind of "digital fence" is needed to set limits, and human intent matters more. AI can move people, but it can't be moved itself. Schools are already adjusting what they teach, and AI will create new jobs. The episode page doesn't say who made these points.
ex: Omniverse's creator contest surfaced many non-professional creators

t90|358.c: Governments wanting their own AI is a real need that would exist even without geopolitical shifts.
t90|358.e: Countries all want control of their own AI infrastructure, and he sees this as genuine government demand. People used to talk about a "sovereign internet," and now the talk is of "sovereign AI." That's because AI carries values and directly drives productivity, so the demand holds even without geopolitical change. On an earnings call, NVIDIA said its sovereign AI revenue is expected to go from zero to about $10 billion this year.
ex: Japan pledged over $65 billion over ten years for chips and AI
NVIDIA expects sovereign AI revenue to go from zero to about $10 billion this year

t90|358.c: Computing power is the most direct opportunity, with room too in AI infrastructure and exporting model talent.
t90|358.e: He sees computing power as the most direct opportunity, though Chinese companies lack production capacity. AI infrastructure, the software and hardware that keep models training and running, is another, and Yunqi has backed a new venture from Lingjie Xu, co-founder of chipmaker Biren. Many countries want their own models, so Chinese model teams can find work abroad. Chinese chips can't easily go overseas for now but may later, and data-center tech like liquid cooling and interconnects also has room.
ex: Kenya is building a Swahili-language model
Some foreign governments work with big Chinese firms like Alibaba and ByteDance

items.d: Countries build models, talent goes abroad
Most direct, but capacity is short

t90|358.c: Local governments chasing investment are driving AI data-center construction, which may not keep up with GPU upgrades.
t90|358.e: By the end of May 2024, mainland China had more than 280 AI computing centers built or under construction. Local governments' need to attract investment is driving this race. But GPUs improve fast, so the centers may fall behind each new generation of chips. The episode puts the scale at 283 projects, over 430 billion yuan of investment and 369,300 petaflops of computing power.
ex: 283 projects and over 430 billion yuan invested
369,300 petaflops of computing power in total

t90|358.c: Investors without seven years of patience shouldn't back AI, and sovereign AI brings new markets and competition.
t90|358.e: He thinks that if you don't have even seven years of patience, you shouldn't invest in AI. Sovereign AI opens new markets but also brings new competition, and NVIDIA's market share is already close to its peak. Companies building apps for governments are embracing large models too, but in China, government clients take a long time to pay, which is a serious problem.
ex: iFlytek can't use NVIDIA chips and works better with Huawei's Ascend

items: NVIDIA's share is near its peak

d.verdict: No seven years of patience, no AI investing

t90|358.c: For ordinary people, sovereign AI could mean better public services, or more pervasive control.
t90|358.e: The episode ends by asking how many governments can reach their goals, how they calculate the return on these investments, and how ordinary people will be affected. It could mean better government services, or management that reaches into everything. The episode page doesn't say which outcome he leans toward.

marks.d: Which way it goes is undecided

t91|442.c: Buddhism shouldn't be treated as a mental painkiller for easing bad feelings.
t91|442.e: The episode title states his position directly. Today Buddhism is often filed under emotional healing and wellness, and young people treat it as something to consume. The episode questions this use and asks what studying Buddhism is really for. The episode page doesn't spell out his answer, so only the view in the title is recorded here.
ex: Discussion question: when young people "consume Buddhism," what are they consuming?

d.verdict: Buddhism is more than personal pain relief

t91|442.c: Modern people live as isolated atoms, struggle to feel others' pain, and miss Buddhism's selfless side.
t91|442.e: The episode page records one core view from him: modern people live as isolated individuals, like atoms, and find it hard to feel other people's suffering. In that state, the side of Buddhism that truly matters, helping others, never comes to the surface. The page doesn't record how he developed the point.

items.d: Modern people cut off from each other
Focused only on their own feelings

t92|446.c: The "go global or go bust" slogan stirs up anxiety, so first ask whether your business suits going abroad.
t92|446.e: He thinks the slogan manufactures anxiety among founders. The episode notes that many founders haven't thought through a few things: whether their product suits overseas markets, whether years of effort abroad might pay off worse than doing well at home, what capabilities they lack, and what investors really care about when funding. The episode then discusses how to judge whether a business is a good fit for going global.
ex: From about minute 27, the episode focuses on judging whether a business should go abroad

items.d: Years abroad might lose to home

t92|446.c: Founders' hesitation about going global comes largely from an unclear global situation.
t92|446.e: A few years ago, almost no one cared about going global. Now everyone is talking about it, and investors see it differently too. He believes founders' hesitation and second-guessing about expanding abroad comes largely from uncertainty in the world situation. His own path ran from investing in Youzan and 51 Credit Card to looking at Africa, then to focusing on overseas expansion.
ex: His path: Youzan and 51 Credit Card, then Africa, then going global

t92|446.c: Chinese founders going global have clear weak spots, and those building brands can learn from Anker.
t92|446.e: As the title says, he meets about 1,000 startups a year and sees the limits of those going global. From an investor's view, the episode discusses where those limits lie and how to fill the gaps. It holds up Anker, the charger maker, as a model for founders who want to build a brand abroad. The episode page doesn't list the specific weaknesses or which of Anker's practices to copy.
ex: He meets about 1,000 overseas-expansion startups a year

t92|446.c: Investors have few overseas-expansion bets left, and Yunshi focuses on five areas.
t92|446.e: He thinks investors now have few directions left to bet on in overseas expansion. Yunshi mainly invests in companies going global, concentrated in five areas: materials and components, software, smart hardware, automation and equipment, and internet businesses. The episode also discusses what kind of globalizing company is most likely to interest investors.
ex: Five areas: materials and parts, software, smart hardware, automation and equipment, internet

t92|446.c: Raising money keeps getting harder, and the root cause is capital misallocated in the past.
t92|446.e: Yunshi built a dual-currency fund, raising both yuan and dollars, from scratch. Looking back on that, he says fundraising is getting harder, but the real reason is that resources were misallocated before. At the end of the episode, he offers advice to young people in venture investing who feel lost.
ex: Yunshi built a dual-currency fund from scratch

d.verdict: Fundraising is hard because of past misallocation

t93|160.c: How AI model startups fare depends on which way the technology improves, and how fast.
t93|160.e: The debate in the market is about how the technology will improve and how quickly. If progress is fast, some founders may win by seeing further ahead, and building the model and the app in one company makes more sense. If progress is slow, product skills matter more, and the leading model companies will struggle to raise money. Either way, free open-source models keep putting pressure on closed ones.
ex: DeepSeek isn't a tech giant, but it has plenty of resources

items: Founders who see further may win
Building model and app together makes sense
Leading labs struggle to raise money

d.verdict: Either way, open source squeezes closed models

t93|160.c: Startups mostly look weak next to the giants, and each of the six is finding its own path.
t93|160.e: The show argues the startups aren't so much failing as looking weak next to the giants, while facing a tangle of linked problems. The "six little dragons", China's best-known AI model startups, each have a path. Kimi focuses on Kimi itself. 01.AI does have products. Zhipu is working with phone makers on AutoGLM, which operates a phone for you. Kimi's big bet on work and study tools is ground the giants will surely fight for. MiniMax ships more products for different audiences, and its apps Xingye and Talkie lead the giants in their niches for now.
ex: MiniMax founder Junjie Yan: bring intelligence to everyone
Moonshot AI founder Zhilin Yang: push intelligence to its limit

items.d: Focused on the Kimi app itself
Partnering with phone makers on AutoGLM

t93|160.c: ByteDance started late on AI models, then pulled ahead: the boss recruited personally, built in-house, and created Flow.
t93|160.e: In the second half of 2023, ByteDance's AI models were still mocked. It started later than other Chinese giants, and Baidu was the first to move. Then a few things changed. The person at the very top recruited talent personally. The company chose to build its own models rather than invest in others. And it set up Flow, a unit for AI apps. Geopolitical pressure abroad was an outside force pushing ByteDance into AI.
ex: Baidu was the first Chinese giant to work on large AI models
Toutiao reached 10 million daily users just over a year after launch

t93|160.c: The giants differ: Alibaba bets on cloud, Tencent can afford to move late, Baidu shines with robotaxis.
t93|160.e: Alibaba's new strategy is AI-driven growth with public cloud, renting computing power to others, as the priority. The contest to watch is Alibaba Cloud versus ByteDance's Volcano Engine. Tencent is well placed to move late and still catch up. Baidu has internal tensions, yet its robotaxi service Apollo Go became its AI highlight this year.
ex: The contest to watch: Alibaba Cloud vs. Volcano Engine

items.d: Can move late and still catch up
Internal tension; robotaxis are the bright spot

t93|160.c: AI apps are springing up, and founders have no time to be gloomy; they will find a way.
t93|160.e: Crossing's in-person AI startup event drew far more sign-ups than it had seats, and a model of one very capable person plus a small team is taking off. The show asks whether apps really haven't broken out, or whether expectations were just too high, and points to useful apps like Recraft and Cursor. The verdict: founders have no time for gloom and will find a way. The episode closes on the line "war is made of waiting and torment."
ex: About 100 seats at the event, more than 700 sign-ups
Useful apps: Recraft for design, Cursor for coding

terms.d: One person can carry a product

result.d: Founders have no time for gloom

t95|454.c: Industrial design is less an industry than a way of thinking about problems.
t95|454.e: The episode opens by framing industrial design as a way of thinking rather than a standalone industry. From there it asks what students learn in an industrial design degree, how it differs from and connects to other kinds of design, whether an industrial designer is the same as a product manager for physical products, and where it fits in the journey from idea to mass production. The show page doesn't record his actual answers.
ex: One prompt: sum up industrial design in about 20 Chinese characters

items.d: How it differs from other design
Are the two the same job?
Which step of making a product

t95|454.c: Much design work hides in plain sight, and what's hard or easy often defies common intuition.
t95|454.e: The pair discuss which humble everyday objects actually involve a lot of design, which details are hard to pull off yet taken for granted, and which things that look hard are actually simple. They also talk about how to judge a new device's design when you first get it, and the design traps that bosses with no manufacturing experience tend to fall into. The show page doesn't list specific examples.
ex: Products reviewed include the iPhone and the Li Auto MEGA

cells.d: Taken for granted by most people

t96|387.c: Copying human drivers can't get you to full self-driving; the system has to practice and learn for itself.
t96|387.e: Imitation learning, where the system copies what human drivers do, can't capture how drivers think, so at best the car drives like a person. But people hold AI drivers to a double standard, and human-like isn't enough. Even copying only excellent drivers fails and can make things worse, because the training is open-loop: the system never sees the consequences of its own actions. Only after despair did he decide closed-loop learning, where the system acts, sees results and improves via reinforcement learning, was the answer. Just as AlphaZero, learning from scratch, beat AlphaGo, which first studied human games.
ex: The old method had run three years and worked fairly well before the switch
The first two years after switching were painful

items: Key inputs: data and computing power
At best drives like a human
Key is how accurate the simulation is

d.verdict: Full self-driving needs closed-loop practice

t96|387.c: The world model is the factory that builds the in-car model; its precision is what sets companies apart.
t96|387.e: About five years ago, Pony.ai shifted its focus to generating its own training data, one job of a "world model", a system that simulates real roads and traffic. He sees the world model as a factory that produces the driving model in the car. Progress depends less on the model in the car than on how precise the factory is. Details decide everything, so the world model's fine-grained accuracy is the real competitive edge. The end goal is cars that never crash because of their own mistakes.
ex: End goal: cars never crash because of their own mistakes

t96|387.c: Driver assistance and full self-driving optimize for different things; neither can replace the other.
t96|387.e: He thinks nobody chose wrong: L2+ driver assistance, where a person must watch the road, and L4, fully driverless within set areas, simply optimize in different directions. Imitation learning suits L2 because L2 wins through scale. But past a certain point you see they are two separate problems. L2 can't stretch into L4, and L4 can't replace L2. Being Tesla doesn't make imitation learning reach L4. He adds that no L2 product will go 1,000 km between human takeovers, because that goes against human nature.
ex: His analogy: MiniMax's products are like L4, coding assistant Copilot like L2
AI models moving into real applications will hit self-driving's old problems

marks.d: Fits assistance, which wins on scale
Past here they're clearly different problems

t96|387.c: Robotaxi fleets start earning gross profit at about a thousand cars; then it's net profit versus growth.
t96|387.e: For five years outsiders could barely see progress in driverless cars, and the mood only shifted once large-scale driverless service appeared. He believes a fleet of a thousand or so robotaxis starts making gross profit, covering its direct costs. Whether to chase overall profit next or keep expanding is a strategic trade-off. Partners help operate and maintain the cars, and the key next step is growing the fleet at a reasonable cost.
ex: In future one remote assistant could oversee 30 cars

t96|387.c: Sticking with it is hard because of temptation, not toil, and copying winners' methods is a mistake.
t96|387.e: He thinks most people quit not because the work is hard but because something else tempts them away. When outsiders can't see progress, a team needs sensible milestones it can actually feel to get through industry swings. People tend to look at who won and assume their methods must have been right, which is exactly why you shouldn't blindly copy them. Commercializing too early and chasing only the biggest prize are both extremes, and he admits he was obsessive at times.
ex: He says he increasingly believes the world is a simulation

items.d: The industry is in a slump
Temptation, not hard work, is the test

t97|459.c: Going abroad isn't easy pickings: religion and culture change what sells, to whom, and how.
t97|459.e: Fierce competition at home makes many Chinese sellers think Southeast Asia will be easy to dominate. He warns against copying what worked in China just because local rivals look weak. Religious calendars, certification rules and cultural taboos decide whether a product can sell at all, and when. So commit to the long haul before going in, then iterate fast to understand local shoppers. Only then do Chinese teams' strengths in content, ad buying and product show up.
ex: About 90% of Indonesians are Muslim, so halal certification can make or break sales
Halal certification works at brand, store and product level; whole-brand is hardest
During Ramadan livestream hosts lose energy, yet mouthwash sells better

root.d: Don't just copy what worked in China

items.d: Halal approval decides whether you can scale
Ramadan shifts daily routines and demand
Think it through first, then iterate fast

t97|459.c: Riding a hot new category earns a brief margin; a brand keeps premium prices going longer.
t97|459.e: When a new category takes off, the earliest sellers make the most money, but as supply floods in the price gap disappears. A brand is how you keep charging more: establish one hero product, tell a story through the founder's journey or ingredient research, then expand the line. He is against spending big for one-off buzz. In his view a brand takes patience and steady investment in R&D, advertising and operations.
ex: Summer ice makers on Amazon US: first movers earned most, then premiums shrank
Brands like Skintific already outprice no-name goods but aren't fully established yet
The path: establish one cleanser, then expand into creams and serums

items: Early movers pocket the price gap
Premium shrinks as supply floods in
Establish one product, then tell a story

d.verdict: Move from riding categories to building a brand

t97|459.c: TikTok creates the desire to buy; shopping marketplaces capture the sales and profit. Plan both together.
t97|459.e: TikTok has to make people aware of a product and want it, so it naturally costs more than a pure marketplace, and on its own it often loses money. But it creates a halo effect. Viewers go on to buy from official and independent stores on Shopee and Lazada, Southeast Asia's big marketplaces, and that profit offsets the content spend. He also suggests asking how the platform wants to make money. Spending above the industry average on ads, for example, can win more platform support.
ex: TikTok ROAS (sales per ad dollar) can climb from 0.1 to 1, 3, even 4–5
A common path: watch a video on TikTok, buy on Shopee
Lacking overseas data, track 14- and 7-day repurchases instead of customer profiles

items.d: Demand spills over to other channels
Shopee and Lazada capture the orders

t97|459.c: Hard isn't the same as small: those entering Southeast Asia in a downturn may win the next cycle.
t97|459.e: He admits Southeast Asia is several small, fragmented markets, with online shopping and logistics far behind China. But hard to crack and small are different things, and some Chinese brands already have real scale there. Developing markets may also skip shopping on computers and jump straight to mobile and content-driven shopping. He believes those who leave during a downturn may not get their place back in the recovery, and new cycles tend to reward newcomers.
ex: He relays that some Southeast Asian markets may run at 40–50% of China's efficiency
Skintific's online and offline sales reportedly reach 1.5–2 billion
He compares it to China reopening college entrance exams in 1977 and the late-1990s business rush

items.d: Those who left may not get back in
Rewards those who entered in the downturn

t97|459.c: A good local partner is your first need abroad, and even referrals should compete in an open pitch.
t97|459.e: His first rule for going abroad is to find a partner who knows the platform, has relationships there, and understands exactly what the brand wants. Start by asking contacts inside the platform and the TikTok team about agency rankings and recommended lists. Overseas Chinese networks are also an edge for Chinese companies. But don't choose on relationships alone. The same agency can be strong in one market and weak in another, so run an open pitch, then grow the winner into a partner you learn from.
ex: North American agencies cost more: he relays running one product costs about 7x China

items.d: Test their strength in this market
Brand knows the platform, partner knows the market

t97|459.c: Chinese teams' fast trial-and-error is a strength, but pace and incentives must adapt to local culture.
t97|459.e: In Japan he found teams leaned on standard processes and paid little attention to results, so changing one page took weeks. Locals like to think things 70–80% through before acting, while Chinese teams start at 10–20%. He suggests meeting in the middle at 30–40% and learning by doing. The Chinese style of harsh criticism and big incentives may also not land in Southeast Asia, so incentives need redesigning for local culture.
ex: In Japan, editing a product page takes two to three weeks; in China, maybe six hours
A Vietnamese livestream host quit on the spot after being told the stream went badly
In Indonesia, many staff quit after Eid, feeling they had earned enough

t97|459.c: Selling abroad is just step one; truly putting down local roots has to be the CEO's own project.
t97|459.e: Overseas business can start small, scattered and loss-making, and you may end up with bad partners. So it can't be a half-hearted test handed to a subordinate: the CEO or founder has to drive it. After selling abroad comes putting down roots, with offices, a local team, R&D and production lines, so the product keeps improving locally. TikTok is just a catalyst and a stage. A platform can blame quality problems on the supply chain, but a brand can't, so quality control always comes first.
ex: After buying an overseas company, send your best people fast; finance and legal must step in
He grew an Indonesian business from zero to about 2.5–3 million in a year (currency unstated)

t98|431.c: Alibaba didn't buy 01.AI; they split roles, with Alibaba raising big "teacher" models and 01.AI the "students."
t98|431.e: 01.AI and Alibaba Cloud set up a joint lab, and the people chasing huge computing clusters and giant models became Alibaba employees. 01.AI keeps smaller training, infrastructure and application teams and stays independent. He likens it to the split between a university and a teachers' college. 01.AI has stopped pre-training giant models, but will still train once or twice a year, depending on whether a new model's gain is worth the cost.
ex: The idea began in May 2024, firmed up in Q3; he denies funding rumors forced it
The core team mostly stayed; some who wanted to build AGI-scale giant models left

items.d: Alibaba joint lab trains the teacher models
Consumer apps abroad, business clients in China

t98|431.c: Training ever-bigger models now yields shrinking returns, so giant models aren't a fight for startups.
t98|431.e: He thinks the scaling law, the rule that bigger models with more compute get smarter, still holds. But each extra batch of GPUs buys less and less, and the return no longer justifies the cost. Only big companies truly chasing AGI and able to absorb huge costs should keep building giant models. Startups shouldn't, unless they have an edge others can hardly copy. In his view giant models will end up as basic infrastructure, like an operating system, so app companies needn't rebuild them.
ex: His analogy: going from 1 to 10 GPUs gets you about 9.5 GPUs' worth of value
Going from 100,000 to 1 million GPUs may only equal about 130,000
In China, he is fairly sure Alibaba and ByteDance can keep going

items.d: Alibaba, ByteDance, maybe one or two more

t98|431.c: Giant models will step back and become teachers; good-enough small models will carry the market.
t98|431.e: A giant model's value lies in labeling data, reinforcement post-training (further tuning with reward signals), and producing better synthetic data, meaning training data written by models, for small models. Synthetic data is pointless if it merely replaces real data. Its value is in improving data that is already close to exhausted. So the models that actually reach the market will be small, fast and cheap enough. Even if a giant model is too slow and costly to sell, it will still teach the small ones.
ex: Yi-Lightning costs about one-thirtieth as much as GPT-4o
Per a friend: Anthropic's Opus was too big and slow, so it teaches Sonnet instead (unverified)

items.d: Trained by giants, not necessarily sold

t98|431.c: If longer "slow thinking" becomes the next breakthrough, answering fast turns into a competitive edge.
t98|431.e: Once a model writes faster than people read, making it several times faster adds little. But slow, long thinking, where a model reasons at length before answering, may be the next breakthrough. If it makes rivals so slow that many apps can't tolerate them, speed becomes a key advantage. A fast inference engine, the system that runs the model to produce answers, also allows more slow-thinking experiments. So going small, fast and cheap is both a cost defense and an early bet on inference-time scaling.
ex: If slow thinking makes rivals ten times slower, 01.AI's speed stays acceptable

terms.d: Much longer reasoning before each answer

result.d: Still usable when rivals get unbearably slow

t98|431.c: AI startups face hard money questions within two or three years; GPU spending must pay back.
t98|431.e: The previous generation of AI companies went through papers, competitions, first orders and expansion, and faced hard financial scrutiny only after four or five years. This generation moves faster, and the faster a company burns cash, the sooner it gets asked. He thinks you must prove, in order, that you understand business, have growing revenue and control costs, and then narrow losses. The cost of training a model should be weighed against the new revenue it brings in over its lifetime.
ex: Training Yi-Lightning cost about $3 million; the model lasts about six months
If losses are still 5 to 20 times revenue, the story is hard to sell
Older AI firms like SenseTime and Megvii faced financial scrutiny only after four or five years

items.d: First prove you can run a business
Treat GPUs as a business expense
From one profit source to several

t98|431.c: Don't fight unwinnable battles: no paid growth for consumer apps, only reusable deals for business clients.
t98|431.e: Fields with no product-market fit, that need years of educating users, or where giants already dominate are off-limits however good the tech. Consumer apps that buy growth with ads stop growing when the ads stop, and free users keep burning GPUs. On the business side, fringe projects are low-value, pay little, and may not even cover sales costs. Worth taking are deals that directly make clients money, or that team up with strong industry partners. A first deal can lose money if the work can be reused widely.
ex: If later clients reuse 60–80% of the deliverables, losing money on the first deal is fine
2024 revenue topped 100 million yuan; the 2025 goal is several-fold growth
01.AI forms joint ventures with industry partners, putting in technology as its stake

cells.d: Share risk, rely on partner's industry knowledge
Lose on the first, reuse later

t98|431.c: In three years there won't be "model companies"; winners will be apps that reinvent a category with AI.
t98|431.e: He predicts that in three years, unless you become OpenAI, no company will still be seen as a model company. The winners will become giants in some field. If AI just adds features to existing products, big companies keep their lead. Only when a category is redefined does the giants' old baggage leave room for newcomers. He thinks China is behind in the model race, but the next contest, over applications and business models, plays to China's strengths.
ex: From PC to mobile, search barely changed, but ride-hailing, payments and local services were rebuilt
Office plus Copilot isn't AI-first; AI drafting while people edit is
He rates Chinese models 90 and US models 98, about six months behind

d.verdict: Startups win only when a category is redefined

t99|466.c: Open-sourcing mainly speeds up research feedback, and it repairs a weak technical reputation abroad.
t99|466.e: He thinks the speed of progress matters more than where the tech stands today. Open-sourcing exposes a model's strengths and flaws faster than shipping a closed model in a product and waiting for user feedback. MiniMax's text models lacked a technical reputation abroad, a past failing, and open-sourcing is a start at fixing it. Models go stale quickly, so hiding a stronger closed version has no lasting value. If he could start over, he'd open-source from day one.
ex: MiniMax uses the open-source MiniMax-01 internally and kept no stronger version
He thinks OpenAI's edge lies more in its brand and its hold on users' minds

items.d: Model shared with researchers and developers
Faster than waiting for product users
Targeted fixes for the next model

t99|466.c: More users don't make a better model: good models create good apps, not the reverse.
t99|466.e: A popular view in China holds that more users mean more feedback and faster model progress, so huge sums go into buying traffic. He calls this a mistake. Capability gains usually come from first defining goals and evaluations, then training toward them, not from user feedback. Technology raises the ceiling on what's possible, and products meet needs and make money. The chain runs one way, and too many users can even slow research down.
ex: ChatGPT may have 50–100x Claude's daily users, yet their abilities are close
SWE-bench coding scores rose from about 10 to 70-plus in a year, thanks to clear goals

items.d: User numbers don't feed back into the model

t99|466.c: The recommendation-engine habit of A/B testing and patching cases can't raise the ceiling for AGI.
t99|466.e: A recommendation system, which picks content for each user, can't judge quality in advance, so it sifts huge volumes with A/B tests. Applied to large models, that becomes sorting by use case, adding data and patching individual failures, which only improves things locally. He argues for first defining capability levels, training data, reasoning processes and difficulty, then using technology to reach those targets. He has seen companies that won users switch to chasing user requests, slow down, and get overtaken.

d.verdict: Build large models the second way

t99|466.c: Being tech-driven means climbing to the next level of capability, not fixing every small problem first.
t99|466.e: With limited resources and plenty of problems after launch, he chose to focus on reaching a higher level of capability, with product and operations serving the algorithms. Once the tech stops leading, the product disappears too. Hailuo's video product had a rough interface but stuck with what the algorithm team wanted. Hailuo's text product tried to patch rare edge cases instead, drifted from being tech-driven, and never took off. He admits some of the wavering came from worrying about the team's feelings.
ex: Hailuo's video product may draw the world's most traffic, yet launched without an English page
He says he judged in May 2024 that ByteDance's Doubao would win on experience

marks.d: Switched to patching edge cases; didn't take off
Rough interface, but followed the algorithm team

t99|466.c: Hitting a wall on scaling is no reason to quit; belief shows in where you put resources.
t99|466.e: He rejects the claim that the industry went from believing in the scaling law, the idea that more data and compute keep making models smarter, to doubting it within a year. Making technology ten times better was always hard. After hitting a wall, find whatever keeps progress going, whether or not it's still called scaling. Startups get few chances to err, but tight resources force new ideas in algorithms and organization. Belief means spending on compute and talent, not big marketing. If no way forward appears, shut down.
ex: He agrees with OpenAI and Anthropic putting most of their money into compute and talent
ByteDance can run rival teams in parallel; a startup has to fight step by step

terms.d: AGI is a long march in one direction

result.d: Stop only when no path remains

t99|466.c: MiniMax-01 lays the architectural groundwork for agents; the actual skills still need building.
t99|466.e: He defines an agent as AI that handles complex multi-step tasks at a professional's level in a specialized field. Long context, how much a model can hold at once, is really memory that keeps growing, and an agent is like an endless conversation along a timeline. MiniMax-01 swaps standard softmax attention for linear attention, whose cost grows only in proportion to length, so its architecture can handle very long inputs. But tool use and planning aren't optimized yet, so this is only step one.
ex: Linear attention isn't an industry consensus; it can coexist with DeepSeek's MLA approach
The next model will improve coding and planning; he denies it will match o3

t99|466.c: Don't distill a model just to earn an o1 label; solid groundwork beats being a month early.
t99|466.e: He says distilling a model that looks like o1, OpenAI's reasoning model, from a few thousand examples isn't hard, and MiniMax has tried it internally. But doing it for a paper or press release is pointless. The best companies of the past two years were usually not the earliest but the most thorough. Distillation is one path, and whether it counts as a shortcut is debatable. Spending more compute at answer time has long existed. o1's advance was building multi-step search into a single end-to-end model.
ex: He notes that training to match GPT-4's outputs can carry an "alignment tax"
His test of research skill: are experiments better designed than a few months ago?

items.d: Smarter design when options are wide open
A month or two early doesn't matter
Business doesn't depend on the o1 name

t99|466.c: Needing paid traffic means the product isn't right yet; AI companies can't copy mobile internet growth playbooks.
t99|466.e: Hailuo has spent almost nothing on promotion at home or abroad. He thinks a product that leans heavily on promotion probably isn't working yet. t100|469.c: R1's breakout is first a win for the open-source community, which helps startups most.
t100|469.e: She rejects the idea that DeepSeek, a lone Chinese company, simply caught up with OpenAI. Since V2 and V3 it has published technical reports and intermediate experiments, and it built on work by open and closed teams worldwide. With many labs pulling back on openness, that openness stands out. Her long-term view: open source helps startups and closed source helps big companies, because startups can cheaply use, distill and modify open models.

t100|469.c: R1 taught itself step-by-step reasoning, which supports the scaling law rather than refuting it.
t100|469.e: She thinks R1's biggest surprise is that, through reinforcement learning (improving by trial and error against rewards), it developed chain-of-thought reasoning, writing out its steps, without large amounts of human-labeled reasoning. Human labeling used to be the bottleneck on progress. Once that bottleneck loosens, adding more compute could still raise capability by another order of magnitude. So when some say this proves the scaling law has failed, she thinks the opposite is true.

t100|469.c: Cheaper models are no reason to short Nvidia; total GPU demand will actually rise.

t101|317.c: Medicine is the jewel in AI's crown: almost every capability of large models applies to it.
t101|317.e: He keeps telling his team that nearly every large-model capability has a direct use in medicine: multimodal perception, embodiment, long memory, literature search and fewer hallucinations. He also opposes building a general model first and starting on medicine separately later, which he says splits the effort in two. Every release should strengthen "general plus medical" together.

t101|317.c: Building an AI doctor is building AGI; a doctor's skills are a good yardstick for general intelligence.
t101|317.e: He criticizes the industry for claiming AI can do anything while calling an AI doctor too hard. True strong AI arrives when machines master language. And people struggle to get care because there aren't enough doctors: booking and consultation platforms only connect patients, they don't add doctors. He gradually steered toward medicine, but early fundraising meant pitching against OpenAI, so medicine became the core only once money and team were in place.

t101|317.c: Even the strongest general model won't swallow medicine; the next era will turn life into mathematics.
t101|317.e: He rejects the idea that the strongest general model will swallow every specialized application: even Einstein couldn't practice medicine without medical data and training. He divides technology into three eras. The scientific era turned physics into math, the intelligence era is turning language into math, and the coming era of coexistence must turn life into math. Medicine is too heavy for startups and not a top priority for big tech companies, which leaves Baichuan a window.

They spot risks early, manage patients, and send people back to hospital when surgery or intensive care is needed. In community clinics, AI fills the service gap left after families sign up with a family doctor.

Half the capability comes from calling outside frontier models and half from Baichuan's own training, but it must still master pre-training, post-training, reinforcement learning and retrieval. t102|486.c: From V2 to FlashMLA, nearly every DeepSeek innovation aims at efficiency.
t102|486.e: He traces DeepSeek's technical thread. V2 used MLA to shrink the memory cache needed while generating answers. V3 added multi-token prediction, low-precision FP8 training, and less idle time as machines pass work down a pipeline. FlashMLA, released on day one of open-source week, uses C++ to optimize the low-level routines, or kernels, that run inference. These sit at different layers but all aim to cut training and inference costs, so he expected the week to cover AI infrastructure, not just models.
ex: FlashMLA optimizes inference for the MLA design introduced in V2
He disclaims predictive power, guessing only that training and inference frameworks may follow

items.d: Multi-token prediction, FP8, less idle time

t102|486.c: Faster low-level computation mostly means moving less data; the gap is engineering skill, not will.
t102|486.e: He uses FlashAttention to explain kernel fusion. A GPU's compute units are fast, but shuttling data back and forth between slow and fast memory eats time. Merge several steps so data is loaded once, processed in one go, then written back, and things speed up noticeably. Many teams can't pull this off, not for lack of will but for lack of engineering skill. He hit this very wall when he tried online training, updating a model while it generates.
ex: The fastest inference frameworks freeze the model and can't update it during generation
Building a library that does both was beyond his team's ability

items.d: Run several steps in a row
Memory access, not compute, is the bottleneck

t102|486.c: "Open-source models" come in at least five levels; most companies release only reports and weights.
t102|486.e: He sorts openness into five levels: technical report, model weights (the trained parameters), inference framework, training framework and dataset. The industry usually opens only the first two. Inference and training frameworks are released less and less, and almost no commercial company publishes full training data. So two things both called "open source" can differ hugely in how far outsiders can reproduce them. DeepSeek's unusually detailed V3 report earned it technical credibility before R1 went viral.
ex: The V3 report runs 50-plus pages, built from many members' separately verified contributions
R1's repository is mainly the paper and run instructions, without full training code

t102|486.c: Judge an open-source project by its issues, not its stars: issues mean people actually use it.
t102|486.e: A star is shallow interest, like a bookmark. Issues about hardware support, build errors and bugs show that people are actually running the code. A pull request means someone has rolled up their sleeves to change the code, usually for no reward beyond love of the work. To learn a codebase, he reads the README, gets the first command running, then follows imports and function calls layer by layer, learning it like a tree.
ex: vLLM came out of Berkeley and has more than 800 contributors
An MIT license plus "as is": the code is open, with no promise of results

items.d: Changing the code and submitting it

t102|486.c: Mature open-source frameworks can handle deployment for everyone, so no company needs to rebuild the tooling.
t102|486.e: When a company releases a model on its own, it often lacks deployment tuning, and community frameworks like vLLM and SGLang can pick up that work. Companies contribute their optimizations to the framework, which then supports more hardware and models and draws more users and contributors. The same goes for open-sourcing training code. The hard part is the extra effort of pulling code out of internal systems and cleaning it up, so it comes down to priorities.
ex: MiniMax contributed its linear attention optimizations to vLLM
SGLang supported V3 and R1 soon after R1's release
He spent over a week rewriting the ESFT code for a public framework

t102|486.c: Whether to release your best model or just smaller ones depends on how you make money.
t102|486.e: Labs that don't earn money from subscriptions or premium API pricing may release their strongest model outright, even hoping to reshape the industry. Companies that need to protect a commercial edge are more likely to release only smaller versions. He thinks keeping models closed can be reasonable too. As for why other companies have been slow to open-source, he leans toward the sheer workload as a major reason.
ex: DeepSeek released its strongest model under the permissive MIT license
He's unsure whether OpenAI will release its strongest model

t102|486.c: The stronger the model, the riskier it is to release; not every top model should be open.
t102|486.e: He suspects his Twitter account was hacked by someone using an AI agent, software that acts on its own, to mass-produce personalized invitations that lure people into clicking. Once models are strong enough, developers can hardly stop malicious use, and cheap harm at scale becomes easy. So releasing small models while holding back the strongest may make more sense. Datasets are similar: once public web pages are gathered into one dataset, personal information becomes easier to find and abuse.

Exceptions: AllenAI and EleutherAI publish data and intermediate checkpoints
