t103|487.c: Attention lets every word look back at everything before it, but cost grows with length squared.
t103|487.e: A word's meaning often depends on its context. Attention computes how relevant each earlier word is to the current one, then pulls in information weighted by that relevance. An RNN squeezes history into a fixed-size memory, so early information gets lost as text grows. A Transformer keeps a representation of every earlier token, the chunks of text a model processes, so distant links survive. But computation and storage grow fast with length, which becomes unsustainable for very long sequences.
ex: He estimates a cache for millions of tokens could take hundreds of gigabytes
Typical GPUs have only tens of gigabytes of memory

d.verdict: Sparse and linear approaches both seek a middle ground

t103|487.sc: From long input to long output
t103|487.c: Long reasoning shifts the strain from long inputs to long outputs, so sparsity must pay off during generation.
t103|487.e: Since R1, the long-sequence problem is no longer just prefill, reading a long document up front, but the model generating long chains of thought itself. Reinforcement learning training repeatedly generates long reasoning traces, so optimization shifts toward decoding and the RL stage. That's why he watches NSA's results on math problems needing long reasoning, and its training loss curves, most closely. Classic needle-in-a-haystack tests, finding one sentence in a long text, usually turn out fine anyway.
ex: Kimi's use case leans toward long inputs; he cares more about NSA on long outputs
He urges not blindly trusting any replication results, including DeepSeek's own

items.d: Long traces generated again and again

t103|487.c: GPU-friendly sparsity must work in blocks; theoretical compute savings don't guarantee real speedups.
t103|487.e: GPUs win through massive parallelism and need contiguous memory access, so scattered operations at random positions can't keep the compute units busy. Sparsity therefore has to be all or nothing per block. But writing the algorithm in blocks isn't enough: real speedups take lots of kernel optimization. He reflects on his own early InfLLM, which promised high theoretical speedups but delivered too little in practice. Believing sparsity was inherently bad for GPUs, he also never took it into training.
ex: NSA uses custom Triton kernels to implement block sparsity
He blames that early retreat on limited understanding more than limited resources

terms.d: Fits parallelism and contiguous memory access
Turns theoretical savings into hardware gains

t103|487.c: Sparsity saves compute but not storage; long tasks need memory that decides what to keep.
t103|487.e: Sparse attention cuts computation, but the amount that must be stored doesn't shrink. As context stretches to months or even years, storage will eventually become the problem. If a model is to work like a scientist, from choosing a topic through experiments to writing the paper, the job could last a long time, and saving every word isn't feasible. He sees long sequences, attention and memory as three separate layers. Memory must learn what to keep, for instance summarizing in layers and rereading the original when needed.
ex: A math problem takes about 10,000–20,000 tokens; a research project may last months
Read 100 papers, keep 20 words from each, and about 2,000 words remain

t103|488.c: NSA and MoBA build sparsity into pre-training, a major boost for the whole field.
t103|488.e: Most earlier methods trained densely and only went sparse at inference, and that mismatch between training and deployment introduced errors. The industry used to care more about a model's ceiling and put efficiency second. Now efficiency is a core constraint, so people are willing to invest in testing sparsity during training. NSA's results show that, trained well, a sparse model can match or even beat full attention, proving you can be smart and fast at once.
ex: Both share a structure: split into blocks, select blocks, plus always watch nearby context
He thinks everyone now agrees on split-then-select; execution is what matters

items.d: Sparse only at inference, causing mismatch
Industry willing to invest in testing
Can match or beat dense models

t103|488.c: Judge sparse attention by the Pareto frontier of speed and smarts, not by quality alone.
t103|488.e: Quality alone isn't enough, because dialing sparsity down can always get close to full attention. A better standard is the Pareto frontier, the edge where you can't improve speed or ability without giving up the other. At the same speed as others, are you the smartest? At the same smarts, are you the fastest? Training curves answer another key question: given enough resources, can a sparse model reach the same ceiling as a dense one?

t103|488.c: Test long-context ability on three levels: fluent output, correct facts, and right answers.
t103|488.e: The first level asks whether output stays fluent once input exceeds the training length, measured by perplexity (how unsure the model is about the next word) or training loss. The second asks whether it finds the right entities and infers the right relationships in long text, measured by accuracy. The third, for reasoning models, looks only at final problem-solving. He warns sparse attention may change how chains of thought look and make them harder to read, but no mature readability metric exists yet.
ex: A second-level example: inferring family relationships across a long text
R1-Zero's chains of thought were at times unreadable and mixed languages

items.d: Still coherent with very long input
Finds the right entities and relationships
Long reasoning reaches the right answer

t103|488.c: Multimodal input inflates context by orders of magnitude, so sparsity patterns must fit each modality.
t103|488.e: In the same hour, text, audio and video produce wildly different numbers of tokens. Even at one frame per second, video approaches a million, and skipping frames loses continuous information. Each type of content also connects information differently: text mostly attends to nearby words, while tracking an object in video means looking back at fixed intervals. So sparsity patterns must be designed per modality. Another angle is redundancy: keep only what is important and distinctive.
ex: At 24 frames per second and 100 tokens per frame, one second is ~2,400 tokens
His team's FrameFusion compresses repeated information in video

items.d: About 1 million even at 1 frame per second

t103|488.c: Sparsity saves compute only by a fixed ratio; as sequences grow without limit, linear attention must fill in.
t103|488.e: Sparse attention barely changes existing architectures and stays highly compatible, so it's the near-term engineering fix. But it only cuts computation by a constant factor, so the problem returns as sequences keep growing. Linear attention, whose cost grows only in proportion to length, scales more slowly and wins at large enough lengths. Pure linear designs still lose some ability today, so hybrids are needed. Storage will also become a hard limit, because GPU memory grows far more slowly than compute.
ex: He estimates compute may grow 10x across chip generations, memory less than 2x

marks.d: Slower cost growth, but some ability lost

t104|494.c: The Transformer's core problem is compute growing with the square of length; better hardware just hides it.
t104|494.e: He sees attention's compute, which grows with the square of text length, as the biggest problem with the Transformer, the architecture behind today's large models. FlashAttention fixed memory use, not the amount of computation. Faster GPUs from V100 to H100 made 128K or 256K tokens tolerable, but covering a squared cost with hardware isn't a structural fix. Reorder the multiplication of Q, K and V, computing K and V first and then multiplying by Q, and the cost drops from quadratic to linear. In essence it becomes a linear RNN, a step-by-step reader, that can still be trained in parallel.
ex: At 1 million tokens, the attention step alone runs about 2,700 times faster than full attention
Analogy: a Transformer rereads the whole book each step; a linear model plays telephone

items: Compute QK, then multiply by V
Compute KV, then multiply by Q

d.verdict: Long context needs a structural fix, not more hardware

t104|494.c: Sparse attention is a lossy shortcut with a low ceiling; linear attention can be lossless.
t104|494.e: In 2021 the team tried sparse attention, which computes only some of the words. It did worse than standard softmax attention and was barely faster, so they switched to linear attention. He grants that newer work like NSA and MoBA fixed sparse attention's speed problems, but notes public tests only go up to about 7 billion parameters, with no proof of its ceiling at hundreds of billions. Sparse methods simply drop the positions they skip, while quadratic computation itself may be partly redundant, so linear plus hybrid could even beat pure full attention.
ex: He tested cache-compression methods like MLA; their edge narrowed as models grew
He guesses big outside labs likely use sliding windows plus full attention

marks.d: Quadratic work may be partly redundant
He thinks it can beat pure full attention

t104|494.c: Early linear attention looked good on paper but was slow and weak; fixing it took three years.
t104|494.e: He admits early linear attention looked good in theory but performed poorly and ran slowly. The team first spent two years fixing accuracy across various linear designs; by late 2022, on the same data, their small models matched Transformers. The speed problem was that the linear form contains a loop, which GPUs handle poorly, and dedicated engineering optimization solved it. Only after testing on a 15-billion-parameter model in late 2023 did they decide it could scale up.
ex: They tried linear attention, linear RNNs, long convolutions and other designs
The CosFormer paper was later published at ICLR, a top machine learning conference

items.d: Weak and barely faster; go linear

t104|494.c: Pure linear models struggle with recall; one softmax layer per seven linear layers beat all-softmax.
t104|494.e: A 15-billion-parameter pure linear model came close to a Transformer on language, but scaled up, it stumbled on needle-in-a-haystack tests, which ask a model to find one sentence in a long text. A fixed-size memory must compress input of any length, so exact recall is naturally harder, and repeating earlier text is basic to learning from context. So the team paired every seven linear layers with one softmax layer. Recall not only recovered but surpassed the all-softmax model, which surprised even the team.
ex: They tried one per 7, 14 or 16 layers, even one in roughly 80
The 1:7 ratio came mostly from experiments, with Jamba as a reference

t104|494.c: Before betting on a new architecture, run many small experiments; the hard part is deciding before training.
t104|494.e: Spending tens of millions of yuan to train a big model only to find the architecture fails is unacceptable, so the groundwork must be solid to convince a company to adopt an architecture untested in industry. The team planned resources ahead and trained thousands of models from scratch, comparing designs and hybrid ratios. They used scaling laws, which predict how performance changes with size, to forecast larger models, then built a mid-size bridge model. When the real large-scale training came, it went relatively smoothly.
ex: They trained about 3,700 models from scratch, mostly small ones
A bridge model with about 9B active parameters came first, taking about a month

items.d: Verified up to 7B dense, then extrapolated

t104|494.c: Someone would build a large linear model soon, so better to find a backer and build it himself.
t104|494.e: His lab's compute topped out at 15 billion parameters, and he figured someone would build a large linear model by late 2024 at the latest. Starting his own company meant a chicken-and-egg trap: proving the architecture needs a top model, and a top model needs vast data and training capacity. In China, mainly ByteDance and MiniMax could take it on. ByteDance showed little interest, since big companies rarely shift major resources to highly uncertain bets. MiniMax founder Junjie Yan was willing to make it the flagship model.
ex: Joining the top tier takes more than 10 trillion tokens of data
Junjie Yan wasn't confident, yet still committed 80 to 90 percent of company resources

items.d: He rated his own confidence above 90%
He guesses Yan's was about half

t104|494.c: Weak long-text performance comes from too little training data, not from the linear architecture.
t104|494.e: When the host tested it, MiniMax-01 drifted off topic on long-article tasks. He doesn't deny it, but argues real performance depends closely on training data, while architecture only provides potential. In strict comparisons with standard architectures on the same data, the new design shows no disadvantage; the current version simply lacks long-text data, so its ability hasn't been fully drawn out. The team has reached a 4-million-token context, but the bottleneck is now building data and finding use cases, so they're making 1 million solid first.
ex: The next version plans native multimodality plus deep reasoning, and will be open-sourced
He thinks the best promotion for a technology is putting it in a product for everyone

t105|496.c: Offline throughput doesn't carry over to production; irregular request lengths drag down machine utilization.
t105|496.e: He stresses that his criticism targets small cloud vendors reselling DeepSeek's API and claiming tenfold faster inference, not DeepSeek itself, and he won't comment on its official figures. In his tests, throughput fell as inputs and outputs got longer. Real model-as-a-service (MaaS) traffic, meaning model access sold by usage, mixes translation, summaries and multi-turn chats, so request lengths are highly irregular and machine utilization swings wildly. Ideal offline numbers can't simply carry over to live service.
ex: Performance peaks at 1K tokens in and out, and drops clearly at 8K output
With 32K input and 8K output, two machines produce just over 100 tokens per second

items.d: Official number, method not broken down

t105|496.c: MaaS is stuck in a billing mismatch: suppliers charge by machine time, customers pay by token.
t105|496.e: Platforms rent GPUs from data centers and pay by machine time, even when idle, while the apps they serve pay only per token and don't care whether machines are fully used. The MaaS platform in the middle carries all the idle risk. It can't throttle traffic either, since that would cap customers' growth, so it must reserve far more capacity than average demand. He thinks a 2x buffer is far from safe: the more apps there are, the bigger the spikes in demand.
ex: His own estimate: serving 100B output tokens a day needs about 500B of capacity
He says small platforms may recover just 1 yuan for every 100 invested

items.d: Charge by machine time, idle or not

t105|496.c: Third-party MaaS without its own model advantage ends in a pure price war.
t105|496.e: Using open-source inference frameworks like vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT as the baseline, he believes most small cloud vendors can't be meaningfully faster. Claimed tenfold speedups mostly come from parameter settings or extreme scenarios, and any speedup must sacrifice something else. Pure resellers have no model of their own and software that rarely beats open source, so they can only compete on price. Big companies can spread idle cost across super-apps and huge user bases, and only companies with a uniquely strong model can make money.
ex: He bets 99% of small cloud vendors won't be clearly faster than open source
He warns that services sold as full-strength may be pruned or quantized
Big companies might get back 30 to 50 yuan for every yuan invested

cells.d: Best placed to sell model access
Like ChatGPT, can charge premium prices

t105|496.c: Dedicated machines beat a shared token pool, because capacity risk goes back to the customer.
t105|496.e: He prefers dedicated instances: a customer reserves one or more tuned machines, one for 100 users, two for 200, so the platform no longer pools random requests from many customers. All-in-one appliances from big vendors are steadier too, because the customer fully controls the machine. Mature cloud customers reserve resources anyway. If apps someday rent model capacity by time slot, that would no longer be today's MaaS model.
ex: He sees all-in-one machines from Alibaba Cloud and Volcano Engine as the safer option

d.verdict: Reserve the machines, and the platform stops eating idle cost

t105|496.c: MaaS brings revenue at too high a cost; startups should narrow their focus again and again.
t105|496.e: In early February, Luchen launched a DeepSeek API service with Huawei Ascend, and within a month it announced a pause. He admits the business brought revenue, but losses ran high and the revenue cost too much to earn. Similar companies abroad are rethinking too: some have dropped MaaS, and others actually earn most of their money from compute platforms and GPU rental. Startups with limited resources should first nail their core revenue and revisit MaaS once pricing and GPU utilization mature.
ex: He thinks Anyscale's exit from MaaS first got the industry rethinking
Together AI earns most of its revenue from compute platforms and GPU rental

t105|496.c: High profits reward innovation, and AI needs one or two giants that make huge money.
t105|496.e: He considers Google the biggest contributor to this wave of AGI, because the high profits of search funded years of frontier research. By the same logic, he defends OpenAI's closed models and high prices: a good model should earn more, and outsized profit is the reward for innovation. China needs companies like that too. DeepSeek's open-sourcing, by contrast, carries a grand idealism and isn't a purely commercial move.
ex: Google's lineage includes the Transformer, BERT and AlphaGo

t105|496.c: Most industries need only a small model plus private data, so Luchen is pivoting to post-training.
t105|496.e: He thinks many industries don't need giant models: a base model of around 7 billion parameters plus valuable private data is often enough. So Luchen is positioning itself as a post-training platform, helping companies train and deploy industry-specific models with reinforcement learning, distillation and supervised fine-tuning. It will build tightly scoped products rather than compete with big companies for tens-of-millions-yuan projects. He also believes infrastructure work for language models is largely done, and the next breakthrough may come from video and other modalities.
ex: Target deals run 100,000 to 1 million yuan; he likens Luchen to an AI Databricks
One Fortune 500 client bought about 1,000 A100/A800 GPUs

Deliverable directly if quality is good

t106|312.c: AI agents became usable in 2025 because reasoning, coding and tool use all crossed the bar together.
t106|312.e: He sees three core skills behind agents, AI that carries out tasks on its own. Reasoning plans the work and checks that it's done. Coding is the universal language for acting in the digital world. Tool use lets a model operate existing software and websites. Over the past year, benchmark scores on all three jumped from very low to good enough, turning agents from an idea into products. But he cautions that superhuman contest coding isn't the same as everyday software engineering, which means reading huge codebases and handling long context.
ex: GPQA science test: o3 scores 70-plus, while PhD students score about 60
SWE-bench: GPT-4o was in single digits early in the year; o3 models reach 70–80
Codeforces: o3 rates about 2703

The universal language for acting digitally
Plugs into existing software and APIs

t106|312.c: DeepSeek succeeded through a mix of tight resources, focus, open source and neutrality.
t106|312.e: He sees DeepSeek's breakthrough as several factors stacking up. Limited chips pushed it toward cost-cutting designs like MoE and MLA. The team stuck to its core work, skipping image and video generation and AI companions. A young, homegrown team dared to go straight to reinforcement learning, where models improve through trial and reward. Open source let platforms like WeChat and Baidu plug it in directly. And since it wasn't chasing a super app or backed by a tech giant, every camp felt safe using it. He calls it AI's "Android moment": strong capability opened up to far more developers.
ex: Publishing that GRPO works and MCTS doesn't saved the industry from dead ends
Tencent plugged DeepSeek into more than ten products, including Yuanbao and WeChat

No image or video generation, no virtual girlfriends
Platforms and developers can plug it in

t106|312.c: The next big products won't fill your time. They'll save it and keep working while you're away.
t106|312.e: The classic internet growth formula is users × time spent × monetization rate. But screen time already takes up nearly half of waking hours, so both users and time are near their ceiling. The industry still judges AI products by daily users, retention and time spent, which favors time-killers like companion chatbots. Agents are different, he argues. They don't need constant attention, yet they handle non-repetitive tasks on their own. No product has combined both before. Their real value is freeing up human attention.
ex: About 16 waking hours a day, with nearly 8 already spent on screens
Deep Research and Devin work on their own once given a task

items: Measured by daily users and time spent

d.verdict: Attention is not all you need

t106|312.c: Agents that only read are working now. Agents that act in the world must clear safety first.
t106|312.e: He sees Deep Research as the clearest case of agent product-market fit: reports it delivers in minutes already beat his interns' work. But "write" agents that place orders, send emails or operate computers are still slow, costly and need confirmation at every step. The bigger worry is that strong models work around limits to hit a local goal, by requesting permissions, getting a person to do it, or killing system processes by mistake. So agents should get their own cloud computers and separately granted permissions, plus monitoring and abuse prevention, rather than chasing task success alone.
ex: Monica's agent couldn't find a timetable, so it drafted an email to city hall
He had a local agent kill a port-hogging process, then feared it could hit system ones

Every step needs confirming; worse than a human

t106|312.c: In the US, replacing human work with AI already makes financial sense.
t106|312.e: His logic: first make a capability exist, then let chips, engineering and scale make it cheap. At the prices then, a coding agent cost less per hour than California's minimum wage. A deep research report worked out to a few dollars, available at midnight and not necessarily worse than a person's. So he believes the future is already here. People fluent with frontier models and people just meeting chatbots experience productivity as if they lived in different eras.
ex: Devin costs about $6–8 an hour; California's minimum wage is about $16
ChatGPT Pro: $200 a month buys about 100 research runs, roughly $2 each

items.d: A coding agent at about $6–8 an hour

t106|312.c: Money can now turn directly into work, which could create super-individuals or concentrate resources further.
t106|312.e: Turning money into output used to mean hiring, training and managing people. Agents shorten that to money into compute, and compute into work. That depends on models improving and on longer thinking time keeping its payoff. Today, an hour of thinking isn't always better than five minutes. To those who doubt society needs this much productivity, he points to cars and electricity: supply creates new demand. Distribution cuts both ways. Individuals can do a big company's work with agents, while the rich and big firms can run tens of thousands of agents at once.
ex: About 13 years from AlexNet to this interview; exponential curves look straight early on

items.d: No hiring, training or managing first
If longer reasoning keeps paying off
Super-individuals and concentration, side by side

t106|312.c: Once reinforcement learning reaches tasks with checkable answers, every industry will get its "Lee Sedol moment."
t106|312.e: He sees a pattern. When a task has clear boundaries and verifiable results, reinforcement learning, where AI improves through trial and reward, quickly pushes AI past the best humans. It happened in Go, StarCraft and competitive programming. Lee Sedol is the Go world champion who lost to AlphaGo. Each such moment shatters people's belief in their intellectual edge and draws more people to AI. He expects AI to beat most people at many more tasks in 2025. He worries that once tests are nearly maxed out, humans will struggle to tell what AI can and can't do.
ex: AlphaGo, AlphaStar and contest coding have all seen superhuman AI
Pick ten people at random, and at least nine research worse than Deep Research

items.d: Rapid gains through trial and error
Like a grade-schooler writing a PhD exam

t106|312.c: Don't rush to monetize while capabilities are soaring. Chatbot product-market fit could even become a trap.
t106|312.e: He points out that BlackBerry's keyboard and Yahoo's portal were winning formats that later held back the next leap. Chatbots, built on short scattered exchanges, also struggle to separate ordinary users from experts, while agents need input closer to a full plan. When capability is rising fast, build capability first. Once the curve flattens, build a business around what has matured. The internet's giants also had products for years before finding business models. There's no need to send a bright high schooler off to haul bricks right away.
ex: Google launched with no ads in 1998 and went public in 2004
Facebook launched in 2005 and added News Feed ads only in 2012

items.d: AdWords and other models in place
Core model found after feed ranking

t107|499.c: AI hardware's earliest and most loyal real users are children, not young adults.
t107|499.e: While working on Tmall Genie, Alibaba's smart speaker, he found that most voice interactions came from kids. Adults expect too much of AI and drop it when older technology falls short, but kids keep talking to it. So he pushed a children's story machine inside Alibaba. It sold tens of thousands of units before being shut down as not strategic enough, and that insight later became Haivivi's starting point. His lesson: people overestimate one to three years of progress and underestimate ten.
ex: Tmall Genie sold about 30 million units in total
Alibaba shut down the Tmall Genie story machine after tens of thousands of sales

items.d: Works on Tmall Genie; sees kids love it
As CMO, incubates a kids' business
Large models open a new opportunity

t107|499.c: Startups can't beat education giants with AI learning gadgets, so they should sell emotional value instead.
t107|499.e: His first venture made learning gadgets and dictionary pens, selling hundreds of thousands. But once Yuanfudao and Xueersi moved in, products started to look alike and a price war broke out, and he realized he wasn't good at squeezing thin margins from the supply chain. After large models arrived, putting ChatGPT into a learning gadget might earn quick money for a year. Within three to five years, though, it would lose to giants that own the models, content, curriculum teams and brands. So he moved the fight from education to emotional value and picked plush toys, a rising category.
ex: He had already noticed the buzz around Jellycat, Pop Mart and Miniso plush toys

items.d: Not built for thin supply-chain margins
Emotional value that commands a premium

t107|499.c: Starting with 3-to-6-year-olds manages expectations; adults must wait for end-to-end voice AI to mature.
t107|499.e: Kids aged 3 to 6 speak fairly fully, ask lots of questions, usually don't have phones, and expect little from AI. A clear character also makes an unanswerable question look like that character's limit, not a product failure. He admits 7- and 10-year-olds find it useless, so he deliberately narrowed the age range to protect word of mouth. He doesn't see birth rates as a ceiling. Adults are plush toys' main buyers, but 2023 models couldn't deliver what adults need. If end-to-end voice, one model that both hears and speaks, works on experience and cost in 2025, the adult market opens.
ex: A Peppa Pig-style character explains quantum entanglement to kids
Kids' lines may be under 20% of leading plush brands' business

items.d: Low expectations; the character is a safety net
Wait for voice AI to work on cost and experience
Many full AI plush characters side by side

t107|499.c: The clip-on form and push-to-talk were deliberate choices under tight cash, not oversights.
t107|499.e: A full AI plush toy needs multiple product versions, character licensing, long reviews and R&D, which 2023 funding couldn't cover. So they first made a charm that clips onto plush toys kids already own, which was also easier to explain to young mothers who aren't into tech. The charm's battery is small, so weighing battery life, cost and speed to market, they chose push-to-talk. Role-play, continuous conversation and memory came before hands-free wake-up. He says hardware takes months from design to tooling, and one wrong call can drain a startup's cash.
ex: The first bad reviews came from Wi-Fi and app setup; most moms skip the manual
After launch, its Douyin livestream peaked at over 3,000 viewers

t107|499.c: Anyone can plug in a large model; the hard part is making an AI toy a lasting brand.
t107|499.e: He reckons at least a hundred teams could hack together a batch of AI toys. But the full chain spans software, hardware, algorithms, emotional understanding, use cases, characters, marketing and supply chain. Getting all of it to 80 out of 100 and into a brand is hard. China's supply chain can make Jellycat-quality plush but won't automatically produce a Jellycat; the difference is marketing, taste and design. A physical product is also unlike a free app. With seven-day no-questions returns, it must prove its worth the moment it's unboxed.
ex: Character.AI and Talkie are free; people expect far more from physical hardware
A team of young moms decided details like the double-bubble shape and hidden logo

items.d: Marketing, design, characters: hardest to copy
Knowing what kids and parents want
Hundreds of teams can do it

t107|499.c: AI toys are like Go, not chess: many brands can coexist, and big tech won't jump in itself.
t107|499.e: He sees phones, earbuds and glasses as tools where one per person is enough, so competition is close to all-or-nothing. Plush and collectible toys get bought again and again, so many characters and brands can each hold ground. His Tmall Genie story-machine experience convinced him big companies struggle to rally cross-team resources for a small toy. Copycats will come. The real opponent is himself: can he run several products in parallel and stay disciplined once money is plentiful? He sees partnerships with listed Chinese toy makers that own factories and characters as a second business model.
ex: The long-term goal is to become the Pop Mart of the AI era
Beware growth that just adds people: 20 people for two products, 40 for four

items: One phone, one pair of earbuds each

d.verdict: AI plush is more like Go; no winner-take-all

t107|499.c: The hardest part of kids' AI isn't blocking harmful content but handling values society disagrees on.
t107|499.e: Kids' products have two customers: parents who pay and children who use them. Kids must feel accompanied, and parents must believe it helps, so parents can set reminders and encouragement themes and get weekly growth reports. But he avoids structured courses, since models still hallucinate and the company has no curriculum team. Harder are questions with no social consensus, like whether to hit back when hit. The product stresses safety and talking it out, and leaves the decision to parents. Religion and death can come up, but only so deep, and users can't create their own characters yet.
ex: A child felt neglected after a baby brother arrived; it explained love hadn't shrunk
Characters are reviewed before launch, trading openness for content control

root.d: Kids want company; parents want peace of mind

items.d: Reminders to drink water, courage, weekly reports
On hitting back, it only stresses safety and talking

t108|359.c: Intelligence means finding predictable structure in a world drifting toward disorder, then using it to decide better.
t108|359.e: He sees the universe as a whole sliding toward disorder, or rising entropy, yet pockets of regularity remain. Life and intelligence are mechanisms that use those regularities to predict and act. The key is compression: the senses take in huge amounts of information, but only a few bits reach the higher levels. Intelligence throws away irrelevant detail and keeps the structure that matters for prediction. This local order isn't free. Even a diffusion model creating an image from noise needs outside energy from power, chips and compute. If the universe ends in pure chaos, intelligence has nothing left to learn.
ex: Diffusion models create local order out of noise, but need outside energy to do it

items.d: Local order needs energy from outside

t108|359.c: DNA was the first large model, and the evolution of species is essentially reinforcement learning.
t108|359.e: He sees DNA as a kind of pretrained model. Random mutation, feedback from the environment and natural selection kept writing experience into genes and passing it on for about three billion years, much like reinforcement learning by trial and reward. Once nervous systems and vision appeared, individuals could form memories after birth, like fine-tuning an inherited model. Smarter animals spend longer learning after birth. Language and writing let experience be shared and kept across generations, taking over part of DNA's job. But intelligence lives in the loop between a species and its environment; a strand of DNA isn't intelligent.
ex: Nervous systems and vision appeared about 550 million years ago
Birds stay with their parents about 3 months; humans about 18 years

items.d: Species-level pretraining over about 3 billion years
Experience shared and kept across generations

t108|359.c: Knowledge is what intelligence produces, not intelligence itself; systems without feedback only cope with closed worlds.
t108|359.e: He argues that a static body of knowledge isn't intelligent. Neither DNA, nor a base model, nor any GPT generation counts. The intelligence is in the ongoing process of spotting errors and improving the model. So he's skeptical of simply stretching the context window, how much a model reads at once, and prefers closed-loop memory that lasts and corrects itself. Open-loop systems learn once and handle familiar settings with what they learned. Only closed-loop systems that keep correcting themselves through feedback can adapt to an open world.
ex: He thinks GPT-1 through GPT-4 aren't intelligent; the human process improving them is

d.verdict: Intelligence is self-correction, not how much is known

t108|359.c: Machine intelligence began with 1940s cybernetics, and today's hype already happened in the 1950s.
t108|359.e: He argues the 1956 Dartmouth conference isn't the real start. Cybernetics, information theory, game theory and mathematical models of neurons are. Their goal was machines that correct themselves in a loop, like animals; researchers even studied how cats hunt to design gun tracking. The Dartmouth generation deliberately sidestepped cybernetics for symbols and logic, describing human intelligence without explaining where abstraction comes from. During the boom around the perceptron, an early neural network, the press said machines would think and become self-aware. The chill that followed wasn't because neural networks were useless. Their structure, learning methods and compute weren't ready.
ex: The 1958 perceptron project cost over $6 million, about $1 billion today

items.d: Wiener, Shannon and others lay out feedback loops
A turn to symbols and logic
Inspired by studies of cat vision
Data, GPUs and deep networks come together

t108|359.c: o1- and R1-style reasoning still imitates problem types, and more compute now brings diminishing returns.
t108|359.e: He splits reasoning into three levels: imitating problem types and patterns, mastering logic and checking your own work, and discovering new laws and axioms. Today's models solve hard math problems yet make silly mistakes on grade-school questions, so they haven't truly mastered logic. He places them mostly at level one. The recipe of supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning and longer chains of thought is like alchemy: scores rise, but it isn't human reasoning. Meanwhile, returns from more compute are falling. Fixed benchmarks can't tell drilling from understanding, so testing should work like an oral exam, probing and rephrasing questions.
ex: Grok used about 200,000 GPUs, yet its base model improved by under 1%
He doesn't think the Turing test has been passed

items.d: No silly mistakes on easy problems
Where today's large models mostly sit

t108|359.c: DeepSeek showed there's no deep secret in large models, and open source will catch up with closed.
t108|359.e: To him, DeepSeek shows the so-called secret sauce isn't deep. A decent base model plus published methods gets close to comparable performance. The real differences come from data, compute, time to experiment and team experience. He also notes that the cost of the final successful training run isn't the full R&D bill. One success doesn't guarantee the next, unless the method has become a system that keeps improving. A longtime open-source advocate, he says open source catching up with closed models is a question of when and where, not whether.
ex: He says shells rarely land in the same crater twice: success is hard to repeat

terms.d: Fine-tuning, RL, long chains of thought

result.d: Only data, compute and trial time differ

t108|359.c: Academia shouldn't compete with industry on scale; it should find where current understanding falls short.
t108|359.e: He sees a scientist's core job as finding where current understanding falls short. Short on resources, academics gain nothing by building lookalike large models and chasing leaderboards. They should pin down what stage intelligence has reached and design tests that separate memorizing, understanding and abstracting. He trained himself to be the hardest person to convince. One of his papers was rejected for results too good to believe, and accepted only after a summer of extra comparisons, so he expects new frameworks may go unrecognized for years. At HKU he has pushed a science course for entrepreneurs and a required AI course for all undergraduates.
ex: HKU's science class for entrepreneurs planned 40–50 students; the first intake had 80
The AI course is required of all undergraduates and worth 6 credits

root.d: Not compete with industry on scale

items.d: New frameworks may go unrecognized for years
Explain the principles and where AI fails

t108|359.c: Next-generation intelligence should be transparent, layered and self-correcting, with embodied AI as its natural killer app.
t108|359.e: He sees today's AI as mechanical compression and generation. Next, mathematical principles should replace the trial-and-error redundancy inside Transformers, giving a "white box" whose workings you can understand. Like the cerebral cortex, it should run parallel, layered, multi-loop systems that predict and correct at every level. Embodied AI, AI with a body acting in the real world, needs a perception-action loop by nature, so it's the most natural fit. End-to-end vision-language-action models may pay off with enough data and compute, just as planes fly without being birds, but not efficiently. New mechanisms may look useless until they cross a tipping point, so they need patient capital.
ex: His team says DINO-style vision systems can be greatly simplified and perform better
1990s robots could run and jump but had "no brain, no eyes"

items.d: A body interacts with the world

t109|507.c: Building an AI product doesn't mean you can sell it; custom software for financial institutions loses money.
t109|507.e: In 2023 his team built Chat Fund, a Q&A product about mutual funds. They saw their edge in fund-analysis methods and processed data, not in owning a model. Technically they moved from fine-tuning to retrieval, using a small model to detect what users wanted and GPT-3.5 to write answers. The product worked, but sales stalled. Standard packages hit procurement caps, while big clients wanted on-premise deployment, only their own funds promoted, and embedding in mini-programs. Each client meant rebuilding databases, prompts and interfaces, plus on-site staff. Expecting losses, he stopped that same year.
ex: Fine-tuning on about 1,000 examples cost about $70; daily fine-tuning wasn't viable
Standard packages capped at about ¥200,000; anything more needed internal review

root.d: Chat Fund could be built, not sold

items.d: It's the methods and processed data

t109|507.c: Mass-producing content with AI raises the floor, but the ceiling still depends on firsthand experience and judgment.
t109|507.e: He built an information pipeline where AI scrapes trending topics, then scores and clusters them. He reviews only the top few dozen and picks ten, which cuts topic selection time sharply. But trying products, forming judgments and voicing opinions can't be outsourced, he says, or you just produce junk. For the same reason he refuses to let a digital avatar or cloned voice stand in for him on camera. A real person sharing knowledge runs on trust, and the audience needs to know who is accountable.
ex: Topic hunting fell from five or six hours a day to about one
When AI content floods in, human traces like typos become rare

items: Appear in person and take responsibility

d.verdict: Scale lifts the floor, not the ceiling

t109|507.c: Anything you've done three times should be handed to AI or automation, freeing time for judgment.
t109|507.e: His rule: by the third time you do something, automate it. He now rarely drags nodes around in workflow builders. Instead he asks AI in plain language to write small plugins or web scrapers. In a multi-dimensional spreadsheet, every column can call a model to tag, translate or summarize. The payoff is biggest for organizations: screening sign-ups and complex grouping that once took several people days now take one night or a dozen minutes. He also matches models to tasks, using GPT for rigorous analysis and occasionally Claude for creative work and coding.
ex: Sign-ups for a 2,400-person event were screened in one night
Grouping by 8 rules took o1 Pro about 11 minutes, versus two days for 11 people

items.d: Have AI write plugins and scrapers

t109|507.c: General-purpose agents are still toys, because success rates multiply downward with every added step.
t109|507.e: He sees an agent, AI that acts on its own, as planning plus tool use plus memory, with memory deciding whether long tasks stay coherent. The problem is that every step can fail, so the overall success rate drops fast as steps add up. That makes zero-tolerance fields like medicine even harder. In his tests, early Manus succeeded on only two of ten tasks, rising to 50–60% only after he narrowed the tasks. Focused tools such as Deep Research for research and Cursor for coding proved more reliable.
ex: Early Manus completed only about 2 of 10 tasks
Deep Research writes a roughly 20,000-character report in about 30 minutes

terms.d: Long tasks often take a dozen or more

result.d: General agents still feel like toys

t109|507.c: Thin apps that just wrap a model in templates get swallowed; community, data and workflows endure.
t109|507.e: He points to Jasper, which grew on marketing-copy templates. Once models got stronger, users had no reason to keep using a middle layer. What survives is what models can't replace: community, proprietary data, workflows woven into users' daily routines, and networks of users. He doesn't start a company himself partly because he has no model background and won't build a thin wrapper around someone else's model. He also thinks big companies hold overwhelming advantages in compute, data, talent and money, so AI startups rarely succeed.
ex: Jasper started with marketing templates and faces rising risk as models improve

marks.d: Focused tools win on experience and habit

t109|507.c: DeepSeek brought huge numbers of new users to AI, but reasoning models are drifting away from ordinary people.
t109|507.e: He estimates DeepSeek may have added hundreds of millions of AI users in China, many of whom met AI through it first. Because it shows its chain of thought, users who get a bad answer first rethink how they asked instead of dismissing the AI. But he cautions that reasoning models pour their effort into math, code and science, so ordinary users notice upgrades less and less. Buzz alone doesn't show who leads overall: in his screenwriting tests, o1 Pro felt more literary.
ex: He calls skipping a post on DeepSeek's launch day a mistake that hurt trust
Manus sent invite codes only to influencers, spawning a scalper market

items.d: DeepSeek brings a flood of new users
Upgrades focus on math, code and science

t109|507.c: Ordinary people should pair their own field with AI, starting with their biggest time sinks, not chasing hype.
t109|507.e: He thinks the scarce people are those who know an industry and can weave AI into its workflows, so the field comes first and AI second. Learning AI starts by asking which tasks eat the most time or are most dreaded, then finding tools for them. Learning every new tool you see swaps tactical busyness for strategic choice. He has seen readers land internships or take over AI projects at state-owned firms. Teachers, judges and even farmers in his groups build small AI tools. To him, that matters more than grand AGI narratives.
ex: He runs 30-plus groups of about 15,000 people; AI summarizes their chats daily
He calls himself a doorman at the gate of AI's temple

cells.d: Learn every AI tool, with no real use
AI woven into their own field's workflows
Bring in AI via the most time-consuming tasks

t110|511.c: After DeepSeek, every company should make agents, AI that finishes tasks on its own, a core R&D direction.
t110|511.e: He sees self-driving cars, robots and software agents as sharing one core: using tools, interacting with the world and finishing tasks people assign. Reasoning models like DeepSeek's outclassed chat products and made teams take agents seriously, level 3 on OpenAI's five-level scale. After talking with model companies, he expects top agents' completion rate on the hardest tier of the GAIA benchmark to rise from just over 50% to above 80% within a year. Startups that don't design products as L3 agents could lose their edge within a year.
ex: Manus scores just over 50% on GAIA's hardest tier
He calls "80% of human work" a rough phrase, not a jobs forecast

items.d: Could lose ground within a year

t110|511.c: A fight over general-purpose phone agents is coming; winners need both a top model and an existing ecosystem.
t110|511.e: He believes model companies have moved beyond base models. Memory, computer use, MCP (a standard way to plug models into tools) and function calling are all part of their agent push. The richer the tools, the more unavoidable the fight over the general-purpose gateway. On an aggressive view, general agent apps will battle on phones in the second half of this year, since food delivery and ride-hailing live on mobile. Meituan and Didi don't want to be dispatched by someone else again, but the prize tempts big tech. Google, ByteDance and Alibaba have ecosystems; OpenAI, Anthropic and DeepSeek lead on models. Lacking either is a handicap.
ex: Manus reportedly connects to about 29 tools, mostly via function calling
Glasses may only fit small 3B or 7B models, leaving fewer openings

terms.d: The strength of OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek
Existing ecosystems at Google, ByteDance, Alibaba

result.d: Missing either puts you on the back foot

t110|511.c: Model companies will take about 80% of a job's generic work, leaving the specialized long tail to vertical players.
t110|511.e: He draws the line between generality and precision. Model companies profit by spreading costs across general use, so they'll keep absorbing generic tasks. What's left is a specialized long tail that needs industry methods, workflows, data and dedicated tools. Customizing it is costly, so it isn't a priority for them. It's not that they can't build vertical tools; they just won't serve every industry themselves. Products close to their main path, like Manus and Perplexity, risk having search and research folded into model makers' own apps, even while growing. Depth beats breadth.
ex: Kimi and Perplexity kept growing despite DeepSeek, possibly helped by paid marketing

marks.d: Model makers cover about 80% of a job
Search and research tools face most risk
Costly to customize; not a model-maker priority

t110|511.c: Vertical agents shouldn't patch old software; they must rebuild workflows in small, fragmented industries.
t110|511.e: After DeepSeek took off, bosses' tech anxiety first benefited RPA, software robots that automate clicks. SaaS companies that add an AI team without changing workflows are just patching, which incumbents can do themselves. He sets three criteria: rebuild the existing process, enter industries that have long been small, scattered and hard to structure, and start with low-hanging fruit current technology can reliably handle. Turning people's standard procedures into detailed workflows can cover model weaknesses, but that edge fades as barriers fall. More durable advantages come from new business flows, new organizations and platform effects.
ex: Full Truck Alliance began by putting freight notice boards online to match trucks and cargo
SHEIN's small, fast reorders pushed upstream factories to digitize

items.d: What tech can reliably deliver now
A more lasting edge than workflows

t110|511.c: Chinese vertical agents should deliver whole outcomes for a cut of results, not copy US per-seat pricing.
t110|511.e: In the US, legal and sales agents assist professionals without owning the outcome, and charge by usage or per seat. Chinese companies have less willingness and ability to pay, and prefer paying for results. They accept either leads they can act on directly or the result of a whole business process. So Chinese vertical agents suit full outsourcing for a percentage, with AI replacing or guiding people so non-experts can run expert processes. He sees this as a very big difference between the two countries.
ex: AI law firm Aiyu Zhineng filed about 15,000 cases in March alone
AI hotel marketing on Douyin takes about 10% of sales; traditional sales cost about 20%

items.d: Aiyu takes about 30% of money recovered

t110|511.c: Agents will weaken search ads, but ads woven into interactive content could work far better.
t110|511.e: When agents search, compare and act for people, nobody sees the raw results, so paid ranking slots lose their meaning. Recommendation systems built for humans can't simply be handed to agents either. He doubts subscriptions are the most efficient way to make money in the AI era, since they offer fewer levers to tune than ads. At the other end, ads that blend naturally into a virtual character's or AI chat's context could convert many times better. That only works if the blend is good; otherwise it just annoys people.
ex: Overseas general AI products rely on subscriptions; in China they're nearly free

items: Agents search and compare for you

d.verdict: Ads won't vanish; they'll move from search to interactive content

t110|511.c: GPT-4o image generation hits mass-market tools first; pros are protected by taste communities and workflows.
t110|511.e: He splits image tools into three tiers: professional creators, marketers and everyday phone users. The broader the audience, the lower the prices and paying rates, and the more people want free, one-step results. GPT-4o's image generation hits casual, low-demand users hardest, not Photoshop's core users, whose work is built on layer-based editing. The defense isn't that models can never do fine control. It's that aesthetic communities, professional workflows and tool combinations don't come bundled with a base model. He even sees it as good news for Liblib, built around a community of LoRA style add-ons.
ex: Adobe's suite: over 100 million monthly users at $50-plus a month (his estimate)
Canva costs about $10–15 a month; Meitu about $2–3

items.d: Canva: low-end uses take a hit
Meitu and others: want one step, hit hardest

t110|511.c: Embodied AI hasn't had its GPT-3 moment, and the biggest risk is sliding back into systems integration.
t110|511.e: He agrees embodied AI, AI with a body working in the physical world, is early to commercialize, but disagrees that it isn't worth backing. Hardware engineering for two- and four-legged robots has clearly matured, and combining imitation learning with reinforcement learning has made them smarter. The core gap is pretraining: the field doesn't know where data comes from, how to process it, or which algorithms generalize across settings. Without that, embodied AI becomes a huge bubble, and companies end up doing grinding integration work like the last generation of robotics. He thinks full commercialization may take three to five years or longer.
ex: Mingshi backed LimX Dynamics in August 2022, reasoning by analogy from end-to-end text models
He checks whether founders have grown noticeably after three months

items.d: Robotics is about matching tech to problems

t111|514.c: Language models should only be an agent's front end; an RL-trained back end should plan and use tools.
t111|514.e: He treats the language model as the interface: it understands what users want and handles conversation. The real planning, reasoning and tool selection go to a non-language model trained with reinforcement learning, which learns by trial and reward. His reason: stuffing tool descriptions, memory and multi-step results into the context window balloons fast. One task can pile up over a million tokens, and the model starts hallucinating. He also rejects letting models build their own tools. Without documentation you can't reliably connect to new platforms, and retraining a language model for each batch of new APIs isn't economical.
ex: 50 tools at 1,000 tokens each means about 50,000 tokens of descriptions alone
The first release connects about 1,000 sub-tools across dozens of platforms

items.d: States the task in plain language
Understands needs and talks with people
Real accounts: social media, e-commerce dashboards

t111|514.c: RL's real challenge is sample efficiency; smart exploration can cut the data needed by an order of magnitude.
t111|514.e: In reinforcement learning, the data needed grows with the number of actions, states and planning steps, so with many tools a naive approach needs an unmanageable amount. When only one of ten thousand tools is right, random exploration yields almost nothing but negative feedback. His approach is to first use generalization to shrink the set of tools worth considering, then explore smartly. Skip tools known to be useless, prune branches already shown to fail, and explore only what's truly unknown. He estimates this cuts data needs to a tenth or less, and calls it the company's core technology.
ex: 10,000 tools needing 100 data points each means a million the naive way
He finds approaches like contrastive learning disappointing

items.d: Data needs may drop to a tenth

t111|514.c: Agents should act through official APIs first, then code; browser automation isn't the future.
t111|514.e: He ranks execution methods. Use an official API whenever possible, then have the system write code to call services. Mimicking a person clicking through a browser is the last resort: slow, token-hungry and unreliable. He doesn't use MCP yet but plans to support it, alongside a lighter JSON-based way to connect. He judges peers the same way. Operator is better at taking actions but has a low success rate. Manus is strong at research and synthesis and well engineered, but doesn't solve the back-end problem he cares about.
ex: Testing Operator and Manus on scheduling meetings and posting, he saw near-zero success

marks.d: Fills gaps where APIs fall short

t111|514.c: The real dividing line for agents is whether they can write to real accounts, so approvals come first.
t111|514.e: He sees Deep Research and Manus as mostly fetching and generating content. He wants to publish and operate directly on social media, websites and e-commerce dashboards. Since that really changes users' accounts, the agent should show its plan first, let users approve or edit it, and say where it's stuck along the way. Enterprise users won't accept changes without consent, while developers find approvals slow, so he keeps both a supervised mode and a fully automatic one. When a subtask fails, it skips if it can but doesn't retry automatically for now, since a retry may stray from what the user meant.
ex: LinkedIn blocks duplicate posts; reworded reposts get through but may not match user intent

d.verdict: The value is in writing, as long as users stay in control

t111|514.c: A good general agent is faster than people, needs little intervention, can read and write, and is cheap.
t111|514.e: He lays out four standards for a general agent and admits his own product still relies on approvals, so it isn't fully hands-off. On speed, a demo with approvals takes about a minute; without them, ten to twenty seconds. On cost, he says a single task is dozens of times cheaper than with comparable products. But he concedes this is a temporary edge from his current architecture. Others will keep pushing compute costs down, so it can't serve as a long-term moat.
ex: A demo takes about 60 seconds with approvals, 10–20 seconds without
He says each task costs dozens of times less than with similar products

items.d: Not just fetching; posts and operates too

t111|514.c: Horizontal agents should start with developers and professionals, then work their way up into enterprises.
t111|514.e: He sees the pain of advertising and social media workers shifting from creating content to distributing and running it across platforms, like replying to comments one by one. They're the first group ready to adopt. Enterprise workflows of dozens to hundreds of steps are the bigger end market. There, agents should cut steps and hand off to people when needed, not copy old processes. Drag-and-drop workflow tools break when processes change, so he's building a higher-level planner. Private clouds, model size and data sensitivity mean enterprises must wait until individuals and small teams prove it out.
ex: A week after the demo, 800-plus joined the waitlist, converting at about 8–9%
Overly general consumer products make users overestimate what they can do

items.d: Accept full automation and give fast feedback

t111|514.c: Technology always gets copied; the moat comes from integrating first, scaling and embedding in users' workflows.
t111|514.e: He admits it's a speed game, and no algorithm stays exclusive for long. What matters is finishing integrations first, scaling up, and building up users' past material and account connections, so one sentence can pull old content and post it to several platforms. He expects at least ten horizontal agent companies within a year, with maybe three to five surviving. Horizontal platforms won't kill vertical companies; they can serve as their foundation. China's model ecosystem is open but its business ecosystem is closed, so cross-platform agents may need to partner with tech giants.
ex: Facebook overtaking MySpace shows why adjusting strategy matters
North America, with its APIs and SDKs, has the most open business ecosystem

terms.d: Keep users' material and account links

t111|514.c: Start research with a tiny but convincing example, and once the direction is right, be a bit stubborn.
t111|514.e: His method is to start with a minimal example that is cheap to compute, intuitive and general, and that other approaches can't solve in principle while his can. That confirms a first-principles advantage before scaling up step by step. Jumping straight to large experiments involves too many variables to tell what's working. Pointing to how Rich Sutton and Geoffrey Hinton were long doubted, he argues direction shouldn't be set by passing consensus. He believed in language models early but felt that boat was full, so he dug into reinforcement learning, where his experience runs deepest.
ex: The travel-planning demo and Shopify project both stress-test the general architecture
A minimal example gives about 80% confidence that an idea will work

items.d: Other methods can't do it in principle

t112|518.c: Embodied AI has moved from scattered research to converging engineering, which opens a window for startups.
t112|518.e: By 2023 he felt there was less and less research left to do. GPT-4 already handled everyday tasks fairly well, leaving little new ground in the basic problems around them. Academic topics in embodied AI also narrowed sharply. It's not that only one path remains; many haven't been disproven but are seen as having limited promise. He agrees with his co-founder Fengtao Han: traditional robots were limited by hand-written programs, large models offer the first foundation for general tasks, and the contest now is engineering.
ex: He estimates academic topics narrowed from about 500 to about 100

t112|518.c: Today's best robots just passed L1; the big leap is L3, doing 70–80% of tasks in one setting.
t112|518.e: He grades robots by ability. L1 does a single task at a fixed spot. L2 moves around one setting and handles five to eight tasks. L3 covers 70–80% of what humans do in that setting, and higher levels cover every task, then any setting. He puts Spirit AI and the industry's best just past L1. Extrapolating, L2 may arrive by mid next year and L3 in another 18 months to two years, though he stresses this isn't a proven timeline. Revenue should follow the levels: L1 customers already pay over ¥100,000 per workstation, and L2 multiplies the doable tasks more than tenfold.
ex: An L2 example: making coffee and tidying desks in an office
You can't expect mature commercialization at the GPT-1 stage

t112|518.c: Embodied AI doesn't mean humanoid; the bottleneck is hands, and wheeled two-armed robots will lead shipments.
t112|518.e: A robot that moves but can't manipulate is worth little, he argues, since people still load and unload it at both ends. Wheeled bases matured long ago yet never made it into offices, which shows the missing piece is hand skills. So the simplest L2 setup is two arms on a wheeled base; legs are needed only for stairs or outdoors. Human form matters because the world is built to human scale, so mimicking people at least guarantees physical feasibility. He sees no fundamental block for two-legged walking, mainly engineering stability. General robots won't replace all specialized machines; both will coexist.
ex: Tables are about 75 cm high; indoor spaces are built to human size
Molds are still fastest for plastic cups; nobody would use a general robot

items.d: Flat settings like offices and factories

t112|518.c: Embodied AI will end up with end-to-end VLA models; hand-built layers are just a convenience for now.
t112|518.e: He treats end-to-end and VLA, vision-language-action models, as the same thing: images and language go in, actions come out. In theory this covers all manipulation, with limits set mainly by sensors. Layered designs are easier today, but given over a decade of self-driving experience, he thinks hand-built layers won't get far. An end-to-end model can still have fast and slow parts. The fast system handles touch and low-level vision at high frequency, holding things steady and regripping instantly. The slow system understands language, forms intent and structures the task. Folding clothes is hard not because of force, but because of reading how tangled they are.
ex: The fast system handles touch feedback at about 50–100 Hz
Around 2016 he researched end-to-end self-driving

items: Vision and language straight to action

d.verdict: It will end up end-to-end

t112|518.c: Internet video teaches a model how to move, real-robot data teaches precision, and reinforcement learning teaches by doing.
t112|518.e: Spirit AI uses data in stages. First it pretrains on internet images, text and videos of people handling things. Only about 1% is truly relevant, and first-person video works best: by predicting how objects and hands move, the model learns how objects should be handled. Next, teleoperation data from real robots fine-tunes it for precision. Finally, reinforcement learning raises the success rate. He admits watching alone doesn't teach doing, like watching your mom cook for ten years and still botching the salt. RL has a threshold effect: after the first success it gets easier, and it transfers across plugging and twisting tasks.
ex: Even with a person guiding the robot's hand, 5–10% of attempts fail
Experience plugging in USB transfers to other plugging tasks

items.d: Learning by doing, past the success threshold

t112|518.c: Embodied AI follows scaling laws too; reaching its "GPT-3.5 moment" means learning nearly all video online.
t112|518.e: Between about 100,000 and several hundred thousand data points, he sees the log of data volume track the gap to best performance in a straight line. Roughly, ten times the data adds one more nine to the success rate. By that math, an embodied GPT-3.5 needs huge amounts of useful video, around 100 million teleoperation examples and tens of millions of RL examples. With only about 1% of video usable, that means learning almost every usable video online, which he thinks takes four to five years. Simulation can generate endless data, but with limited variety, so the same rule doesn't apply per example.
ex: He estimates about 10 billion useful videos and 100 million teleoperation examples
AI is the shortest stave in the barrel; scaling laws are only the theory

terms.d: Useful clips filtered from 100x raw footage

t112|518.c: Brain and body must be built together so the model develops "muscle memory" for a specific body.
t112|518.e: Building only the brain lets you study methods, he argues, but rarely solves real problems. Humans can't just switch bodies either, and a model not trained on a specific body lacks the muscle memory for quick, fine movements. Building only the body doesn't work either. Robot bodies haven't fundamentally changed in over a decade; the market grew because AI brains changed, so most of the value sits in the brain. Long term, the industry may look like cars: makers define specs and integrate systems while buying parts. But touch sensors and dexterous hands aren't good enough yet, so for now they build their own.
ex: Chinese hardware gets fixed fast: Unitree repairs take about a week and a half
He rejects trading late nights for output; method matters more

root.d: Spirit AI's choice from day one

items.d: No muscle memory for a specific body
No fundamental change in a decade
The model fits a specific body
Integrate the whole, buy the parts

t113|522.c: The real shift was large-scale pretraining; the Transformer was just the engineering that made it work.
t113|522.e: He believes pretraining, where a model first reads vast amounts of text to learn general knowledge, replaced labeling data from scratch for every task with transferring knowledge. Sentiment analysis once needed tens of thousands of labels; after pretraining, a little fine-tuning did better and even handled unfamiliar phrasing. People had tried pretraining with recurrent networks before BERT, but they were hard to parallelize, so he guesses that without the Transformer, GPT might have arrived just two years later. GPT-3 barely changed the architecture; the key was scaling past 100 billion parameters. He first saw it as a fun experiment, until ChatGPT and GPT-4 proved scale itself is an industrial barrier.
ex: Sentiment analysis needed about 10,000 labels; after pretraining, about 1,000 for fine-tuning
BERT Base has about 100 million parameters; GPT-3 has over 100 billion

items.d: Build data from scratch each time
Hard to reproduce with limited resources

t113|522.c: Rule-based systems are only as smart as the human effort behind them, so they can't scale.
t113|522.e: Rules conflict with each other, resolving conflicts takes new rules, and new rules create new conflicts, so the bigger the system, the harder it is to keep consistent. Knowledge graphs, which organize facts as networks of entities and relations, have the same problem: he thinks keeping such hand-built data current across every industry is basically impossible. By contrast, any task with logic and patterns, even a complex one needing several reasoning steps, can be done very well by data-driven methods. That's why Metaso started with legal translation.
ex: Even Google, investing in knowledge graphs, struggles to cover every industry in real time

items.d: Spins out of control at scale

t113|522.c: Arguing BERT versus GPT is like red pen versus blue; decoder-only won on engineering cost.
t113|522.e: He believes architecture should serve the task. Pitting a 100-billion-parameter decoder-only (GPT-style) model against 10-billion-scale alternatives and declaring the architecture superior isn't fair. No one ever ran a fair comparison at equal size, and encoder-decoder models like T5 traded wins with GPT at similar scale. Decoder-only more likely won on engineering: a single computation path means simpler scheduling and higher throughput, so it scales more easily. He also resists mythologizing certain genius papers, arguing that simple ideas backed by solid experiments are just as valuable.
ex: He estimates decoder-only models have about a 20 to 30 percent throughput edge

d.verdict: Won on engineering and cost, not architecture myth

t113|522.c: Generative AI for every search doesn't pay off; only expensive professional services make the math work.
t113|522.e: Using the generation costs Qihoo 360 disclosed, he calculated that calling a generative model for every search would cost more per year than the company's ad revenue. At prices back then, it didn't work without a new business model. Professional services are the opposite: good law firms charge per word for human translation, senior lawyers bill high hourly rates, and a machine subscription looks cheap by comparison. That's the opening Jasper found. Likewise, Metaso was confident it could beat Google at news translation but skipped it, because users won't pay for low-value content however good it is.
ex: Generating about 200 characters cost about 0.04 yuan
A senior lawyer might charge 5,000 yuan an hour

items.d: His estimate: over 10B yuan a year

t113|522.c: Subscriptions and enterprise sales are both hard in China; standard products dragged into custom projects hurt everyone.
t113|522.e: He thinks Chinese users are less used to paying than users abroad: Jasper quickly passed $100 million in annual recurring revenue, but the same product would struggle in China. Enterprise sales can reach 100 million yuan, but $100 million is rare. Metaso prefers selling standard products to companies, yet clients often drag them into custom work, revising until they're back where they started. Heavy enterprise deals drag on: a small team may spend six months landing a few-hundred-thousand-yuan project that doesn't cover salaries. Clients think paying entitles them to demands, and the vendor loses money just to get a logo for fundraising.
ex: Xiezuocat has over 7 million registered users, with 2 to 5 percent paying
Legal translation reaches about 30 to 50 percent of lawyers doing cross-border work

marks.d: Sell standard products, pay only sales costs
Ten drafts later, back to draft one
Six months for a few hundred thousand yuan

t113|522.c: Startups shouldn't wage all-out war on giants; take the edge markets giants don't care about.
t113|522.e: Once users have tried GPT-4, they'll only ask why you're worse, not sympathize with your costs, so head-on competition is hopeless. A sliver of a giant's revenue can matter a lot to a startup, yet the giant may not commit its best people. Writing alone splits into civil-service writing, e-commerce copy, email marketing, SEO and more, each needing different knowledge, interaction and workflow, so one general model is unlikely to solve them all at once. He also insists the next market be at least ten times bigger than the current one, rather than copying small tools earning a million a year.
ex: Legal translation is widely adopted, but its market ceiling is limited
Asked about differentiation, he answered: wait and see

items.d: Civil service, e-commerce, SEO all differ
The next market must be 10x bigger

t113|522.c: Prompts can't create abilities the base model lacks; training, fine-tuning and prompting trade cost for control.
t113|522.e: He sees the three routes as a spectrum of investment and control. Training from scratch costs the most and gives the most control, fine-tuning an open model sits in the middle, and prompting is cheapest but depends entirely on what the base model can already do. If the base model can't do something, prompts won't help. Metaso first looks for high-value problems that prompting can't solve and fine-tuning can't solve well, then goes back to data, architecture and pretraining, rather than training first and hunting for uses. In products, it uses whatever works, mixing models by cost and capability.
ex: Metaso has trained its own models from scratch since 2018, iterating every two or three months
Early on, it trained on a few dozen consumer gaming GPUs

items.d: Cheapest, limited by the base model

t113|522.c: Open source cut innovation costs about a hundredfold, but the strongest model may still be closed.
t113|522.e: Once training code, inference code and weights are fully open, he says, developers can fine-tune on their own data, turning a year of training from scratch into a few days, slashing the cost of innovation. But language models aren't like traditional software: it's hard even to define the goal, so a community can't improve them the way it fixes bugs. If one player can spend a hundred times more and get in a day the feedback others wait months for, the strongest closed model will likely stay ahead. He also warns many Chinese models merely run without being well trained, and expects 90% of users to stay with ChatGPT.
ex: He estimates training a 20-30B model from scratch takes a year; fine-tuning, three days
At hundreds of billions of parameters each, OPT clearly lagged GPT-3

items.d: A year's work shrinks to days

t114|522.c: AI should help people get into long works, not just shrink them into summaries.
t114|522.e: He thinks the few hundred words an AI search engine returns are fine for checking a specific fact but fall far short on a broad topic. There, AI should point people to the original text or papers. Pure compression throws away the deeper details different readers care about. A good course fills in the basics experts take for granted, adding diagrams, analogies and notes automatically. Learn Something Today is the first product to link sorting material, building a course, visuals and narration, but he gives it only 70 out of 100. The interface, scripts and looks all need work.
ex: For One Hundred Years of Solitude, the aim is getting people through all 800 pages
Explaining Transformers, it adds background: older LSTM models could only process one step at a time

items.d: Lower the barrier, don't replace it

t114|522.c: A founder deciding in ten minutes makes a small company fast, and is also its clearest bottleneck.
t114|522.e: He says most of his product calls are gut decisions made within ten minutes, while big companies go through research, reviews, technical sign-off and scheduling. He rarely does formal user interviews. He skips requests that keep coming up but don't hold up, and moves scattered feedback up the list if he can reason out why it matters. Professional and business customers are different: you can't just ask what they want, you have to understand them deeply. He splits projects into hundreds of tasks for a team of about 60. That speeds decisions, he admits, but the team should gradually take over the splitting.
ex: He says over 80% of product strategy decisions are made on gut feel
He runs product, engineering and model training, and even sketches the UI himself

items: Scattered feedback can jump the queue
But one person splits all the tasks

d.verdict: Speed is an edge; the team should slowly take over planning

t114|522.c: General-purpose AI agents are far from reliable. Users want them to succeed at least 95% of the time.
t114|522.e: Rather than chase the agent trend (AI that carries out tasks on its own), he looks at success rates first. Over two years, general agents got about ten times better at finishing tasks, but they're still far from what users expect. Treating one like a genie you make wishes to isn't realistic. Agents built for one industry need each result to be worth a lot. In Chinese law, he doubts tools that make lawyers more efficient. For business customers, outright replacing the lawyer is likelier to work. Metaso explored fully automating one type of legal case. It looked very efficient on paper but was shelved because Metaso couldn't win clients.
ex: He estimates automating one type of legal case could beat lawyers' efficiency about 100-fold

items.d: About 3 in 100 tasks succeeded, he estimates
At least 95 succeed and meet expectations

t114|522.c: Metaso moved from professional tools to consumer products because China's professional and business markets are too small.
t114|522.e: Metaso started with legal translation, then built Xiezuocat (a writing assistant), AI search and Learn Something Today, moving step by step toward everyday users. The main reason, he says, is that China's markets for business and professional software are small, and customers are reluctant to pay. The same professional-services product in the US might earn over $100 million a year. After ChatGPT launched, writing features quickly became a free standard in every model. That convinced him to look for markets at least ten times bigger than the ones he had.
ex: He points to Harvey, the US legal AI company, as proof of America's big professional market
Metaso's AI search has close to 1 million daily active users

items.d: Mass market, nearly a million daily users

t114|522.c: When tech giants pour in billions, a startup must first make sure it can survive on its own.
t114|522.e: In late 2024 he concluded that his 2025 rivals would be companies worth hundreds of billions or trillions, each spending billions of yuan. A startup must chase users or revenue, and revenue matters most because it lets a company survive independently. People treat AI search as free, and fees don't cover the computing cost of answering queries, so Metaso shifted toward revenue this year.
