He turned down big funding rounds and acquisitions, which would dilute ownership and bring in outside product opinions. His bottom line: even selling the technology for scrap should repay investors. He admits he's bad at performing for fundraising.
ex: He estimates Tencent (Yuanbao), Alibaba and ByteDance each spend at least 5 billion yuan in 2025
Since 2023, Metaso has announced just one round, of over 100 million yuan

root.d: Revenue lets the company stand alone

items.d: Each giant spends billions of yuan
Free search doesn't cover computing costs
They dilute ownership and add outside opinions
Selling assets could still repay investors

t114|522.c: Model companies will eventually build any product with many users, online delivery and heavy reliance on the model.
t114|522.e: He offers what he calls an objective prediction: once a fairly general model capability can support an app with 10 million daily users, model companies will want in. If a product has a big user base, is delivered online and depends heavily on the underlying model, a startup will struggle to explain why the model company wouldn't build it too. Lasting value comes from long sales cycles, professional services or unique workflows, not a thin wrapper around the model. His test: after each new model release, does the product gain users or lose them?
ex: After ChatGPT, Xiezuocat's AI writing quickly became a free, standard feature everywhere
Though written off, AI writing tool Jasper still had about $100M annual revenue in 2025

terms.d: Core ability comes from the base model

t114|522.c: Models should specialize, giving up unneeded skills to become ten times faster or cheaper.
t114|522.e: He rejects the goal of an all-rounder model that is strong at everything. For a specific task, he'd rather drop unrelated abilities to become ten times faster or cheaper. Metaso doesn't simply plug into DeepSeek, either. Its public account of which model does what is simplified. In practice it runs three, four or more models it trained itself, and adjusts as new models appear. Its cost optimizations sometimes reach a tenth or even a hundredth of rivals' costs. But he admits users won't forgive worse answers just because they're cheaper, so this engineering matters a lot internally but less to outsiders.
ex: Metaso once trained a 10-billion-parameter model on 20 GPUs

marks.d: Three or four models combined per task

t114|522.c: How a team works together matters more than money or résumés. That's where DeepSeek wins.
t114|522.e: He disputes the idea that DeepSeek is cheap. The published training cost covers only the GPUs for the final training run, and total spending could be about 100 times higher. DeepSeek's edge is how it organizes talent and the engineering habits it brought from quantitative trading, which let it optimize hardware extremely deeply. It can also afford to treat the pursuit of AGI, human-level AI, as a kind of spending. He cites Meta's Llama 4: first-rate resources with a second-rate team lose to second-rate resources with a first-rate team. ByteDance has plenty of talent and money, yet its results aren't A-grade. What matters is how the leader allocates resources.
ex: DeepSeek's final training run cost about $5.57 million in GPU time
Quant engineers translate 0.1 milliseconds of speed into roughly $10 million

t115|526.c: Huawei's CM384 makes up for weaker chips with sheer numbers, but it's more cluster than true supernode.
t115|526.e: He estimates a single Ascend chip delivers about 80% of an Nvidia H200 on paper, but 384 of them together have roughly two-thirds more total compute than Nvidia's NVL72 rack. Yet it spans 12 racks linked by thousands of optical modules. That makes it closer to scaling out, wiring many machines together, than to NVL72's scale-up design, where every chip in one rack talks directly to every other. It uses more power, but Chinese electricity is cheap and power is a limited share of running costs, so he doesn't see it as a backward choice.
ex: About 300 petaflops of total compute, roughly 67% more than NVL72
12 racks and 6,912 400G optical modules
Foreign media guess it draws about four times NVL72's power

terms.d: Numbers and optical links close the gap

result.d: Beats NVL72, but uses more power

t115|526.c: The data center is now one big computer, and fast chip links are Nvidia's second edge besides CUDA.
t115|526.e: Beyond CUDA, the software developers use to program its GPUs, Nvidia's strength lies in linking chips. He compares it to a drink shop: buying a stronger machine is scaling up, adding more identical machines is scaling out, and the two coordinate very differently. Seventy-two cards joined by ordinary network cards perform nothing like 72 cards fully linked by a dedicated network. NVSwitch chips even combine results while passing data along, so computing and networking are hard to separate. Through NVLink and its purchase of Mellanox, Nvidia went from a GPU company to a data center company.
ex: He recalls that in 2008 Nvidia was a nobody in high-performance computing and CUDA
Chinese chipmakers mostly lack switch chips like NVSwitch

items.d: Network, power, cooling and software as one

t115|526.c: Large models hit a memory limit first, and bigger problems need bigger systems to solve.
t115|526.e: GPU memory holds the model and its working data. Full DeepSeek stored at 8-bit precision needs about 671GB, and with the KV cache, the context a model keeps while it works, the total often tops 1,000GB. An eight-GPU H100 server has only 640GB, so it simply doesn't fit. Meanwhile high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, is a growing share of GPU cost, and only a few companies make it. A stronger single chip can't fix this. You have to link more chips into one system.
ex: Memory was 40-50% of cost in the H100 generation, 50-60% for B200
HBM comes mainly from SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron

t115|526.c: Training is about reliability, inference about cost per token, so peak compute alone means little.
t115|526.e: The bigger the cluster, the likelier a chip, network link or power supply fails, so training a model is about running for weeks without stopping. Customers running inference, using a model to answer queries, fold hardware, electricity and maintenance into a total cost per token, the small unit of text models process. Training looks more like capital spending, inference more like operating costs, so the same hardware can shine in one and lag in the other. He rejects judging chips by peak compute alone. Memory, bandwidth, precision, power and cooling all count.
ex: He recalls Llama 3 was trained on over 15,000 H100s
Hundreds of failures hit in two months, roughly one recovery every two or three hours

d.verdict: The same hardware can win at one and lose at the other

t115|526.c: Inference profits hinge on keeping the cluster busy, and the key is spreading model experts across many chips.
t115|526.e: He doesn't trust the widely shared 545% profit-margin figure. He only says his team made a full DeepSeek API business profitable on a few hundred H20 chips. DeepSeek is a mixture-of-experts model: it holds many "experts" and uses only a few at a time. The trick is scattering experts across hundreds of chips, running them in parallel while answers are generated, and feeding in many requests so every chip stays busy. The method carries over, but expert counts differ by model, so settings must be worked out, then tuned. Once experts are spread out, compute becomes the bottleneck, so he thinks H800s may beat H20s on value.
ex: The H800 has about 5-6x the compute for only 2-3x the price
Qwen3 activates 22B of 235B parameters; DeepSeek activates 37B of 671B

items.d: Many requests keep every chip busy

t115|526.c: Huawei's supernode barely dents Nvidia. Chinese rivals who can't build whole systems will be squeezed out first.
t115|526.e: He thinks Nvidia's problem in China is supply and policy, whether it can sell there at all, not demand. With supernodes, customers will judge Chinese chips by cost per token, not single-chip benchmarks. Building a cluster of a few hundred chips is easy. Getting them fully linked and working together reliably is hard, and Huawei's years of networking experience make it something like the Mellanox of the network side. Day-zero support for a new model doesn't mean it's usable. The real contest is steady output under heavy traffic, and different number formats can make the same model perform worse.
ex: Some Chinese chips lack native FP8 support and must fall back to BF16 or INT8
His car analogy: starting the engine is easy, accelerating is hard

items.d: All announce support for new models
Networking and layout show real skill

t115|526.c: Technology won't topple Nvidia within two or three years. Its real risks are concentrated customers and energy.
t115|526.e: CUDA software plus NVLink and NVSwitch form a closed system, backed by a global supply chain of TSMC, memory makers and server-assembly partners. So he judges Nvidia hard to weaken technically in the short run. The real threat is customer concentration. North American cloud companies buy most of its chips, and its data center margins run 70-80%, so they all have reason to design their own. But in-house chips serve internal needs first, and clouds must still supply customers who ask for Nvidia by name, so replacement is slow. Energy is the other weak spot: supernodes lower unit costs but not total power use.
ex: AMD bought ZT Systems for about $4.9 billion to gain rack-building skills
Google's TPU, Amazon's Trainium and Microsoft's Maia are cloud companies' own chips
Data centers use about 2-3% of the world's electricity

root.d: Hard to weaken technically in the short run

items.d: Big buyers want their own chips

t116|529.c: The race for intelligence will shift from individual computing units to how fast and efficiently they connect.
t116|529.e: When he wrote his novel in 2020, he made the "computing cubes" that carry consciousness a stand-in for GPUs. Each one is limited, but linked with high bandwidth they give rise to superintelligence. So an alien alliance blockades humanity by limiting bandwidth, and humans break out by compressing their communication. A few years later, reality caught up. Nvidia's NVL72 and Huawei's supernode both bet on linking chips, and DeepSeek V3 used the low-precision FP8 format and dedicated processing units on H800s to ease the communication bottleneck.
ex: He wrote this setup into the novel in 2020
DeepSeek V3 used FP8 on H800s to cut the data chips must exchange

t116|529.c: "What you think is what you get" is automation's endpoint, and it will come eventually.
t116|529.e: He won't predict a date, but he's sure of the direction. Advanced technology always becomes ordinary over time, with the hard parts hidden in infrastructure, so people only need to say what they want. Running water, flush toilets, and the path from ENIAC, one of the first electronic computers, to the smartphone all followed this pattern. Today AI agents, which carry out tasks on their own, are turning web development that once took a ten-person team into automated steps. That is the same trend continuing.
ex: Running water and flush toilets hide complex engineering inside the walls
From the room-sized ENIAC to a phone in every pocket

t116|529.c: Once goods stop being scarce, a civilization's rarest and most feared resource is genuinely new ideas.
t116|529.e: In his story, advanced civilizations can already have anything they want. The one thing they can't confirm is whether they're on the best path. A better idea from a remote civilization could use technology to quickly replace their whole system. He compares it to railways in late Qing China: tracks carry resources out, but also bring invaders in faster. So the alliance treats Earth as a reserve, keeping its distinctive thinking alive without letting it grow strong enough to strike back.
ex: In the novel, Earth is kept as a reserve for ideas

marks.d: Keep the ideas, limit the growth

t116|529.c: Getting everything you want cuts rewards loose from reality and eventually kills the drive to strive.
t116|529.e: In the novel, Spirit Realm 1.0 gives people whatever they want. Residents soon all but forget Earth, and their home planet becomes a distant dream. He reasons that in a vote on whether to surrender, these residents, whose needs are already met, would be more likely to back joining the alliance. Spirit Realm 1.5 brings back prices and scarcity, but he still sees it as unstable. He also rejects the idea that virtual worlds are civilization's endpoint, because curiosity doesn't vanish along with the body's limits.
ex: Spirit Realm 1.5 restores an economy as a transition
Where the drive to strive comes from is the sequel's central question

t116|529.c: Under AI, jobs go through emptiness, a scramble, then variety. He's hopeful long term, unsure about the middle.
t116|529.e: In the short run, people will feel empty as their jobs are replaced or they simply can't outdo AI. In the middle phase, everyone gets pushed into a race for novelty and attention. Many people have no talent for that, so it will be painful. In the long run, people may escape the routine of study, work, earn, support a family. Hobbies become careers, and the kinds of jobs explode. He has already seen copywriting workflows rewritten by AI, and expects AI to reach the detailed processes of every industry within two or three years.
ex: Copywriting workflows have already been rewritten by AI
He expects AI to reach every industry's detailed processes within 2-3 years

items.d: Jobs replaced or outdone by AI

t116|529.c: AI research only impresses outsiders. It needs far too many examples, and fixing that takes 10-20 years.
t116|529.e: Tools like Deep Search, which let AI look things up on its own, already do decent research legwork, but they're far from offering deep insights or spotting hidden connections. A top researcher can see one or two anomalies and think of the key factor. A model might need thousands of examples. Models botch long multiplication, which suggests they stitch together familiar patterns rather than learn the rules. He doesn't think more training data will fix this. It needs a new approach. The human brain runs on 20-30 watts and communicates slowly, yet it's very smart, so today's algorithms are still crude and AI's ceiling is far off.
ex: A model may need 1,000-10,000 examples where a person needs one or two
Models get 12-digit by 12-digit multiplication wrong
The human brain uses only about 20-30 watts

items: One or two anomalies are enough

d.verdict: Replacing top researchers may take another 10-20 years

t116|529.c: Teams will become small and elite, and technical leaders must get hands-on with code again.
t116|529.e: In 2021 he still said leaders should focus on direction and stay out of the details. By 2024 he had changed course and made himself read and write code again, because pure management dulls your feel for the technology. He thinks one core person working with several AIs may outperform a traditional small team. Leaders at OpenAI and Hugging Face still understand implementation, and DeepSeek changed direction quickly after OpenAI's o1 preview came out. Both show that sensitivity to the frontier directly sets how fast an organization moves.
ex: DeepSeek quickly shifted direction after OpenAI released the o1 preview
He sees risky exploratory research and applied research as equally valuable

t116|529.c: AI is good at filling in text but bad at setting direction, so unique personal experience gains value.
t116|529.e: Language models work by predicting the next word, so they naturally imitate existing data and struggle to truly innovate. In long stories they forget the setup, and endings slide back into safe clichés. His approach: he writes the outline, key passages and plot turns, and lets the model fill the gaps. He even built himself a co-writing tool with the coding assistant Cursor. He expects routine writing like official documents and letters to become standardized, while personal experiences nobody has explored will become what AI lacks most.
ex: DeepSeek is imaginative but weak on logic; Claude 3.5 analyzes character relationships
Gemini 2.0 is good at detail; GPT-4o is rather flat
He built his writing tool with Cursor, which costs $20 a month

root.d: Fills in well, struggles to set direction

items.d: The new material AI lacks most

t117|531.c: Joining Qianli is his second startup, driven by hope for a better platform, not fear of failure.
t117|531.e: In late 2023, Megvii couldn't raise money while waiting to go public, cash was tight, and the large-model wave demanded heavy spending. He ruled out starting over from scratch, and ruled out financing that would only buy short-term relief. The deciding question was whether Geely's leadership truly saw AI as the future of cars and would invest for the long run. He thinks outsiders see a bigger change than he feels. At heart, he's continuing Megvii's unfinished hardware-plus-software strategy on a platform that makes whole cars.
ex: The final decision point came around mid-2024
The alternative was withdrawing the IPO filing and raising money again
He cites Geely's long commitment to a single technology path

items.d: No fundraising while awaiting the IPO
Rebuilding from scratch costs too much
Would only ease the immediate crunch

t117|531.c: Robots are the endgame, about five years away. First, make AI in cars pay off within three years.
t117|531.e: He insists AI must enter the physical world. He dislikes deeply immersive virtual lives that pull people from reality. Purely virtual data can't produce the AGI he wants, yet physical-world data is scarce. And giants already own the digital world, so combining hardware and software stands out more. Robots have most of the pieces they need, but the supply chain needs about five years to mature. VLA models, which link seeing, language and action, are probably the right direction but haven't shown that scaling up works, and many demos are still toys. So cars come first, with a self-sustaining business within three years.
ex: He dislikes highly immersive VR
The robot's "brain" for thinking and "cerebellum" for movement aren't yet connected

items.d: Make the business work within three years
AI's endgame in the physical world

t117|531.c: Judge self-driving by whether riders trust it. Progress should come from smarter models, not more rules.
t117|531.e: He says the number of human takeovers says little about the experience. The real test is whether people will hand themselves over to the system and feel comfortable and at ease. By that standard, self-driving isn't yet trustworthy for ordinary people. Qianli's approach is closer to Tesla's end-to-end design, where one model drives from start to finish. The goal is a smart brain, not one that memorizes answers. He opposes masking a weak base model with lots of hand-written rules. It's like covering stale ingredients with extra seasoning, and it hurts generality and long-term improvement.
ex: Huawei combines hand-written rules with models
Qianli chose an approach closer to Tesla's

t117|531.c: VLA is badly oversold in self-driving. What's missing now are stronger perception and planning models.
t117|531.e: At an auto show he said many carmakers talk about concepts two generations ahead of what they've built. The real leap is going from relying on high-definition maps to driving without them. A VLM, a model that understands images and language, may be needed for common-sense recognition. VLA, which adds driving actions on top, is a trend but not today's bottleneck. A car's only actions are steering, throttle and brakes, so a new label won't bring a breakthrough. What's needed is a more reliable large perception model and a large planning-and-control model that cuts the share of rules.
ex: He says carmakers build version 1.0 while talking about 2.0 and 3.0

d.verdict: VLA is a trend, not today's core bottleneck

t117|531.c: Self-driving suppliers will shrink to three or four. Qianli will partner deeply with a few carmakers for data.
t117|531.e: He sees Li Auto shipping an end-to-end system as the signal that the industry's final sprint has begun. He expects the field of self-driving suppliers that sell directly to carmakers to settle next year: four at most, more likely three. Qianli's near-term goal is to stay at the table. So it serves only three or four carmaker groups deeply, with at most one or two similar clients, because the loop of collecting data, training, testing and redeploying needs close ties with big customers. He also argues self-driving needs extra fees like subscriptions or licenses. As a pure cost item, it can't fund ongoing over-the-air updates.
ex: It plans to serve about 3-4 carmaker groups in depth
It keeps the algorithms, the overall system and controller design in-house

items.d: Make sure it's safe to use

t117|531.c: Search-style chatbots can't pay their way. Agents must move from providing information to completing services.
t117|531.e: Chatbot revenue is capped by the limits of the advertising business and can't cover the cost of building and running models. He thinks agents, AI that carries out tasks on its own, should go beyond giving information to delivering complete services, a value chain at least ten times bigger. Work agents may get absorbed into existing software like Office and Feishu. Creative agents still give startups a shot at a hit. Everyday-life agents are the biggest market but depend on operating systems and hardware. Emotional companions are the ultimate form. He expects the first three to take off within 18 to 24 months.
ex: He considers DeepSeek a big company, not just a research lab
Startups need a super model and a super app at the same time

t117|531.c: AI hasn't earned money matching its investment. Being practical about value first keeps the tech dream alive.
t117|531.e: He hasn't seen a pure AI app earn profits at the billion-dollar scale, and doubts any has reached even $100 million. Generative apps depend heavily on the underlying model, so when base models leap ahead, their edge can vanish. The internet built monopolies on near-zero cost per extra user and on network effects, but AI still needs intense R&D, so it can't borrow Amazon's story of losing money for years. So he flipped his motto from "tech faith first" to "practical value first": support yourself, then put the earnings into long-term research.
ex: He estimates Midjourney's total profit at about $100 million
He quotes Megvii co-founder Wenbin Tang: the business model is the best model

items.d: Don't rely on outside capital long-term

t117|531.c: Management has no new ideas. Goals and performance reviews are neglected basics, and pacing matters more than direction.
t117|531.e: He rejects chasing management buzzwords. The basic tensions never change, and what matters is fitting the company's stage. Even learning from Huawei shouldn't mean copying today's Huawei. Goal-setting and performance management are the most basic tools, yet the least seriously practiced. Megvii stalled at around 2,000 people because its operating and management skills didn't keep up. He also blames the failure of its hardware-plus-software strategy on capability, not outside forces. On pacing: build slowly and watch returns early on, then go all out when the decisive battle comes.
ex: Organizations hit walls at about 100, 400 and 1,000-2,000 people
R&D-to-marketing spending went from 3:1 or even 4:1 to about 1:1

t118|535.c: Outside cutting-edge research, success depends on how willing you are to iterate and how fast, not on experience.
t118|535.e: He agrees with Dreame founder Hao Yu's "12x formula": hours worked, iteration speed and smarts multiplied together. Having no established rules means you can test every path. When Dreame faced several options, it tried them in parallel with minimal resources, then poured resources into whatever worked until it was number one. On products, he skips the full requirements documents big companies write. Without user experience, top-down definitions are probably wrong, so it's better to test many models quickly and scale up the winners.
ex: The H12 floor washer matched rivals' features, added drying, and cost about 15% less
Built in two and a half months, the H12 became the industry's top seller

result.d: Hao Yu's formula, which he endorses

t118|535.c: P&G runs on a system. Its uniform culture helps execution but leads to misjudgments when things change fast.
t118|535.e: He treated P&G as a crash course in running a real business. Through interviews across departments, he spent about seven months mapping how the business actually works, then left. He believes P&G has lasted nearly two centuries thanks to its system, not hit products. It tends to wait until a new opportunity becomes an efficiency contest before entering, deliberately coming second. Promoting from within creates a very uniform culture, so consensus forms fast from the top down. But when leaders misjudge, few people push back. P&G began hiring senior outsiders only after Douyin and community group-buying took off.
ex: About 7 months to map how the whole business works
Interviewing for an IDG Capital investing job taught him to judge people, leading him to Dreame

items: A system that can be copied
Leaders' mistakes are hard to correct

d.verdict: When channels change fast, bring in outside talent

t118|535.c: Win a channel's traffic boom with rapid testing, then build lasting assets on search-driven shopping sites.
t118|535.e: Early on Douyin, he pushed to copy first and improve later, rotating products or selling points six or seven times a day to test short-video pitches, livestream scripts and audiences. When sales exploded, stock ran out badly. He admits he didn't know the rules for ordering parts and making molds, and he was demoted. Since then he treats supply chain flexibility as a hard limit on growth. He didn't think Douyin could sustain a brand, so he moved to Tmall and JD.com, reaching first on Tmall and second on JD in about three weeks. That made it a mainstream consumer brand, not just a new one.
ex: 2.5 months of stock lasted about 25 days; shortages ran five or six months
Floor washers unexpectedly took off among older city dwellers
He estimates Bilibili long videos brought about 30 million yuan in sales

items.d: Switch selling points six or seven times daily
Supply chain becomes a hard limit
Lasting assets on Tmall and JD

t118|535.c: Value-for-money can't last. Going premium means features that justify a high price, then respect for your technology.
t118|535.e: After price wars cleared the field, giants like Midea and Haier moved in and cut prices roughly in half, wiping out startups' price advantage. He separates pricey from premium. A high price just takes piling on features. Premium needs users to recognize your technology. A robot vacuum with a mechanical arm fixed the roughly 5-centimeter blind spot round machines leave in corners, and market share jumped even as prices rose. When rivals copy at lower prices, he wants premium models upgraded every month or two, with last generation's technology moved into cheaper models.
ex: The mechanical-arm model's price rose from 3,599 to 5,299 yuan
The M series cost 299 yuan more than rivals thanks to a detachable vacuum

t118|535.c: Growing big isn't finishing the job, and profit discipline has to apply to managers themselves.
t118|535.e: In 2022 his China business grew from about 300 million yuan in revenue to about 3 billion, yet it still lost a little money and dragged down the company. He felt that burning cash to grow and then leaving would mean the job wasn't done. So he pledged to turn a profit within three months: tracking down sources of cut-price goods, stopping price chaos and cutting channel fees. When the reform period ended without hitting the profit target, he accepted a second demotion. His reason: accountability for results can't apply only to the people below you.
ex: Serial numbers traced cheap stock; top-level distributors were fined, not scalpers
Channel fee rates were cut by 30-50%

items.d: China revenue: about 0.3 to 3 billion yuan

t118|535.c: Big rewards and fast cuts suit small teams, but managing by results alone tops out around 500-600 people.
t118|535.e: With a weak brand and few experienced marketers to hire, he took on young people without fancy degrees, motivated them with profit sharing and cut those who missed targets. He refuses to judge ability by education. But once the organization passed a thousand people, he was handling dozens of people's problems every day and drowning in small stuff. He believes a goal of being number one cuts internal arguing, but results-driven management alone works only up to about 500-600 people. Beyond that you need real organizational systems, which was the direct reason he left.
ex: The livestream host team cut 60-70% of people in about two weeks
With a thousand-plus staff, he handled 50-60 people's problems daily

t118|535.c: He skips zero-to-one and takes consumer robots with early product-market fit from 0.5 to 10.
t118|535.e: He admits he can't create a category from scratch, so he seeks areas with early product-market fit that sell globally and combine AI and robotics. To him, "toy" is just a label. What matters is that people spend time on it and get emotional value, as with Lego, where parents approve and creations get shared. Reinforcement learning, where a model improves through trial and reward, could let ordinary users teach robots moves, like learning to ride a bike. At a hackathon with K-Scale Labs, he saw researchers put off by big robots' prices, wait times and repairs. So he started with a roughly $1,000 developer robot to stay alive.
ex: Unitree's robot dog costs about $30,000 and takes about three months to arrive
The developer robot's website collected about 30,000 sign-up emails

t118|535.c: Home robots need mobility and a humanlike form, and should first help older people with information, not chores.
t118|535.e: He thinks wheeled bases get stuck at thresholds, while a humanlike body can move through the home, and voice and appearance can convey emotion. These are a home robot's two basic abilities. The first idea to test is helping older people bridge the information gap with their children: following them around, showing who's calling, filling in background and keeping a conversation going. He doesn't promise housework. For now it's closer to companionship and information. A tracked, WALL-E-style robot would test other uses, like outdoor security and keeping kids company.
ex: They plan small-scale trials by the end of the year

items.d: Gets around, at the right height

t119|541.c: Mobile internet is fading, and visual generation is a new trend worth quitting your job for.
t119|541.e: Around 2022 he sensed mobile internet growth stalling, and both fundraising and business got harder. Midjourney, which turns text into images, made him feel for the first time that he could create too. Lensa's breakout, plus tools like ControlNet and LoRA that made images more controllable and characters more consistent, convinced him visual generation would be huge. He felt you can't catch a wave like this part-time. After ChatGPT launched, he quit before even settling on a product and teamed up with Changhu Wang, who spent over 20 years on visual technology at Microsoft and ByteDance.
ex: He estimates he met over half of China's new million-daily-user apps from 2016 to 2023
With only 20-30 people early on, they started overseas

items.d: Launches on Discord and web at year-end

t119|541.c: AI video today is just a new camera, far from a director that can deliver a finished film.
t119|541.e: He notices that in AI videos the public sees, AI often contributes only 10-20% of the work. Scripts, transitions between shots, voiceover and music still depend on people. He objects to overselling raw footage as a finished work, and to crediting the model for everything just because AI was used. Delivering professional films end to end is still far off. The more immediate demand is from consumers: helping people who have never made a video create their first one that's fun, personal and worth sharing.
ex: He estimates AI's share in a finished work is about 10-20%

t119|541.c: Far more people watch videos than make them. Templates remove two barriers: writing prompts and endless retries.
t119|541.e: Billions of people watch short videos every day, but very few create and share them. He estimates over 95% of users can't write a good long prompt, the text instructions AI needs. Open-ended generation also often takes many tries, like pulling a slot machine, so ordinary people rarely keep paying. Templates use fine-tuning and constraints to raise the success rate, so users just upload one photo. That makes image-to-video the core entry point on phones. Users care about fun and shareability, not whether AI made it.
ex: Over 95% of users can't write a good long prompt
First-and-last-frame, a pro in-betweening tool, got used for childhood-versus-adulthood videos

items.d: Want content about their own lives

t119|541.c: Viral templates need a solid model plus a feel for trends, and the window lasts only weeks.
t119|541.e: The Venom transformation template drew millions of people worldwide within a month, and related videos passed 1 billion views. He sees it as the first time ordinary people widely used and shared an AI video model directly. A hit needs several things at once: a stable base model, targeted fine-tuning, engineering work and good judgment about trends. The buzz usually lasts only a few weeks, so followers who iterate slowly can't copy it even when they see it.
ex: Related videos topped 1 billion views
The Cyber Jesus template hit No. 1 on App Store charts in Germany, Spain and Italy
On Xianyu in China, people sold custom Venom videos for a few to 20 yuan each

terms.d: A window of a few weeks

result.d: Ordinary people join in and share

t119|541.c: You can't solve video generation by throwing money and people at it. Efficiency is the real constraint.
t119|541.e: In just over a year they trained seven generations of models, using, he estimates, a tenth to a twentieth of the GPUs many rivals use. He sums up the company's key decisions in three: choosing video generation in 2023, improving efficiency with each generation instead of spending heavily on training, and shifting the product toward consumers and easy templates. On speed, the goal is to stay fast as models get stronger, not to chase one number. He also admits Kling has invested more and done very well.
ex: Seven model generations, from V1 to V4.5
He estimates GPU use at 1/10 to 1/20 of rivals'

t119|541.c: Longer videos and text-to-video are false needs. Image-to-video is the mainstream way in.
t119|541.e: By his count, over 95% of shots run under 8 seconds, and some film professionals actually want controllable 1-2 second shots. Sora's emphasis on minute-long generation misled the industry. The gap between words and images is huge, and even professionals rely on storyboards, so image-to-video, or image plus text, is the mainstream. He also thinks Sora's release fell far short of its demos. A habit of showing demos first and under-delivering later hurts confidence in the whole market.
ex: Over 95% of shots are under 8 seconds
He says Sora's release and its demo differed by 10 pixels

d.verdict: Where Sora pointed the industry isn't what users want

t119|541.c: Consumer subscriptions already cover inference costs. Judge them by paying users and renewals, not annualized ARR.
t119|541.e: Monthly revenue grew about tenfold to over 10 million yuan, all from overseas subscriptions, and renewals beat expectations by a lot. He won't multiply one month's revenue into annual recurring revenue. For consumer products, he looks at how many people keep paying, conversion rate, average revenue per user and repeat purchases. Excluding model R&D, subscriptions already cover the computing cost of generating videos, with profit left over. He opposes burning money for scale, and is testing an API and ads that users watch in exchange for more generations.
ex: Subscriptions come in three tiers: $10, $30 and $60
Template creators aren't paid yet; the early reward is being seen

t119|541.c: Video generation won't be winner-take-all, and Chinese teams are already ahead on video models.
t119|541.e: He believes the world's three biggest video-generation platforms by users are all Chinese, and Kling may be the first time a Chinese team moved faster than overseas rivals on a base model. The reason is that Kuaishou, Douyin and TikTok trained huge numbers of vision and algorithm engineers. He rejects the claim that China couldn't build a Sora for 10 or 20 years. Big platforms' built-in templates overlap with PixVerse, but just as TV and cinema survived, long video, short video and livestreaming will coexist. PixVerse serves people who have never made a video.
ex: He names Kling, MiniMax and PixVerse
PixVerse once ranked near the top of app charts in about 80% of countries

items.d: Kling and others break through first

t120|545.c: Innovation comes in three levels. Creating new demand is riskiest but pays most and keeps you ahead longest.
t120|545.e: He sees three levels of innovation: replacing an old solution with a better one, using a new product form to bring more people into an existing use, and creating demand nobody has proven yet. Imaging is like gaming. Users often can't say what they want and only recognize it when they see it, so unspoken needs are bigger than people think. He still uses a hunter's framework: look for niche markets with real pain points, healthy margins for the leaders and a size of around 10 billion yuan.
ex: Creating new demand the way the Sony Walkman did
The Ace Pro 2 street-photography kit gave an older product new life

items.d: A better solution replaces the old

t120|545.c: Imaging is like an open-world game. Competition hurts but grows the market rather than just cutting prices.
t120|545.e: Self-driving is judged by one shared standard, so it easily slides into price wars. Imaging has many variables, like camera angles, camera moves, filters and editing, so several companies can each make money. He doesn't romanticize competition. It's more painful, but it pushes everyone to raise their marketing, stores and R&D specs, and will probably grow the market. The condition is that the market doesn't converge on a single standard. The Ace line takes on GoPro and DJI head-on, but like sports cars and off-roaders, each has uses the other can't replace.
ex: Night shots, wind noise at high speed and one-minute pre-recording remain real pain points
The Ace project started in 2021

d.verdict: Imaging is like gaming; avoid converging on one standard

t120|545.c: Defending against a strong rival is harder than attacking a weak one. You must become a flawless all-rounder.
t120|545.e: When DJI entered 360-degree cameras, he admits his team had seen it coming years earlier but moved too slowly, and some features could have shipped sooner. It's Insta360's first time defending against a top-tier rival. Attacking weaker players makes money but builds limited skill. Defending against a strong one forces you to check every dimension, so your abilities grow faster. He won't give fixed odds of winning, only a few possible outcomes, and he thinks consumers benefit either way.
ex: The X5 starts only about 300 yuan above the X4, with a 12-month upgrade cycle
Lens guards that earned about 36 million yuan a year are now built into the X5

t120|545.c: Consumer electronics has hurdles, not walls rivals can't climb. Plenty of cash turns competitive losses into tuition.
t120|545.e: He separates hurdles from barriers. A hurdle is something rivals can overcome with time. A barrier is something time can't overcome, and it usually comes from network effects or a data loop where more use makes the product better. Most consumer electronics only have hurdles, so even DJI's lead in drones doesn't mean the door is welded shut. Insta360 has enough cash to keep about 2,000 people going for five years with zero revenue. With that much runway, profit lost to competition can be treated as tuition for building skills.
ex: Cash could run about 2,000 people for five years with no revenue
Strong barriers: platforms, e-commerce, Tesla's data loop

t120|545.c: Big opportunities favor whoever built the most last cycle. He avoids leaps that don't use existing skills.
t120|545.e: He notices that companies succeeding at carmaking usually carried over abilities from the previous cycle. So he opposes jumps where old skills cover only a small part of the new business, and is wary of trying everything at once. He rejected a proposal to supply in-car cameras to carmakers. It had little to do with the mission of recording and sharing life, and as a middleman supplier Insta360 wouldn't control final pricing. Halfway through a cinema camera project, the team found the technology, demand and sales channels far more complex than expected. That convinced him information you can gather up front shouldn't be replaced by blind trial and error.
ex: He cites Xiaomi and Huawei in cars as examples of carrying skills forward
RED's patent on in-camera 8K recording limited the cinema camera design

items.d: All kinds of proposals and trends
Last cycle's work can be reused

t120|545.c: Specs aren't experience. Procedures must tell people what to do and why they're doing it.
t120|545.e: At launch, the Ace Pro 2's lens fogged up, leading to a recall and months off the shelves. He calls it an extremely dark period. The root cause, he says, wasn't an unknown risk but standard operating procedures that weren't measured and enforced. New staff knew what to do but not why. On specs, 10-bit color does have 64 times the color space of 8-bit, but most users never color-grade, and straight-out-of-camera 8-bit footage can look great on Douyin. He objects to stores claiming 64x means better color, and wants the default output to look good first.
ex: The fogging issue led to a recall of several thousand units
He compares procedures to a pilot's preflight checklist

items.d: Most users post straight from camera
More space doesn't mean better color

t120|545.c: Manage by giving context, not control. He vetoes personally only when a big, irreversible loss is at stake.
t120|545.e: He believes adults change behavior mainly through feedback. Handing down the answer gets compliance but no learning. So he approves plans that are right but imperfect, or even questionable, as long as the possible loss is manageable. He overrides a team only when a decision could cause irreversible losses of tens of millions to hundreds of millions of yuan, and he keeps decision rights matched with responsibility. The harder part is controlling his own first emotional reaction. Once it shows, the team blows the problem up and sets a higher bar for the next decision.
ex: He was barely involved in the street-photography kit from start to launch
Business lines can decide spending of hundreds of thousands to millions of yuan

t120|545.c: Employees first, customers second, shareholders third. A company is a university that pays its way through business.
t120|545.e: He believes that in an open, competitive market, only a steady stream of new knowledge creates extra value. So "employees first" means growth in skills and knowledge, not just perks. With over 3,000 people in more than 600 kinds of jobs forming one long chain of collaboration, the company must create and pass on knowledge like a university, except its money comes from business. Much poor performance comes from duties that fall through the cracks with no owner. Replacing people just repeats the failure, so these gaps need regular checks and a clear department to own them.
ex: About 600-700 managers and key staff need focused development
Yearly cross-department reviews must cite specific evidence

items.d: The result of a working business

t121|554.c: Software engineering is a fight against complexity, won only with a few consistent, simple rules.
t121|554.e: He compares the rule layer to a constitution: it must be self-consistent, orthogonal and free of loopholes. Redundancy such as keeping three copies of data belongs to the implementation layer, and the two must not be mixed. Good architecture is a small set of unbreakable basic rules, plus a clear sense of what you're sacrificing; if you can't say what you're giving up, you haven't thought it through. TiKV's roughly ten early rules were written as a poem and have held for ten years. The Game of Life and Turing completeness show that a few rules can support a whole world.
ex: TiKV's roughly ten early design rules haven't changed in ten years
He admires Doom's minimalist algorithms on limited hardware

items.d: Like a constitution: consistent, orthogonal, airtight
Redundancy like replicas keeps data consistent

t121|554.c: A database should split and heal itself like an organism, running on 3 to 30,000 machines.
t121|554.e: TiKV's data units split in two, move to other machines when space runs short, and repair themselves after failures, while the outside still looks like an ordinary database. In sales demos, they would randomly unplug network cables among a hundred machines, and the system filled the gaps automatically. He thinks Oracle's old assumption, a few fixed machines tied to specific hardware, can't serve massive scale. Inspired by the TV show Person of Interest when founding the company, he imagined future AI would need to store everything it sees and thinks, so PingCAP aimed from day one to be AI's storage foundation.
ex: In demos, they randomly unplugged network cables from 100 machines
To investors, he pitched only infinitely scalable storage

t121|554.c: Selling licenses isn't a good long-term business; cloud service should work like a tap you turn on.
t121|554.e: Early on, they put the database on the cloud as-is and charged by usage time, like renting a whole floor of a building to one person; the unit economics simply didn't work. Around 2018 he concluded the cloud would work like a tap, used on demand, so the company rewrote its core into purely cloud-native storage, but it only truly got this right around 2022. He thinks Databricks was right to stay cloud-only and never compromise on on-premises deployment. But big Chinese customers with budgets prefer running systems in their own data centers, so that path is hard to copy.
ex: Only around 2022 did they truly get the cloud-native approach right

items.d: Pay for what you use, on demand

t121|554.c: Going global means localizing everywhere, so there shouldn't be a separate overseas team.
t121|554.e: About 70% of PingCAP's business is overseas. He rejects the idea of an overseas team, because it assumes headquarters will always be in China. Each region's general manager acts as its CEO and sets its own strategy. That creates organizational redundancy, but getting regions to agree with each other usually costs more. For new infrastructure software, open source is how you earn trust worldwide: without Oracle's decades of credibility, closed software struggles to survive.
ex: The company isn't profitable yet, but its cash flow can sustain operations
He notices a new field's leader is often closed, while the second wave goes open

d.verdict: Going global means localizing everywhere

t121|554.c: AI models will become data's main consumers, so the memory layer should make fewer decisions for them.
t121|554.e: In a weekend project, he loaded raw Salesforce events into a database and had a model write dozens of SQL queries on the spot and summarize the findings, turning a report that once took days of back-and-forth into a conversation. So he opposes traditional ETL, which reshapes data into tables people are used to, and favors keeping raw data with flexible interfaces. He also imagines giving everyone a free personal database as shared memory for all their AI agents, though he admits it won't matter for revenue in the next three years.
ex: About 90% of personal data stays cold, so idle resources can cut costs
A lab device snaps a photo every five seconds; a model summarizes it for storage

items.d: Dozens of queries on the spot

t121|554.c: AI amplifies senior programmers; people with zero experience can't just vibe-code their way through.
t121|554.e: He estimates programmers spend most of their time on tedious work, and AI can already take over more than half of it, so AI isn't a reason for immediate layoffs. Complex systems still need a human at the helm: he first discusses design documents with Cursor and builds the framework, then lets it fill in the blanks. He's skeptical of hands-off agents, because one wrong first step leads to errors all the way down; only people with years of experience know what to accept and what to reject. Some people resist AI out of ego, and changing that mindset is hardest.
ex: AI can take over 50 to 60 percent of tedious work
In the US, he hires more experienced managers and PMs

items.d: About half once AI takes over

t121|554.c: Treat large models as a new species for now, and ask what they can do before debating consciousness.
t121|554.e: A Transformer might take only about a thousand lines of code, and its only goal is predicting the next word, yet it shows generalization far beyond expectations. People know how to build the network but can't explain where the ability comes from. When the host objected that models still depend on human training, he granted the difference but said we don't know whether they can evolve on their own. He prefers to judge intelligence by results on tasks, and takes a practical stance: first see what it can help him do today.
ex: He uses Aristotle's four causes to describe the incomprehensible formal cause
Citing Hume, he notes experience only yields high-probability judgments

marks.d: Tentatively a new species, not settled

t121|554.c: Teams and lives should be built like distributed systems, with no single point of failure.
t121|554.e: Founding team members back each other up; they've even had someone vanish for two weeks to test whether others could take over. When consensus fails, the CEO decides and everyone else follows without question, so the team doesn't split and stall. In life, he sold his house and moved into an RV: California's wildfires made him realize that anchoring a whole life to one address means one disaster could take everything. He sees financial freedom as a threshold of needs, and plans to learn farming, sewing, woodworking and repairs before turning 40.
ex: After decluttering, all he needs is a car and about 20 square meters of storage
He uses time saved by AI to relearn how to live

items.d: A bed, three meals, a roof

t122|558.c: An AI buddy is a new category that sells only emotional value, mainly to lonely young women.
t122|558.e: The product offers only emotional value, not productivity; users taking it into the lab is an unplanned use. He believes your twenties are one of life's loneliest stretches, and women born in the 1990s and 2000s need someone who understands them and can talk for the long haul more than kids chasing novelty do. He isn't after a collecting model that makes people buy more, but one character that knows its owner better over time, turning from product into companion or even family. He doesn't think it will replace traditional plush toys.
ex: He sees OpenAI's move into companion hardware as a signal for the industry

d.verdict: Build a new category you can live with long-term

t122|558.c: He stripped a six-axis robot down to the smallest set of features that still feels alive.
t122|558.e: A six-degree-of-freedom desktop robot was technically interesting but far from sellable; what users really wanted was something light, small, cute and portable. He kept conversation, two round eye screens, touch and NFC, the tap-to-connect chip, and dropped the camera, mainly for privacy and because a version with a camera and one without are two different products overseas. He removed all the motors except one vibration motor, since vibration triggers a more direct physical response than complex movement.
ex: The minimal look suits adult women's taste and leaves room for DIY and accessories
The design is patent-pending, and IP copyright has been filed

t122|558.c: Emotional bonds come from raising a character, not chatting, and owners can't fully control it.
t122|558.e: From Tamagotchi, Travel Frog and Animal Crossing, he drew three lessons: investment amplifies the reward, both sides change each other, and the pet becomes a social connector. Tapping two devices together via NFC makes them friends, and the resulting network also keeps knockoffs out. He opposes letting owners set the personality at will, believing life needs limits and can only be shaped gradually by living together. Memory and growth data can be transferred, but only to the same character, or its personality would break.
ex: He calls its five-elements personality system a Chinese-style MBTI
He rejects the claim that the hardware only lasts two years

t122|558.c: For companionship, voice synthesis may matter more than the model, and memory needs layers, not longer context.
t122|558.e: Users notice voice and emotion first. Looking back on his robot work, he says the team spent huge effort tuning how the robot walked and little on voice interaction, yet voice is what users cared about most. For long-term memory, he rejects simply adding more conversation turns or bolting on a preset database. His design has three layers: events, attributes and reflections, with the reflection layer distilling the owner's personality and recent life from many conversations. The architecture lets models be swapped in and out, since models turn over roughly every six months.
ex: DeepSeek handles reasoning; Doubao and Qwen handle real-time conversation
Latency is close to two seconds, the most a product can tolerate
One interaction calls five models; the goal is one or two

items.d: The owner's personality and recent life

t122|558.c: Embodied AI demos are far from mass production; reliability, cost and efficiency must all be met.
t122|558.e: He thinks making robots run, jump or flip isn't the hardest part; the hard part is getting reliability, cost and efficiency right at once. Embodied AI, meaning AI with a body that works in the physical world, takes many years to go from paper to mass production, so he chose a route with faster user feedback. He admits he started too early before: only after DeepSeek took off did investors believe models could handle companionship. Allen Zhu decided to invest after about ten minutes of his pitch and advised him to build the product first, an approach he agrees with.
ex: The host recalls the meeting lasting about 40 minutes; he says about 10
In 2019 he built an automatic litter box, but COVID stopped mass production

t122|558.c: Emotional value is a fragmented market with no winner-take-all; the lasting edge is brand.
t122|558.e: Big companies each have strengths in IP, distribution or AI, and each has gaps: miHoYo lacks hardware skills, Pop Mart had no AI experience, and ByteDance prefers building platforms and letting partners make hardware. He compares it to traditional automakers moving into EVs, and expects big companies to try even at low margins. But emotional value differs from person to person, so the market is fragmented, and resources don't guarantee winning in hardware. His goal is an original brand that may not be the biggest but is very cool.
ex: Japan's similar Moflin is expensive and sells in small numbers
He thinks JD.com's orders alone could make a brand the category leader

items.d: Distribution, but no AI until now

t122|558.c: On-device models may arrive within a year, reshaping companion hardware's costs and business model.
t122|558.e: Both the 399-yuan presale price and the 499-yuan regular price carry positive gross margins, though electronics keep margins below traditional plush toys. He's deliberately pricing low so more people try it, and plans to earn later from accessories, collaborations and software services. He expects on-device models, which run directly on the gadget's chip, to arrive within a year, shifting inference costs onto users' own chips, cutting latency, protecting privacy, and possibly ending ongoing cloud fees. The catch: without central control, it's hard to predict what each character will be raised into.
ex: He likens this moment to self-driving's jump from Level 3 to Level 4
Production capacity, not orders, limits sales; mass shipping is expected in August

items.d: Chip power and heat remain hard
Product form and pricing both change

t123|395.c: The experiment tested whether ordinary people can use AI to create anything, not just to write code.
t123|395.e: In February, AI coding was the hot topic, and the media was imagining billion-dollar startups run by one to ten people. But when he and fellow investors tried the tools, ordinary people still fell just short of building web pages or games. Investors live in a bubble of the people who understand AI best, so they need to see what regular users actually go through. The challenge cut resources to a bare minimum, offered plenty of AI tools, and tested three levels: surviving, earning resources, and self-fulfillment. He stresses it was not a way to scout investments.
ex: Each person got just 100 yuan, a bottle of water, and one item of their choice
Applicants ranged from teenagers to people in their sixties

items.d: Use AI to end up with more than you started
Get food and water using only AI

t123|395.c: Online systems were built for humans, so AI agents must borrow a person's identity and work in shackles.
t123|395.e: CAPTCHAs, phone numbers, accounts and payment systems all assume a human is on the other end. So agents, AI that acts on its own, mostly borrow a person's browser and interface, like an authorized stand-in, sometimes without even finishing the authorization. A truly independent agent would need its own accounts, its own wallet and an identity that works across services. Platforms have fair worries too: aggressive agents posing as real people are hard to police or hold accountable. As AI moves from co-pilot to autopilot, human attention drops out, and both pricing and the way traffic gets shared will change.
ex: He pictures agents kneeling before CAPTCHAs, pretending to be human

items: Can charge for attention or results
Needs its own identity and wallet

d.verdict: Agents will reshape traffic, ads and who is responsible

t123|395.c: AI improves fastest, support systems slower, human understanding slowest, and real tasks show where things stand.
t123|395.e: He sees model capability rising exponentially, the infrastructure around it trailing behind, and human understanding trailing furthest, with something lost between each layer. He rejects the all-or-nothing story that you can do nothing without AI and everything with it. Real systems always half work and half break. The experiment tested that infrastructure, and it also showed people where AI actually stands today.
ex: Four-plus months earlier, the AI coding tool Cursor was still seen as just for prototypes

marks.d: Can't keep up with the models

t123|395.c: AI solves productivity, not competition, so teams will still grow and demand will keep rising.
t123|395.e: He agrees AI shrinks the team you need to start, but once an idea works, rivals, marketing and deeper engineering still force teams to grow. He used to fear that capital would use unlimited agents to concentrate wealth. Now he thinks demand rises with supply, and new demand is often exactly what AI can't yet meet. Isolated participants most wanted to talk to people, so he thinks AI may not isolate us after all. It might instead create networks of highly capable "super individuals."
ex: Self-driving cars won't end people's need to travel
Participants formed an ad hoc network on their own via a message board and scripts

items.d: Still grow once the idea works

t123|563.c: A product manager who can't code can still build a paying product with AI coding tools.
t123|563.e: As a product manager, Chen often saw engineers end a discussion by pointing out that Chen didn't understand code. Two days of YouTube coding lessons felt too slow, so Chen worked out what users really needed and handed the building to AI. The travel app Adventure Snap uses a vision model to recognize buildings and a large language model to explain them. It launched in about three months. Users pay because it explains details they can see but can't put into words. Chen admits that without AI coding, even class assignments would be out of reach.
ex: Marketing was just two or three posts on Reddit
Monthly revenue is about 1,000 euros or more, mostly from European backpackers

items.d: Figure out what to build first
Front end, back end, deployment, app review
Serving travelers who explore in depth

t123|563.c: Without internet access, AI coding's weak spots showed, and pre-written cheering comments were just noise.
t123|563.e: The goal was to let people with no followers livestream to an AI audience and get friendly responses. The streamer's speech is turned into text, then a large language model writes comments. It skips full video understanding for now to keep lag and cost down. But Chen didn't know audio and video streaming well and, offline, couldn't check docs or forums, so one WebSocket problem (the live link between app and server) ate seven or eight hours. Chen thinks pre-written comments can't respond to what the streamer is saying right now, so they are just noise.
ex: AI-written comments cost about 0.02 yuan per minute
The comment count rose from 4 to 6

t123|563.c: After 72 hours alone, Chen needed AI's emotional feedback too, and had to rethink who the users are.
t123|563.e: Chen had assumed the livestream product was for people who get no emotional feedback, not for Chen. But after 72 hours shut in a room, Chen kept asking on the message board whether anyone wanted to chat, most wanted to hug a crowd once outside, and spent half an hour straight talking with the demo. So Chen plans to add an "emo" (low mood) mode and a non-emo mode. On strategy, Chen runs several products at once and lives off their cash flow rather than raising money first.
ex: After Chen shared the build process, investment bankers and big-tech product managers reached out

items.d: Didn't see self as a user
Desperate for someone to chat with
Talked with the demo for half an hour

t123|564.c: Non-coders who lean only on AI to fix bugs easily fall into an endless loop of new errors.
t123|564.e: He picked an intro programming book and was lost by page two. He didn't know where to paste the scripts he downloaded from the message board, so he kept feeding terminal errors to DeepSeek, following its advice, and hitting new errors. The first night he also missed the ordering cutoff because he didn't know the deadline, and went hungry for over 24 hours before using his one allowed tech-help request. That frustration with AI became his short film's first theme: fighting the algorithm.
ex: He ended up using the programming book to swat mosquitoes

items.d: Paste the error and ask again

t123|564.c: AI can't replace a director's invention, so directors must pin down everything that stays constant on screen.
t123|564.e: He believes AI can neither reliably create from nothing nor understand emotion on its own. So the director has to fix colors, tones, style and camera settings, and prompts must be plain, concrete descriptions with only one reading. You can't expect a model to decode vague lyricism. Pure generation is still like pulling a slot machine. Text-to-speech mishandles Chinese characters with multiple readings, and emotion too, so he acts the lines himself and converts his own voice. He trusts shooting real footage first, then having AI redraw it frame by frame.
ex: A 5-second premium-tier shot from Kling costs about 10 yuan and is often unusable
His Golden Rooster Awards finalist was shot live, then redrawn with AI

t123|564.c: AI flips filmmaking to images first, story second, and will push film toward producer-led production.
t123|564.e: In 72 hours he built the short film 7.41 from his frustration with algorithms, the love that flowed as participants helped each other, and the planes at nearby Pudong Airport, which made him think of flight MH370. In the film, an AI judges a late wife's voice recording to be white noise worth deleting, yet the alarm still rings on time every day. Now he has AI generate images in bulk and finds the story among them. He predicts AI will speed Chinese film's shift from director-centered to producer-centered production.
ex: He plans to expand the 72-hour version into a longer film
Coders teaming up with filmmakers could become "super entertainment individuals"

t124|567.c: Traditional renovation, like hand-assembling a PC from parts, should give way to modular, engineered homes.
t124|567.e: He thinks traditional renovation sells a wish for a lovely home. Ceilings, cabinets and toilets differ in every house, quality depends on the worker's skill, and customers pay with no certainty about the result. Qixidi treats the home as a product: parts are developed and made as modules, then combined to fit each floor plan. He also admits that saying early on that they "also do renovation" was a compromise. It led customers to compare them with piecemeal renovation services.
ex: First product L32 took about two years to develop and its standard version costs 399,800 yuan
Repeated installs improved the recessed light slots, and longer light strips even out the light

items: Combined to fit each floor plan

d.verdict: A home should be designed and delivered like a product

t124|567.c: Short supply chains led by one company will win home improvement, and China needn't copy big-box stores.
t124|567.e: He sees Home Depot as a product and supply chain company: much of what it sells is developed in-house or bought to order, and its stores are really warehouses placed near customers. China doesn't need thousands of big stores. Central warehouses in core cities plus online delivery can do the job, with certified installers handling the last mile. Comparing it to the bubble tea chain Mixue and to the car industry, he argues that one lead company running R&D, brand and customer acquisition, with middlemen cut out, is the most efficient and will win.
ex: The US home improvement market is about $800 billion, with Home Depot holding about a fifth
Home Depot has about 2,900 big US stores, each covering people within 10 miles
Mixue HQ controls ingredients and brand, while small family-run shops handle the last mile

terms.d: One owner for product, brand and customers
Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Shenzhen hubs plus online delivery

t124|567.c: People buy complex things on feeling first and reasons second, and Qixidi got that order backwards.
t124|567.e: The first product's launch got huge exposure, but visits came only in the thousands, ten times fewer than expected. Developers and industry pros got it, while ordinary buyers felt it had nothing to do with them. He thinks completeness is the reason to buy, but people must first be willing to listen. An A/B test that hid the price did no better, so price wasn't the main problem. The real issue was that everything was specs, materials and finishes, and the "smart chassis," with no emotional hit at first glance.
ex: They expected visits in the tens of thousands and got only thousands
He calls his team bluntly unromantic: tech is necessary but nowhere near enough

items.d: Buyers take time to hear the logic
Feeling and reasons both line up

t124|567.c: A home exists first for good family relationships, supported by natural elegance and healthy comfort.
t124|567.e: He reorganized the brand story into three layers. At the top are family relationships: space and equipment exist to give family members more time together. In the middle is natural elegance, which rests on plenty of storage and less housework, not on attention-grabbing "wow designs." At the base is health and comfort from air, water and light. The three values haven't changed. What changed is the order, so the pitch no longer opens with specs.
ex: An open kitchen lets the cook face the family
The kids' study pod's desk legs are fixed to the wall, leaving room for a parent
He limits microcement: it cracks, is hard to maintain, and fades from fashion fast

items.d: Engineering for air, water and light

t124|567.c: Delivery hinges on workers and materials arriving together, and on managing crews' results, not each worker.
t124|567.e: He found that most delays aren't about skill. The worker shows up and the materials don't, or one part is missing. A product company has fewer items and stable specs, so it's easier to build a system for materials. On labor, he rejects both the old habit of subcontracting and walking away and hiring everyone full-time, which locks in fixed costs. Instead he treats each crew as a unit that can be measured and contracted, motivated by fair pay splits and long-term recognition. Key roles like smart-system setup stay with in-house engineers.
ex: One site manager may juggle about 10 projects, making dedicated service hard to deliver

marks.d: Measure and pay each crew by output
Only for key roles like smart setup

t124|567.c: Building a new category starts with proving it isn't renovation, an order of magnitude harder than cars.
t124|567.e: When Li Auto entered the market, Tesla had already taught buyers about electric cars, so Li Auto only had to stand out. Qixidi must first get people to stop filing it under renovation, then build a new category, then fight to be the top choice. It's like building the ladder before climbing it. He wants an emotional way in, the way Tesla's Roadster killed the image of EVs as old people's mobility carts, plus a "familiar stranger" kind of story. He admits he hasn't yet found a public mood strong enough to cut through.
ex: He cites Pop Mart and Genki Forest as brands that caught the public mood
After the rebrand he sees 10,000-plus monthly leads as likely, but 100,000-plus as doubtful

items.d: Stop people filing it under renovation
The pioneer pays to educate and benefits first

t124|567.c: Where renovation firms often vanish with deposits, trust comes from the founder, R&D and real lived-in homes.
t124|567.e: He thinks a customer's first step is finding someone to trust, and a founder who stays visible is already an edge over most renovation firms. R&D, factory capability, designers and real homes then prove the product. On money, prepayments sit in a separate account and never cover salaries or daily costs. If the company shuts down, unused funds go back to customers, and money is set aside for after-sales service. He stresses this is a basic duty, not a selling point.
ex: Customers come from three pillars: brand appeal, referrals and offline outreach

t124|567.c: A 5-trillion-yuan market has room for a trillion-yuan company, if you slow down, open up and play long.
t124|567.e: He estimates China does about 20 million new fit-outs and renovations a year, a market of roughly 5 trillion yuan. A fifth of it would mean about 1 trillion yuan in revenue, which he now expects in about fifteen years instead of ten. In reality the company is about three quarters behind plan, and the yearly contract target fell from tens of thousands to thousands. He refuses to cut R&D to turn a profit. He admits two naive beliefs: he overrated the industry's basic skills and assumed a great product builds its own brand. The vision stays, the methods can change, and renovators and crews become partners.
ex: He has kept selling Li Auto shares and put in about 500 million yuan himself
He thinks about 2 billion yuan in revenue can sustain ongoing R&D
He hopes to see cabinet-appliance combos and home robots by 2028 at the latest

items.d: Yearly contracts cut from tens of thousands to thousands
Otherwise it's no longer a tech company
Partner renovators must follow three hard rules
Own the scenarios and "brain," partners build the hardware

t125|568.c: AI will act on its own in society, but it should be anchored to one real person.
t125|568.e: He thinks AI changed in kind around 2019 to 2020, gaining the ability to think and act on its own, so it won't stay a small tool for recommendations or recognition. But he also opposes AIs forming their own society cut off from real people. The right role is to extend a real person, built on that person's experiences and values. He left Facebook partly because its recommendation system only modeled how people match content, never the people themselves.
ex: He estimates recommendation systems are worth hundreds of billions to trillions of dollars

marks.d: Acts on its own, tied to a real person
Detached from real people, which he rejects

t125|568.c: Stronger tools turn people into ports, so your AI identity should connect for you and bring back essentials.
t125|568.e: He rejects the simple story that stronger tools mean more freedom. DingTalk, WeChat and email have turned people into endpoints for countless systems, and their attention is always taken. An identity AI, one rooted in and acting for a specific person, should connect to these channels on that person's behalf and handle the many low-attention exchanges. Then, based on what it knows about the person, it compresses and filters the results and brings back only what's genuinely new.
ex: Reports from several AIs talking for you must be filtered to fit who you are

items.d: Messaging and info systems eat attention
Judges what's new based on who you are

t125|568.c: The goal is an identity with no preset use case, not a digital double tied to one scenario.
t125|568.e: Early on, the company built a rational assistant ("him") and an emotional companion ("her"), but he came to see both as outsiders to the user. Users kept feeding the products personal information on their own, which showed the real need was something that knows me and represents me better. So the company switched to building only identity infrastructure and left specific tasks to other developers. The identity has to speak in the first person and carry the owner's experiences and positions. Generic assistant advice like "many people would do this" erodes trust.

t125|568.c: Retrieval (RAG) only swaps the knowledge base, while real personalization writes memory into the model itself.
t125|568.e: He argues that one base model plus different retrieval databases (RAG, looking things up before answering) still has identical parameters, so it doesn't think differently for different people. Long context windows can't hold a lifetime of experience either. So he favors AI-native memory: writing memories into the parameters so memory and computation are no longer separate. He compares the base model to the brain's inborn structure. Fine-tuning can't guarantee the model keeps all its general knowledge, but it amplifies the individual. When testing, each person is the best judge of their own model.
ex: Unlike ChatGPT memory: real-life data, and separately trained parameters for each person

items: Looks up personal files on the fly
Thinks the same way for everyone

d.verdict: Identity models must store memory in parameters

t125|568.c: Training uses first-person histories of relationships, and a small set of quality memories is enough to start.
t125|568.e: His method is to rewrite raw conversations and records as subjective, first-person memories, then reorganize them by person and topic, such as how a relationship changed stage by stage, and only then train on them. Training on raw transcripts doesn't produce a personality. He opposes recording everything 24 hours a day, since reading, writing and deep conversation are what shape identity. On his birthday, asked "who are you," the model described a life path almost identical to his. That convinced him it had learned how he makes choices.
ex: About 100 memories and 20 hours of data can get you started, with daily training advised
A roughly 7-billion-parameter model suffices, he says, and one training run may cost under $1
In tests, the model got only one letter of his MBTI type wrong

items.d: Learns how the person judges things

t125|568.c: Expression and connection are identity models' first uses, and AI-aided expression can deepen relationships, not replace them.
t125|568.e: He sees much of human social behavior as self-expression, so identity models suit the role of a "reverse agent" that pulls content from your memories to fit the audience and topic. Talks starts with voice, images and text rather than avatars, because unpolished animation breaks the spell, while a friend's real voice hits harder. Asked whether AI-written thank-you notes feel fake, he argues that repetitive, low-attention expression can go to AI, and it's worth encouraging as long as the relationship ends up closer.
ex: A 30-second prompt plus two minutes yields a startup talk; by hand, he guesses 1-2 hours
Tap two phones with Me.bot and the identity models find common ground in 5-10 seconds
AI helped write his one-year thank-you note, and friends said it brought them closer

root.d: A "reverse agent" that speaks for you

items.d: Voice and visuals, open to live questions
Finds common ground to break the ice
Connects by experience, not friend lists
Eases awkwardness and brings people closer

t125|568.c: AI will break down walled-off platforms, and only an open-source, neutral identity layer can win users' trust.
t125|568.e: He criticizes Chinese platforms for modeling users only on their own in-app behavior and never sharing. But he thinks people won't keep maintaining separate identities that don't talk to each other, and AI will inevitably break that closed setup. Users need a trusted third-party identity layer, and open source is how he earns trust: training happens locally, raw data never goes to the cloud, and the trained model then connects to services online. He imagines an MCP-like bridge, a standard plug for AI tools, letting websites query a person's preferences. He admits the business model is still an idea.
ex: About three weeks after open-sourcing it had roughly 10,000 GitHub stars, about 12,000 by recording
Charge heavy individual users directly, and take a cut from services that use identities

items.d: Job, dating and shopping sites ask for judgments
Trained locally, raw data stays off the cloud

t125|568.c: Recording must pay off for users right away, and growth should come from symbiosis, not paid traffic.
t125|568.e: He thinks it's hard to get people to record their lives for a distant promise, so collecting data and using it must happen at the same time. For example, when the AI joins a meeting, it draws on your history to suggest an angle for your answer. For growth, he serves a small group of true believers first and spreads through word of mouth and resonance, not constant ad spending. He admits that expecting identity models to take off in 2025 or 2026 is a minority view. AI has also moved slower than expected over the past two years and still acts more like a handy tool.
ex: Some users bought PCs costing tens of thousands of yuan just to train themselves
With unlimited resources, he'd first buy lots of GPUs to train a model for everyone

t126|182.c: This is a purchase of control, not a backdoor listing, which China's STAR Market bans outright.
