t126|182.e: He says to start with the filing itself. What has been disclosed is a 784 million yuan purchase of 29.99% of Swancor Advanced Materials, plus the control that comes with it. The roughly 2.1 billion yuan figure is only a theoretical total if the buyer later raises its stake to nearly 66%. A backdoor listing is judged by whether the incoming assets, revenue, net profit and net assets exceed the listed company's size, and the STAR Market flatly forbids it. "Quasi-backdoor listing" is just outsiders' shorthand for a possible future path. Market hopes are not a disclosed plan.
ex: The filing mentions possibly buying another 33.63% to 37% later

items: 2.1 billion yuan buys the whole company
Robots list through the back door
A name change means a listing
No plan yet to inject assets

d.verdict: Respect the market and regulators, and go by the filing

t126|182.c: Stopping at 29.99% was deliberate: it gains control through voting rights without a mandatory offer to all shareholders.
t126|182.e: He explains there are two kinds of control: absolute control with over half the shares, and relative control through effective voting rights. Once the original controlling shareholder gave up its voting rights, AgiBot's side became the largest voting bloc with just 29.99%. Crossing 30% generally requires a tender offer to all shareholders, buying any shares they want to sell. The offer price in the filing is far below the market price anyway, so small shareholders wouldn't sell at it. He also notes the deal still needs approval, so the outcome isn't guaranteed.
ex: The filing's offer price was 7.78 yuan, while the stock topped 13 yuan at recording
He expects negotiated share transfers like this rarely change much

terms.d: Gives up voting rights on its shares

result.d: Control without a mandatory full offer

t126|182.c: Putting the robot business into the listed company means clearing share-swap, business-fit and financial hurdles.
t126|182.e: He stresses that changing a registered company name won't list AgiBot. Injecting assets requires the listed company to issue new shares to buy them, so AgiBot's shareholders swap into listed stock. If that counts as a backdoor listing, it gets reviewed like an IPO. STAR Market mergers also require the businesses to be similar or linked in the supply chain. A "robot concept" isn't real business fit, and Swancor's resin business has no natural link to humanoid robots. He guesses it may take a long time to grow adjacent businesses inside the listed company, but stresses this is speculation.
ex: Swancor once said its thermoset resin testing was aimed at industrial robots
He recalls rules like three years in business and about 300 million yuan in latest-year revenue

root.d: Listed firm issues shares to buy assets

items.d: Years in business, revenue, cash flow

t126|182.c: Private valuations are ten times what A-share mergers pay, so a share-swap at today's price is unlikely.
t126|182.e: He estimates A-share mergers in 2022 to 2024 paid about 12 to 15 times earnings. Even if AgiBot earned 100 million yuan in profit, 12 times that is only a little over 1 billion yuan, far below its roughly 15 billion yuan private valuation. Its private investors wouldn't accept that, and regulators would scrutinize the price anyway. He thinks a lighter path is for the listed company to buy assets from AgiBot's supply chain for cash, without new shares, which is usually fine at a fair price. But this too is just his reasoning.
ex: Beijing Stock Exchange IPOs price at about 15-16 times earnings, above merger levels

t126|182.c: AgiBot's other shareholders gained no tradable public stock from this deal.
t126|182.e: He points out that the Swancor shares will be held by acquisition vehicles above AgiBot, so ordinary shareholders sit at least two layers away from the listed stock. To exit, they would have to ask the controller to sell shares and pass the money back down layer by layer. Targeted payouts like that are hard in China's system, and ordinary shareholders have no say. The deal helps AgiBot's fundraising story but promises nothing. He adds that private-company restructuring answers to only two things, the shareholder agreement and company law. Cash on the books doesn't mean founders can spend it on a shell.
ex: The buyers are two partnerships, Zhiyuan Hengyue and Zhiyuan Xinchuang
He sees Taihua Deng, not the more visible Zhihui Peng, as the real controller

items.d: Zhiyuan Hengyue and Zhiyuan Xinchuang partnerships
Still a limited company, not yet joint-stock
No direct access to listed shares

t126|182.c: Companies hoping to copy AgiBot face hurdle after hurdle, and need money, governance and a clean shell.
t126|182.e: He rejects the idea that this deal is a shortcut anyone can copy. The first hurdle is money: a change of control usually takes 500 million to 1 billion yuan at minimum. Then come the shareholder agreement, the shareholder meeting and the board. You also need a clean shell: tidy business, no pledged shares or regulatory problems, concentrated ownership, and a seller willing to hand over control. A private placement of new shares can substitute, but it dilutes existing holders, and sellers may not want to trade cash for shares. He likens it to a carp leaping the dragon gate.
ex: Private placements are usually priced at 80% of the prior 20-day average
He cites Qiming-linked buyers taking Tianmai Technology and Meihua-linked buyers taking Mengjie
At least three companies he knows are in deep talks with listed firms

items.d: 500 million to 1 billion yuan for control
No pledges, no risk warning, concentrated ownership

t126|182.c: When IPOs fully reopen depends on the index, and buying a shell is a long-haul choice among exits.
t126|182.e: He thinks an IPO is usually still the first choice, but there's a backlog. With little new money coming in, new listings drain existing funds, and blue chips and state-owned firms are tasked with keeping markets stable, so IPOs won't open up fast. Hong Kong's Chapter 18C route for tech firms needs a strong investor lineup and big cornerstone investors, with no valuation guarantee. Unitree may already be a joint-stock company with strong state shareholders, and whoever gets a window first becomes the sector's first listing. AgiBot's shell route means high risk and a long timeline, not a proven shortcut.
ex: He notes 18C requires over HK$600 million in cornerstone investment, among other rules

items.d: The market's pool of funds is limited
Pace of opening is tied to the index

t127|312.c: A general model scoring at gold level on the International Math Olympiad shows AI generalizing to hard-to-check tasks.
t127|312.e: He sees this as bigger than Google's math-specific system last year: OpenAI's model had no internet, no math-specific tuning and no tools. Math proofs are hard both to produce and to check, and were long seen as a weak spot for large models. Much entry-level code just reuses existing modules, but a proof has to build new reasoning where no ready-made steps exist. So the spillover value may be bigger than for coding. He also notes Google's objection that the result wasn't officially certified.
ex: He thinks AI helping find small theorems and proofs has moved from distant to near
Fields that run on reasoning rather than experiments may benefit first

items: Reasoning carries over to other areas

d.verdict: General reasoning passed on the hardest-to-check task

t127|312.c: Even if pretraining stalls, post-training and longer thinking at answer time still have a long way to go.
t127|312.e: He splits model progress into three stages: pretraining on huge amounts of text, post-training that refines the model with methods like reinforcement learning, and inference, the thinking done while answering. If rumors are right, the IMO model's base is close to GPT-4o, so the gains came mainly from post-training and longer thinking. That leaves lots of room after pretraining. He compares it to the atomic bomb: once people know it can be done, the field quickly finds the path and reasoning improves everywhere. But if experts need a long time to check a proof, AI still can't replace researchers soon.
ex: He calls going from "sparks of AGI" 2.5 years ago to now a moon-landing moment
He reads "multi-agent" as several roles collaborating inside one model, with details still unpublished

items.d: The longer it thinks, the better

t127|312.c: The talent war shows top researchers are valuable, but stacking stars doesn't guarantee they work well together.
t127|312.e: He thinks Meta's huge pay offers hurt the teams being raided, dent morale on Meta's own existing teams, and push up salaries across the industry. How top people mesh and how the organization works matter just as much. All-star teams have failed to gel plenty of times, and money alone can't fix organizational problems. Competition is heating up in China too. He admits he lacks the full picture, but sees startups' costs rising for talent, token subsidies and fundraising.
ex: He sees Tencent as one of China's most aggressive recruiters lately

items.d: Talent, token and funding costs rise

t127|312.c: In the agent era, apps are undervalued, because context and environment give them an edge others can't copy.
t127|312.e: In the chatbot era, he thinks model companies had a clear edge from owning everything end to end. In the agent era, context, tools and environment matter more, and app companies can supply them. Context has three layers: the quality of a single session, memory across sessions, and new data sources the product creates. A trained model's weights are static, like an engine without a car, and apps turn it into the whole vehicle. That's why all three big labs build their own apps. He rejects the idea that "wrapper" apps get crushed once model makers move in.
ex: ChatGPT Agent's slide decks are worse than some Chinese products'
Smart glasses supply real-time visual context models can't get on their own
OpenAI leans on apps, Anthropic on coding, Google on its full stack and TPU chips

items.d: Access and tools turn output into results
Session quality, memory, new data sources

t127|312.c: Coding and reasoning have gone mainstream, agents work for early adopters, and robots are overhyped.
t127|312.e: He judges that coding and reasoning are now mainstream paid uses. Cursor and Claude Code can handle large codebases and fix their own mistakes, and Deep Research drove ChatGPT's growth. Agents and multimodal AI, which handles text, images and sound together, are still unreliable but already create value for early adopters. He was impressed by GPT-4o's image generation and Veo 3's synced sound and video. By contrast, people underestimate how hard physical manipulation is for robots, so he focuses on productivity already being delivered in the digital world.
ex: Tesla cut its Optimus robot production forecast, confirming manipulation is hard
He calls 10,000-plus factory robots driving screws this year far too aggressive

t127|312.c: Kimi K2's comeback came from a stable team and better pretraining, not just reinforcement learning.
t127|312.e: As of recording, he called K2 the best open-source model he knew, standing out in coding, agent workflows and Chinese writing. He trusts real users' choices on OpenRouter more than leaderboards. He rejects the claim that pretraining doesn't matter: without a strong base like DeepSeek's V3, R1's reinforcement-learning gains wouldn't exist. Moonshot's core team held together under pressure, and its early bet on long context is now exactly what agents need. He also stresses that open source's value lies in control and community feedback. It is no cure-all.
ex: K2 rose from 13th to 10th on OpenRouter's coding chart within days
K2 has 1 trillion total parameters, with about 32 billion active at a time
He thinks DeepSeek's R2 may have to wait for a new base model

terms.d: Stayed together, and predates the company

result.d: Among the best open models at the time

t127|312.c: Agents use over a thousand times more tokens than chat, so demand for computing power is underestimated.
t127|312.e: Agents search, read and write files, call tools and check their work again and again, so he estimates they can use over a thousand times the tokens of an ordinary chatbot. Estimating Nvidia demand from chat alone is like sizing bandwidth in the dial-up era by QQ chats alone. Productivity demand can also multiply in parallel: tools let people write more code and ask questions they never would have asked, while companionship demand is capped by a person's time. He personally spends nearly $1,000 a month on AI to try new products and find ideas.
ex: He imagines AI tracking earnings reports for 50 stocks at once
He cautions that OpenRouter only reflects small and mid-sized developers' relative preferences

t127|312.c: Agents are about letting AI take the wheel, and by year-end the test is success rates and memory.
t127|312.e: He compares the core of agents to Level 3 self-driving: the human stops doing the work and the AI does it. Users must learn to be the AI's boss, setting goals, providing resources and granting permissions instead of watching every step. Micromanaging stops the system from building experience. He isn't rushing to pick a winning approach, since end-to-end training and app-level orchestration can coexist. By year-end he most wants to see whether task success rates jump, whether memory compounds, and what risks come from AI code no one has fully reviewed.
ex: Claude Code hands over more fully than Cursor, which stays inside the editor
Cursor only took off with Sonnet 3.5 and 3.7, so design products for future models

t128|574.c: Cece meets people's need for explanation and comfort, not for predicting their fate.
t128|574.e: He started the company after a heartbreak, looking for a framework to make sense of his confusion, and he believes comfort has always been a core part of medicine. Astrology, psychology and personality tests are topics people happily discuss every day, and they support less frequent paid counseling. Medical content has a small audience and costly education, so it doesn't suit a consumer app. He sees astrology and birth charts as broad hypotheses about life cycles, not reproducible science, since no one can rerun their life as an experiment. Their staying power lies in helping people organize experience and feel more certain.
ex: Cece works with a Peking University medical humanities team on narrative medicine research
He thinks top programmers looked down on this need, leaving room early on

items.d: Love and other problems bring uncertainty

t128|574.c: Each stage of the product solved the previous stage's bottleneck, moving from tools to a physical robot.
t128|574.e: Early on he wanted an AI that could answer questions comprehensively, but traditional machine learning couldn't pull many conclusions together. So he started with buffet-style tools that laid out scores, astrology readings and MBTI results for users to pick from. Next, borrowing from paid-knowledge platforms, he built a marketplace of human experts. One-on-one human sessions have a ceiling, so he planned AI conversations to add supply. Pure software is still a passive tool, though, and only a physical product can become a proactive companion in daily life.
ex: He uses names like "birth chart" and "wisdom cards" to play down the mystical label

items.d: From passive tool to active companion

t128|574.c: AI now serves more users than human counselors, but building AI made him value human presence more.
t128|574.e: He sees that AI is easy to start with and cheap, and some users even find a machine more objective, so more people now use AI than human counseling. But it's not a simple swap. The longer he works on AI, the more he feels that eye contact, hugs and being physically together are hard to replicate, and the human experts' numbers on the platform keep growing. The company bets on both: AI expands low-cost supply, humans keep the value of relationships, and a robot adds back some sense of presence.
ex: About 50 million registered users, roughly half of whom have used AI features

d.verdict: Not a replacement: bet on both

t128|574.c: General models excel at one-off answers, while specialized products deliver results using long accumulated context.
t128|574.e: He says every Chinese New Year brings a panic, over ChatGPT, Sora or DeepSeek, but on reflection he judges that DeepSeek hit base-model makers hardest. A specialized product's value is in combining a user's history, expert tools and multiple services into a longer context that delivers results. Single features like AI astrology are low-hanging fruit anyone can pick. Psychological needs vary from person to person and one-on-one help is hard to standardize, so the field has long stayed fragmented. That fragmentation is the room for going deep.
ex: They fine-tune general base models and hire psychology graduates to label data
Next, they want a Deep Research-style analysis of a person's situation

terms.d: Builds on the best base models

t128|574.c: Building a companion robot was a gut decision, starting with a family's first robot: proactive but never intrusive.
t128|574.e: He admits the online business already has an edge, while hardware means getting software, hardware and service right at once, and his managers worry the company lacks hardware DNA. So it's a gut call, but it's funded from company profits and stays within a safe range. He thinks large models' biggest breakthrough is in interaction, while doing housework is still far off. So the first generation focuses on proactive companionship at home, covering education and emotions. He doesn't believe a category needs tens of millions of units to count, and will serve early users first.
ex: Last year he turned down a lucrative acquisition offer to keep control of decisions
Sensitive video stays on the device, which keeps the price high
The first batch is expected internally at about 10,000 units, an experimental scale

root.d: Proactive interaction before an all-purpose body

items.d: Knows when to approach, when to stay quiet
Not focused on school test scores

t128|574.c: Companion products shouldn't copy short video's dopamine playbook, and should support both connection and growth.
t128|574.e: He uses three reward systems as a design framework: dopamine for instant stimulation, oxytocin for lasting, family-like connection, and endorphins for the delayed reward of overcoming hardship. He opposes building a robot that maximizes instant stimulation. The ideal path is to ease pain first, then build support and attachment, while keeping the difficulties people need to grow. He stresses this is only a design lens, and he wouldn't dare use it to define love.
ex: Drawing on LOVOT, which uses big eyes, movement and hugs to spark affection
Pets and stuffed toys are early models

marks.d: Lasting connection, the core of companionship

t128|574.c: AI will replace tool-like jobs, and the future will depend more on human emotion and empathy.
t128|574.e: He's fairly pessimistic about AI's social impact. The industrial era used division of labor to give people professions and a place in how income is shared. AI replaces exactly those tool-like roles, and new jobs such as AI training are far fewer than the ones lost. He rejects the optimistic view that AI will surely create new professions, and thinks handing out money can hardly restore people's sense of competence and dignity. He reasons that farming ran on strength and industry on intellect, while the AI era may rely more on people themselves. Counseling and companionship could be one way forward.
ex: AI-boosted coding may not mean more programmers, and could even cut jobs

items.d: Runs on intellect and division of labor
Relies more on emotion and empathy

t129|581.c: Chat-style AI is already behind, and the future is real-time AI that watches, listens and helps unprompted.
t129|581.e: He thinks AI shouldn't wait to be asked. Like Jarvis in Iron Man, it should watch and listen in real time and step in to help, which is why he started with a meeting assistant. One user said they had an interview in ten minutes and would pay right away, which showed him how painful job hunting is. So he narrowed the product to an interview assistant, then grew it into an end-to-end job search platform. He also refuses to add a bot that joins the meeting.
ex: About 7 million users, with paying users in over 150 countries
A team of about 20 across San Francisco, Shanghai and Bangalore

items.d: Watches, listens and prompts on its own
Interview in 10 minutes, ready to pay now

t129|581.c: Innovation always challenges old norms, and someone else would build it anyway, so he doesn't dodge the controversy.
t129|581.e: Asked whether an invisible interview assistant is cheating, he admits the product challenges traditional norms, but says all innovation does, and if they didn't build it, someone else would. He distinguishes it from Cluely, another real-time AI helper: Cluely needs a screenshot to activate by hand, while his product is hands-free, keeps listening and prompts on its own. On possible future regulation, he offered no prediction, saying only that it depends on how the market changes.
ex: He admires Cluely's no-holds-barred marketing and its founder's personality

marks.d: Activated by hand after a screenshot

t129|581.c: Job-search products naturally lose users, so growth depends on constant acquisition and company-wide systems.
t129|581.e: He accepts that job seekers leave once they find work, but notes over a billion people look for jobs worldwide each year, so the key is constant acquisition. He calculates annual recurring revenue (ARR) as last quarter's revenue times four, which he considers conservative. He criticizes inflated ways of calculating it and prefers checking against real user feedback. Going from a few million to over ten million dollars, he says, took steady feature releases, reliable global deployment, multichannel marketing and a data flywheel, where more data improves the product and a better product brings more data.
ex: ARR tripled from about $1 million to $3 million within 12 weeks at the HF0 accelerator
The seed round raised about $6.88 million from 13 investors

t129|581.c: Growth comes not from inspiration or taste but from many small experiments compounding over time.
t129|581.e: He wants real traffic data, not internal debates about taste, to settle questions. When an adviser suggested raising prices, they moved the monthly fee from $99 to $150, and willingness to pay didn't noticeably drop. Ending the free trial and redoing the brand gave mixed results. He thinks most growth comes from small 5% to 10% improvements stacking up, and even a button's position and color affect conversion. So every team, from operations to marketing, can take a slice of traffic to run experiments.
ex: Over 100 experiments run at the same time every week

items.d: Any team can test with live traffic

t129|581.c: Marketing should be run entirely by AI agents, not just partly automated with AI.
t129|581.e: He credits AI-driven growth infrastructure for letting a 20-person team reach this scale. For SEO, they turn licensed real interview questions into huge numbers of pages that each focus on a single question, and now also aim to be cited in ChatGPT and Gemini answers. When news breaks, they quickly generate landing pages and content. They test ad creatives in bulk instead of fully trusting platforms' auto-optimization. Expensive US labor also pushed them to replace manual ad buying with agents early.
ex: About 4,000 to 5,000 SEO pages generated each week
Pages and content go live within about 10 minutes of news like layoffs
About 500 ad creatives tested every week

root.d: Big growth from a small team

items.d: Real interview questions become countless pages
From news to content in minutes
Bulk tests, not just platform optimization

t129|581.c: AI has turned Silicon Valley money toward young founders, and grueling hours only make sense with equity.
t129|581.e: He saw that before 2024, established VCs favored big-tech executives and foundation-model teams. After that, they started backing young people using AI to remake traditional industries like HR, payments and healthcare, which he likens to scrappy newcomers beating old masters. He thinks the app layer's ability to make money is underrated. The 996 schedule, 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. six days a week, is clearly back in US AI startups. He thinks it only makes sense when employees hold equity and share in the growth, since traditional 996's problem is high effort for low reward.
ex: He has personally angel-invested in 28 companies, at $3,000 to $10,000 each
The company offers unlimited paid leave and actively urges staff to take it
He criticizes how Windsurf was absorbed, leaving the rest of the team behind

d.verdict: The app layer's business value is underrated

t129|581.c: Once anyone can use AI to deliver results, hiring must judge the process, not the outcome.
t129|581.e: He thinks as AI job-search tools spread, résumés and traditional screening will tell employers less. His plan for companies is a "programmable workspace": AI simulates a company's first day or first week, and candidates complete real tasks while employers watch how they pick tools, collaborate and approach the work. He admits this workshop-style hiring is hard to scale, and how fast companies adopt it and which roles to start with are open questions. He leans toward high prices or charging by results to avoid vanity revenue.
ex: He estimates 40 to 50 companies worldwide are copying FinalRound
The product for companies is slated for September

terms.d: AI builds a company's first week

t130|584.c: Phone agents should stop hogging your screen and instead run in the cloud, working in the background.
t130|584.e: He says last October's version ran on the phone itself and fought the user for the screen. Heavy users hated it, and it could only handle short tasks. Version 2.0 runs on cloud phones and cloud computers that work in the background for long stretches, and users can take over anytime. Phones lean toward everyday services and computers toward knowledge work, so both need covering. Partnerships with phone makers still decide in the cloud and act on the device, which suits short tasks. Zhipu's own consumer product takes long tasks and doubles as a testbed for its algorithms.
ex: 2.0 covers iOS, Android and the web, and is free for now with no invite code
Last year's beta could handle only single-digit concurrent sessions

items.d: Hogs the screen, short tasks only
Cloud phones and PCs work in the background
Glasses, fridges and more tap the cloud

t130|584.c: Seconds-long tasks aren't worth giving an AI agent, but hands-busy or time-consuming ones are.
t130|584.e: His rule of thumb: anything you can do in a few seconds, like sending a WeChat message, isn't worth delegating. The value comes when your hands are busy, while driving, doing chores or running, or when a task takes time, like booking trips, researching or planning an outing. He thinks deciding what to eat is the daily question most likely to become a habit, and today's recommendation systems don't capture what users really want. Operating WeChat is technically feasible but carries big privacy risks, so it's not a priority.
ex: He often eats braised chicken rice simply because he can't be bothered to look further
He most wants scheduled tasks, like coffee ordered before he wakes up

cells.d: Quick commands while driving or doing chores
Hands busy and the task takes time

t130|584.c: Confirming payments is today's biggest friction, so users should grant agents tiered authority, like a boss.
t130|584.e: He admits that if you still have to pay by hand at the end, ordering takeout through an agent may not beat doing it yourself, and users might forget to confirm. For safety, the cloud device is like a new phone that users log into themselves. Zhipu doesn't store account passwords, and sensitive steps like logging in and paying go back to the user. The plan is to shorten the flow with notifications and voice confirmation, then allow small payments without asking, and eventually give agents their own wallet with limits on amount, frequency and category. Refunds are still undecided.
ex: For example, purchases under 30 yuan could skip confirmation

marks.d: Sensitive steps go back to the user
Pays directly below a set amount
Limits on amount, frequency and category

t130|584.c: Agents won't cost apps their traffic, and will actually visit them more often.
t130|584.e: Some platforms worry agents will browse in place of users. He argues an agent's information still comes from the apps themselves. It passes along the platform's recommendations and ads faithfully, just filtered with the user's history, so visits may even go up. The urge to compare prices across several food delivery apps already exists, and agents simply automate it. Still, he expects big apps are more likely to build their own agents first than to open up to partners.
ex: An agent could find a restaurant on Xiaohongshu, then order on Meituan

items.d: Keeps recommendations and ads, adds user history

t130|584.c: AI that taps through screens like a person ships fastest, and will long coexist with direct API calls.
t130|584.e: The GUI route has the model look at the screen and tap buttons like a person, reusing the app's existing accounts, payments and fraud controls. Platforms don't need to adapt anything, and the agent developer pays the price: reading images is slow and burns more tokens. APIs, direct software-to-software connections, are fast and accurate, but account linking, ordering and payment after search are broken. Platforms also fear bulk data scraping, and maintaining thousands of interfaces for a big app is costly. He compares it to self-driving cars, which won't eliminate human drivers. Both will coexist.
ex: He thinks a visible, step-by-step process also makes people feel safer because they can follow it

items: Ordering and payment steps are broken

d.verdict: Both will coexist, and screen tapping ships first

t130|584.c: Personal agents work for the user, platform-specific agents work for the service, and both will exist.
t130|584.e: He thinks specialized agents built for a platform or industry can improve the quality of existing traffic, but users must open that app first, so they may not bring new traffic. A personal agent manages a user's whole life and work and sits closest to the user, which makes it most valuable. Ideally, your personal assistant sends requests to each service's front-desk agent, which handles them and reports back. That could eventually form a service network hidden behind social networks. He expects each person to have three or four assistants.
ex: He imagines two people's agents reading calendars and booking a podcast recording slot

t130|584.c: Agents still fall short of human level, held back by training environments and reward signals.
t130|584.e: GPT-4 in 2023 convinced him models would move beyond the chat box. Since then his team has built AgentBench, a test of agent skills, and web agents, and he believes this ability must be grown from pretraining onward. He calls it "heavy industry." Imitating correct action paths isn't enough. A model has to make mistakes, back up and retry in real environments to learn recovery, so he trusts supervision based on outcomes. The hard parts are massively parallel virtual environments and turning expert judgment into checkable reward signals. 2.0's clearest gain is fixing itself after something goes wrong.
ex: Online reinforcement learning needs over a thousand virtual computers collecting data in parallel
Early on WebArena, models scored about 20 and humans about 70-80

t130|584.c: Agents are still being introduced to the market, so welcome competition, ship early and improve through real use.
t130|584.e: He estimates only 10% to 20% of people have used a chatbot, and maybe under 1% have really used an agent, so the whole industry needs to grow the market together. That's why he welcomes OpenAI, ByteDance and others. Like the early iPhone, he'd rather release an imperfect version and let real demand shape the algorithms and engineering. A single task still costs about ten times a search, and the business model isn't clear yet, but he thinks the value is higher. In the end, whoever has the stronger AGI wins.
ex: About $0.20 per task versus about $0.02 per Google search, though measures may differ
His minimum bar for AGI: an ordinary-coworker-level agent working reliably around the clock
New features planned every one to two weeks

t131|586.c: Judge AI by business results like revenue, not just by how much time it saves.
t131|586.e: She finds that "hours saved" doesn't win over business teams. What matters is whether AI brings in more deals and revenue. After rolling out Copilot, Microsoft's AI assistant, across its own sales force, Microsoft tracked new opportunities created, how fast deals closed and revenue per person. Copilot for Sales pulls customer profiles, CRM records, meetings and emails into agendas before meetings and notes after them. An internal agent, an AI that carries out tasks on its own, suggests resources for deals still open. But it only advises. People still make the decisions and review whatever gets sent.
ex: About 65,000 people in Microsoft's sales organization got M365 Copilot licenses

t131|586.c: Copilot became indispensable not at one turning point, but as its quality gradually crossed a usable threshold.
t131|586.e: She recalls that early on, Copilot's simplified Chinese was far worse than its English, and the first customers weren't impressed. The stronger selling points then were enterprise-grade security and compliance, plus access to work data in email, meetings and documents. As the underlying models improved, quality in Chinese, Japanese and traditional Chinese rose sharply. Only then did the value of pulling context together across apps really show. For example, after a vacation you can ask it to list last week's to-dos, deadlines and the people involved.
ex: Teams translation lets Chinese, English and Korean speakers meet, each heard in their own voice
She uses Copilot to polish her English emails so they sound more professional

items.d: Compliance and access to work data

t131|586.c: Enterprise AI should serve different people at different layers and not lock into any one model.
t131|586.e: She sums up Microsoft's approach as "Copilot is the interface for AI." Business staff use it directly inside familiar Office apps. People with a little technical skill build their own tools in Copilot Studio, a low-code tool that needs little programming. IT staff and developers go deeper with Azure AI Foundry and GitHub Copilot. At the bottom sits a safety foundation of data governance and responsible AI. The platform doesn't bet on one model. It offers models from many companies, plus tools to choose, fine-tune and test them, so AI doesn't stay stuck as an idea because it's too hard to use.
ex: She says the platform hosts over 11,000 models, including OpenAI, Mistral and DeepSeek

items.d: Business staff use it in Office
Build your own tools in Copilot Studio

t131|586.c: Getting everyone to use AI takes firm requirements and role models, but not mindless clicking to hit targets.
t131|586.e: She believes customer-facing teams must use AI well themselves before they can answer customers' questions. New habits need some pressure and required routines, and usually take three weeks or more to form. Microsoft runs boot camps, internal communities, workshops and hackathons, short contests to build something quickly. It picks "pioneers" to set an example and tracks usage app by app, in Teams, Outlook and others. She firmly opposes a Great Leap Forward–style rush to pad usage numbers just for the metrics.
ex: She thinks a new habit takes about 21 days or longer to form

root.d: Use it well before serving customers

t131|586.c: More certain than any single model upgrade is a shift toward many AI agents working together.
t131|586.e: GPT-5 hadn't been released when they recorded. She expected clear gains in multimodality (handling text, images and audio together), structured output and reasoning, but stressed this was only an expectation. What she sees as more certain is a change in how people work with AI: from question and answer, to taking an instruction and acting on it, to several agents (AIs that carry out tasks on their own) and models jointly handling complex work. So the discussion shouldn't fixate on how strong any one model is.

t131|587.c: AI in advertising now covers every step, from opening an account to creative, placement and review.
t131|587.e: She splits Microsoft Advertising's AI into four stages: managing the ad account, generating ad creative with Creative Studio, automated placement with Performance Max, and Copilot analyzing results and suggesting improvements. Clients mainly supply the creative, their goals and their KPIs. Ads run mostly on Bing search and the MSN display network, with more of Microsoft's own traffic being added over time. She cautions that every client is different, and case figures only cover ads run on Microsoft's side.
ex: Samsung's click-through rate on Microsoft ads rose 2.8 times after adopting the AI tools
Samsung cut the time to produce account analysis reports by 35%

t131|587.c: What makes or breaks enterprise AI is how data and access are managed, not what it can generate.
t131|587.e: She argues that if a model can't reach the email, documents and other work data employees use daily, its answers may look polished but are useless. Before connecting that data, though, a company must sort out classification, labels and who can see what. Otherwise an ordinary employee might use Copilot to look up the boss's salary. For clients with weak data foundations, Microsoft does a full overhaul, which is also pushing office systems to the cloud. She opposes rolling out AI without governance, and doesn't think more data is always better.
ex: Access control is built on Microsoft Entra ID, its identity system

terms.d: Labels and governance in place first

t131|587.c: Agents let non-technical people build products, and grassroots adoption works better than mandates.
t131|587.e: With a humanities background, she used AI tools to generate code and built a "24" math card game that made it onto Apple's App Store. That convinced her the point of an agent, an AI that acts on its own, is to get the job done, not just answer questions. Bottom-up ideas are appearing on her team too. A technical support colleague taught themselves to build an AI customer service bot that answers common questions from public ad documentation, then demoed it to the global team. She feels a learning culture doesn't have to rely on mandatory sign-ups.
ex: She used AI to plan a seven-day trip to Osaka with her two kids
Now when she hits a problem, she asks Copilot first, then colleagues

items: Staff build tools on their own

d.verdict: Once tools are easy to use, grassroots innovation works better

t132|590.c: Chip design software (EDA) is hard to beat thanks to algorithms, fab process ties and full toolchains.
t132|590.e: He breaks EDA's barriers into three layers. At the bottom are algorithms, which are really problems of physics simulation and computational science. In the middle, tools must keep up with the new manufacturing processes of fabs like TSMC, Samsung and Intel, constantly updating their libraries of design rules. Tools that fall behind get dropped. On top is a complete toolchain covering design, simulation, verification and testing, which makes switching vendors extremely costly. That is why Chinese tools struggle to win customers from the giants.
ex: Moving from 28nm to a more advanced process can mean rebuilding algorithms, scripts and everything underneath

items.d: Design to testing; costly to switch
Rule libraries track new fab processes

t132|590.c: A few giants already dominate EDA, but new processes and new uses keep creating niche openings.
t132|590.e: Asked why there's no monopoly, he says first ask whether there already is one. The top three to five firms hold 70–80% of the market, which makes it an oligopoly. The giants grow by constantly buying companies. Synopsys buying Ansys links chip-level and system-level physics simulation. But the big three aren't the best at every step. New processes and new uses keep appearing, so niche markets still offer openings. Analog and radio-frequency tools are also where Chinese products are more likely to be used.
ex: By his count, Synopsys had bought over 100 companies by 2022, about 3 a year
He designs digital circuits and hasn't used Chinese tools; RF and analog teams might

items.d: Gaps from new processes and uses

t132|590.c: AI and EDA will improve each other, given enough data, connected tools and customer trust.
t132|590.e: He sees AI's impact in three phases. Short term, AI chips grow so large that traditional placement and routing, deciding where parts go and how wires connect, becomes too slow to run. Medium term, AI reaches deep into EDA, for example using neural networks to predict timing delays. Long term, chips power AI and AI improves chip design, so the two evolve together. Getting there takes training on huge amounts of process data, linking chip-level and system-level tools, and convincing customers their confidential data won't leak during training or use.
ex: He understands Synopsys's DSO.ai is used at many firms to improve power, performance and area
A single AI computing chip is often 600–700 square millimeters

items.d: Predicts delays, improves power, performance, area

t132|590.c: AI is good at local optimization, but whole-chip trade-offs remain top chip companies' edge.
t132|590.e: He thinks AI is already strong at local tasks. But making global trade-offs across an entire SoC, a system-on-chip that packs many functions onto one chip, within a given area and set of constraints is the core skill of the world's top chip companies. That experience isn't shared outside, and AI can't do it yet. So junior, execution-focused roles are easier to replace, while senior engineers who make judgment calls and take responsibility are harder to automate. Good engineers can't just run tools. They need to understand, use and even build AI.
ex: He estimates big firms may have 3–4 design-for-test engineers per 10 designers

t132|590.c: Advanced packaging has gone from a back-end step to what defines chip performance, reshaping the supply chain.
t132|590.e: With single chips hitting size limits, he says the main path is now packaging several chiplets and different kinds of chips together. TSMC's CoWoS packaging capacity has a waiting list, while panel-level, fan-out and other approaches advance in parallel. How many chiplets, what each does and how they connect must be decided when a project starts, so packaging now decides performance. The supply chain is reorganizing vertically, though not always in-house. Intel runs design, manufacturing and packaging itself, while fabless firms tie themselves closely to foundries, IP vendors, packaging-and-test houses and EDA vendors.
ex: He cites $87 billion in combined Q2 2025 capex at Google, Microsoft, Meta and Amazon
Synopsys predicted half of new high-performance chips this year would use 2.5D/3D designs

items: Chiplets and links set at project start
Many chiplets combined in one package

d.verdict: Plan packaging together with design and manufacturing

t132|591.c: EDA is like chopsticks at a meal: until a chip is made, engineers have nothing but data files.
t132|591.e: He compares EDA, chip design software, to chopsticks to show how essential it is, and refines the common "renovating a house" analogy. From architecture and verification to back-end design, engineers never touch anything physical. They just produce data files in EDA tools, and only after those files go to the fab is the chip made. The one-time engineering cost has three main parts: IP (ready-made circuit blocks) bought or built in-house, back-end design, and the masks used for tape-out, the first production run. In-house IP is costed in person-months.
ex: 20 engineers working for a year equals 240 person-months

root.d: Up-front engineering spend for a chip

items.d: Bought at a price, or person-months in-house
Handed to the fab for manufacturing

t132|591.c: EDA costs little to sell to more customers and earns steadily, but only at the design stage.
t132|591.e: He points out that selling a software license to ten companies or a thousand costs about the same, so EDA revenue is steady. But a customer who spends $1 million on tools might be backing a $100 million chip project. However many chips ship once production starts, EDA vendors usually get none of that. They only sell the shovels. The most common pricing is a time-based license. The vendor lists features, customers tick what they need and renew every year.
ex: He compares: perpetual licenses strain cash up front, while pay-per-use can spiral

t132|591.c: Chinese EDA struggles to enter mainstream projects because nobody wants to be blamed for switching tools.
t132|591.e: Even his own employer, a Chinese chip company, won't let a project take on the risk of unfamiliar tools. Mature tools already meet the needs of ordinary chips. Switching brings extra costs, plus the opportunity cost of time that could go elsewhere. If something goes wrong, the person who made the call takes the blame, so even Chinese companies have little reason to switch. His conclusion is that Chinese EDA must first build a reputation in the steps where users are willing to try something new.

t132|591.c: If AI cuts headcount and shortens verification, small teams can build chips and more chip companies will emerge.
t132|591.e: He sums up this year's chip industry as compute, stability and AI. Investment is concentrated in computing chips like GPUs and TPUs. The industry is settling into a balance between closures and new startups. AI both creates demand for chips and is entering front-end design, verification and back-end design. He imagines "AI-generated chips," automated all the way from writing code to drawing the physical layout. The capital barrier won't disappear, but with fewer people and shorter cycles, a lean small team might build chips that once needed a big one.
ex: He agreed when the host compared this to the earlier wave of fabless chip startups

terms.d: From code to netlist and layout

result.d: Capital barrier remains; staffing barrier drops

t132|591.c: Engineers must learn fast, shifting from storing knowledge like a warehouse to connecting it like a router.
t132|591.e: He borrows AMD CEO Lisa Su's advice on learning agility. Engineers should move from Perl to Python, keep up with advanced processes and learn to master AI. Engineers used to be like knowledge warehouses, winning through accumulated experience. Now what matters more is connecting scattered information and building a knowledge network that keeps changing. In future they may even go from using tools to training AI. He admits that most chip design work is pretty tedious.
ex: He estimates about 70% of chip design work is fairly tedious

items.d: From using tools to training them

t133|599.c: Paying AI researchers $10 million a year is a calculated bet on returns, not a pay bubble.
t133|599.e: He rejects the idea that Meta's poaching spree is just an absurd salary bubble. One layer is measurable savings and revenue. Compute spending often runs to $10 billion or more, so talent that raises efficiency by 10% is worth around a billion dollars. Lifting total ad revenue by 0.1% is worth $200 million. The other layer doesn't show up in this year's profit. Falling a model generation behind could shake a company's position, and only those who get a ticket to AGI, AI that can do most human work, survive the next round. That's why Meta is in such a hurry.
ex: He estimates saving 10% on compute is worth about $1 billion
Ad revenue is nearly $200 billion, so a 0.1% lift is about $200 million

terms.d: Don't fall behind in the next model race

result.d: A small outlay with a huge payoff

t133|599.c: Past a certain point, pay stops mattering; culture and the chance to get things done keep people.
t133|599.e: Once income far exceeds what someone needs to live, even ten times more rarely changes their choice. Top talent looks instead at team culture, who they'll work with, whether their direction is trusted and whether the pay will last. So people hired at a high price who are constantly overruled or boxed in tend to leave quickly. He estimates the range where pay still works is about $5–10 million in the US and 5–10 million yuan in China. Beyond that it means little, and this tier is only a tiny fraction of AI talent.
ex: He estimates the top tier is a few hundred people, a tiny share of AI talent
Top pay in China and the US differs by "one exchange rate": same numbers, different currency

marks.d: More money no longer changes choices

t133|599.c: AGI, AI as capable as people at most work, could arrive within three years. He's 80% convinced.
t133|599.e: He didn't believe it before his Silicon Valley trip, but conversations there changed his mind. Reinforcement learning, where models improve through trial and reward, has produced leaps on tasks with clear answers, like coding and math. Models judge writing better than they produce it, so one model can grade another, moving toward machines improving from machine feedback. Running out of internet data doesn't mean data stops growing, since conversations between people and AI keep creating more. He suggests measuring AGI task by task, like self-driving levels: science and engineering first, then sales and interviews, which have no single right answer. He keeps 20% doubt.
ex: A large model placed 8th in the world at the IOI informatics olympiad
Last year Silicon Valley's core teams disagreed; this year consensus is much stronger

items.d: Leaps first where answers are clear

t133|599.c: The US already replaces junior programmers with AI; cheap labor means China will lag a year or two.
t133|599.e: At big US tech companies, programmers who leave often aren't replaced. Startups that once needed R&D teams of eight to ten now get by with one strong engineer plus AI. In China labor is cheaper, so there's less pressure to replace people, and so far the effect shows up as slower job growth. But he expects a more visible phase next year or the year after. The impact hits standardized, repetitive roles first. Hiring for several kinds of developer jobs in China is already down year on year, and executive openings have fallen by about a quarter.
ex: Hiring for embedded, front-end, testing and Android roles fell about 20–30% year on year
One video site cut review, labeling and support staff from 6,000+ to 1,000+

items: Cheap labor, less pressure to replace
Shows up as slower job growth
Expected to lag one to two years

d.verdict: Standardized, repetitive roles get hit first

t133|599.c: Big tech has moved from layoffs to spending more, using reviews and stock grants to keep talent.
t133|599.e: After two years of slimming down, further cuts save little, so the question for big tech is where to spend and on whom. He calls this "spending more to get more." Resources flow to AI and core teams that deliver, while ordinary roles keep shrinking. To fend off rivals offering raises of about 30%, companies give core teams a bigger share of top performance ratings, make it easier to transfer into AI work and front-load stock vesting so key people get rewarded right away. Rivals then often need to offer 50% to 100% raises to lure them.
ex: Core teams' share of top ratings can rise to 30–50%
Tencent reportedly cut transfers into Hunyuan and Yuanbao from a one-year wait to three months
About 40% of staff at China's six AI "little dragon" startups say they're open to offers

items.d: Money goes to AI and core teams

t133|599.c: The gains go mainly to science and engineering grad students from top schools; academics are priced by citations.
t133|599.e: This round's gains are concentrated among master's and PhD students in science and engineering from the C9, China's nine elite universities, and strong computing schools like BUPT and Xidian. Strength in a specific field matters more than overall ranking. After DeepSeek, companies found interns could make key contributions, and interns now make up over 10% of AI hires. A few top interns earn 4,000–5,000 yuan a day, but he stresses this is a tiny minority. Academic talent is priced roughly by paper citations, engineering talent by downloads of their code on GitHub.
ex: AI talent by degree: about 20% bachelor's, 54% master's, 25% PhD
BUPT ranks second as a source of AI talent, which surprised him
Daily pay of 4,000–5,000 yuan usually means papers with 100+ citations

t133|599.c: For now AI boosts efficiency without pushing people out, and its impact ripples outward from the internet industry.
t133|599.e: He hasn't seen brand-new jobs appear from nowhere, or whole categories of jobs vanish. In China, people working alongside AI is still the norm. The impact spreads like ripples from a stone dropped in water. The first ring is internet giants and AI startups. The second has reached cars, robotics and consumer electronics, where hardware firms like Xiaomi and BYD now compete with internet companies for the same people. In two or three years more industries may be affected. He also cautions that model capability alone doesn't make a business. Technology, demand and commercialization must mature together.
ex: ByteDance has about three to four times as many AI roles as Tencent
Megvii was a hammer looking for nails until banks adopted face verification

items.d: More industries in two to three years

t133|599.c: White-collar work will go from human-AI teamwork, to gig tasks online, to most people not working.
t133|599.e: He sees AI tools for cheating in job interviews as a bridge between old assessments and new ways of working. Just as using a calculator or Excel now counts as a skill, hiring will eventually test whether a person and AI can deliver together. Later, white-collar tasks that can be broken apart will be handed out online, like delivery orders for couriers. The top 5–10% stay at big companies, while most do outsourced and gig work, perhaps for slightly less pay and less satisfaction. In the end most people may not need to work, though he admits he hasn't figured out what happens in between.
ex: One Silicon Valley firm rates programmers weekly on four levels, up or down
He advises office workers to pay for AI and use it ten-plus times daily

items.d: Hiring tests joint delivery with AI
Tasks split up and dispatched via platforms
He estimates about 95% won't need to

t134|514.c: Meta's pay can't keep people because layers of approval and more staff than key tasks breed credit fights.
t134|514.e: He guesses that new hires leaving after two or three months, which is rare in Silicon Valley, isn't mainly about money. After the pandemic Meta added layers, so each iteration needed sign-off from several VPs who didn't know the project well and often contradicted each other. The deeper problem is structural. Once a business matures, even a 1–2% gain is worth chasing, so the company keeps hiring. When people outnumber key tasks, some get pushed to side work and everyone fights over the core 20%. Credit is hard to divide, and politics follows.
ex: At Meta in 2017–2019, he swapped out every model for Facebook's push notifications within six months
One team ships a model, another owns a 2% daily-user goal; credit is hard to split

items.d: Some get pushed to side work

t134|514.c: A state-of-the-art model needs a core of about 50; 5,000 people racing each other just burns energy.
t134|514.e: He estimates Meta Superintelligence Labs has about 5,000 people, more than all of OpenAI. In his experience, the core team behind a state-of-the-art model is twenty-odd people tuning the model and twenty-odd on training infrastructure and engineering, plus a few PMs setting capability priorities. If the goal is just getting Llama past GPT-5, a focused team of 150–250 is enough. Meta's bottom-up culture also lets several teams race each other and train duplicate models. No one clearly owns the result, and a finished model may have nowhere to ship.
ex: Anthropic has about 1,900 employees in total
Amazon also runs internal races, but research sits under business units, so results get used

t134|514.c: Mission-driven companies are united but fragile, because one company can't hold two missions.
t134|514.e: OpenAI and Anthropic use their mission and public benchmarks to pull the whole company in one direction. As long as key tasks outnumber people, even thousands of staff needn't fight over credit. But the mission is the only glue. When directions split, you can't fix it the way you fix a clash of interests, by redividing the gains. That's why he thinks shared financial interests are actually the sturdier bond. He suspects the clash between Sam Altman and Ilya Sutskever was two paths, wider user reach versus safety and reliability, competing for the same resources.
ex: He suspects OpenAI's infighting came from "user reach" versus "safety and reliability"

items: No way to reconcile split paths
He sees it as the sturdiest bond

d.verdict: A mission-driven company facing a split must pick a side

t134|514.c: Frontier research needs leaders with past breakthroughs: scientists shape the decade, engineers the next few years.
t134|514.e: He believes a sense of direction, technical taste and an eye for people come from years of experience, and a CEO can't substitute for them. Even OpenAI's CEO and CTO don't run research directly. Meta isn't short of people. It hasn't put the right leaders in the right seats. The ideal setup pairs five or six pioneering scientists with five or six technical leaders who ship, since pure researchers often lose interest once a direction is proven. He sees Elon Musk as engineering-minded and Google as science-driven. One shapes the next two or three years, the other the next decade, but a company may not last two or three years.
ex: Qualified leaders mostly did key work before ChatGPT and are in their thirties or forties
He points to AlphaGo's David Silver as an example

items.d: Five or six, make it real

t134|514.c: Past a pay threshold, top researchers want their names on the author list of the AGI moment.
t134|514.e: He thinks top researchers care most about being core members of the "AGI moment," when general AI is truly achieved, with their names on that author list of about ten. Like scientists chasing a Nobel or Turing Award, they want history to see their contribution. He poses a hypothetical: no pay at all, but a 90% chance of making the list. Many would accept, maybe even him. So past a threshold, money is just a number, and direction and collaborators decide where people go. That's why OpenAI and Anthropic attract talent best, while a chaotic Meta struggles even with huge packages.
ex: His ranking for attracting talent: OpenAI, Anthropic, then Google

items.d: Past a threshold, just a number
A core part of the AGI moment

t134|514.c: He agrees a billion daily users comes before AGI, and the three giants each capture value differently.
t134|514.e: He agrees with Altman that a billion daily users comes before AGI. A billion users cover almost every job and question, and an AI that handles all those tasks is close to AGI. Anthropic pushes text-based actions to the limit and is strongest at coding. OpenAI wants to win every consumer use case. Google opens its models to developers and lets them fight it out, and he guesses it will later buy the winners or build similar products. He likes Google's research depth and the distribution it gets from Chrome on desktop. ChatGPT still needs to become the first app people open on their phones.
ex: For Google, late 2023 to late 2025 is exactly one release cycle for a major product
He estimates Gemini may already have 300–400 million users

root.d: A billion daily users nears AGI

items.d: Text-based actions taken to the limit

t134|514.c: AI-native companies first ask whether AI can do a job, then replace the pyramid with a network.
t134|514.e: Pokee AI has only eight full-time employees. Before opening any role, it asks whether AI could handle the job within two or three months, and if so, it doesn't hire. Hierarchy exists because leaders can't see what's happening on the front line. In a small company, AI can track everyone's skills and spare capacity, so the founder can set company-wide priorities directly. Tasks are assigned at a higher level: engineers design the architecture and AI does the execution. When each person's output multiplies, leaders can't review everything, so trust and complementary skills matter more. He opposes internal races as a fix for overlapping work.
ex: Pokee AI raised a $12 million seed round
A feature that used to take 5–10 days took AI about two hours

items.d: First ask if AI can do it
Output too large to review item by item

t135|604.c: His key breakthrough on Landau–Siegel zeros came in 2022; the hard part now is writing the proof clearly.
t135|604.e: He sees bounded prime gaps as his first lightning strike and Landau–Siegel zeros, a famous number theory problem about how primes are distributed, as his second. He admits his 2022 paper was unfinished, with some ideas left undeveloped and some calculation errors, but believes the key ideas hold. Now he works on it a little each day, comparing ways to simplify and rewriting. Some doubt that the power of a logarithm term can be brought down. He compares that to bounded gaps not reaching 2: not a fundamental problem. Still, a mathematician's certainty must become something peers can check.
ex: He started on it in the late 1990s; a 2007 paper he now considers weak
Cracking it in 2022 took six months to a year, with no dramatic epiphany

t135|604.c: In math, almost there means not there; breakthroughs come from going around where everyone is stuck.
t135|604.e: He rejects the idea of being "just a hair away." People on the same path get stuck at the same spot, and in math, almost means you didn't make it. He came in through how primes are distributed in arithmetic progressions, and at first didn't even know this related to twin primes, pairs of primes that differ by 2. Working alone for years may mean more detours, but it also kept him from fully following mainstream methods, and that became the source of his breakthrough.
ex: Method found in July 2012; the 2013 proof: infinitely many prime pairs under 70 million apart
He admits his method can't shrink the gap to 2, as twin primes require

t135|604.c: Picking a problem takes little judgment; the real hurdle is accepting you may never solve it.
t135|604.e: Number theory problems open for decades or centuries are already agreed to be important, so choosing one is easy. What's hard is daring to bet on it and living with the odds of failure. He has little interest in material or worldly goals. From 1992 to 1999, when he was out of academia, he kept thinking with library books, paper and pencil. Pure math needs only a brain, paper and a pen. He says he'd have no regrets even if he never produced a result. The reward of research is the joy of it.
ex: He helped an Intel classmate with encryption, earning a patent he sees as a minor episode

items.d: No regrets if it never works

t135|604.c: Intuition is mostly innate but builds up over time; older mathematicians lack new intuition, not ability.
t135|604.e: He thinks mathematical intuition is hard to learn, but the longer you think, the likelier inspiration becomes, so intuition also accumulates. Choosing a method is a matter of intuition, and the key is to think of what others don't. Many ideas that seem unique turn out useless, but without pursuing them you never find anything new. He doesn't fully agree with the British mathematician G.H. Hardy that original work is rare after 60. He thinks it's less that intuition fades and more that new intuition stops coming. At 70, he still feels he can do it.

terms.d: The longer you think, the likelier inspiration

t135|604.c: AI will advance math, but it won't solve the Riemann hypothesis without people involved.
t135|604.e: He sees AI as powerful, and since many AI problems are ultimately math problems, it will push math forward. But competition problems have known answers, are timed in hours and can be trained for by learning common patterns. Research faces the unknown and takes long exploration. When the four color theorem was proved with computer help, some predicted traditional math would be replaced, yet decades later the main research is still done by people. He won't comment on AI winning gold at the International Mathematical Olympiad, since he doesn't know the details.
ex: If he set AI a task, he'd have it read centuries of papers for unnoticed connections

d.verdict: AI is a powerful tool, but research still needs people

t135|604.c: Focus is a mathematician's most important gift; olympiad results and early brilliance aren't required.
t135|604.e: At nine he read the popular science series One Hundred Thousand Whys and became fascinated by Fermat's Last Theorem and the Goldbach conjecture. He never attended high school and only entered Peking University in 1978. He thinks olympiad results may raise the odds of success but aren't necessary. Talent takes long observation to see, and mathematician Hong Wang is an example. Children should first feel the satisfaction of going from stuck to solved. Back in China, he'll finish his paper before taking students, choosing them for interest and mathematical sensitivity rather than résumés. He admits he couldn't be a leader.
ex: He supervised only two PhD students in the US and hopes to demand more in China

items.d: First feel the thrill of solving

t136|542.c: Sora is really AI social, not AI TikTok, and it grows through videos starring friends and celebrities.
t136|542.e: His wow moment came when a colleague made a video using his face. The fun was in the relationship, not the video itself. Pure AI video feeds had been tried before without making much noise. Meta's Vibes is buried inside Meta AI, has no real-person cameos and gets almost no attention. Sora's Remix lets you swipe left or right to build on someone else's video, turning meme-sharing into an easy game, like meme culture on Bilibili or CapCut's "use this template." Long term he imagines real and virtual friend circles side by side, but stresses that's just imagination.
ex: He thinks the best interactions will never go beyond swiping and tapping
He likens Sora's low-quality first-day content to early doubts about Kuaishou

items.d: Put friends and celebrities in videos

t136|542.c: Even a 10–20% chance Sora becomes a super app forces the giants in; mid-sized startups can't hold on.
t136|542.e: Losing a top daily app costs far more than fighting for it, so giants can't sit out. Social apps have network effects, improving as more people join, so the window to follow is about three to six months. A mid-sized startup that takes off first still faces privacy and regulatory pressure over real faces, the huge cost of free generation, and quick copying once the idea is proven. He admits he underestimated how fast OpenAI builds consumer apps. He also warns that capital is arriving far faster than compute and energy, so money may not pay back in the short term, but the trend is clear.
ex: He agrees with OpenAI trading free use for growth: super apps can lose money early

items: Privacy and regulation over real faces

d.verdict: AI social looks like a giants' battlefield

t136|542.c: An industry-specific agent's edge is its interface, context and domain experience, not an exclusive model.
t136|542.e: General models are "building a person with a high IQ," while industry-specific companies are "training a designer." In design work, people point at the screen and say "change this," so he built Chat Canvas, chat plus a canvas, instead of a plain chat box. Context, the background the model gets, comes in two kinds: references, like a company's past materials and public style examples, and long-term preferences. He also plans to have the system ask for missing information. He no longer agonizes over open versus closed models. Open source only affects cost and room for post-training, and context and prompt engineering still run deep.
ex: A preference might be: always reject skeuomorphism, prefer minimalism
No community: the inspiration feed only exists to improve what users put in

result.d: General models bring knowledge; vertical firms bring craft

t136|542.c: App companies should design for mature models first, then scale up once the capabilities arrive.
t136|542.e: Lovart began designing Chat Canvas before GPT Image 1 came out, betting that complex instructions, consistency and "point and edit" would be solved. GPT Image 1, Nano Banana and Seedream 4.0 then delivered one after another, and the interface built in advance paid off. The reverse is also true: patches for old models can become useless all at once. Special control structures once made up for weak understanding, and they faded away as models improved. But for last-mile tweaks like brightness or contrast, dragging a slider still beats describing it in words.
ex: Text rendering was patched with traditional tools; the next model made the patch obsolete

items.d: Instructions and consistency will be solved
From GPT Image 1 to Nano Banana

t136|542.c: Lovart expects over $30 million in revenue this year, but he rates the product below a passing grade.
t136|542.e: Lovart grew by word of mouth, with well-targeted users. During the invite-only beta, daily active users were around 10,000–20,000, rising to 80,000–100,000 after it ended. After the public launch on July 28 and the arrival of Nano Banana, it climbed again and has recently held at 150,000–200,000. US users are over a third of the total and a slightly bigger share of subscription revenue. Revenue roughly covers model costs, but with many free users and slow conversion, it still loses money overall. He's sure the price of running models will fall, allowing tiered pricing by how much work is delivered.
ex: No paid acquisition yet: influencers and brand story first, then test ads
He says fundraising is a means, not an end

t136|542.c: The window for productivity tools is closing; as production gets cheaper, the next wave is consumer products.
t136|542.e: In 2023 he split productivity tools into two kinds, Office and Adobe, and still does. Coding is this generation's new Office, but it's where startups most easily collide head-on with model makers, while design sits further from language, the models' main line. The productivity race is red-hot, and teams formed this year may have missed the window. As models get cheaper, competition will shift to what new content people consume. He also urges caution about sudden consumer hits. Douyin, Xiaohongshu and Bilibili all grew slowly from humble beginnings.
ex: Veo 3 cut prices 70%, and Nano Banana is cheaper than GPT Image 1
He guesses Canva and Adobe will bet big only when design agents hit $100M annual revenue

items.d: Video, image and language models cut prices
To what new content people consume

t136|542.c: Designers who only copy will shrink in number, but AI will turn far more people into creators.
t136|542.e: Narrow design jobs built on repetitive delivery may shrink. But as design ability spreads, people who lacked the skill or budget can express themselves, so creators in the broad sense will multiply. Wedding materials and art photos are examples of individuals wanting to set the look themselves. For non-professionals, Lovart delivers usable results with little back-and-forth. For professional designers, it's like a junior team that brainstorms and drafts. He believes people will always raise the ceiling of creative work, and objects to professionals handing in machine output as finished work.
ex: North American small businesses buy a substitute for costly labor; Western designers want inspiration
Chinese designers care more about efficiency and chain workflows together with ComfyUI

t136|542.c: An AI product's window may be just two years, so hire for learning speed and keep managing anxiety.
t136|542.e: He sees three waves for Lovart. In 2023 he judged it too late for a global image tool and started in China. When the agent wave arrived, he went global again. The third wave depends on future consumer products. Because windows are short, he hires people who understand AI, learn constantly and accept change. What matters isn't whether someone has experience, but how they treat it. During a hard stretch a company wanted to buy Lovart, and he gave it no chance to proceed. While the technology keeps advancing fast, he sees no reason to quit. If it stalls, there's no need to persist blindly.
ex: Three months in the US shifted his question from who wins to why it must exist

items.d: Too late for global image tools

t137|612.c: Drag-and-drop Agent Builder isn't very new; its value is letting non-technical business staff build agents.
t137|612.e: AgentKit packages OpenAI's own experience running sales and support with AI into a full toolkit for building, deploying, evaluating and optimizing agents. Its drag-and-drop Agent Builder looks a lot like Dify, Coze and n8n. Silicon Valley developers already write agents directly with Claude Code or Codex, so the real new users are non-technical business staff. Flowcharts hard-code the steps, the opposite of the AGI path where models plan for themselves. He sees it as a shortcut to revenue now, not the end state. Evaluation and tuning have also been standardized, so some startups' advantages will erode.
ex: OpenAI gets about 13,000 sales leads a month; staff could personalize replies to only about 1,000

items: People draw the steps as a chart
The model plans its own steps

d.verdict: Builders are a practical shortcut to revenue, not the end state

t137|612.c: ChatGPT's app platform offers distribution to 800 million weekly users, but developers build on someone else's land.
t137|612.e: The GPTs of 2023 were mostly a prompt plus a skin. The new Apps SDK is built on MCP, a standard way for AI to call outside tools, so apps can log in to accounts, use external tools and embed interactive widgets. The biggest benefit is distribution: new apps don't have to solve the cold start. The risk is that context and user behavior stay inside ChatGPT, so developers struggle to own user relationships. The platform sees full conversations and may build popular ideas itself, and for now only OpenAI models work. He thinks ChatGPT could become a "WeChatGPT," and services plugging in is an unstoppable trend.
ex: The new Canva can link your account and use your existing assets
A future 30% cut is only a guess based on Apple's App Store

root.d: An app platform built on MCP

items.d: About 800M weekly users, no cold start
User relationships stay with the platform
Hit ideas may get built in

t137|612.c: Every leap in model capability spawns a new wave of infrastructure companies for agents.
t137|612.e: He sees an agent as a virtual digital person. The model is the brain, LangChain the skeleton, MCP the left hand that uses tools, browser control the right hand, ElevenLabs the mouth, LiveKit the eyes and ears, and evaluation companies the coach. Each piece took off after a particular leap in capability: scaffolding frameworks, function calling, real-time voice, coding sandboxes, reasoning and cloud browsers, and a tool protocol reusable across models, in that order. He admits it's hard to predict what will change in the next three to six months.
ex: LiveKit's daily calls grew from about 1 million to about 20 million
He calls MCP Anthropic's gift to the community

items.d: AI coding soars; code sandboxes rise
Demand for complex evals and cloud browsers

t137|612.c: Agents aren't reliable enough yet; everyone calls evaluation important, but almost no one does it seriously.
t137|612.e: On benchmarks like OSWorld and WebArena, the best computer- and browser-use models succeed only 60–70% of the time. That's unworkable for critical flows like opening a medical account. So for now, high-stakes write actions still need reliable tool calls, and browser use fits long-tail cases better. Evals are hard because labeling is expensive and teams don't agree on metrics. Coding and math give clear signals, which suits reinforcement learning, training by trial and reward. For subjective, complex tasks, evaluation may cost more than the task itself.
ex: One big client changed a prompt and shipped after engineers tried just three or four calls
Browsers can scrape vacancies from Japanese boutique hotels not listed on travel sites

marks.d: Clear signals, suited to reinforcement learning
Run hundreds of calls before judging metrics
Evals may cost more than the task

t137|612.c: Once AI turns services into software, agent tooling could be 10–15 times today's developer tools market.
t137|612.e: He does an order-of-magnitude estimate. The global software market is about $650 billion, and developer tools are a low-to-mid single-digit percentage of it. If AI raises software's ceiling to about $10 trillion and tooling takes about 5%, that's $200–500 billion. He stresses this isn't a near-term revenue forecast. Companies that grow to $10 billion will need to own workflow chokepoints like identity, communications, observability and evaluation, and build a data loop where more use means better results, higher success rates and lower costs.
ex: For reference: Okta earns about $2 billion a year, Twilio about $4 billion
Reinforcement learning's second spring: building environments for labs, RL services for enterprises

t137|613.c: The industry is moving from calling tools to completing tasks, so the tool layer must own outcomes.
t137|613.e: Her signal to invest in Composio came from AGI House's Agent Build Day, where the community broadly found it more reliable. Composio started in India with a product that auto-generated API integration code, but accuracy fell short. The team then realized agents' bigger problem was unreliable tool calling, and pivoted to a general skills layer before MCP was even released. Too many tools, or tools that look alike, confuse models and lower success rates. So Rube, its product for individual users, uses a single meta-MCP to pick tools for each task.
ex: Composio has about 30 people, moved to San Francisco, and serves ClickUp and Glean
Lightspeed led its Series A

items.d: Pick tools per task and execute

t137|613.c: Model companies only need to define interfaces; specialist teams should do the messy third-party integration work.
t137|613.e: She doesn't think Anthropic will build a full Composio itself. Maintaining scattered third-party APIs doesn't make models smarter or strengthen core advantages like safety, and it takes a lot of people. Platform companies also want to stay neutral, so growing Claude's tool ecosystem through open protocols is enough. Model companies define the interfaces, and specialist teams handle maintenance and error handling. That's exactly the room for tooling companies. She also thinks the app market is fragmented enough that model companies building their own apps pose a limited threat.
