ex: OpenAI bought Statsig for about $1.1 billion; many A/B testing people moved into evals

items.d: Many of them, with scattered interfaces

t137|613.c: Investors keep doubling down on agent tooling, and valuations are rising fast.
t137|613.e: She cites several deals. ElevenLabs, an AI voice company, ran an employee share sale of about $100 million at a valuation of about $6.6 billion, roughly double its last round just nine months earlier. LangChain is closing a roughly $100 million raise at about $1.1 billion. David AI, which supplies voice data to top AI labs, raised about $25 million in a Series A. She sees OpenAI, Google and Grok as the main players in voice, and thinks Anthropic may not be at the table.
ex: San Francisco rents reportedly rose about 20–30% as teams move closer to customers and talent

t137|613.c: Chinese teams excel at consumer product sense and execution, complementing business-focused Silicon Valley.
t137|613.e: In HF0's last three or four batches, about 20–30% of founding teams had Chinese backgrounds. Most had already started companies in China, then used a US accelerator to build connections and growth channels. Their teams, products and valuations are often more mature than comparable YC teams. Silicon Valley offers a good environment and clear exits for B2B startups, so it has many B2B founders and relatively few in consumer and hardware. China is the opposite. She sees this as a natural division of labor between the two.

t138|616.c: As models get smaller and stronger, AI will move from the cloud onto phones, with both working together.
t138|616.e: OPPO divides its AI strategy into new computing, new sensing and a new ecosystem. The aim is to rebuild the phone experience, not bolt on a few AI features. As models shrink and improve, inference that once ran only in the cloud will gradually move onto the phone. Splitting work between device and cloud cuts costs and speeds things up. Sensitive payment and financial data can be anonymized and processed locally by small on-device models rather than sent to the cloud. Every phone maker has compute, personal data and the home screen. The difference lies in gathering context, building habits and connecting services.
ex: Breeno spans phones, watches, tablets, earbuds; monthly users went from about 150M to nearly 170M

items.d: More can run on the phone
Some tasks stay on the device
Sensitive data stays off the cloud

t138|616.c: Memory is a phone AI's most valuable asset, and it should cover far more than chat history.
t138|616.e: He sorts memory into three kinds: conversations with Breeno, things users explicitly ask the AI to remember, and the files and photos already on the phone. So health checkup reports and photo albums can feed personalized answers, which he thinks fits daily life better than ChatGPT's focus on chat memory. OPPO may be the first phone maker to give memory its own physical button, making it easy to trigger so saving things becomes muscle memory. One-press capture has expanded from screenshots to videos, voice, bills and food pickup codes.
ex: Long videos become key points and to-dos; bills get analyzed across apps
Photo search uses on-device search plus RAG, which looks things up before answering

items.d: One-press capture with a physical button
Found via on-device search and RAG

t138|616.c: The model just processes information; how good its answer is depends on the context it's given.
t138|616.e: A user's question is only part of the input. The open app, what's on screen and past memories matter just as much. The same "how do I make this?" means a recipe if a dish is on screen, and a solution if it's a homework problem. The phone's hardware and software sensors, app states and personal data together form the context. That's what he means by new sensing, which isn't just adding cameras and microphones. As model costs fall fast, competition shifts to interaction design, context engineering and understanding the situation.
ex: Ask about the screen, ask about what the camera sees, voiceprint ID answering only the speaker

terms.d: Who you are, what you saved

t138|616.c: Pretraining is no longer a phone maker's key lever; build only layers that create data feedback loops.
t138|616.e: After the "battle of a hundred models," model costs fall tens to hundreds of times a year, and suppliers are consolidating. OPPO considered pretraining its own model from scratch around 2023, but in the first half of last year judged the strategic value too low and turned to partners for general capabilities. In-house work covers three layers: fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on open-source models, product-focused context engineering, and sensing and small models. The test is whether real user data can feed a loop at controlled cost. He rejects the idea that owning a model is a moat. What matters is using models well.
ex: Partners for general capabilities include DeepSeek, StepFun and Qwen
OPPO was among the first phone makers to adopt DeepSeek R1 after its release

items: Fine-tuning and RL on open models

d.verdict: Alone is fast, together goes far: using models well matters most

t138|616.c: A phone assistant must pass four tests at once, a higher bar than any standalone chat app faces.
t138|616.e: He admits 170 million monthly users is below expectations, and the share using it daily, counted against all phone buyers, isn't great either. It's not only Siri's bad reputation. Breeno's first version in 2018 came before large language models and didn't work well, so users learned to skip it. The deeper reason is that the job is hard: general Q&A, personalized answers using on-phone data, thousands of device controls, and carrying out tasks across third-party apps. If any link fails, users think the assistant is dumb.
ex: Asked "where should I stay in Chengdu," it should find the hotel the user saved
"Navigate home" means opening maps, entering the address and starting navigation

items.d: On par with standalone AI apps
Uses third-party services to finish jobs

t138|616.c: AI products can't be designed in a meeting room; ship first, then chase the horizon with real feedback.
t138|616.e: The same words can hide completely different needs, and being able to do everything isn't the same as understanding everything. So features can't be designed only in meeting rooms. Breeno has strategy product managers who analyze implicit feedback like likes, dislikes, copies, shares and multi-turn chats. It also brings users, store sales staff and product teams together to talk through pain points. The experience can go from 60–70 points to 80–90, but user expectations rise just as fast. He also thinks AI isn't yet a reason to buy a phone, but an after-sale experience that shapes reputation and repeat purchases.
ex: He doesn't track spending and missed that need until interviews kept raising it
Updates went from roughly monthly in 2021 to as often as weekly this year

t138|616.c: An assistant needn't cook hotpot itself; agents will shrink finding a service down to one sentence.
t138|616.e: Breeno works with Alipay. Once it understands what the user wants, it hands the request to Alipay's agent, which returns the service as a card in the chat. That will change how daily users and time spent are counted, and how ads work. A trustworthy answer may itself become the ad, but paid placement that hurts quality destroys trust. Mobile protocols are still split across several tracks, and he wants Android makers to unite as they did with "quick apps." He opposes just layering a screen-tapping GUI agent onto the old Android interface. An AI-native OS should differ from the ground up, and needs hit products to kick-start its ecosystem.
ex: One merchant advertised "Recommended by DeepSeek"
Apple has App Intents; Google has two or three protocols

t138|616.c: The endgame is a personal butler plus expert advisors, not one butler ruling every device.
t138|616.e: The butler knows the user best and handles understanding intent and handing out tasks. Advisors for law, medicine, travel and so on go deep on specialist work. Phones can complete more services and act as the hub for other devices, so they may be the butler's main home. But cars and other devices will still have their own assistants and cooperate only on some tasks. In the short term, glasses are just an extension of the phone's senses. Voice's biggest obstacle is psychological and generational. People don't mind phone calls but feel awkward talking to machines. Kids growing up with AI will find it more natural.
ex: The butler knows you skip cilantro and numbing spice, and tells the food service

items.d: Law, medicine, travel and other specialties

t139|619.c: Pick problems that matter most, have high ceilings and are still early, then execute them fully.
t139|619.e: From Swin Transformer (an image-recognition model design he co-created) to BAAI to AI video, he has used the same test: the problem should be the most important one in its field and still have clear room to grow. A direction that is already too hot usually means the chance has passed. The call comes from intuition built over years in a field. A signal outsiders find faint can look loud to insiders. But ideas aren't enough. Swin worked because the team went all in on task coverage, benchmarks and polish. Chasing trends without solid execution produces work that doesn't last.
ex: In 2014 many Chinese professors doubted deep networks, but his group bought GPUs early.
Swin aimed to be one general base for image classification, detection and segmentation.

t139|619.c: Teams built around papers resist collaboration, while systems that scale with compute get the most from it.
t139|619.e: Author order on papers naturally sets up fights over who is first or second author. Reviewers ask about novelty, so teams optimize for a story that sounds new instead of solving the problem. OpenAI designs a system that gets better as compute grows, rather than piling on hand-crafted assumptions and tricks. That takes collaboration across scraping and cleaning data, training, infrastructure and evaluation, with people caring about the system, not credit. In essence, it's a startup. After winning best paper at ICCV, a top computer vision conference, seeing the scale of AlphaFold and OpenAI showed him the ceiling of the paper-driven path.

items: Pile on hand-made rules and tricks
Care about the system, not credit

d.verdict: A team building big systems is essentially a startup

t139|619.c: China lacked OpenAI-style organizations because it wasn't "rich enough" yet, and is now shifting to original work.
t139|619.e: He agrees with Wang Huiwen, Meituan co-founder and founder of Light Years Beyond. While catching up, goals are clear, and efficiency gains, business-model innovation and bringing proven foreign ideas to China offer the most certainty and the best returns. Closer to the frontier, the direction gets blurry, so investors, founders and society all have to reset how much failure they tolerate. He sees Ne Zha, Black Myth: Wukong, DeepSeek and Unitree as signs of the shift, but thinks it is far from complete.

t139|619.c: By 2023 general language models were a late bet, while early, high-ceiling AI video was worth backing.
t139|619.e: In March 2023 he talked only with Wang Huiwen and Liang Wenfeng, DeepSeek's founder, and joined Light Years Beyond because he had already promised Wang. In hiring, he favored PhDs within three to five years of graduating, whatever their field. After Light Years Beyond ended, by that August he judged it too late for another general language model, and the teams he met weren't complete across models, infrastructure, product and fundraising. Weighing language models, agents (AI that does tasks on its own) and companion chatbots, he picked AI video. The tech was young but had a high ceiling, and each new capability could open new uses.
ex: When Light Years Beyond was hiring, DeepSeek was its fiercest rival for talent.

items.d: Video model that generates clip by clip, in order

t139|619.c: Magi-1's core intuition was right, but they underestimated the difficulty, and tech and business never fed each other.
t139|619.e: Video plays out over time and has an order, like language, so compressing it by predicting the next piece, as language models do, felt right. But nobody had done it, so algorithms, infrastructure and code all had to be built from scratch. The 30-to-40-person team bet all its key people on this "autoregressive" approach, underinvested in data, evaluation and post-training, and took 13 to 14 months to launch. The model won praise among engineers and on GitHub and brought hundreds of thousands of sign-ups, but no clear business numbers. He opposes overemphasizing pure tech, yet won't be led by short-term demand. Every iteration should matter for the business.
ex: He says a six-month deadline for a usable model would have changed the team's mindset.

Every iteration matters for the business
Led by demand, falls behind on tech

t139|619.c: Sora 2's real leap is ten-second storytelling, made possible by tightly integrating product and model teams.
t139|619.e: He breaks Sora 2, OpenAI's video model, into three layers. Generating sound and picture together already existed in Google's Veo 3, and keeping characters consistent had been studied. What amazed him was several shots forming a story. He had assumed that would need a pipeline of AI steps stitched together, so seeing one model produce it directly changed his mind. Behind it, product defines the need and the model team delivers to a shared standard, while Cameo, which puts users into videos, amplifies the model's most distinctive ability. At Sand.ai, model and product leads also pair up one-on-one, with him as the hub for information.
ex: He calls Meta's Vibes stitched-together features with no memorable selling point.
He won't guess whether Sora 2 is autoregressive, generating in sequence, underneath.

items.d: Shots form a story: the biggest leap
Faces and voices stay the same

t139|619.c: AI short dramas aren't yet ten times cheaper than live action, and character acting is the biggest gap.
t139|619.e: AI short dramas cost about 2,000 to 5,000 yuan per minute, or roughly 200,000 yuan per series. That isn't an order of magnitude cheaper than filming, and the quality isn't there, so viewers haven't bought in. Older models are good at B-roll like empty scenes and transitions, but story characters have to talk and act, and lip-syncing afterward looks fake. The most common complaint from short-drama makers is that characters look fake and don't act. He estimates people fill over half the frame in ordinary video, so Sand.ai's new model focuses on character performance with sound and picture generated together.
ex: He says in internal tests its acting looks at least as real as Sora 2's.

t139|619.c: The Sora app is more tool than platform for now, and retention, not hype, will decide its fate.
t139|619.e: For consumers, speed, resolution and cost matter most. With sound and picture generated together, dropping to 270p-360p only costs sharpness, the audio is unaffected, and it's good enough to share on WeChat. Generation time has fallen from one to three minutes to about ten seconds, which could make people create ten times as often. Whether it becomes a platform depends on new content formats and new distribution channels, yet most generated videos still get reposted to WeChat Moments, Xiaohongshu and Douyin. The early rush only helps the team find the right audience. Nobody knows yet whether users will stay.
ex: Sora cut its daily free quota from 100 videos to 30, a sign of cost pressure.

root.d: More like a tool for now

items.d: Watchable clips with sound and picture
Still relies on existing social apps

t140|621.c: Using AI as a stand-in for first-principles physics keeps accuracy while running about a million times faster.
t140|621.e: The Schrödinger equation can in principle describe most matter, but it can't be solved directly. Density functional theory, the usual workaround, scales roughly with the cube of the number of atoms, and molecular dynamics simulations only cover short time spans. His approach trains a neural network to map atom positions to energy, standing in for the exact calculation. The hard part is making the network respect physical symmetries: shifting, rotating or swapping identical atoms shouldn't change the energy. And it uses general symmetry handling plus a general network, instead of hand-designing features for each system like water or silicon.
ex: A roughly 200-million-core-hour supercomputer calculation was reproduced on a laptop in under half an hour.
He made Princeton's idle P100 GPUs train about ten times faster.

items.d: Accurate but too slow to run
Learns how atom positions map to energy
Shift, rotate or swap atoms: same energy

t140|621.c: Research only counts when something gets made, so agents must link reading, computing and experimenting.
t140|621.e: He breaks research into reading the literature, running computations and doing experiments, plus people. Machine learning and pretraining strengthen the signals from computation and experiments, large language models improve literature search, and agents, AI that acts on its own, change the human role. The bar for faster discovery is actually making the thing, not just having an idea, so literature, computation, and both simulated and lab experiments must check each other in one loop. Databases, software and equipment were built for people. More and more, they'll be built for AI.
ex: Today agents assist scientists; later they may call tools on their own.

result.d: Linked by agents, each step checking the others

t140|621.c: AI makes papers and narrow specialties less scarce, so the old way of doing research stops working.
t140|621.e: AI can write papers and review them, which threatens the siloed arguments in narrow fields that rest on approximations. The old division of labor loosens, so research needs organizations, tools and evaluation systems that allow a smooth transition. He also worries about AI simply handing over every answer. As a student, he felt classes worked backward from conclusions and taught only derivations, erasing how scientists actually groped their way forward. In 2016 he dropped all his Princeton courses and switched to machine learning.
ex: Einstein spent about ten years on gravity theory, but classes flatten it into a straight line.

items.d: Use read, compute and make tools to do research

t140|621.c: "Science has no borders" can no longer be assumed, so research through industrial R&D should stay open.
t140|621.e: He points to funding cuts at some US universities and research centers as a sign that the idea of borderless science is being shaken. He argues for values that keep everything open and open source, from basic research to industrial R&D, and believes this is even more necessary, and more firmly held, in China. He opposes shrinking science into a contest between nations. Looking back, the team saw chances like AlphaFold-style problems, AI-designed materials and nuclear fusion, but with limited resources it could only keep the spark alive.
ex: He calls 2022 the team's lowest point, with competing demands deadlocked.

items: Open from research to industrial R&D

d.verdict: Science shouldn't shrink into a contest between nations

t140|621.c: Over the next 10-20 years, almost every Nobel will involve AI, and AI for Science will reach products.
t140|621.e: AlphaFold's 2024 Nobel Prize moved them, but they don't regret returning to China to start a company. He separates Nobels for being "first" to a breakthrough from the infrastructure that supports everyone who comes after. He expects that around 2030, many drugs, materials, batteries, alloys and polymers will be developed with AI for Science, meaning AI used to do research, though specific paths such as solid-state batteries remain uncertain. Models also can't just optimize for predicting the next word. They need to truly innovate. They don't buy claims that lifespans will double in five to ten years.
ex: He thinks FutureHouse, a US AI research lab, is overhyping its new-drug claims.

items.d: May go beyond what typical scientists know
Could become a treatable chronic disease

t140|622.c: Industrial R&D matures when it can be done on a computer, yet quantum mechanics is barely used.
t140|622.e: He points to Dassault Systèmes, the French industrial software maker: planes and cars have long been designed and tested on computers with CAD and simulation software. Traditional industrial software captures plenty of large-scale physics but hasn't tapped quantum mechanics, the micro level, so drug R&D still feels like alchemy and materials R&D like cooking by feel. He figured the upside was changing how drugs, materials and even science itself get done. The downside was going back to teach in his home county, a risk he could live with. In 2016 he decided to start a company once the right chance came.
ex: He estimated molecular simulation infrastructure needed about 1 billion yuan; they had about 200,000.
Three years of competition prizes, 12 million yuan total, got them started; Baidu Ventures then led.

items.d: CAD and simulation already happen on computers
Still trial and error, like alchemy

t140|622.c: Where data is scarce, you can first generate it from physical laws, then train models on it.
t140|622.e: He sees AlphaFold 2 and Deep Potential as two paths. The first tackled a problem where data already existed and the goal was clear. The second works in fields short on experimental data: it uses physics equations to generate data on atom positions and energies, then trains a model. He stresses that the "AI for Science" they talked about in 2018 meant using machine learning to speed up physical and mathematical modeling, unlike today's idea, which includes large models and agents. Generating data from principles first also works for robots, rockets and similar areas.
ex: Slides from 2019-2020 already mapped a path from small models and data to pretrained large models.

t140|622.c: A platform suits DP Technology better than its own drug pipeline, and grows stronger with every customer.
t140|622.e: Drugs were the first entry point because pharma can pay, roles are clearly divided, outsourced R&D is mature, and computed results can quickly go to lab testing. But a drug pipeline means betting on a few drug candidates and requires clinical judgment and project selection, which don't match the team's strengths. Platform and pipeline logic don't mix well either, a view they reached around 2023. He thinks computational software is mature but its market is limited. Bigger growth lies in Science Navigator and research agents, and they won't rebuild mature lab-automation hardware.
ex: He thinks a deep platform, a drugmaker or a materials company could each reach $100 billion.

t140|622.c: When AI takes junior tasks, the real danger is that young people lose the chance to practice.
t140|622.e: He pushes learning by doing on his team, picking up whatever each problem needs. AI has lowered the cost of getting knowledge, so the hard part is judging what to learn. That makes foundations like math, physics, computer science, politics, economics and philosophy, even literature, art and sports, more important. He worries that once AI takes over interns' and junior work, young people lose their practice ground, and the standards for judging universities, majors and scientists stop working. Risks like dangerous molecules or drugs have physical supply chains that can be regulated. A gap in how people grow is harder to fix.
ex: He imagines everyone having a cross-disciplinary, professor-level AI scientist as a friend.

root.d: From getting knowledge to choosing what to learn

items.d: Math, humanities and sports matter more
Standards for universities and majors need rebuilding

t141|630.c: Embodied AI has a clear goal, but going straight to humanoids doesn't work yet because data is missing.
t141|630.e: Embodied AI, AI with a body that acts in the real world, is stuck on data. Large language models train on about a trillion tokens, but that's a one-dimensional sequence of text. Robots need at least time, 3D space, touch and sound, and each added dimension makes the data needed balloon. He grants that language already encodes a lot of logic and the senses are closely linked, so data needs may not grow exponentially. Still, a few hundred hours of video is nowhere near enough, and no setting yet keeps producing household data. Physical-world data is far harder to get than text, so OpenAI's scale-it-up playbook can't simply be copied.

items: Hundreds of hours of video fall short
No setting that keeps producing data

d.verdict: Clear goal, but the humanoid path doesn't work yet

t141|630.c: Aim for embodied AI's summit, but ship sellable, useful products along the way to gather data.
t141|630.e: He borrows a line from Huawei founder Ren Zhengfei: aim for Everest like an idealist, but lay eggs along the way like a realist, building products as you climb, the way chips evolved from PCs to phones to AI. Between late 2022 and early 2023, Google work like PaLM-E and RT-2 convinced him the past decade was robotics' silver age and the next would be its golden age, so he started. He rejects using "products along the way" as an excuse for thin resources. Breakthroughs keep popping up in universities and labs, and a company's skill is spotting the signals and betting big.
ex: Livox got its price low because it was designed for mass production from day one.

items.d: Google's PaLM-E, RT-2 and similar work
Four-wheel drive, driver assistance, sensor fusion
A CES prototype in about three months

t141|630.c: Home robots face a chicken-and-egg trap: unreliable robots don't sell, and unsold robots produce no data.
t141|630.e: A consumer robot that can only handle half of everyday household tasks will fail, because the half it can't do leaves the home a mess. Without data it can't be reliable, without reliability it won't sell, and without sales there's no data. He criticizes 1X's NEO Gamma, priced around $20,000 and still needing a remote human operator for complex tasks. People won't pay for a machine that is expensive and needs someone to drive it. The way out is a use case people pay for today, where every use produces real-life data.
ex: 1X's NEO Gamma costs about $20,000 and still needs a remote operator for complex tasks.

items.d: Home data is hard to get
Expensive and needs a human operator

t141|630.c: Getting around as people age is a real need, and the product should shed the "wheelchair" label.
t141|630.e: Wealthy regions are aging faster and caregivers are scarce, while getting around is everyone's most basic need. Many people can walk, but it hurts, their balance is poor or they tire easily. So EV One is positioned as an everyday mobility device, not a medical wheelchair. He thinks the wheelchair label holds adoption back. When a disabled customer enters a store, staff often turn to the caregiver instead, as if using a wheelchair meant something was wrong with your mind. Traditional wheelchairs only cover basic living, are awkward to control and can't handle rough ground.
ex: Some high-end US and Japanese senior homes charge $500,000 to $1 million to enter.
His grandmother went from a bicycle to a tricycle, and now can't ride that either.

root.d: Not unable to walk, just worn out by it

items.d: Not enough staff to push wheelchairs
Wants to walk less at expos and parks

t141|630.c: Driver assistance should feel like the user lets the vehicle help, and every smart feature serves safety.
t141|630.e: He nearly tipped over test-driving a rival's mobility scooter on a sideways slope in the US, so he treats smart features and terrain handling as safety, not premium extras. Basic assistance slows and stops before obstacles. In narrow aisles, elevators or when reversing, the user holds a button to let the vehicle correct its steering, and letting go hands control back, so it never feels out of control. Auto mode drives to set spots like the fridge or bathroom, or to a spot picked on a map. Four-wheel drive with suspension, self-balancing and anti-slip handles slopes, grass and mud, though he admits sand may be a problem.
ex: Say "I'm thirsty" and the vehicle takes you to get a drink.

marks.d: Steers only while you hold the button
Set spots or a destination you pick

t141|630.c: Prototypes are easy but stable mass production is hard, so the first version drops all shape-changing parts.
t141|630.e: Shape-changing features like a lifting or tilting seat add lots of motors and linkages, hurting reliability and consistency and lengthening testing, so the first generation drops them all and leaves them for later. The driver assistance also skips the newest embodied AI models, which are hard to make stable with low cost, little computing power and little data. The team follows a path closer to early self-driving cars. For reliability, it set test standards ten times the safety requirements, which delayed the project by nearly six months.
ex: The twin-drum test machine has 5-centimeter bumps on its drums.
The body has 200-500 watt power ports and more, so a robot arm could attach later.

t141|630.c: Often "no market" just means the product isn't good enough yet, not that demand is missing.
t141|630.e: He uses 3D printers as an example. Leveling, assembly and long print jobs kept ordinary people out, and the market only grew once the product got easier. Robot lawnmowers went from buried boundary wires to wire-free, and robot vacuums followed a similar path. Power wheelchairs lack decent market research, so instead of trusting shaky data he looks at real users. A Florida girl with a fragile neck had crashed a rented power wheelchair at home. With EV One she went back to a muddy stable to groom horses, and her mother cried on the spot.
ex: In research, willingness to pay ranged from $1,000 to $20,000.
The first generation sells as a personal mobility device and may not be insurance-covered.

items.d: Better products push the boundary out

t141|630.c: Being first only slows copycats. Crossing the chasm takes a second and third generation of steady iteration.
t141|630.e: A brand people trust for safety, patents and a team that combines motors and mechanics with sensors and algorithms give a first-mover edge, but that only slows imitation. No single product stays ahead for five to ten years. Who the innovators and early adopters are, and how to reach the early majority, he admits are still unproven. A small chasm also means fierce competition arrives fast, as robot vacuums showed, but he'd rather face that kind of "hard problem amid optimism." He also wonders whether starting earlier would have been better, but building the technology and understanding people both take time.
ex: Co-founder Nick is strong in motors and mechanics; he leans toward sensors and algorithms.

items.d: A small chasm means competition comes faster

t142|631.c: An AI tutor must be rebuilt from interface to lessons. Bolting chat onto old courses is outdated.
t142|631.e: He chose to start with the narrow problem of children's spoken English rather than a general education assistant. The front end, back end, interface and course materials are all designed around AI, and the agent, the AI that acts on its own, is just one piece. Adding a chatbot to an old product is, to him, still last-era product thinking. By the time the project started, models were mostly capable enough. The real challenge was making every lesson predictable.
ex: A three-part screen: a 2D AI tutor, the child's video, animated lesson slides.
25-minute lessons, 6 levels, 96 lessons per level.
Over two years of R&D, about 200 people, roughly 200 million yuan invested.

items: Front end, back end and UI built around AI
The agent is only one piece

d.verdict: To nail spoken English, you must rebuild everything

t142|631.c: Learning to speak needs a live conversation partner, and a good product will unlock that demand.
t142|631.e: Listening, reading, vocabulary and grammar can be self-taught or taught in large classes. Speaking needs a live partner who knows the learner's level and offers lots of chances to talk. When writing you can stop to look up a word or cram, but in conversation a pause breaks the flow. Teachers who are both trained and fluent are scarce, so many kids plateau at some level and cram only before going abroad. He won't pin down the market size, but thinks every child learning English has this need, just as demand for cars only became visible once cars spread.
ex: Many kids plateau at Cambridge KET level, or PET in China's biggest cities.
Like cars: until the product exists, you can't see the demand.

root.d: Other skills can be self-taught or taught in bulk

t142|631.c: A chatty AI only keeps kids where they are. Progress needs AI that decides what to learn next.
t142|631.e: He thinks chat-style AI usually tops out at keeping a child's current level. Real progress means controlling how much difficulty to add each time, how much practice to give and which materials to use, and that can't be left to a general model's improvisation. Cambridge English vocabulary matches children's lives and understanding, but general models don't know that path and have no year-long teaching plan. So long-term memory lives outside the model, in a separate database for each child, used to generate feedback and plan the next step.
ex: Each child's database stores what they've said, their level, interests, even pet names.
Lessons run on an in-house model; after-class summaries sometimes use DeepSeek.

terms.d: Vocabulary that fits how kids think

result.d: Not just holding the current level

t142|631.c: The hard part is predictability: split lessons into small goals and stack guardrails instead of proving safety once.
t142|631.e: Each lesson is split into a dozen or so segments of two to three minutes, each with a clear goal and a pass standard. The AI knows the goal in advance and speaks around it, and a child moves on only after the whole lesson checks out. He doesn't try to eliminate hallucinations, AI confidently making things up, since that is sometimes creativity, but keeps them within teaching limits. Safety comes from stacking training, test sets, real-time monitoring and human review, then using real cases to keep shrinking the room for error.
ex: Training adds adversarial "gotcha" examples and rewards good examples.
Off-topic kids get steered back within two turns; sensitive topics are declined.

items.d: Clean data, adversarial tests, reward good examples
Watches for sensitive words and errors
Labeled real cases feed new guardrails

t142|631.c: Lower difficulty step by step when kids get stuck, and praise the exact sentence they just said.
t142|631.e: When a child can't answer, the key choice is dropping one level or two: turn a what or why question into multiple choice or a yes-or-no question, give hints, read along, then return to the original goal. He prefers using rules the child already knows to lead them to the answer themselves. Feedback should be positive but specific, pointing out which sentence was good. That lowers the anxiety of speaking a foreign language so kids keep talking. A generic "great job" isn't the point. Nor is the AI tutor meant to seem human. It's a new kind of character kids can form a stable sense of.
ex: From come→came, the child works out become→became on their own.
The 2D tutor doesn't try to look human. As he puts it, a dog is a dog.

items.d: Can't answer a what or why question
Switch to multiple choice or yes-or-no

t142|631.c: Speaking progress isn't linear, so it takes intense practice and a year per level to get past plateaus.
t142|631.e: In each 25-minute lesson a child speaks meaningfully more than 100 times, about four times a minute, and that intensity is deliberate. He has seen that progress isn't a straight line. Around three months in, kids hit a plateau, and breaking through takes another two weeks to a month. So each level spans a year and isn't meant for cramming. Measuring results is also shifting from counting how often kids speak to a combined "speaking score" of accuracy, fluency and richness. To him, every lesson is itself a test.
ex: Beta testing covered 7,000+ lessons; the longest user has finished 26 weeks.
Level 4 will be checked externally with a Cambridge KET speaking mock exam.

items.d: Push through two weeks to a month

t142|631.c: The real edge is experience in how to teach, and education can't tolerate 97% reliability.
t142|631.e: What to teach a particular child first, and how to step down difficulty, is a matter of experience to him. General data can't answer it, and it's hard to copy even if the materials are public. New curriculum and product staff train for two months and still master only one part. If reliability drops from 99.9% to 97%, three in a hundred children are taught wrong, which he won't accept. He expects big tech companies to build general tools rather than dig this deep. Pricing follows learning results rather than AI-tool logic, because parents care about what gets delivered.
ex: Each level costs 3,600 yuan a year; the beta price was about 1,500-2,000 yuan.
New curriculum staff train for two months and master just one part.

t143|480.c: A model doesn't need to compare every word with every other word to understand text.
t143|480.e: Today's models mostly read with "attention": every pair of words in a passage gets compared directly. Nothing is missed, but the cost grows with the square of the length. She sees attention as simply mixing information from different positions, and pairwise comparison is only one way to do that. "Linear attention" instead squeezes what has been read into a fixed-size memory, so the cost grows only in proportion to length. Every attention variant is a choice somewhere between "remember everything" and "compress it into a small memory."
ex: Linear attention can run step by step, so cost grows only in proportion to length

marks.d: A few full-attention layers as backup

t143|480.c: DeltaNet once lost out on slow training and missing parts; her parallel algorithm let it scale.
t143|480.e: The 2021 DeltaNet computed one step at a time, so training was slow, and it lacked modern parts like short convolutions, output normalization and output gates, so results were unremarkable. The hard part was that unrolling the steps means multiplying a long chain of matrices. She linked these to Householder matrices and their efficient WY product form from linear algebra, which let the Delta Rule, DeltaNet's memory-update rule, train in parallel across a whole sequence. She stresses she didn't invent DeltaNet and kept its name. Her contribution was making an old technique usable again, an idea built over years rather than a sudden flash.
ex: She began working on parallelizing it in September 2023; it took shape around March 2024.
She drew on QR decomposition and GPU parallel programming experience.

items.d: The Delta Rule can scale up

t143|480.c: A fixed-size memory has to learn to forget, and finer-grained forgetting works better.
t143|480.e: A linear attention layer's memory has a fixed capacity, so without forgetting it fills up. Gated DeltaNet, which she built as an NVIDIA intern, combined the Delta Rule with Mamba-2-style decay that gradually fades old memory. But having a whole group of channels share one forgetting rate is still crude. Kimi's KDA lets each dimension decay on its own, so some forget fast while others keep long-range information. It can be seen as GLA's fine-grained decay combined with DeltaNet. She thinks Qwen's choice of Gated DeltaNet was a sound one after comparing the options.
ex: In Gated DeltaNet, a group of 128 channels shares one forgetting rate.
She expects Kimi K3 will likely keep using KDA.

items.d: Adds decay shared across a group
Each dimension forgets on its own

t143|480.c: Hybrids trade memory capacity against cost: most layers go linear, with a few full-attention layers as backup.
t143|480.e: Pure linear models have fixed-size memory and degrade noticeably on long text. Full attention stores every past word in a cache, the KV cache, which grows without limit, so when large models read long contexts, just reading that cache gets too costly. Hybrids keep a few full-attention layers as backup and make the rest linear, shrinking the cache sharply and allowing bigger batches of requests. Qwen and Kimi validated this on small and mid-size models first. She sees that as normal industry risk reduction: failure is too expensive to try at the largest scale right away.
ex: Her estimate: making about 75% of layers linear cuts the KV cache by roughly three quarters.
Qwen3-Next and Kimi Linear were validated at smaller scale first.

t143|480.c: MiniMax's return to full attention exposed a weak module and weak evaluation, not a failure of linear attention.
t143|480.e: She thinks MiniMax's worry came mainly from multi-hop reasoning, where A leads to B and B leads to C. Those cross-step dependencies are more sensitive to attention, and M2 targets agents, AI that carries out tasks, which need exactly that. Short-range benchmarks like MMLU can't measure long-range mixing, so if internal evaluation missed it, the risk stays hidden until the model is scaled up. MiniMax's Lightning Attention is also a weaker linear module that doesn't represent Gated DeltaNet or KDA. She won't vouch for Qwen or Kimi either. The real test is flagship models at full scale.
ex: Multi-hop benchmarks like BBH can be gamed and say little about real agent performance.
She hopes agent-ability signals will show up already at the base-model stage.

root.d: Why it returned to full attention

items.d: Agents depend more on cross-step links
Not a failure of the linear path

t143|480.c: Dynamic sparse attention is stronger per layer but saves no storage; linear layers' lasting value is small memory.
t143|480.e: Dynamic sparse attention keeps everything it has read and precisely picks out the relevant words at each step, so a single layer is definitely stronger than a linear one. But it only cuts how much is read per step. The total cache stays the same, so with long contexts storage becomes a bottleneck sooner or later. A linear layer's fixed memory is both a theoretical weakness and the source of its speed. She most wants to see DeepSeek-style sparse attention mixed directly with KDA, replacing the remaining full-attention layers. But each step should be validated first, rather than stacking several bold changes at once.
ex: DeepSeek moved from picking whole blocks to picking individual tokens, which is more flexible.
Its indexer needs no softmax, so it can be sped up with FP8.

items: Big cache savings on long text

d.verdict: Next, try mixing sparse attention directly with KDA

t143|480.c: The bitter lesson doesn't make built-in assumptions useless. What matters is whether a method scales.
t143|480.e: Her test for a method is whether it scales: hardware-friendly, trainable at large scale, still useful in deep networks, and proven by experiments rather than debate. With unlimited data and compute she'd just use full attention. But high-quality data will run short first, and linear or hybrid designs with a built-in bias toward nearby words may need less data, an edge that might show first in post-training and reinforcement learning. In theory DeltaNet is NC¹-complete, a stronger computational class, so it may track state better, keeping code variables or web page state with shorter reasoning chains. That still needs large-scale experiments.
ex: In circuit complexity terms, softmax attention is TC⁰, while DeltaNet is NC¹-complete.
FLA filled in features like variable-length training, since only easy-to-use tools reach industry.

t144|636.c: AI progress shouldn't be judged by compute alone, but by how much intelligence each unit of resources yields.
t144|636.e: From 2022 to 2024, the dominant story read scaling laws as piling up data, compute and parameters, even implying you shouldn't enter without 100,000 GPUs. He thinks that misleads researchers and decision-makers. The density law sets a metric for how much intelligence a unit of resources produces. Like Moore's law, it began as an observation and became an industry roadmap that has to be kept true through constant innovation. He also opposes intelligence being available only through expensive APIs, which limits how widely the technology spreads.
ex: DeepSeek V3 trained on far fewer resources than the threshold people had implied.
The density law complements scaling laws, asking whether the curve can get steeper.

d.verdict: Models costlier for the same ability will be weeded out

t144|636.c: Capability density doubles roughly every 3.5 months, and the curve steepened sharply after ChatGPT arrived.
t144|636.e: The team tracks density by how many parameters a model needs to reach a given ability. The first estimate was a doubling every 3.3 months, and adding 2025 models made it about 3.5. He sees the gap as normal noise. What matters is the exponential trend. The curve steepened around early 2023 because the competition and money ChatGPT brought sped up efficiency work. The curve covers only base models, so gains from reinforcement learning aren't counted yet, and the team is working on a version that includes post-training.
ex: Fast-falling GPT API prices are seen as an outward sign of density gains.
o1 and R1 gain by thinking longer when answering, so they don't belong on this curve.

t144|636.c: Skip the race to 100-billion-parameter models, use small models as a "wind tunnel," and bet on on-device AI.
t144|636.e: ModelBest calculated that training a roughly 140-billion-parameter model would cost tens of millions of yuan, and several Chinese teams would soon match its abilities, so there was no clear way to earn the money back. It turned to a "model wind tunnel": small experiments that break down efficiency and predict a large model's abilities before training starts. In January 2024 it released the 2.4-billion-parameter MiniCPM. He thinks general APIs lack differentiation, and big companies can subsidize them with profits from other businesses, so startups can't hold prices. On-device models were a less crowded race.
ex: MiniCPM 2.4B rivals Llama 2 13B and runs on a phone.
The API price war of May 2024 was seen as confirmation.

items.d: 140B costs tens of millions, hard to recoup
Avoid the general API price war

t144|636.c: On-device AI comes to cars first, then PCs and phones; by 2030 devices could run 60-billion-parameter models.
t144|636.e: Once the chip and power budget are fixed, model density decides what a car's cockpit can do. Cars have the loosest space and power limits, so they come first. Phones are still constrained but could leap ahead within two to three years. Extending chip roadmaps in a straight line, by 2030 devices could run a model with about 60 billion total parameters and 8 billion active at a time. Add density gains, and GPT-4 to GPT-5 level ability could fit on a device within five years. He leaves room for breakthroughs beyond the straight line too.
ex: One Mazda and one Geely model are in mass production; 6+ expected next year.
A standardized fine-tuning toolchain cuts the cost of customizing for each carmaker.

items.d: Devices can run sizable reinforcement learning

t144|636.c: Intelligence will spread out, with personal on-device models and cloud expert models forming an internet of agents.
t144|636.e: He cites China Telecom Research Institute figures showing that in 2023, China's on-device computing power was about 12 times that of its data centers. So he rejects the centralized view that the world needs only a few large models, comparing it to the 1943 claim that the world needed only five computers. He imagines everyone having an on-device model that holds their personal data. Wearables just collect data, a portable device runs the intelligence, and it works with cloud models built for each industry. He also warns that routine knowledge work will be replaced, and grand narratives shouldn't gloss over the toll on individuals and families.
ex: Wearables like blood glucose monitors only collect data.
One-person companies staffed by AI are, he says, just his personal speculation.

t144|487.c: Raising density takes four levers: architecture, data, algorithms and infrastructure, plus using compute fully.
t144|487.e: He compares architecture to a container that holds intelligence, data to textbooks, learning algorithms to how a model grows, and infrastructure to what fits training to hardware. The team wants to measure each one's contribution, but there's no clear formula yet. On hardware-software fit, a GPU used at half capacity still burns power, so even an elegant architecture isn't economical. One reason Transformers won is that attention uses GPUs more fully. The fit runs both ways: designing block-sparse algorithms for today's GPUs, and designing dedicated AI hardware such as phone NPUs.
ex: FlashAttention reworks attention around how the hardware works.
DeepSeek V3 changed low-level assembly code, another case of hardware-software co-design.

items.d: Makes training use the hardware fully

t144|487.c: Attention's new bottleneck is long outputs, and sparse attention, not linear, is the real substitute for full attention.
t144|487.e: Agents reading whole code repositories or doing deep research create long inputs, and reasoning chains create long outputs, so attention has become an efficiency bottleneck. He sees linear attention as closer to a replacement for sliding windows, which only look at recent text, while sparse attention corresponds to full attention. The two will eventually combine. The industry treats long context as "feed it a book, then ask questions," but the untested battleground is long output: remembering early state and keeping plans consistent. The worst failure is forgetting step one after step two. He guesses this relates to MiniMax M2's return to full attention, but stresses it's only a guess.
ex: InfLLM V2 needs to attend to only about 4K-6K tokens of a 128K context.
NSA's three-part design triples computing cost on short text.

cells.d: Read a repository, then plan long-range

t144|487.c: Less but better data directly yields stronger models and lower costs.
t144|487.e: The team processes data from raw text through deduplication and filtering, quality selection and synthetic rewriting, all the way to "textbook-grade" data checked by formal proof or by people. Ultra FunWeb uses less than a tenth of the original data yet trains a stronger model, which suggests training costs could fall to about a tenth. Data matters beyond pretraining too: the quality of fine-tuning and reinforcement learning data sets the ceiling for post-training. He goes further and asks what the smallest possible dataset is, which gets at what experience intelligence truly can't do without.
ex: Ultra FunWeb: under a tenth of the original data, yet a more capable model.
He cites Pengfei Liu's team and its "Less is More" series of papers.

t144|487.c: Reinforcement learning has no scaling law of its own yet; the bottleneck is environments models can't game.
t144|487.e: Pretraining often runs tens of trillions of tokens over hundreds of thousands of steps, while reinforcement learning usually runs a few thousand steps, too few to prove a stable scaling effect. Beyond math and code, environments where answers can be checked are hard to build, and real software development involves dependencies, system state and long-term maintenance. Borrowing from AI researcher Jason Wei, RL's "magic" requires an environment that can't be gamed. Otherwise more compute just amplifies cheating. There are two ways out: expand environments and wait for generalization, or improve sample efficiency. For now RL still learns far less efficiently than people.
ex: R1's reinforcement learning ran fewer than 10,000 steps.
People read negative feedback from a facial expression; machines need explicit rewards.

terms.d: Hard to build beyond math and code

t144|487.c: AGI won't be one model doing everything; it's more likely an AI that produces other AIs.
t144|487.e: He sees three steps toward AGI, artificial general intelligence. First, become an efficient learner. Then let specialized models work together. Finally, gain the ability to create new concepts, not just searching within existing symbol systems but building new frameworks, the way physics went from Newton to relativity. Handing self-driving to a small specialized model doesn't mean a general model isn't AGI. AGI can produce data and train specialized models for a given compute budget. Robotics is still in a "Warring States" era, with no settled way for the thinking "brain" and the motor "cerebellum" to work together. Vision-language-action models are just one attempt.
ex: For example, training a self-driving model for a given compute budget.
He thinks AGI's shape may start to emerge within a year or two.

t145|639.c: Exoskeletons augment people rather than replace them, giving basic mobility the way cars do.
t145|639.e: Humanoid robots aim to replace people in all kinds of settings. He chose to side with people, using technology to help them break past physical limits rather than withdraw from the real world. He compares exoskeletons to cars: they provide mobility, a basic capability, and the more basic it is, the more ways of living grow out of it. The long-term goal is a "programmable" body, with the device as the interface between people and the physical world. He admits the benefit has only just passed break-even. It's good for climbing volcanoes or touring museums, not yet for popping downstairs for coffee.
ex: Aging and digital life are lowering people's average mobility.
Units were donated to disaster rescue in Hong Kong, easing rescuers' physical strain.

items: Take over all kinds of work

d.verdict: Choosing to side with people

t145|639.c: Start with hardcore outdoor users, not elderly mobility aids, then widen circle by circle to daily commuting.
t145|639.e: The team ran Facebook ads with product renderings, comparing click rates across one to two hundred audience types. Mountaineers, backpackers and photographers showed the most consistent need. He deliberately avoided the elderly market. A medical-brace label would drive away young and old alike, the way parents resist hearing aids. Hardcore outdoor users have strong needs and naturally create content, which can reach casual hikers, travelers and then everyday commuters. Each circle needs a strong enough pain point, good enough tech and users willing to spread the word. To him, the turning point is someone wearing one naturally on the subway.
ex: Facebook ad tests covered one to two hundred audience profiles.
A user said about seven in ten US hikers they met recognized the brand.

items.d: Climbers and photographers who make content

t145|639.c: The first job is offsetting the device's own burden, and every spec serves the benefit-to-burden ratio.
t145|639.e: Each extra kilogram a person carries raises energy use by about 2-3%, and early exoskeletons could leave people more tired. So "actually useful" comes first: peak power in the hundreds of watts, battery life for a full day, and ideally recovering energy downhill. He balances the design by the ratio of benefits to drawbacks. The shape follows the body's curves and folds into a backpack, and weight fell from 4-5 kg in the prototype to about 2 kg in production. The first generation's range was 17.5 km, a bit short of the roughly 20 km serious hikers need. X Ultra raised it to 30 km.
ex: Weight came off through carbon fiber, titanium, aluminum and system-level optimization.
X Ultra weighs 1.8 kg and assists about 20-30% more effectively.

t145|639.c: Keeping only a power button forces the AI to read movement intent automatically, like a cerebellum.
t145|639.e: Engineers wanted backup mode buttons, but he refused. If users can only switch it on and off, automatic recognition has to be good enough for people to keep using and recommending it, just as touchscreens replaced keypad phones. The device now adapts automatically between walking, running, stairs, slopes and cycling, which he rates as "basically usable." The app still offers mode selection, but mainly to collect users' manual choices as learning feedback and reduce manual input over time. Software updates ship over the air every two to three weeks, far faster than hardware's one-to-two-year cycle.
ex: On a bike, you feel the assist within two pedal strokes.
Some software bugs get fixed over the air in about two days.

items.d: Works as soon as it's on
Users pick a mode in the app
A data loop that improves accuracy

t145|639.c: The best design in simulation isn't the product answer; better to delay than ship a 40-out-of-100 product.
t145|639.e: Minutes of simulation replaced six months to a year of human trials, proved the idea worked on energy and found a design where one motor assisted both legs. But in limited beta tests, every metric passed while user scores sat in the 40s out of 100. The motor's axis didn't line up with the body's joints, and fit with backpacks and body types was off, worst for slim users and Asian women. He scrapped a near-final design for two motors, nearly doubling cost and delaying delivery. He admits the conservatives were right about cost and timing, but won't let a bad product make the whole category cry wolf.
ex: Internal experience scores must reach at least 70-80 before shipping.
Before the first generation launched, the company had only about 200,000 yuan left.

t145|639.c: The hardest part is where it touches the body; defining the category means setting safety and durability rules.
t145|639.e: There's no existing consumer standard for exoskeletons, so the team had to write its own. Under repeated load, belts, straps and fabric turn mild pressure into rubbing and pain. Borrowing from bike saddles, he put the load on bony spots near the lower back. Early on, buckles came loose and devices sprang up, so the team spent two to three months on an algorithm that constantly checks the device is worn properly. For reliability, he spent about half a year at a partner factory doing failure analysis. Nearly every part broke during testing, and something worn on the body can't fail that way.
ex: Extreme impact tests ran about 2 million cycles, versus 100,000-200,000 for bikes.
Each leg adjusts separately to suit users whose legs differ.

items.d: Not a medical brace or a movie villain

t145|639.c: Hardware with no precedent needs time, and at scale, experience must be locked into processes.
t145|639.e: It took about 40 months from founding to first deliveries. He believes a category with no history has to respect time. The judgment, standards and supply chain built from detours became an "arsenal," so X Ultra went from kickoff to mass production in just four and a half months. After the team grew from about 40 people to over 200, he revised his view that talent density can replace process. A shipment to Europe missing its CE mark, the EU's required safety label, was returned in full at a loss of several million yuan, so checkpoints now guard high-risk steps. He tolerates trial and error on unknowns, but not carelessness.
ex: The first batch shipped in about four months; the official community nears 10,000.
He borrowed Bambu Lab's high performance bar, high rewards and cutting the bottom performers.

items.d: Global exoskeleton sales just 2,000-3,000 a year
Won over by simulations run online during quarantine
Shipping from August while ramping production

t145|639.c: Price cuts can't eat R&D margins; mass adoption starts at a half to a third of today's price.
t145|639.e: X Ultra costs $1,999 and existing products average just over $1,000, but buyers are mostly early adopters, so they say little about the mass market. He puts the mass-market tipping point at a half to a third of current prices, about 3,000 to 5,000 yuan in China. But he rejects the idea that margins are high and a price cut alone would break through. Prices are already near cost, with room needed for R&D. Cost cuts come from more in-house parts, better manufacturing, mass-producible lightweight materials replacing some carbon fiber, and investing in titanium suppliers. The biggest enemy is the category's weak overall experience, not any rival.
ex: He puts industry revenue at a few hundred million yuan a year, about 90% Hypershell's.
Medical and industrial players like ULS Robotics and Haier have launched consumer products.

t146|642.c: Gemini 3's comeback came from Google designing chips and software together and feeding product data back into training.
t146|642.e: He thinks Google is slow to decide but good at long-term bets. From its own TPU chips to its software libraries, the JAX framework and its model infrastructure, everything was designed to fit together. Data from apps like Workspace flows back into training, creating a loop of train, ship, retrain. That system simply happened to pay off now. He is more cautious about TPUs challenging Nvidia's CUDA software platform: big cloud providers haven't deployed many, retrofitting data centers is costly, and few people use JAX. For now CUDA still leads.
ex: He worked at both Brain and DeepMind: the first more bottom-up, the second more top-down
As competition heated up, paper releases tightened and many results were delayed

items.d: Feeds the next round of training

t146|642.c: Benchmark scores mean little without token use and cost, and long multi-step tasks reveal real ability.
t146|642.e: He thinks scores alone mislead. GPT-5.2 packs more intelligence into each token, so the total cost of a task can actually fall. GDPval's questions skew toward toy problems, and Databricks' OfficeQA shows real enterprise tasks are much harder. Public leaderboards also leak test data and can be gamed, so how high a lab climbs is down to its own restraint. He puts more weight on long, multi-step tasks like SWE-bench Pro and Mind2Web, and he rejects reading scores as real-world automation rates.
ex: τ²-bench adds a simulated user, making it closer to real back-and-forth

marks.d: Find one fact in long text
e.g. SWE-bench Pro: long, many steps

t146|642.c: Models will absorb generic agent scaffolding, but not the long tail of each company's private workflows.
t146|642.e: He expects foundation models to learn some generic agent scaffolding, the code wrapped around a model so it can act, by practicing with simulated tools. But the long tail of private company workflows is hard for any model to cover. He warns founders not to assume AGI has arrived: intelligence today still depends on how much data you have. Horizontal opportunities come from enterprise anxiety, such as using reinforcement learning to optimize orchestration and building data connectors and tool layers. Vertical startups need π-shaped people who know both AI and the industry.
ex: A data-connector example: Composio

items.d: Need people who know AI and the field

t146|642.c: Real open-sourcing means sharing training details, and cramming image and video skills into small models backfires.
t146|642.e: He thinks Google's Gemma falls short on sincerity: a small model is asked to handle text, images and more at once, so quality suffers. He admires DeepSeek for publishing its training details, which he sees as a more honest kind of openness. He also criticizes fake open source that carries the label but shares little. And he notes that humans are naturally multimodal, but video and mixed media put heavy pressure on model capacity and resources.
ex: Video and mixed media add a lot of pressure on model capacity

d.verdict: Sharing the details is what makes openness real

t146|642.c: Self-improvement goes far beyond retrieval and add-on memory; learning from real use is right, but feedback is hard.
t146|642.e: He sees RAG (letting a model look things up before answering) and add-on memory as early attempts at self-improvement, and thinks the real thing must go much further. He backs the direction Cursor, the AI coding tool, is taking with online reinforcement learning, which means learning straight from real use. But outsiders can't tell how far along it is, and whether user feedback is reliable is a hard problem. So he doesn't accept add-on memory as the end state.
ex: Cursor is trying online RL to learn from real-world use

items.d: The model keeps getting better by itself

t146|643.c: Tools shouldn't stay static: they should learn from failures, and failure traces become company assets.
t146|643.e: Precur builds a trainable, stateful tool layer for AI agents. Each tool has some intelligence built in, so when a call fails it learns and improves, and failure traces become assets that build up over time rather than throwaway logs. They drive tools with code to keep irrelevant information out of the model's context, and customers keep their existing agents. She thinks Anthropic has pushed hard on agents since October, with programmatic tool calling and MCP, a standard for connecting AI to outside tools, working as a loop. Claude's edge is that its coding skill carries over into taking action.
ex: In blind tests customers designed, about 12% better than their original tools

items.d: Traces pile up and get reused

t146|643.c: Agents, not people, will become the main users of tools, so products must be agent-friendly first.
t146|643.e: She splits tool users into three groups: consumers, businesses and agents. She expects agents to make most tool calls, so interfaces and reliability should be designed around what agents need. Models and agent frameworks push each other forward, and the usage data agents generate flows back into model training. The key question is whether the new market grows bigger than the part models swallow. She hopes for open models trained on lots of agent traces that also allow further post-training.

items.d: The future main callers of tools

t146|643.c: Companies pick models first by which cloud holds their data, then by price, and by performance last.
t146|643.e: Which cloud holds a company's years of data often decides its candidate models before performance does, because migrating usually takes a year or two. Partnerships with Azure or Google Cloud, plus cloud credits, change the real cost. Real-time agents care most about how well they perform within a response-time limit, so small models are often the better choice. In her view, model performance is usually the last filter.
ex: Real-time uses often pick small models like Gemini Flash or OpenAI's mini models

items.d: Migration takes a year or two

t146|612.c: RL startups come in three layers: environments, services and vertical apps, and environments now need real domain depth.
t146|612.e: He splits reinforcement learning opportunities into three layers. RL environments are where models practice and get tested. RL-as-a-service trains custom AI workers for companies that can't do RL themselves. Then come high-value verticals like drug discovery, financial trading and scientific discovery. Early on, having a coding agent clone software like Jira was enough to build an environment, but that's no longer a barrier. Environments for cybersecurity, robotics and self-driving depend far more on domain knowledge. He sees Tinker as closer to infrastructure-as-a-service, since users still need to understand RL.
ex: On the environment layer, they invested in Preference Model
A vertical example: Periodic Labs

items.d: Where models practice and get tested

t146|612.c: Gemini 3 wins by combining many strengths, and pretraining still has room to improve.
t146|612.e: Citing DeepMind's Oriol Vinyals, he believes pretraining, the stage where models learn from huge amounts of data, is far from its limit, so there is still runway after Gemini 3. Gemini 3's edge isn't one standout breakthrough but how it brings together long context, cost and multimodal ability. That's why he is optimistic about the versions that follow.

result.d: Broad integration, not a single breakthrough

t146|613.c: GDPval defines AGI by economic value again, and naming a rival's model as best makes it more credible.
t146|613.e: She sees GDPval as a return to how OpenAI's 2018 charter defined AGI: measuring a model's economic contribution through real job tasks. It covers industries that each contribute more than 5% of GDP, spanning 44 occupations and 1,320 tasks. When OpenAI released it, the top-scoring model was from Anthropic. She thinks that makes the benchmark more credible and shows OpenAI's researchers can keep research separate from marketing.
ex: 44 occupations and 1,320 tasks

t146|613.c: Gemini 3 went viral with native web page generation, while GPT-5.2's practical gains spread less.
t146|613.e: She thinks Gemini 3 lived up to sky-high expectations. The web pages it generates natively look good and work well, which makes it especially easy to share. GPT-5.2's improvements are more practical and don't spread as easily. The two offer different kinds of value, so comparing them head to head isn't fair.

items: Native web pages look good and work

d.verdict: A direct comparison isn't fair

t147|645.c: In the AI era, community-first no longer works: build tools to stock content, then open the community.
t147|645.e: In the mobile internet era the order was Douyin first, CapCut later: community first, creation tools second. Early Douyin had little content, and users accepted plain videos. Today's audiences are used to rich content, so a community built only on user uploads struggles to keep people, a lesson she learned building Lipu. The test for models has also shifted from whether output looks good to whether anyone wants to watch it. So OiiOii first uses agents to package professional animation skills into tools and stocks content across genres, so there's something to watch when the community opens.
ex: She estimates going from tool to community takes most of a year

d.verdict: Timing changed, so the path must change

t147|645.c: Animation is scarce because it's hard to make; lower the barrier and hidden demand will appear.
t147|645.e: Animation's audience now includes adults, but supply is concentrated among a few big studios. Live-action video got so easy you can edit it on a phone, while animation is still stuck on drawing and 3D modeling. Bilibili creators keep making animation even with clunky tools like Live2D, which shows supply has been held back. She admits she can't be sure viewing will grow, but before Douyin nobody believed ordinary people's lives were worth watching. If animation costs less than live action, topics like history, finance, education and science could all gain new content.
ex: Live2D is hard to use, yet creators still want to learn it

t147|645.c: Start with semi-pro teams of two or three, moving them from weekly posts to several a day.
t147|645.e: She sorts content makers into four groups: everyday users (UGC), semi-professional small teams (PUGC), professional studios (PGC) and rights holders (OGV). The semi-pro middle lacks tools the most. She estimates China has about 1.8 to 2 million anime, comics and games accounts, mostly two- or three-person teams posting once a week. The goal is ten posts a day, and even two a day would be a breakthrough for animation. The team started around August and opened a closed beta on November 10, about two and a half months later.
ex: About 1.8 to 2 million anime and gaming accounts, most posting weekly

marks.d: Two or three people; the biggest gap

t147|645.c: Instead of one-click finished videos, OiiOii shows its workflow so users can step in like a director.
t147|645.e: She doesn't think multi-agent setups are a universal answer for video generation. Animation and film have mature handoffs between stages, while ads may just need a pile of assets. She also opposes fully automatic packaging: AI can't yet make good films on its own, and creators need a sense of control and ownership. OiiOii makes its workflow visible, so users can edit or step in at any node. The cost is a combinatorial explosion across task assignment, entering and leaving nodes, and two-way sync between canvas and chat, which is the main source of bugs.
ex: A contrast with one-click approaches like MovieFlow

terms.d: Edit or step in at any node

t147|645.c: Every model has weak spots; the edge is people with taste and technical skill who combine them well.
t147|645.e: She sees natural trade-offs: Midjourney holds a style well but lets characters drift, while GPT-4o and Nano Banana are the reverse. For images, the team hard-codes fixed branches instead of letting an agent choose, because character consistency must be nearly certain. For video, an agent used to pick among about six models, but Sora 2 stood out for synced sound and natural motion, so it now has its own main path. She compares tuning models to opening loot boxes: double down on what works, pull what's unstable. People who understand content, tech and aesthetics are extremely rare.
ex: About 1.5 people orchestrate models, with 3 designers checking quality
Illustration styles look great as stills but lack animation data for video

root.d: Combine models to cover weak spots

items.d: Strong on style, weak on characters
Strong on characters, weaker on style

t147|645.c: OiiOii won't start with AI comic dramas or heavy enterprise work, which drag products into custom jobs.
t147|645.e: AI comic dramas depend on scripts and paid promotion, and the team is good at neither. Those clients want one step of a mature, still manual process made faster, the opposite of her goal of relying less on human labor. Top studios each have different workflows, so serving them turns you into a custom-work shop, while smaller studios look much like semi-pro teams. After the beta, comic drama companies still came knocking, mostly wanting scripts turned quickly into many storyboards they edit themselves. She may set up a small separate team for that, but it won't be the focus.
ex: A small-business angle: licensing game and toy characters for creators to remix

items.d: Overseas Lipu, AI comic dramas, animation tools
No strength in scripts or ad buying

t147|645.c: She wants an ecosystem, not hits: hits bring people in, but rich content keeps them.
t147|645.e: She rejects treating animation as a tool for quick profit or manufactured hits, and avoids formulas that whip up emotion fast. Her aim is to let people express imagination through animation. For growth, hits bring new users, while the rich content the tools build up keeps them. Hits without a stocked shelf of content become a one-off spike. Invite codes now go only to users active for two or three days, five each, so viral spread doesn't dilute user quality.
ex: Roadmap: music stories first, then comedy, music videos and science explainers
The overseas version starts in mid-to-late January and should grow slower

items.d: Every genre has more to watch

t147|645.c: From a hobby-niche startup to big tech, she turned every low point into an antibody.
t147|645.e: In 2014, after three years in product at WeChat, she quit to study animation, only to find low pay and internships that charged fees. She couldn't sacrifice that much for her passion. She then ran an extreme-sports content company, mistaking a hobby niche for a big market. It broke even but couldn't scale. At ByteDance she worked on CapCut and Douyin effects, and sees her biggest contribution as picking people and clarifying business logic. At Bilibili she confirmed that animation is scarce because it's hard to make. She believes climbing out of a low point beats starting from zero.
ex: CapCut had about 5 to 6 million daily users when she joined, later 36 million
She led the real-time comic filter, which she calls the world's first

items.d: Quit in 2014 to study for six months
Using AI to pursue animation dreams

t148|650.c: Embodied AI has three breakthroughs: RL for movement, large models for planning, end-to-end networks tying it together.
t148|650.e: The first breakthrough is reinforcement learning solving motor control. MIT's Mini Cheetah got four-legged hardware and software working together, and ETH Zurich then used RL to control the whole body directly. That relied on running huge numbers of simulations in parallel, plus hardware designed to shrink the gap between simulation and reality. He considers this path largely figured out. Second, large models are good at breaking a sentence into steps, but robots still lack a shared task map like self-driving has. Third is end-to-end: one neural network going straight from sensors to actions.
ex: RL-driven motor control from MIT's Mini Cheetah and ETH Zurich

t148|650.c: Embodied AI is where self-driving was in 2019; he conservatively expects a clear breakthrough in 2027.
t148|650.e: At Huawei, self-driving had piled up about 2 million lines of hand-written rules, and problems grew faster than fixes. He saw planning and control as closed-loop, since each move changes what comes next, and harder than perception. So he had the network plan trajectories directly. About 100 cars collected human driving data, and at roughly 10,000 hours the network could smoothly navigate crowded urban villages. That convinced him AI could plan. Self-driving took about two years from going end-to-end to results, so he expects robot data to explode in 2026 and pay off in 2027.
ex: He asserts US founders will be no match at all for Chinese rivals in embodied AI
His reason: hardware, settings, data and algorithms must work as one system

t148|650.c: Robots first hit a data wall; the next leap needs at least 10 million hours of real data.
t148|650.e: He sees three walls. First is the data wall: a network can only grow complex enough with enough data. Second is what's often called the algorithm wall, which he thinks is really about compute, since more data actually allows simpler model designs. Third is interaction and post-training, where the model must predict how its actions change the world. In self-driving, results began around 10,000 hours, and a product needed 100,000 to 1 million hours. For robots to jump another order of magnitude, he estimates a starting point of 10 million hours.
ex: TARS has collected about 100,000 hours of data
Product-grade self-driving needed 100,000 to 1 million hours

t148|650.c: Internet video and simulation can't replace real data; only motor control suits simulation.
t148|650.e: Internet video like dashcam and travel footage is limited in scale, uneven in quality and hard to link to specific failures, so his team has crossed that path off. Rendered city reconstructions mainly improve visual realism, but perception isn't the hardest part. Traditional physics simulation still approximates the world with rules. Only problems with fairly simple mechanics, like motor control, are well suited to generating data in simulation, just as a self-driving test track can't replace driving in real cities.
ex: Cloth and cables change state with every touch; describing pictures can't teach that

d.verdict: Simulation only suits simple problems like motor control

t148|650.c: Teleoperation captures motions, while wearable capture records skills and costs two orders of magnitude less.
t148|650.e: He favors human-centered collection: record how people do things, then transfer that experience to robots. Data must be real settings plus real actions, and collectors must be able to do the task correctly.
