Teleoperation, where a person remotely steers a robot, is slow, often fails and disrupts work on site. TARS uses a first-person camera and lightweight gloves to record hand position and orientation, every finger's state and the force applied. Vision alone fails when hands are blocked. He firmly backs dexterous hands, so collection must capture the human hand's twenty-plus degrees of freedom rather than reduce people to grippers.
ex: The main cost of collection is compute, not hardware

t148|650.c: Robots deserve their own foundation model, not an action head bolted onto a vision-language model.
t148|650.e: He sees next-token prediction as GPT's greatest invention, and the Transformer's value as being simple, efficient and able to absorb huge amounts of data. Physical-world AI should prioritize time, space, contact and force over texture and color. So TARS's AWE devotes most of its neurons to these physical quantities and recommends next steps as the world changes with each action. Adding an action head to a vision-language model amounts to saying robots don't deserve their own foundation model. He compares behaviors to meaning and low-level trajectories to sound waves, and planning at the behavior level makes long tasks easier.
ex: The test: from motion alone, you can't tell if a human or robot is dressing

items.d: Behavior is like meaning; helps long tasks

t148|650.c: Pick the route by the problem: world models for closed games, VLA models for the open world.
t148|650.e: He defines end-to-end broadly: solve as much as possible with neural networks, whether through imitation learning or reinforcement learning. Labels like VLA (vision-language-action models) and world models have no agreed definitions either; what matters is the task. Self-driving's top problem now is the back-and-forth with other cars and pedestrians, which suits a closed system of world models plus RL and can reach Level 3 and 4. Open-world problems like reading road signs or handling unfamiliar obstacles and flooding need language and VLA more, mapping to Level 4 to 5.
ex: TARS's first target: flexible assembly like routing wire harnesses and plugging connectors
To judge a company, first see whether it knows what it wants to become

marks.d: World models plus RL, up to L3 and L4
Flooding and debris need common sense
Language and VLA, L4 to L5

t149|655.c: A cherry-picked demo proves something worked once; robotics needs large-scale, standardized testing on real robots.
t149|655.e: Robotics research often leans on cherry-picked demos, which only show a task succeeded at least once, not how often or how reliably. Paper-style evaluations often test just three or four tasks. He wants each task run hundreds of times on real robots, using the average success rate to squeeze out luck. The first goal is to reliably tell whether a model has an ability at all, not to fuss over 99% versus 99.5%. His belief that sound algorithms pay off with sustained investment comes from his face recognition days.
ex: RoboChallenge was launched jointly by Dexmal and Hugging Face
Anonymous submissions allowed; only the last result counts, to stop cherry-picking

result.d: First tell if the ability exists

t149|655.c: Test tasks drawn from real-life needs expose each model's different blind spots.
t149|655.e: Table 30 started as a wish list: everyone at the company wrote down what robots should definitely be able to do next. Thousands of entries came in, and the data team narrowed them to 30. The tasks cover soft objects, millimeter-level positioning, remembering context, contact between the gripper and objects, and contact between objects, and each one fails in its own way. He thinks real needs expose blind spots better than artificial academic categories. The barcode-scanning task, for instance, revealed that single-frame models forget what they just saw.
ex: Shredding paper: the paper blocks the wrist camera and must enter a narrow slot
Arranging flowers: sensing when a stem touches something else

items.d: Thousands of ideas from the company

t149|655.c: Many data routes can work; what sets the ceiling is how much you invest in capturing real-world knowledge.
t149|655.e: He doesn't think the label on a data type sets a model's ceiling. What matters is how much a team invests in capturing knowledge of the physical world. Dexmal builds on its past experience collecting face data offline at scale and relies mainly on data from real robots. He calls the idea that internet data is free for language model companies a fairy tale, since cleaning and organizing it takes huge human effort. He also relayed other companies' claims about their data volumes, while making clear he doesn't vouch for them.
ex: Generalist AI says it has 270,000 hours, adding 10,000 hours a week
One wearables team says it will collect 10 million hours in a year

t149|655.c: Robot AI is still at its CIFAR stage; China's DeepSeek moment in robotics is about three years away.
t149|655.e: He borrows from computer vision's history: the field is still at the stage of small datasets like CIFAR, and its ImageNet moment hasn't arrived. In 2026 he most wants to see whether China gets a DeepSeek moment in robotics, with domestic teams truly matching overseas models. Based on how vision caught up, he estimates about three years. Breaking into the mainstream means making customers believe, and that takes a few jaw-dropping demos. His personal test: a robot that folds the duvet every day on its own.
ex: Folding a duvet tests payload, balance, precision and the whole robot's hardware
Many failures that look algorithmic first require clearing a hardware bar

items.d: Small scale; where we are now
China matches overseas in about three years

t149|518.c: Look at generational gaps and trends; physical noise drowns out improvements in the decimal places.
t149|518.e: Cup handle shapes, placement, lighting and mechanical error all affect results, and it's hard to tell whether a failure comes from the model or the environment. So small gains on real robots mean little; focus on generational gaps and trends. The top score is still under 60, the range where differences between models show up most. Spirit AI ran every task with one base model and one standard fine-tuning process. He opposes hand-crafting tricks per task, because a foundation model's value lies in learning any task through the same process.
ex: Spirit AI's Spirit V1.5 passed π0.5 to top the leaderboard

t149|518.c: For now, test models after fine-tuning; zero-shot head-to-head matchups are still too hard for today's models.
t149|518.e: RoboArena, launched by Physical Intelligence, tests zero-shot ability, with no demonstrations, through distributed pairwise comparisons. That suits more mature future models. For today's models most tasks have success rates so low that, with everything near zero, pairwise comparisons can't tell models apart. RoboChallenge tests few-shot or fine-tuned ability, with about 1,000 human demonstrations per task. Simulation is reproducible, but its trajectories are mostly scripted and narrower than real teleoperation, so reviewers usually reject sim-only papers. University-built remote robot setups are hard to maintain long term.
ex: World Labs' Marble is more like a static 3D scene, hard to interact with dynamically

d.verdict: For now, test real ability after fine-tuning

t149|518.c: Data is the biggest bottleneck, and robots can copy language models' recipe: pretraining, SFT, then RL.
t149|518.e: He believes that once robots have data on the scale of language models, the problem will most likely be solved. The recipe follows language models: large-scale pretraining, then supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on high-quality expert data, then RL post-training. Spirit AI bets on three kinds of real data: human video, wearables and teleoperation. Plentiful, lower-quality data goes into pretraining, and scarce, high-quality data that matches robot actions goes into post-training. It isn't betting on simulation yet, since each scene needs professional artists and the tools are hard to use. VLA only describes inputs and outputs and doesn't require an LLM base.
ex: He admits he'd change his mind if simulation tools became easy enough

t149|518.c: Foundation models decide what robots can do; 2026 may bring a jump from GPT-2 to GPT-3 level.
t149|518.e: He believes foundation models decide what robots can do, while business logic decides what they actually do. Ability is still lacking, so raising it matters more than rushing to find one universal application. Robotics hasn't yet found a killer app like AI coding. Many vertical companies will emerge, in areas like housekeeping and roof repair, possibly earlier in the US and Europe where labor is expensive. When watching demos, beware four risks: cherry-picking, editing, hidden teleoperation and AI-generated video. He's confident in a leap in 2026, but a GPT-4-style mainstream breakthrough will take three to four years.
ex: The strongest evidence for a demo: go there and interact with it yourself

t149|518.c: Single-frame VLA models have no memory, and adding past frames or an agent isn't training memory in.
t149|518.e: In the scanning task, a robot must remember whether it has already scanned an item. Most open-source VLA models look only at the current frame and have no memory mechanism, so they keep making mistakes. The usual fixes are feeding in past frames or bolting on an agent, but he argues none of these truly trains memory into the foundation model. That's why Table 30 includes tasks that test memory of context.
ex: The scanning task: the model can't tell whether it already scanned the code

items.d: Memory must be trained into the model

t150|160.c: R1 broke out on open weights, a detailed report and a low-cost story, proving small teams can lead.
t150|160.e: She thinks DeepSeek R1 had far more impact than Kimi K1.5 or the original o1 from the same period. It open-sourced its strongest version, published a detailed technical report and cited a training cost of about $5.57 million, which caught the attention of US politicians and executives. It first won respect among top researchers, then went viral in China over the Spring Festival. She has reservations about the habit of valuing things at home only once America praises them. R1 also changed investors' minds: young, small teams can do world-class work with modest resources.
ex: The roughly $5.57 million training cost claim caught attention in US politics and business

result.d: Praise abroad first, then fame at home

t150|160.c: Claude Code is a general agent: an AI that codes has hands and feet in the digital world.
t150|160.e: She breaks down what agents need into reasoning and planning, coding, multimodal understanding, tool use and long-term memory. Not all of it must be trained into the model; add-on systems and protocols like MCP can supply some. Coding matters most: writing code gives an AI hands and feet in the digital world, which is why Claude Code is more than a coding tool. The barrier has dropped to a single person. She can't code, yet she uses an agent to track tech workers' social posts and summarize them weekly, a niche need nobody would have built for before.
ex: Codex, Grok Code Fast and Antigravity are all doubling down on coding
Agent platforms keep pivoting to tools, a sign that frequent creators are still rare

items.d: One person can serve niche needs

t150|160.c: Model competition has become system design, from chips all the way up to apps.
t150|160.e: She sees Google's vertical integration, from TPUs, JAX, infrastructure and cloud up to Gemini and its apps, as its core advantage. Alibaba's combination of Qwen, Alibaba Cloud and its chip unit T-Head, Tencent putting one person over both infrastructure and algorithms, and DeepSeek's infrastructure team helping design algorithms all point the same way. Long-context limits ultimately come down to GPU compute, interconnect and storage, so competition has moved to the system level. She also thinks training large models is closer to engineering and needs hands-on feel.
ex: Huawei's CloudMatrix 384 and Nvidia's NVL72 show competition at the system level
DeepSeek estimated an 84.5% gross margin; the industry disputes how it was calculated

t150|160.c: Pretraining plus post-training may be hitting its limit; the next way to learn needs a return to research.
t150|160.e: Citing Ilya Sutskever, Demis Hassabis and Yann LeCun, she leans toward defining AGI by few-shot learning, continual learning and understanding physical laws. She agrees with Yuandong Tian that the next approach should be simpler and explainable. If LLMs alone reached AGI, the rules of the world would have been captured in ways no one can explain, which bodes poorly for humans. Genie 3 and SIMA 2 can generate and explore environments but can't yet manipulate objects. If AI can improve technology itself and become an inventor, she asks whether humanity is ready.
ex: DP Technology: from accelerated computing to agents covering the whole research process

d.verdict: Breakthroughs require going back to research

t150|160.c: Big tech's AI race is about organization: ByteDance coordinates best, Alibaba grows from the edges, Tencent hires catfish.
t150|160.e: She thinks ByteDance's standalone AI unit and startup-style setup help it escape inertia, with models and products working most closely together. The risk is locking in people and tasks before a direction is proven. Alibaba's Qwen grew bottom-up from the company's edges and built strength through open source, but Quark and Qwen have been renamed and swapped as flagships several times, which looks like treating symptoms. Tencent brought in outside talent to oversee both infrastructure and algorithms, a rare, aggressive catfish move to stir things up. The results won't be clear until 2026.
ex: She notes Yuanbao's daily users once jumped tenfold after adding DeepSeek
WeChat blocked Yuanbao's red-envelope links: group resources aren't automatically available

items.d: An edge team became the main force
Brings in catfish, borrows outside models

t150|160.c: AI can't copy the internet playbook: every call costs money, and super apps won't work under agents.
t150|160.e: Mobile internet's build-once, sell-many economies of scale don't apply to large models, because every call costs compute. ByteDance's highest-traffic product, Doubao, is free, while revenue comes mainly from tools like TRAE and Coze, which shows the mismatch. The Doubao phone assistant was restricted by WeChat, Meituan and others, a sign that super apps refuse to become agents' downstream suppliers. Efficiency uses like food delivery and ticket booking face big disruption, while content platforms are less affected. Who sees the ads, and whether revenue goes to the agent or the platform, are still open questions.
ex: Vertical agents selling outcomes, not seats, is harder: they must own the workflow and delivery

items: Super apps are the front door

d.verdict: Economies of scale don't simply carry over

t150|160.c: Investors are pricing robotics and model companies far ahead of their revenue and real-world deployment.
t150|160.e: By her count, Chinese embodied AI and robotics companies raised 73.5 billion yuan in 2025, far more than the 18.2 billion yuan raised by companies still training large models. Zhipu and MiniMax are worth tens of billions of dollars, yet their revenue is only tens of millions, around $50 million at most. She sees an IPO as the start of the next race and a safety net for survival, not a trophy. On robots, she doubts simulation can easily solve the data problem, and flags hardware durability and hype around government training grounds and orders. Next, watch orders, delivery, repeat purchases and autonomous work.
ex: Optimus's dexterous hands last about six weeks and cost over $6,000 each
Plaud's recorder sold over 1 million units by solving a concrete pain point

t150|160.c: AI won't automatically free people to enjoy life; meaning has to be found again outside work.
t150|160.e: She sees sky-high AI salaries and funding stories alongside layoffs at big companies. She rejects the idea that once AI takes over work, people will naturally enjoy life. People were never trained to find passion and meaning; it's like going from being forbidden to date as a teen to suddenly being pushed to marry. The emptiness Yuandong Tian describes during the period of replacement also deserves attention. She admits AI hasn't freed her either: it brings more story ideas, but face-to-face interviews and careful deliberation are hard to replace. She closes with Dongxu Huang's line: a model can't live your life for you.
ex: AI brings more story ideas, but interviews and careful thought still need people

items.d: People never learned to seek meaning

t151|663.c: An AI that can code can operate a computer, so Claude Code is already the strongest general agent.
t151|663.e: He sees coding as the bridge that lets AI do computer work for people. Users want tasks done; writing code is just the agent building itself a tool on the fly. Once a model can code, what's missing is no longer intelligence but task knowledge, a runtime environment and reliable delivery. Without a browser it can't operate web pages, so you need the full runtime and skills. On the flip side, pure web-coding products quickly become interchangeable, because the same model API sets everyone's ceiling.
ex: With the same prompt, their product and Lovable or v0.dev give similar results
Anthropic employees also use Claude Code for chores like email

result.d: In theory, can do anything on a computer

t151|663.c: Production systems should be mostly standard procedures plus a little AI, with code handling anything deterministic.
t151|663.e: He has reread The Bitter Lesson many times and concluded that anything code can solve reliably shouldn't be stuffed into a long context for the model to work out. What large models really add is judgment glue: whether to restock, which workflow a request should go to, whether a candidate meets unwritten criteria. These are hard to spell out as rules. Software handles the standard steps, models handle judgment, and AI's round-the-clock, copyable nature multiplies efficiency. Unless an all-powerful AGI arrives, this combination will hold for a long time.
ex: Comparing 9.11 and 9.2 can test a model, but production should call code
Restocking and routing calls in CRM and ERP systems suit models

d.verdict: Mostly SOPs plus a little AI will last

t151|663.c: Skills are layered, on-demand context loading; anything that can live outside the context shouldn't stay in it.
t151|663.e: He has seen that once context gets out of control, hallucinations multiply, so engineering effort has shifted to context engineering. A skill first exposes only a one-line description of the problem it solves, and the agent reads the full text only if it seems relevant. Skills can also bundle programs or APIs so the model doesn't compute things itself. Agents no longer hard-code branches with if-else like traditional software; the model weighs the task and skills to choose a path. The platform's job is to judge which of several similar skills works best and audit them for security.
ex: GitHub may have a dozen versions of a skill for the same task
A malicious skill could open a reverse shell through a local Claude Code

items.d: The agent picks likely useful ones

t151|663.c: The raw supply for agents sits in experts' heads, and low-code tools actually keep those experts out.
t151|663.e: Much professional knowledge still lives in people's heads, offline processes and inside organizations, not in models, and new tasks keep appearing. If experts can spell out their experience, criteria and steps, they can copy most of their ability into an agent that others reuse cheaply. But he thinks people who can use low-code tools could already write code. The ones to activate are HR staff who know how to screen candidates and support staff who know returns. They only need to describe needs and judgments in plain language.
ex: He approves of Coze moving from drag-and-drop low-code to natural-language creation
He thinks simple web pages and mini-games offer thin value

marks.d: Domain experts like HR and support

t151|663.c: Three months in, the storefront hadn't found product-market fit, mainly because supply wasn't rich or reliable enough.
t151|663.e: The plan assumed about 100 daily users per narrow use case. In reality only a few use cases had a handful to a dozen power users. He thinks two-sided marketplaces are hard to cold-start anyway, and creating, deploying and reviewing agents was too complicated, so the Agent Builder went from add-on to prerequisite. The company shouldn't flood the platform with its own supply, or the ecosystem won't grow, though he admits building a few clear-cut use cases early isn't necessarily bad. The quality bar must be strict: anything that fails five runs out of ten should go.
ex: The team of about 50 says it can't build everything itself
Pivoted in January 2026; Agent Builder entered closed beta in mid-January

items.d: New users don't know what's possible
Describe a problem, get matched automatically

t151|663.c: As development costs approach zero, software will be built for one purpose, then thrown away.
t151|663.e: He compares it to 3D printing. Industrial production only serves large numbers of people, and traditional software also needs thousands of users to spread its costs. With creation spread out, needs of one to ten people become worth serving, and ultimately code will be created, run and destroyed for a single task. But he stresses that AI is manufacturing: every run consumes tokens, compute and electricity, so marginal cost isn't zero. Price wars only happen when several models are about equally capable, and demand for the strongest intelligence is nearly unlimited.
ex: In the short run, it's more realistic to build agents a few people love daily

t151|663.c: Lowering barriers often breaks through more than technical leads, and technical founders tend to underestimate it.
t151|663.e: He thinks people with technical backgrounds push lowering barriers far down the list, as if it didn't matter. From a pure tech view, the layer MuleRun added might look like it does nothing. But breakout cases often come from accessibility: DeepSeek was free, showed its full chain of thought and wrote fun Chinese, while ChatGPT's Ghibli-style images and NotebookLM also drove growth. He also thinks that even if models stopped improving, fully using today's abilities would take a year or two, so 2026 will be a boom year for apps.
ex: Someone packaged a Nano Banana figurine prompt and charged per use
He expects AI-native apps earning $500 million to $1 billion a year in 2026

items.d: Help ordinary people past the hurdles

t151|663.c: His second startup failed from split focus, funding-inflated ambitions and too little respect for a new industry.
t151|663.e: Chaitin Tech's success gave him the illusion he could do anything, and in 2021 he founded two companies at once, one in gaming and one in data security. The gaming venture was overconfident about its first product, and its large funding pushed it toward big projects instead of cheap experiments. He reflects that learning fast doesn't mean getting it right the first time. In 2023, with tens of millions of yuan still in the bank, he judged he lacked the energy and shut the gaming company. Starting over, he set two rules: only do what fits his abilities, and work on the front line himself.
ex: Chaitin was founded in 2014 and sold to Alibaba Cloud in October 2019
At his low point, a friend spent two days gaming with him at an internet cafe

items.d: Back to Alibaba after anxiety and insomnia

t152|668.c: In 2026 the real fight in embodied AI is over models, not orders; mass deployment comes after 2027.
t152|668.e: He rejects the idea that the industry is finished if it can't deploy in 2026. In his view, robot models are roughly at GPT-2: somewhat intelligent, but painful to use as agents or deploy at scale. Replicable products arrive near GPT-3.5. The turning point is when a robot entering a new environment succeeds 70 to 80 percent of the time zero-shot, with little teaching needed afterward. Until then, every site needs its own data collection and fine-tuning, so revenue can only grow slowly.
ex: He expects mass deployment from the second half of 2027 into 2028
Demand, hardware, supply chain and funding are ready; only core capability lags

items.d: Today: collect data and fine-tune per site
Standard products enter many settings at once

t152|668.c: Robots are rare because they're dumb; a capable brain could raise demand tenfold.
t152|668.e: He has run the numbers on industrial robots: about 500,000 units a year worldwide at around $20,000 each comes to only about $10 billion, far smaller than people assume. Domestic substitution fulfilled its industrial mission but didn't bring high profits. The bottleneck is that machines can only do simple, structured work. If robot models could take on about 30% of tasks, industrial demand could grow by an order of magnitude, and the same brain could extend to hotels, retail, logistics and homes.
ex: China has about 100 million factory workers and about 3 million robots
Installed penetration is about 3%, adding roughly 0.3% a year

t152|668.c: Chinese embodied AI startups must own the brain, the robot body and the customer relationship.
t152|668.e: US companies can build just the brain because they can be acquired by Google, Tesla and others. Big Chinese companies tend to build in-house, so acquisition can't be the main exit. Customers want a smarter robot and don't want to buy a body and install a brain themselves. Owning the hardware lets a startup guarantee the experience, deal with customers directly and build up data from real sites. He stresses that full-stack doesn't mean dabbling in everything: you must be strong at AI, robotics and enterprise sales.
ex: From building controllers at Rokae, he learned performance depends on the robot body

items: Must prove both tech and business

d.verdict: Chinese teams must go full-stack and excel at all three

t152|668.c: Simulation struggles to transfer to reality, so data must layer video, teleoperation, wearables and on-site RL.
t152|668.e: He thinks the gap between simulation and reality is hard to close, especially for tasks involving contact. Spirit AI's recipe has four layers. Internet videos of people working are plentiful but coarse, so they go into pretraining. Teleoperation is precise but can't scale, so it's used for fine-tuning. Wearables capture real motions cheaply at scale, filling the gap in between. Robots doing real work on site collect failures for reinforcement learning. Nor does it bet on one wearable form: UMI only records hands, so it must be combined with exoskeletons and motion capture.
ex: Pretraining used about 200,000 hours of video of people working

t152|668.c: To compare rivals, look at how fast their data collection is accelerating, not how much they already have.
t152|668.e: Early on, wearable data was only 20 to 30 percent as usable as teleoperation data, so learning the same motion took three to five times as much. Since May 2024 the team has gone through four hardware generations and nearly 100 improvements, raising usability to about 95%. He credits the acceleration to accumulated work on devices, the data platform, training pipelines and engineering efficiency. He admits 100 times more data doesn't mean 100 times better performance; whether the model scales as expected is the real test.
ex: Rollout began in January 2026, aiming for over 100,000 hours by Q2
He puts over 80% of his energy into the data bottleneck

items.d: About two years at PI and others

t152|668.c: The right production step is scarcer than demand; the first site must keep feeding training data back.
t152|668.e: CATL sent its needs to several embodied AI companies, and Spirit AI picked end-of-line battery plug-and-unplug testing out of nearly 200 production steps. It needs no major line retrofits, calls for a VLA model plus force control, runs at a slow pace, tolerates errors and allows retries. More importantly, robots actually entered the line and could run the full loop of collecting data, training, deploying and feeding results back. He also thinks the best first targets are tasks where traditional automation already does 90% and only the last 10% of adaptability is missing.
ex: The project took about 11 months to acceptance; he estimates a month with newer models
One team chose a job needing three robots per factory: no market even if it works

t152|668.c: Startups must reach 100,000 robots a year before big tech goes all in around 2028.
t152|668.e: He sees the real long-term rivals as giants like Huawei, Xiaomi and Li Auto that can do both hardware and software. The market is just too small for them now, and their big push may not come until 2028 or 2029. For big companies it's a job; for startups it's life or death. Selling 100,000 units a year is the threshold for a profitable mid-sized maker, and only five to eight full-range makers may survive. Latecomers can still catch up, but need at least $100 to $200 million to buy time, and robot brains won't be winner-take-all.
ex: First round valued at 300 million yuan; now nearly 2 billion raised, valued over 10 billion
He caps revenue plans at about 100 million yuan and skips low-quality orders

t152|668.c: Technical virtuosity isn't a business; deployment needs a big market and a product you can sell repeatedly.
t152|668.e: Rokae once built a ceramic-knife sharpening workstation for Kyocera. By coordinating 3D vision, force sensing and trajectory planning, it outperformed Mitsubishi, and he calls it the best in the world, but global demand was just eight units. The previous generation of AI could only conquer specialized steps one at a time and couldn't create a general market. He also admits he long thought like a robotics engineer, only accepting in the second half of 2024 that embodied AI is first an AI race, where data matters more than existing control modules.
ex: The global market for sharpening workstations was about 8 million yuan
Rokae expanded too fast in 2018; a year later it had about four months of cash

cells.d: Long on-site work, hard to copy
Customers fine-tune with their own data
Best in class, eight units worldwide
No market even if it works

t153|160.c: Junyang Lin chose to leave; claims about Qwen app user targets or Hao Zhou replacing him are wrong.
t153|160.e: She believes Junyang Lin had long pushed himself hard toward his goals, ran out of drive at the last step and decided suddenly, leaving management almost no time to react. Claims that the model team was judged on the Qwen app's daily users lack evidence and make no organizational sense: the app belongs to the intelligent information business group under Eddie Wu, while the model team's goals remain performance, efficiency and open models in many sizes. Hao Zhou joined in January to replace post-training lead Bowen Yu, reporting to Jingren Zhou, not to replace Lin.
ex: Announced on DingTalk the afternoon of March 3, posted on WeChat before dawn next day
Qwen Code lead Binyuan Hui had already left

items: Still judged on performance and open source
Hao Zhou replaces the post-training lead

t153|160.c: The proposed split cuts the tight collaboration between pretraining, post-training and infrastructure.
t153|160.e: She thinks Qwen trained efficiently because one small team kept pretraining, post-training, infrastructure and multimodal work together. Members had worked side by side for years, talked constantly and didn't pass the buck. The proposed reorganization slices the team by modality and training stage into parallel groups, and it came just as Qwen 3.5 finished training and the team was exhausted from long overtime. At an all-hands meeting, management called it more investment in base models, not a retreat, and admitted the communication was mishandled, but offered no concrete plan.
ex: Eddie Wu, Jingren Zhou and Fang Jiang attended the all-hands meeting

root.d: From one integrated team to parallel teams

t153|160.c: RL exposed infrastructure gaps, and going over his boss's head for an in-house infra team set things up.
t153|160.e: After OpenAI's o1, Qwen stepped up reinforcement learning, but results were poor at first. The team suspected its algorithms, and only by changing one variable at a time did it trace the problem to infrastructure. Switching to ByteDance's open-source veRL brought a clear improvement. For models with hundreds of billions of parameters, that wasn't enough either. Qwen wanted to hire its own infrastructure staff, but Jingren Zhou preferred that the PAI platform keep providing unified support. Junyang Lin went around him to Eddie Wu for hiring support, which she sees as foreshadowing the later reshuffle.
ex: The team felt Alibaba Cloud supported Kimi and Zhipu better than Qwen
Management said no individual should be put on a pedestal

items.d: Goes over his boss to Eddie Wu

t153|160.c: Qwen's open-source reputation is clashing with the group's hopes for cloud and API revenue.
t153|160.e: She sees Qwen as one of the two best-known Chinese models abroad, alongside DeepSeek. Its open models in many sizes are fine-tuned by small and mid-sized companies and many robotics firms. But some inside Alibaba question whether open source converts directly into AI cloud business, or whether it diverts API revenue, and some executives saw Qwen 3.5, released on Lunar New Year's Eve, as half-finished. Outside, Volcano Engine is catching up in cloud, and the Qwen app didn't noticeably close the gap with Doubao in the Spring Festival subsidy war.
ex: The flagship Qwen Max isn't open; Lin had wanted to open-source a 1-trillion-parameter model
Companies such as Cursor fine-tune on top of Qwen

marks.d: Used by startups and robotics firms
Lin had wanted to push it

t153|160.c: AI is now a must-win war for big companies, so a fringe team's freedom can't last.
t153|160.e: She frames the conflict as a mismatch between a small team's goals and a big organization's. Qwen grew up in a corner few people noticed, where it could focus on improving models with little interference. Now that AI is a company-wide war, that kind of fringe space is hard to preserve. Headhunters and investors contacted Qwen members overnight, and she thinks this may be Qwen's biggest organizational crisis yet. How much individuality a big company tolerates is both a principle and a choice, and the outcome will take longer to see.
ex: Lin told colleagues to stick to the plan; she says his intent is only her guess

t154|672.c: By open-sourcing a full family of models in every size and type, Qwen became academia's default.
t154|672.e: He thinks Qwen's influence lies in developer mindshare, not revenue. It wasn't first to open source, but it offered a complete family: from a tiny 0.6-billion-parameter model to models for images, video, reasoning and embeddings (turning text into numbers for search). Schools, developers and robotics teams with limited resources could just use it. Once people are used to it, rivals pay a lot to win them over. He also sees ModelScope, Alibaba's model community, as the GitHub of the AI era: how developers use and comment on models matters more for research direction than hosting revenue.
ex: He says Qwen's downloads exceed all other Chinese open models combined, and lead Mistral's
After the shake-up, Qwen-related searches on DINQ roughly tripled

terms.d: Schools and small teams use it directly

t154|672.c: If labs still believe scaling works, resources will shift from open-source buzz to post-training and tool use.
t154|672.e: He expects Meta, xAI, OpenAI and others to compete for people from the Qwen team. His reasoning: as long as companies believe scaling (bigger models, more data and compute) still buys more intelligence, they'll care about how models do on real tasks, not benchmarks or open-source fame. So resources flow to post-training (refining a model after its initial training), reinforcement learning (improving through trial and reward) and teaching agents, AIs that act for you, to use tools. Open-source spending may shrink by comparison. He guesses 2026 will bring more third-party sellers of data and RL training environments, and environment sellers already make good money.
ex: He guesses the SpaceX–xAI merger's wealth effect will intensify poaching, but calls it speculation

items.d: Intelligence can still be piled up
Vendors of data and RL environments

t154|672.c: AI research teams resemble Renaissance workshops and will spread into outside studios and independent companies.
t154|672.e: He compares AI labs to Renaissance workshops: researchers are apprentices, and the companies paying for them are like the Medici family, who funded artists. People who can put expensive compute to good use command a big premium, and it will keep rising. He sees research organizations evolving in three steps: teams inside big companies, then outside studios that specialize in jobs like reinforcement learning for AI agents, then independent companies selling models to businesses. When the host countered that big companies will keep core technology in-house, he didn't disagree. He only said the change would come in stages.
ex: Cohere is one example of an independent model company
Thinking Machines Lab's Tinker offers model training as a service

items.d: Core tech stays inside big companies

t154|672.c: Real talent can take a problem from discovery all the way to a finished result on their own.
t154|672.e: He thinks great creative talent is like a Renaissance craftsman: they find and frame problems, design experiments, solve them and deliver a complete result. Employers can judge them by their work, without relying on degrees or interview puzzles. This also breaks screening by age and pedigree. Many key breakthroughs came from people under 30, and interns can carry core work. When the field's approach changes, say from GANs and VAEs to diffusion models for generating images, old big-company experience quickly loses value.
ex: Most authors behind CLIP, RoPE, MoE and Llama were under 30
He recalls ICLR submissions growing from one or two thousand to over 30,000

items.d: No one else to bail you out

t154|672.c: Real work lets you get past the degree barrier. He started by fixing typos in PyTorch.
t154|672.e: He studied civil engineering and switched to AI in 2017, inspired by Andrew Ng's course. He picked PyTorch, a popular tool for writing AI code, because it was easy to debug. When he couldn't follow the internals, he fixed spelling errors, and getting a few changes accepted kept him going. Later he worked on DeepFaceLab, a face-swap project, and big companies came to him. He concluded that once you have real work, nobody tests your coding. Porting StyleGAN, he admired its code and began collecting researchers' stories. Kingma later advised him to build agents, which reward individual creativity more than thousand-GPU infrastructure.
ex: Porting StyleGAN to PyTorch earned about a thousand GitHub stars
DINQ Roast once capped salary estimates at $10 million a year, which later looked low

items.d: Witty reviews and valuations of researchers

t154|672.c: "Drivers" who build products with models draw more public attention than the researchers who build models.
t154|672.e: He compares researchers to the engineers who build F1 cars, and people who make products with models to the drivers. Ordinary users can't feel a model getting better, but they instantly notice an agent, an AI that acts for them, sorting their email or running a workflow. So posts from app builders get far more engagement than paper announcements. The host summed it up as AI shifting from a race for model capability to spreading applications. He also sees younger researchers speaking out more, because speaking up is now how you get discovered.
ex: A paper announcement often gets only a few hundred likes
Posts by Karpathy and others get about one comment for every four or five likes

root.d: Users feel the apps, not the models

t154|672.c: Hiring will shift from employing a person to buying a result, judged by how people use AI.
t154|672.e: He reasons that fine-tuning or reinforcement learning jobs that once needed six months or more of ramp-up might soon be done by one expert in a few weeks. Loyalty between people and companies weakens, and top researchers switching jobs three times in five years is already common. Hiring signals will become AI-native: how many tokens (units of text a model processes) someone uses, how many products they've tried, how much of their work is automated. He doesn't think degrees are useless. They still show likely ability but no longer guarantee anything. Building in public has a high ceiling and a low floor.
ex: Cursor, the AI coding tool, hires from its heaviest users
DINQ plans to launch short-term project matching in April–May 2026

items: Match a person to one job

d.verdict: Degrees still signal the odds but no longer guarantee

t155|676.c: Nvidia builds tools for others, far from users and real data, so he left.
t155|676.e: In late 2015 he became Nvidia's first full-time self-driving employee in China, demoing its PX in-car computers to automakers and filling software gaps like perception and localization. He felt Nvidia excelled at broad toolchains for everyone but avoided facing users, so it never got the real data needed to keep improving a product. It also leaned toward L4, fully driverless in set areas, built on high-definition maps and rules. To build a good product, you have to let users criticize you. In 2020 he didn't see sense in starting another algorithm supplier, so he joined an automaker to build the final product.
ex: He recalls autos made up under 2% of Nvidia's revenue in 2020
From 2015 to 2019 the industry was in a "To A" stage of research and demos

d.verdict: A good product means letting users criticize you

t155|676.c: Standard dual high-power chips are an early bet on scaling, and shadow mode lets new models improve safely.
t155|676.e: He thinks Tesla, back in 2016 and 2017, bundled powerful compute, dual chips and pre-installed hardware, fitting it even when buyers skipped FSD, its Full Self-Driving package. That was an early bet on scaling laws: bigger models, data and compute keep getting better. His company follows the same idea. One chip runs the stable version for the user, while the other quietly runs a new model in "shadow mode." Cases where they disagree go to the cloud, and large A/B tests become possible. Selling the product becomes the best data collection system.
ex: Pre-installed hardware lets every car already sold send data back

items.d: The other runs the new model

t155|676.c: A team playing catch-up must first agree on one approach, then work in projects, while keeping researchers.
t155|676.e: When he joined Li Auto in 2020, its driver-assistance team had only 20 or 30 people, an underdog with no reputation. He believed a team split between Waymo's, Tesla's and Nvidia's methods was doomed. So he first got everyone on one path: copy Tesla, make hardware standard, and build the data feedback loop first. Then the team worked in sealed-off projects, running as much in parallel as possible, "splitting time into three." He kept researchers too, so proven new techniques reached production cars quickly. For suppliers he chose the industry's No. 2 and No. 3, because the project's success mattered to their survival too.
ex: In 2021, about 80 people delivered highway navigation assist in 100 days
The team publishes about 20 to 30 papers a year at top conferences

root.d: How Li Auto's team came from behind

items.d: Copy Tesla, build the data loop first
New tech moves fast into production

t155|676.c: Dropping HD maps gives small-city drivers the same experience. The team must climb out of the pit together.
t155|676.e: Systems built on high-definition maps depend on map providers' coverage, so the same car at the same price works worse in smaller cities. He found that unacceptable. A small team in Shenzhen first proved a map-free approach could work. After the 2023 switch, the experience got worse for a while. For every problem the team laid out the data, root cause, fix and timeline, cleared most issues within weeks, then rolled it out to everyone. He opposes people who sneer afterward or pile the old system back on. Success is measured by daily users, the share of miles driven with assistance, and NPS (willingness to recommend).
ex: Max costs ~30,000 yuan more than Pro; its share rose from the teens to over 70%

items.d: Track daily users, mileage share, NPS

t155|676.c: Fast and slow systems clash and are hard to referee, so one model should reason, predict and act.
t155|676.e: He opposes "fast and slow" dual systems, where one part acts quickly and another thinks slowly. They run at different speeds, their disagreements are hard to settle, and training them together takes lots of paired data. He wants one model that reasons in language, predicts upcoming frames and outputs actions. He thinks OpenAI, Gemini and Tesla's newer versions are all moving toward this, though there's no consensus on the exact design. His company doesn't train an internet-scale base model from scratch. It builds on open-source models and partners with big companies. He even suspects bolting an action module onto a vision-language model may be a dead end.
ex: The name Zhijian, "utmost simplicity," means Simple Scaling: fewer modules and rules scale better
The team starts from open-source models such as Janus-Pro

terms.d: Writes out its thinking step by step
Imagines how the world will change

t155|676.c: Synthetic data helps but isn't the main source. Real rare cases only come from commercial use.
t155|676.e: He rejects splitting things into "forget business, just build models and data," because the long tail of rare real-world cases can't be produced in a lab. Synthetic data is good for adding rare cases, training motion control and testing, but it can't replace real manipulation data. Nvidia promotes simulation because that fits the business of a company selling tools. His company has about 10,000 hours of data, mostly collected in a "semi-real-robot" way. Early on, about a third was unusable. After improvements, about 90% is usable.
ex: Interference with the data-collection gloves was the main reason early data was unusable

t155|676.c: Embodied AI is still in the research-and-demo stage, and inconsistent hardware is an underrated bottleneck.
t155|676.e: He thinks embodied AI lacks a mature method, naturally available data and room for error. The window for startups is longer than it was for large language models, but it's closing, and mass production is still far off. There are only a few thousand robots, mostly hand-assembled. Two dexterous hands of the same model can replay the same data and behave differently, so noise may outweigh gains. He sees repair rates near 100%. So robot bodies must follow what today's models can do, and hardware teams shouldn't race ahead. Home robots must wait for safe interaction, durable hands and lower prices.
ex: He expects selling to businesses to start around late 2026 to early 2027
He expects the industry to find product-market fit around 2028

t155|676.c: The first deployments should take over a whole workflow, not replace one station on an assembly line.
t155|676.e: He thinks assembly-line stations demand too strict a rhythm and too little tolerance for error. Customizing one station is no different from what over 7,000 custom-automation firms already do. Better are flexible tasks that run start to finish and can be standardized and copied, covering a whole workflow within what robots can do now: move around, do simple manipulation and handle varied objects. He likes flexible manufacturing, European factories and supermarkets. He also expects each industry to end up with a few dominant players. Humanoids won't take over everything, and many lower-body designs will coexist for a long time.
ex: He says a service worker in Europe can cost about €3,000
Goal: adapt to a new task in 20 to 30 minutes, still a work in progress

t156|612.c: OpenClaw's breakthrough is packaging, not technology, and its "long-term memory" is really compressed short-term context.
t156|612.e: He points out that local computer access, chat-app commands, scheduled tasks, long-term memory and tool loops all existed already. OpenClaw packaged them into a mass-market product, like the iPhone, which is why researchers paid it little attention. Power users who spend a long time configuring it get big rewards, but ordinary people struggle to repeat that. It also faces three problems at once: cost, instability and safety. Its so-called memory often gets lost when compressed, so working with it longer doesn't make it more reliable.
ex: Getting it to register one LinkedIn account cost about $20
A Meta alignment lead's safety instruction was lost in compression, and hundreds of emails got deleted

terms.d: Give orders like sending a message
Always on, acts on its own

result.d: Clever packaging, not a tech breakthrough

t156|612.c: Anthropic became OpenAI's equal through a killer product, while OpenAI's risk is too many side projects.
t156|612.e: He thinks over 70% of Anthropic's revenue comes from businesses and the API, the paid interface other software uses to call its models. Its growth comes from Claude Code becoming a killer product, not from a huge model lead. For the first time OpenAI faces a rival of similar size. OpenAI's research is still strong, and it has ChatGPT's reach and plenty of money. The problem is spreading across too many directions at once. He sees Sam Altman as a portfolio manager who, if he reallocates resources, can still strike back hard.
ex: He thinks Claude Code's annual revenue already tops Cursor's roughly $2 billion
Several xAI co-founders left this quarter, which he called a disastrous quarter

items: ~70% of revenue from businesses and API
Claude Code is the killer product
Too many side bets, scattered focus

d.verdict: OpenAI's comeback depends on cutting side projects

t156|612.c: Model makers must move up into products. The layer that owns users is harder to replace than executors.
t156|612.e: A popular setup is to have Opus plan and communicate inside Claude Code, then call Codex when code needs writing. He thinks the executor is easy to swap, while the layer that owns the user relationship is not. Selling only models risks becoming a commodity, like Cisco. Products also bring real tasks and records of failure that feed back into training. Once benchmark scores converge, ecosystem, trust, reliability and cost decide the choice, just as Apple wins on the whole experience, not on single benchmarks.
ex: On OfficeQA, models failed mostly at parsing files and retrieval, not reasoning

t156|612.c: AI improving itself is already paying off, but only on tasks with clear goals and fast checks.
t156|612.e: He cites AlphaEvolve optimizing Google's own kernels (low-level code that runs on chips), models helping debug themselves, and AutoResearch running nearly 100 experiments overnight. Research itself is starting to be automated, so progress will speed up again. But for now humans still define the search space and AI searches it efficiently. Tasks with measurable metrics and quick feedback, like performance tuning, kernels and database queries, fit best. Subjective tasks break the loop, and when goals are vague and too much can be changed, AI may break things beyond repair.
ex: Shopify's CEO used a similar method for 93 automatic commits, speeding rendering about 53%
Asked to add dark mode, an agent ran for over an hour without finishing

cells.d: Like color schemes; the loop fails

t156|612.c: Coding agents are pushing the global software industry into China's predicament, where high margins can't last.
t156|612.e: He recalls the struggles of Chinese SaaS, subscription software for businesses: big companies that could afford programmers built their own, and software often ended up as outsourcing work. AI is spreading "cheap programmers" worldwide, so customers will redo the math. Instead of paying hundreds of thousands for software, they can have Claude Code write it. He expects SaaS's 80–90% gross margins to be hard to sustain. Teams will also shrink. A few great people with a set of AI agents may be enough.
ex: Block, the payments company, cut 40% of staff, and Meta plans to cut about 20%
Some people leave Claude Code idling to burn tokens and game productivity reviews

t156|160.c: China's OpenClaw craze is real, but agents built into office platforms may beat ones installed locally.
t156|160.e: She has seen OpenClaw, nicknamed "little lobster" in China, spread to schoolchildren and retired teachers, with in-home installation offered on the resale app Xianyu. Snapping a photo on your phone and sending it into a chat saves many steps compared with moving it to a computer and dragging it into a terminal. But her own documents and collaboration live in Feishu (Lark), so a local agent feels clumsy. She is more optimistic about all-in-one office platforms with built-in agents, and Henry agrees.
ex: In-home installation on Xianyu costs about 500 to 1,000 yuan

items.d: Schoolkids and retired teachers use it

t156|160.c: Teams will shift from stars with average staff to elite people plus agents. People-facing work is safest.
t156|160.e: She maps America's AI layoffs onto China: companies will concentrate budgets on top people who use AI best. Headcount falls, but labor costs may not fall as much. In Henry's example of an AI-native law firm, document analysis, spotting conflicts and drafting shrink dramatically, while client relationships, negotiation and taking responsibility still need people. So she thinks work that deals with people is safest. She also jokes that judging staff by token use, the units AI usage is measured in, is like the old practice of judging programmers by lines of code.
ex: Two or three lawyers revised a contract in hours, work that once took far longer

t157|678.c: Unitree's real advantage is mass-production experience, and hardware leads last far longer than AI model leads.
t157|678.e: He thinks the hard part of the Spring Festival Gala show wasn't any single move. It was 21 mass-produced robots performing complex moves together, reliably, which tests hardware quality and control. Unitree had already sold tens of thousands of four-legged robots, meaning it had designed and built on the order of a million motors. Latecomers can't catch up by copying specs, and the G1 humanoid still has no real challenger long after launch. On the "brain," the AI that controls robots, Unitree tends to follow. But as long as frontier research runs on G1, open and closed models alike strengthen its hardware ecosystem.
ex: Humanoids went from under 2% of revenue in 2023 to about 51%
The IPO filing seeks 4 billion yuan, about half for the "brain"

t157|678.c: The cost penalty of legs is overstated. Compact and light, humanoids may not cost more than wheeled robots.
t157|678.e: He used to think warehouse robots only needed two arms. This quarter he redid the math. A humanoid stands on about 40 by 60 centimeters, yet can pick things off the floor and reach about 2 meters high, so it uses space well in narrow aisles. Wheeled designs look simpler, but to carry the same heavy boxes the whole machine weighs around a ton. Each of four wheels needs its own drive and steering motors, plus a lifting mechanism and a heavy base. He admits he still doesn't know whether humanoids are the best form for general-purpose robots.
ex: The new Atlas uses about two motor types, and its legs swap for easy repair

items: Needs a lift and heavy base
Reaches from floor to about 2 m

d.verdict: Legs may not cost more, but the best form is unsettled

t157|678.c: Dexterous hands are the next frontier, and whoever builds "the G1 of hands" becomes the platform.
t157|678.e: He traces research moving from four-legged locomotion, VLA models (which turn images and instructions into actions) and UMI-style data collection with handheld grippers, to humanoid walking. Since 2025, researchers broadly see dexterous hands as next. The market will compete for a standard part: reliable, with enough degrees of freedom, affordable, and equipped with sensors and developer tools. He warns that chasing a fully closed product too early and shunning research partners can cost the platform chance. In the four-legged boom, Unitree went furthest by steadily selling research gear. He doubts Optimus's tendon-driven hand can be reliably mass-produced and repaired.
ex: Optimus's hand threads over 40 tendons, so repairs are almost surgery
XPeng's robot horse went wrong by aiming for a finished consumer product too early

t157|678.c: World models are capped by their video foundations and missing sense of touch, not by speed.
t157|678.e: He sees world models, which predict what happens next on screen, as complementing VLA models, not replacing them. DreamZero runs at about 7 Hz, which is slow, but speed can be fixed. The real problem is that these models rely on outside video foundation models, so robot companies struggle to fix spatial inconsistencies and physics errors. Video also has no touch: whether a cup slips or how soft things deform can't be reliably fed back. Video generation aims to look good, which isn't necessarily the world robots need. Data forms a pyramid. A million hours is just a target, and he's unsure there are enough useful hours.
ex: Many robot world models are built on Alibaba's Wan 2.1/2.2 video models
Nvidia's EgoScale used over 20,000 hours of first-person data

t157|678.c: Over 20 embodied AI firms valued above 10 billion yuan have outrun deployment. A shakeout is inevitable.
t157|678.e: He sees robotics as China's national technology priority for the next decade, and Unitree, with real users and revenue, as a credible benchmark. But more than 20 Chinese humanoid or embodied AI companies are now valued above 10 billion yuan. At the height of the large-model craze, only four or five reached that level. Even Unitree, the top earner, brings in only a little over $200 million. He expects consolidation and failures, most likely triggered by technology falling short of expectations. The many makers of onboard robot chips will also consolidate, as happens with complex chips.
ex: Complex chip markets often end with two players splitting about 80/20

items.d: Concentration once a good design emerges

t157|160.c: A robot model is more than a VLA. It's an agent system with stricter real-time and safety demands.
t157|160.e: She argues that around the core model, robots also need task orchestration, skills, tools, memory and state management. Like AI agents in the digital world, that's systems engineering, only with tougher real-time and safety requirements. Judging only how well the VLA model (which turns images and instructions into actions) performs overlooks these modules, which decide whether a robot can reliably finish long tasks.

t157|160.c: World models sense time, so they can judge whether an action is done better than imitation-based VLAs.
t157|160.e: She notes that a VLA's tokens, the basic units it processes, mostly describe a frozen moment, and the model essentially imitates demonstrations, an approach called behavior cloning. Train it with a blue cup, then test with a red one or move the cup, and it may fail. A world model explicitly predicts what happens next, making it easier to tell when an action is complete, and in theory it can handle more new situations. Zhe Chen added that for now this advantage is only theoretical.
ex: In RoboChallenge's barcode-scanning task, a VLA needs a bolt-on detector to know it's done

items.d: How the world looks after acting

t158|160.c: Key authors leaving is a sign of strain, not a mass exodus. Unclear option value makes retention harder.
t158|160.e: She confirmed that several key authors have left one after another. But in a research team of over 100, three to five people isn't many. The rumored group departures didn't happen, and most still back Liang Wenfeng's direction. The problem is soaring talent prices. DeepSeek staff have stock option agreements, but the company has no clear valuation, so nobody knows what the options are worth. Rivals' share surges after going public have amplified the anxiety, and Liang is trying to set clearer valuation expectations.
ex: R1 core author Daya Guo and OCR author Haoran Wei recently left
Tencent reportedly pays top interns 5,500 yuan a day, over 100,000 a month with full attendance

items.d: Big firms pay more; new leaders recruit

t158|160.c: Liang Wenfeng's AGI goal isn't just the strongest model. It also backs Chinese chips and original research.
t158|160.e: She sees DeepSeek's goal of AGI, general-purpose AI, as unlike most companies'. Beyond model performance, it adapts its work to Chinese chips and their software stack, and funds original research with no clear short-term payoff. That creates tension with some young researchers, who would rather keep building the strongest model, get their names on technical reports, have plenty of GPUs and get instant outside feedback.
ex: V3.2 switched its low-level compute library to TileLang, a Chinese open-source tool
AgiBot's robot model GO-1 is built on DeepSeek's Janus-Pro-7B

t158|160.c: Agents have redefined "strongest," and DeepSeek lags in product reach and update speed.
t158|160.e: She thinks benchmarks increasingly fail to reflect real experience. In the race to build agents, AIs that act for you, models with similar scores can feel very different in use, and the rare cases and varied data that products bring matter more and more. DeepSeek invests little in coding and general agents, its consumer app is still mostly chat, and it updates less often than Chinese rivals. V3.2 ranked 12th in OpenClaw usage and made the paid top ten once free models were excluded. How to read that is up for debate.
ex: Based on OpenRouter data from February 24 to March 26
Even if V4 is still the best open model, it can't meet every definition of "strong"

t158|160.c: A flat, two-layer structure gets denser research out of fewer people and fewer hours.
t158|160.e: The research team has only two layers, Liang Wenfeng and researchers, with no second-in-command. He directly leads a base-model architecture team of a few dozen, links the data and infrastructure groups, and joins every team's weekly meeting, acting as connector and glue. Meetings are open to other teams. New directions usually start as small experiments by three to five people and get more resources once proven, so infrastructure staff don't become an internal contractor taking orders. Staff usually leave by 6 or 7 p.m. Liang believes mistakes from fatigue waste compute.
ex: Of 84 traceable résumés, over 70% have bachelor's or master's degrees and are under 30
Before V3 and R1, it reached the top tier with a tenth of big firms' staff

items: Open meetings, small teams test ideas

d.verdict: Talent density and teamwork buy research efficiency

t158|160.c: Stockpiling GPUs early matters less in the global compute race, so DeepSeek is starting to change.
t158|160.e: Liang Wenfeng once compared buying GPUs early to a family buying a piano: it was about curiosity. Now there are more people who want to play and more pieces to study, but being able to afford the piano is no longer secure in the global compute race. He is sorting out valuation and options while investing more in products. She points out that R1 was a miracle precisely because it was unlikely. It shouldn't become the bar for every release, and DeepSeek doesn't have to be everyone's hope.
ex: In 2023 he wanted to raise money with capped returns, but VCs refused
March job ads named Claude Code, OpenClaw and Manus for the first time

t159|469.c: With Terafab, Musk wants to control his own compute and copy Google's chip-to-app full stack.
t159|469.e: She sees Terafab as more than a chip plant. It brings chip design, manufacturing and deployment inside Musk's empire, so outside suppliers can't choke his growth in compute. The model is Google, whose own TPU chips, models and data let Gemini catch up fast. Musk wants to extend that full-stack advantage to cars, robots and satellites. The strategic value is huge, but she expects the timeline and the money required to far exceed Musk's expectations.
ex: Tesla and SpaceX's 3D real-world data is a unique edge for building world models

t159|469.c: Orbital data centers are at least seven to ten years off. Startups entering now are too early.
t159|469.e: She lists three obstacles. Cosmic radiation hurts chip performance more than people think, and shielding through packaging is still hard. Even as launch costs fall, running and repairing large clusters gets more expensive. And if they serve users on the ground, transmission delays undercut the economics. Why not build first in cold places with plenty of hydropower? She thinks the technology may take seven to ten years to mature. Startups should wait three to five years, and are better off building tools that make clusters more efficient, or services for space infrastructure.
ex: She thinks one of Musk's core motives is escaping government regulation in space

t159|469.c: A space economy needs local demand from factories, satellites and robots before orbital compute makes sense.
t159|469.e: She thinks space naturally favors AI and robots, since robots need far less life support than people. Microgravity can produce crystals, materials and protein structures that are hard to make on Earth, so space factories are a nearer-term use. Only when local needs like satellite traffic management and lunar refueling reach scale, and every satellite becomes an edge device computing on the spot, will near-Earth data centers make sense. Moving Earth's workloads into orbit doesn't. SpaceX's trillion-dollar valuation also needs this space-economy story behind it.
ex: One portfolio company uses AI to manage satellite traffic, cutting collisions and space junk
Another extracts water from lunar soil, splitting hydrogen and oxygen to refuel rockets

t159|469.c: Nvidia now sells whole AI factories, not chips, and inference will bring steady, recurring cash flow.
t159|469.e: She thinks Jensen Huang has redefined Nvidia as a full-stack AI infrastructure company built around the token economy, where AI output is metered in tokens. This year's GTC launched seven chips at once, plus networking, inference systems and software. Customers no longer ask which chip to pick but whom to buy a whole AI factory from. Training is a one-time burst of spending. Inference, a model answering requests, keeps running as long as products are used, especially once agents run nonstop. Nvidia's rosy data center forecasts rest on inference far exceeding training.
ex: She favors fast, low-power networking and optical switching, since communication uses so much power

t159|469.c: In the agent era CPUs matter again, and Groq's value is completing Nvidia's platform, not its chip.
t159|469.e: Agents, AIs that act for you, constantly call tools, run code and coordinate with other agents, and reinforcement learning and simulation also lean heavily on CPUs. Fusion Fund's research found some new architectures run more efficiently on CPUs, so she doesn't expect a single computing architecture to win. Owning the CPU lets Nvidia define the performance of whole machines and racks, a clear one-stop-shop advantage. She says bluntly that Groq's chip alone isn't worth the reported price. Its low-latency inference fills out the Vera Rubin platform story.
ex: Vera CPU's first partners include Alibaba, ByteDance, Oracle and Meta
Portfolio companies Lepton AI and Nexusflow were bought by Nvidia within two years of founding

t159|469.c: TPUs shine inside Google's own full stack and won't threaten GPUs in the near term.
t159|469.e: She notes Google has invested in TPUs for over a decade and prioritized inference early, tuning chips together with models, data, cash flow and feedback from apps. That system-level optimization, not any single chip, is why Gemini improved so quickly. Outsiders lack that stack, so they get worse performance and cost, and Nvidia's CUDA software platform makes switching expensive. Besides, AI adoption in finance, healthcare and insurance is still under 1%, so the market has room for many architectures.
ex: She recalls Google's internal TPU training costs about a third of OpenAI's

d.verdict: TPUs can't seriously threaten GPUs soon

t159|469.c: Traditional companies prefer working with startups, and fast US buying and acquisitions keep talent circulating.
t159|469.e: She thinks regulated industries like finance, healthcare and insurance need small, industry-specific models deployed on their own servers or private clouds, with low latency, few hallucinations (made-up answers) and strong privacy. Traditional companies also don't want to hand core data to big platforms, so they prefer startups. US companies buy quickly, with deals closing in as little as one or two months, and acquisitions are frequent. She'd rather see companies grow big over time, but admits quick exits keep money, talent and serial founders cycling back.
ex: Some B2B teams of under ten went from zero to $20M in annual revenue
Five Fusion Fund portfolio companies were acquired last year, four under two years old

items.d: Deals in one or two months

t160|685.c: GPU rendering was a hammer. The direction came from demo after demo, chosen by users willing to pay.
t160|685.e: At Nvidia he believed in general-purpose GPU computing and proposed putting GPUs in the cloud, but the company feared hurting hardware sales and said no. Back in China, investors didn't understand GPU infrastructure, so the team raised money on the hot O2O (online-to-offline services) story. In reality they kept demoing their rendering technology everywhere to see who would actually pay. Homeowners left once renovation was done, so retention was poor. Designers and renovation firms stayed. He dropped the furniture-selling story and switched to selling software.
ex: Huai Wang invested about 500,000 yuan as a personal angel
After IDG invested, they moved from outsourcing-style projects to building a product

items.d: Nvidia feared cloud would hurt hardware sales

t160|685.c: GPU costs rise with usage, so annual subscriptions never fit. Usage-based pricing finally removed the shackles.
t160|685.e: For CPU-based software, the cost per user falls as the user base grows. GPU rendering costs rise with usage, and optimization saves only a few dozen percent. So annual or monthly plans survived only by capping image sizes and pushing heavy jobs to nighttime. Ads didn't add up either: one design action burned about 1 yuan of compute, while one ad view earned a few hundredths of a yuan. Ad revenue reached tens of millions of yuan and was still cut. In the AI era, paying per use or per token finally gives this cost structure a matching price model.
ex: An action costs ~1 yuan in compute; an ad view earns a few hundredths of that
The ad business was cut after reaching tens of millions of yuan

items: More users, lower cost per user
Only a few dozen percent to optimize

d.verdict: Paying per token makes GPU product pricing sensible again

t160|685.c: Lasting matters more than dazzling: stay out of the giants' way and keep two fallback options.
t160|685.e: He has watched Chinese startup fads turn over every three to five years. Investors chased O2O one moment and wouldn't let you mention it the next. When big companies copied his product and poached his team, he refused a price war and bet on industrial software, the grinding work giants lack patience for. He set a worst-case rule: if all online business vanished, there would still be industrial manufacturing. If all China business vanished, there would still be overseas. He also turned down investment from BAT (Baidu, Alibaba, Tencent) to avoid being locked into one camp and its internet wars.
ex: He turned down BAT money to avoid being tied to Alibaba's or Tencent's camp

terms.d: No price wars with big companies
Industry if online fails, overseas if China fails

result.d: Outlast fads that change every few years

t160|685.c: In China pure algorithms are easily copied, but neglecting them is also wrong. You need algorithms and data.
t160|685.e: After his rendering engine team was poached and his product copied, he decided relying on algorithms alone for protection was too risky. He bet instead on harder-to-copy things: data, network effects (the product gets better as more people use it) and customer service. Then he overcorrected and cut back on hiring algorithm engineers. His conclusion now is that you need both. Algorithms are the engine, data is the fuel, and neither runs without the other.
ex: A competitor once poached his entire rendering engine team

items.d: Algorithms the engine, data the fuel

t160|685.c: AI replacing workflow software is a trend, not a cycle. Software closer to the physical world is safer.
t160|685.e: In 2020 and 2021, money was easy and real estate clients paid fast, so the company overexpanded. Many workflow features were just add-ons around its 3D capabilities, with no real defensibility. He sees industrial software as essential demand that still rises and falls with the economy. Copilot-style AI assistants disrupting ERP and CRM business software, by contrast, are a productivity revolution. You can wait out a cycle, but a trend requires the leader to drive change, even shutting down units that used to make money. He also rejected opportunities unrelated to core technology, like renovation loans and crypto mining.
ex: Eight of its top ten real estate clients went bankrupt
Three tests for projects: uses core tech, has social value, builds lasting assets

cells.d: Essential demand that rides the cycle

t160|685.c: Rather than fight giants on general models, building its own spatial models is slow and costly but defensible.
t160|685.e: In 2023 he concluded that language and image models were a battlefield for big companies, and Manycore shouldn't fight head-on. Building add-ons around others' foundation models is fast, but the next model generation can wipe them out, and platforms can easily lure the team away. Developing its own spatial models is slow and expensive, but builds something hard to copy. He splits spatial intelligence into three layers: models for rendering, understanding and generating spaces at the bottom, an API for outside developers in the middle, and products serving people and machines on top.
ex: The algorithm and model team grew from under 10 in 2023 to about 60
Fame as one of the "Six Little Dragons" brought about 9 times more résumés

items.d: Design tools for people, solutions for machines

t160|685.c: Video models only aim for smooth visuals. 3D content is physically correct, which suits robots better.
t160|685.e: Video generation aims to look continuous but doesn't guarantee that sizes, distances, interactions and which objects hide which are correct. 3D content carries this information by nature, so it suits training and planning real physical tasks better. He positions Spatial LM as translating the physical world into a script large models can read, reusable across different robots and the company's business lines. He admits two uncertainties: how good his own models can get, and whether the video approach will eventually replace 3D.

marks.d: Smooth, but sizes and occlusion unreliable

t160|685.c: Robots today resemble self-driving a decade ago, so spatial intelligence must serve many uses and make money.
t160|685.e: He thinks robotics is a sure direction, but nobody knows when it will scale, and batteries, battery life and compute are beyond what Manycore can solve alone. So spatial intelligence can't bet only on humanoids. Factory planning, AGVs (automated guided vehicles), film and tourism are all worth doing, even though each niche is small. The company is past pure cash-burning, and R&D usually has to pay back within three years, with spatial intelligence as the exception. On data, China favors real-robot data while the West trusts synthetic data more. He's doing both.
ex: Add-on compute purchases bring in about 5% of total revenue
The goal: compute-based and subscription revenue at 1:1 within three years

t161|689.c: A pure tech lead only buys time. What rivals can't copy is a flywheel where usage creates data.
t161|689.e: Megvii's first business at scale was bank-grade face verification. Deep learning lifted accuracy from about 90% to 98–99%, which even the team found hard to believe at first. Looking back, he thinks algorithm leads always get caught. What lasts is a loop where use creates data and data improves the product. Identity verification had that loop. A beauty-filter SDK, a toolkit sold to other apps, did not, so the first survived and the second died.
ex: Account verification for Alipay was Megvii's first business at scale
He says its verification business still holds about 70–80% of the market

items.d: Product runs in the real world

t161|689.c: The biggest trap in B2B is overpromising, because saying "we can't" looks like weakness.
t161|689.e: His B2B rules: value must be measurable, the problem should be common but a small share of the customer's costs, and beware of sliding into one-off custom projects. In 2019, a Uniqlo warehouse project used over a thousand robots. To win the deal they overpromised, and at first reached only 40% of target efficiency. They delivered only after winning a six-month extension and rewriting the code from scratch. In competitive bidding, honestly saying you can't counts as failure, and failed projects get hidden, so the whole industry inflates expectations. Only with trust can both sides use small experiments to turn "can't" into "how."
ex: Early on, the Uniqlo project hit only 40% of target efficiency
Logistics revenue reached several hundred million yuan, half projects, half products

d.verdict: With trust, "can't" becomes "how can we"

t161|689.c: The biggest bottleneck now is model intelligence, so robot data should be trained in from pretraining on.
t161|689.e: Dexmal's mission is to be intelligent, useful and trustworthy. He thinks the main obstacle to the last two is that models aren't smart enough, so the model comes first, and commercial work feeds back into it. He opposes bolting an action module onto an off-the-shelf vision-language model, which he believes damages its existing multimodal skills. DM0 was trained from the start on internet video and images, driving data and robot data together, alongside localization and question answering. Navigation, in his view, is just another kind of action.
ex: DM0 trained in three stages, in partnership with StepFun and Qianli Technology
Mainly real-robot data, plus teleoperation, exoskeletons and other collection methods

terms.d: Helps with varied environments and navigation

result.d: Not an action module bolted onto a VLM

t161|689.c: Robot systems may split into slow reasoning, manipulation and force control. Big labs lead only the top layer.
t161|689.e: He pictures slow reasoning on top, a manipulation model running about 10 times a second (10 Hz) in the middle, and force and touch control at 100 Hz or more at the bottom.
