What the layers should pass to each other is still an open question. You can't learn embodied skills from video, just as watching soccer won't teach you to play. Large-model companies have an edge in reasoning, but the lower two layers need hardware and software designed together. Simulation works for rigid objects, but soft objects and contact forces are hard to simulate, so it suits locomotion and high-level planning better.
ex: He estimates end-to-end success rates at about 50–60%
He's open to world-model-generated data but not optimistic about it

items.d: Slow reasoning and planning; big labs lead
Force and touch control above 100 Hz

t161|689.c: Good use cases allow errors, slack pacing, moderate variety and long hours. Logistics is a greenhouse.
t161|689.e: His logic: without enough capability there's no large-scale use, and without large-scale use there's no data. Whoever first keeps a limited model running in the right setting can build a lasting edge. Logistics already has people and existing automation that can absorb a single robot's failures, the way self-driving cars and human drivers coexist in ride-hailing. He defines "keeps running" as a real setting, powered on 10+ hours a day, for two straight months, in meaningful numbers. He thinks almost no case in the industry meets that bar.
ex: He treats about 100 units as a rough threshold for real volume
He won't do car assembly lines, despite having supply-chain connections

items.d: Mistakes OK; humans or remote takeover

t161|689.c: Models don't define hardware: test the task by teleoperation, then let the use case shape the robot.
t161|689.e: He thinks hardware sets the ceiling on capability. To judge whether a task is feasible, first see if a person can do it by teleoperating the robot. A fully standardized robot body ends up either underpowered or overbuilt in different settings. High-center-of-gravity humanoids or wheeled two-armed robots move slowly, low-slung AGVs (automated guided vehicles) are much faster, and some workstations don't need the robot to move at all. So the company's approach is: models unlock use cases, use cases define hardware, and standard modules combine into different forms.

items.d: High center of gravity, tops out ~0.8–1

t161|689.c: Core technology should be open-sourced early, and a leaderboard is fair only if anyone can reproduce it.
t161|689.e: Megvii built its own deep learning framework, MegEngine, early but open-sourced it years later and missed the window to build an ecosystem. So he argues core infrastructure should open up early. Open source is also a trust mechanism: users don't fear being locked in. Drawing on his experience setting contest problems, he says a good problem separates people well rather than just being hard, and a good evaluator must first be a good practitioner. DM0 ranks first on RoboChallenge, and he believes fairness requires public code and training details that others can rerun.
ex: After DexBotic was open-sourced, about 1,000 outside developers used it
For RLinf, already built by others, they chose to integrate rather than rebuild

t161|689.c: Many fronts add up to roughly your strongest one, so Dexmal sticks to two or three use cases.
t161|689.e: Reflecting on Megvii's many fronts, he concludes that A plus B plus C roughly equals the biggest of the three. He expects embodied AI to first produce lots of industry-specific companies, then consolidate into a handful of platforms, mostly Chinese. Winners will be decided by model intelligence, data flywheels in real use cases and long-term focus. So the company turns down performance robots, Spring Festival Gala-style publicity and car assembly lines, avoids scattershot expansion, and is saving money ahead of an industry downturn.
ex: The 2026 goal: a thousand robots running in one use case
About 100 staff, roughly 40% from Megvii's original team

items.d: Avoid becoming a small, going-nowhere shop

t162|692.c: Chinese companies abroad are moving from selling goods to building brands, and 2025 was the tipping point.
t162|692.e: He sees four levels of going global: commodities with only basic functions, products backed by R&D, brands people remember and like, and finally whole companies with a soul going worldwide. Slapping on a label or logo doesn't make a brand. Xiaomi became a global brand by combining R&D with its own spirit. In Meetsocial's first decade, most clients were still just selling goods. From 2025, more companies began moving from products to brands. But it's gradual accumulation, not an overnight change.
ex: Xiaomi went global by combining R&D with its company spirit

t162|692.c: With pricier traffic and tighter rules, cheap-price competition is a dead end. Build the brand while selling.
t162|692.e: When buying traffic was enough to sell goods, companies had no reason to make customers remember or like them. Now traffic is pricier, products look alike, and platforms demand more on quality and compliance, so even sellers doing hundreds of millions of yuan a year hit a ceiling. Companies that didn't prepare face a painful shift and may not survive. Anker kept investing in R&D and building its brand even while selling charging cables, planning step two while taking step one. The mindset must shift from "sell what we make" to "make what users need."
ex: Anker improved connector craftsmanship and charging efficiency while still just selling goods
Anker and Xiaomi run lots of user research every year

items: Only ask if it pays back now

d.verdict: Step one must prepare for step two

t162|692.c: Digitization isn't one item alongside sales, product and brand. It's a multiplier on all of them.
t162|692.e: He sums up a company's global capability as D-MES: S is sales conversion, E is product iteration, M is brand influence, how people think of you, and D is digitization. Digitization first makes the existing setup more efficient, then improves the speed and quality of decisions. Among rivals at the same level, whoever senses market changes faster, understands them better and acts more precisely wins. L'Oréal is strong on all three, yet has spent heavily in recent years connecting online and offline processes, suggesting digitization may be the key gap in top-tier competition.
ex: Starbucks linked its mini-program, payments and membership to speed up ordering
Meituan uses data to keep rebalancing riders, capacity and incentives

t162|692.c: AI can't be accountable for high-stakes results. Hand it content, but humans must steer ad budgets.
t162|692.e: The industry agrees AI must be adopted now, but not on what it actually solves. So first set goals and expected outputs, then decide what goes to AI, to people or to both. Simple customer service can go to AI. But decisions like ad buying can't be judged by average accuracy, because one mistake can badly hurt a client, just as self-driving can't escape the question of who's responsible, however low its error rate. Media buyers make countless daily judgments on bids and budgets, and for now AI can only supply background information. It's like a fresh PhD who must first learn from a mentor.
ex: McDonald's Netherlands pulled an AI-made holiday ad
He sees AI coding as revolutionary, with people shifting to review

marks.d: Text, images and video change first

t162|692.c: Splitting creative work across multiple agents, with human checkpoints, multiplies output of standardized ad materials.
t162|692.e: He thinks AI isn't a button you bolt on. Business processes must be redesigned, as they were in the internet era. One creative is split into steps such as understanding the brief, identifying goals, strategy, choosing a format, production and quality checks. Different AI agents handle each step, while project or product managers coordinate and insert human review. He's in no hurry to sell agents to clients, because most can't say what they deliver or what counts as good enough. Claiming clients can create value through technology alone is, in his view, irresponsible.
ex: Creatives went from 5–10 assets a day to hundreds or thousands
A short-drama client got 6,000 video-edit concepts during Spring Festival week

items.d: Understand the result the client wants
Pick images, video or other formats

t162|692.c: Once generation becomes a commodity, quality is what's scarce, and people must define what good looks like.
t162|692.e: Ad materials steer ever larger media budgets, so small quality differences get magnified. He estimates a 1% gap in quality can mean a 10%+ gap in final results. Large models can tag materials with hundreds or thousands of labels, but they don't know what makes a creative good. People must first distill their knowledge and define the method, and then AI can iterate within that framework. After calculators spread, bridge engineers still had to know when to use them. Competing with machines on simple skills that are now tools is pointless.
ex: A short-drama client's daily ad spend rose from thousands of dollars to over $100,000

t162|692.c: Fixing client websites and data pipelines beats squeezing media buys. Marketing will become a digital hub.
t162|692.e: He refuses to promise clients a generic number like "at least 30% better ROI," and rejects treating AI as magic that brings growth once plugged in. You first have to understand the client's product, current returns and where the problems are. Media-side optimization usually wins only one or two percentage points. Fixing the website, data collection and user data flows can add 10–20%, and the effects multiply. Meetsocial built a unified data warehouse in 2015, while traditional ad groups have data scattered across competing subsidiaries, making change hard. He expects marketing within three to five years to connect everything from viewing an ad to repeat purchases and the supply chain.
ex: Its AI infrastructure serves over 100,000 clients
The system logs over $20 million in daily ad spend data

t163|693.c: DeepSeek V4 isn't a new paradigm. It follows R1's path and makes million-token context and low cost real.
t163|693.e: He thinks "paradigm" has become an overused storytelling word in AI. Real paradigm shifts are rare: the Transformer, scaling laws, RLHF (training models on human feedback) and test-time scaling (letting models think longer when answering). V4 opens no new capability area. It does known goals more completely and more cheaply. In use, it is clearly better than V3 at math, code and following instructions as an agent, and it makes things up less. But its coding still trails the top overseas models, and it feels about on par with Kimi K2.6.
ex: V3 disclosed only about $5.57 million for its final training run; V4 disclosed nothing
He estimates full R&D spending is dozens of times the final training run

d.verdict: V4 is an engineering breakthrough, not a new paradigm

t163|693.c: Cheaper tokens don't mean cheaper tasks. Over-compression forces the model to reason longer to make up.
t163|693.e: Many users found V4 used more tokens (the units models read and write) to solve the same problem. He suspects two reasons. First, the training reward only checks whether the task got done and doesn't penalize length. Second, compression at the token level is so aggressive that each token carries less information, so the model reasons longer to make up for it. He compares it to watering flowers with a pressure washer. He argues people building agents should think about using context efficiently instead of assuming more is better.
ex: Kimi K1.5 tried penalizing length, but its replies still got longer

terms.d: Only checks if the task is done

result.d: Total tokens per task go up

t163|693.c: Linear attention has a hard limit on distant information, so big models will favor sparse or sliding-window attention.
t163|693.e: Linear attention keeps updating a fixed-size memory, so the longer the text, the more the earliest information gets squeezed again and again. With a sliding window, where each layer only looks at nearby text, stacked layers let distant information hop over in a few steps almost intact. So he thinks linear attention suits small and mid-sized models, while frontier models will bet on sparse attention (reading only selected parts) or sliding windows. V4 dropped MLA, DeepSeek's earlier memory-compression design, for a more basic structure. He guesses heavy token compression plus low-rank compression was too complex. Model design is far from settled.
ex: MiniMax went from linear attention in M1 back to full attention in M2

items.d: At 1,024 tokens, the first is squeezed 1,023 times

t163|693.c: Muon updates each weight matrix as a whole and is replacing AdamW, which adjusts numbers one by one.
t163|693.e: An optimizer decides how a model's weights change at each training step. The long-standard AdamW treats every number separately and ignores links within a weight matrix, which can slow training. Muon updates the whole matrix at once. One-dimensional parameters such as embeddings and LayerNorm still use AdamW, so optimizers are now mixed. Original Muon needed a separate learning rate for each module. Kimi's Moonlight fixed the ratio between the two at about 0.2, so only one global learning rate needs tuning. V4 uses 0.18.
ex: He thinks it's worth testing whether Newton-Schulz iteration should run 5 steps or 10

root.d: From single numbers to whole matrices

items.d: Keeps the structure inside each matrix

t163|693.c: MHC widens information flow between layers, helping reasoning at low cost. Cross-layer attention may go further.
t163|693.e: A model is a stack of layers, and a traditional residual connection passes just one stream of information between them. MHC widens this into several streams and uses a Sinkhorn-Knopp constraint to keep values in range, easing the exploding and vanishing gradients that naive widening causes. He thinks the main payoff is in reasoning. Kimi's Attention Residual is more like DenseNet-style links across layers. It captures how layers relate more precisely and may have a higher ceiling, but it demands more of the infrastructure. Teams with limited resources should start with MHC.
ex: His own Deep Delta Learning also follows the hyper-connection direction

marks.d: Kimi's cross-layer links, heavy infrastructure needs

t163|694.c: V4 shines at systems engineering: many new parts working at once, keeping open-source infrastructure busy for a year.
t163|694.e: Each DeepSeek release gives the open-source community about a year of catching up. It took a year to fully digest V3's MLA and mixture-of-experts details. V4's attention changes force a rebuild of prefix caching, speculative decoding and the KV cache, the tricks that speed up serving. Hybrid sparse attention, MHC, Muon and FP4 all shipped at once and worked. He sees this kind of systems engineering as the main theme of the next year or two. FP4 quantization-aware training, which trains at ultra-low precision from the start, has finally moved that idea off chipmakers' slides.
ex: His team got inference and RL running end to end on launch day
He thinks open and closed models are close on serving but open still trails in training

items.d: Split into experts, then distill back into one model

t163|694.c: The compute and cache savings only appear with long inputs, and need good caching systems to pay off.
t163|694.e: V4 claims big cuts in compute per token and in the KV cache, the stored memory of text already read. But that only holds when inputs are long. Tests with 8K tokens in and 4K out show no edge. Agents working near a million tokens benefit most. Hybrid attention makes prefix caching hard to keep consistent. His team keeps separate compressed states for the three attention types, built three different cache pools, and moved sparse attention's cache to host memory. Only this kind of groundwork turns a paper advantage into real, deployable cost savings.
ex: With long inputs, compute per token drops to about 27% and KV cache to 10%
He says offloading lifts long-context throughput more than fivefold

items.d: Prefill, decode and speculative decoding in sync

t163|694.c: Activating only 3% of parameters trades engineering risk for low serving cost. It's not a recipe to copy.
t163|694.e: V4 is a mixture-of-experts model: it has many "experts" and calls on only a few for each token. He likes to look at the ratio of total experts to active ones. It has gone from about 5:1 to 10:1 to 20:1, and now past 30, nearly 40:1. The more extreme the ratio, the more evenly experts must be trained, and the better token routing and cross-chip communication must be. Otherwise loads get uneven and routing jitters. V4 uses hash routing in its first layers so early tokens don't pile onto a few experts. DeepSeek is trading engineering risk for cheaper serving and more knowledge capacity.
ex: V4 Pro has about 1.6 trillion parameters, with about 49 billion active
Engram needs many parameters for limited gains, so it stayed out of V4

t163|694.c: Benchmarks max out in a year or two, so scores can't be trusted. Shift to real evaluation.
t163|694.e: Public scores are mostly above 90, yet users can tell a model got worse after a few chats. Scores and experience have come apart. Models are bunched in a narrow range, and small ranking gaps don't mean real differences in use. When he switched from Claude Code to Codex, his work didn't noticeably suffer. He wants less talk of benchmarks and more of evaluation: stability over many steps, long conversations, a consistent personality and robust tool use. Those needs won't disappear just because some test set gets maxed out.
ex: "Vibe checking": users judging a model got worse from a few chats

items.d: Scores pass 90 within a year or two

t163|694.c: US models lead in long-running agents and feedback loops; Chinese models in architecture innovation and value for money.
t163|694.e: He has seen US models improve sharply at multi-turn agentic coding since Claude 4.5, driven by a data loop built on high-quality human feedback. Chinese teams stand out for how much they innovate in architecture and how polished their engineering is. V4 swapped several components at once and still worked. With more compute, the US can push the capability ceiling first and cut costs later. China focuses on value, and the same capability may cost an order of magnitude less, though sparsity also gives up some ceiling.
ex: He admits Chinese teams also rely heavily on US closed models in real work

items: Ample compute, push the ceiling first
Same capability, an order of magnitude cheaper

d.verdict: Each path has strengths; sparsity trades ceiling for cost

t164|609.c: Closed-source SaaS is dead: AI can quickly copy code, so software is no longer a mine-like asset.
t164|609.e: Software used to be like a mine or a factory: once built, a fixed asset others couldn't easily take. Now AI can write code that copies it fast, so closed code alone is no longer worth charging for. Companies that stay closed-source, big or small, have little future. Mininglamp is less exposed because its core is a data supply chain that keeps collecting and labeling data, more like Wind or Bloomberg. Customers will call that data through command-line tools or their own agents, so usage may actually grow.
ex: Mininglamp's data comes from web scraping, ads, loyalty programs and offline retail

items.d: Hard to copy, like a mine or factory
Closed code is no longer worth charging for

t164|609.c: Software firms must stop selling licenses and sell results, charging a management fee on top of token costs.
t164|609.e: His plan is to gradually open-source the software capabilities that can be copied anyway, and earn money from results delivered by digital labor. The wrapper might be advertising, legal or outsourcing services, but the core is still software. Custom development used to be billed by the person-month or person-day. In future it will be a management fee on top of token spending. US knowledge services price by the value they save clients, so AI will force a cost comparison and hit them harder than China, where work is priced by cost.
ex: Say a project burns $1 million in tokens; charge an extra $200,000 management fee
He used Yum China's restaurant business to show industry-specific models work better

items.d: Copyable parts are no longer charged for
Service on the outside, software inside

t164|609.c: Efficiency from general AI gets copied by rivals and passed on to customers. Data and taste are defensible.
t164|609.e: Once rivals learn the same tools, cost structures converge and the savings end up passed to customers as lower prices. What lasts is proprietary AI, proprietary data, industry context and judgment built over years, like Mininglamp analysts' taste for their industries. AI is good at reasoning from clear premises. Where people can't be replaced is deciding what they want and judging what is beautiful. He has even cut back his child's math-olympiad drills to build that kind of judgment instead.
ex: He thinks leaders in industries like advertising and retail are stuck in the old era

result.d: General efficiency gains get competed away

t164|609.c: OpenClaw lets ordinary people edit an AI's readable memory so it keeps learning, but teams must assign owners.
t164|609.e: Centralized models are frozen once released, and individuals can't tune them efficiently. OpenClaw, an open-source personal AI assistant, keeps its memory, "soul" and skills in readable, editable text. Ask it to reflect or to remember something, and it updates itself. He compares how widely this spreads the benefit to DeepSeek. But it was built for individuals. In a team it mistakes who is who, mixes up permissions and can even be tricked into leaking secrets. He wants every agent bound to one owner, with shared agents belonging to the department head, so a person bears the consequences.
ex: After Chinese New Year, Mininglamp launched an internal analysis agent called Deep Miner
He thinks merging contributions has become the bottleneck for open-source projects

items.d: No need to change model weights

t164|609.c: AI-native companies take people out of execution so small teams can cover more fronts, not to cut jobs.
t164|609.e: At Mininglamp, people supply ideas, find context and judge results, while agents write code and do repetitive analysis. The change starts with programmers and data analysts, then spreads to finance and HR. Influence comes from "taste credit", how consistently others endorse your judgment, rather than from rank. People still handle customers for now, because whoever is accountable has to be a person or a company. After the big 2022 layoffs, he now avoids cutting jobs whenever he can. He also rejects one-person companies and favors three-person teams handing work across time zones.
ex: In 2022 the company had about 4,000 people and cut roughly half
With about 1,800 staff now, he imagines about 100 three-person teams

items.d: People decide what they want and what's good
People supply background and judge results

t164|609.c: A team of specialist agents beats one agent stuffed with material. Octo is the network where they collaborate.
t164|609.e: A colleague fed a huge library of classical texts to one agent, and it did worse than a specialist trained only on math and AI. He proposes MOA, a mixture of agents, as the counterpart to mixture-of-experts models. Different people train math, philosophy or game-theory agents, which then work and learn together in one organizational network. Octo doesn't rebuild OpenClaw. It aims to be a boat that rises with the tide: a communication layer as the backbone, with apps like paper collaboration and data analysis on top. It removes overlap by domain and only sends people what needs their judgment.
ex: Octo's backbone has about five core engineers
The top engineer spends about $8,000 a day on tokens

items.d: Trained by someone good at math

t164|609.c: Don't concentrate intelligence in a few servers. Once base models are good enough, scale out across people.
t164|609.e: He isn't against smarter AI. He opposes simply making one black-box model bigger so that intellectual work concentrates on a few servers. That could cause mass unemployment and damage the economy's circulation. He thinks base models only need to be good enough. Then intelligence should spread across individuals, small teams and organizational networks, with intellectual property staying with the contributors. He is glad a big 2021 funding round fell through, or Mininglamp might have been locked into the scale-up path of pretraining ever-larger models.
ex: In 2021 it nearly raised $500 million at a $5 billion valuation
For now it won't train large base models, focusing on small and multimodal ones

items: Intelligence concentrated in a few servers

d.verdict: Spread intelligence out instead of concentrating it

t164|609.c: Graphical interfaces will always exist. Fixed-coordinate automation will break, so GUI models need production-grade accuracy.
t164|609.e: He disagrees that APIs and command lines will replace graphical interfaces. People need visual screens, and we should keep systems humans can operate in case AI causes an accident. Interfaces will become personalized and get rebuilt often, so RPA, automation that clicks through fixed layouts, will keep breaking. General leaderboards only prove you can train a model. Seventy percent accuracy means three errors in ten tries, which is useless in production. He thinks the biggest near-term market for GUI models is testing the custom software that coding agents just built, because graphical interfaces are hard to verify by reading output.

items.d: About 70, wrong three times in ten
Early cross-border e-commerce accuracy, per him

t165|700.c: A world model for decisions must predict the future given an action. General robots should first model themselves.
t165|700.e: A model that knows about the world and makes realistic video only meets a loose definition: text can edit the scene, but it can't take in joint trajectories. He sees an action as an intervention in the world, so decisions need a model that predicts what happens next given the history and an action. A general policy should only assume it controls its own actions. Editing other agents helps build rare scenarios for self-driving or games, and multi-agent communication has long-term value. But to deploy in any environment, getting the single robot right is the most general approach.
ex: Without a world model, deciding means ignoring the consequences

items.d: Predicts the future from a given action
Doesn't assume it can edit other agents

t165|700.c: Bet on video in, video out: build foundations on data-rich video, then align to scarce robot actions.
t165|700.e: Particles and graphs save compute and data, but soft objects need special definitions and they generalize poorly across objects. Explicit 3D is consistent and stable over time, yet depends on reconstruction, rendering and labeling, so it isn't end to end. JEPA-style latent spaces, which predict in an abstract internal representation instead of pixels, are compact and promising, but hard to plug into today's large-model ecosystem. Language and video are the two most data-rich modalities. He wants foundations built on them, then aligned to scarce robot action data. Predicting pixels is just the training target and doesn't stop it helping decisions.
ex: Explicit 3D example: World Labs' Marble
Latent-space examples: Yann LeCun's JEPA and AMI

marks.d: Stable but not end to end
Compact but hard to plug in

t165|700.c: World models are hot this year because generation quality, robot data and policy skill all arrived together.
t165|700.e: Generative models led by Sora crossed the bar for realistic images and some correct physics, so simulators went from concept to something you can experiment with. Robot-data vendors and open datasets have multiplied, and world models need exactly the data on successes, failures and random actions, unlike policies, which only need expert demonstrations. Policies now handle simple tasks reliably and produce a narrower range of actions, so a world model only has to cover that range, which makes the job easier.
ex: Running on the robot or in the cloud depends on latency and bandwidth, not model size

t165|700.c: DreamZero proposes actions, and DreamDojo checks their consequences before the robot moves.
t165|700.e: DreamZero is a world action model. Given a task in text, it outputs both future video and robot actions, doing the same job as a VLA (a model that maps vision and language straight to actions). DreamDojo is an action-conditioned simulator: it takes real trajectories and predicts future frames. Chained together, the high level first compares steps as text subtasks. Then the low level uses DreamDojo to compare what different grasp angles, forces and speeds would lead to. Trial and error moves to before the action happens.
ex: DreamDojo builds on Cosmos and was pretrained on about 45,000 hours of first-person video
He's unsure whether latent actions are the final answer

items.d: A general agent splits out subtasks

t165|700.c: World models needn't be perfect to help: safety, evaluation, data collection and virtual training come first.
t165|700.e: Foreseeing consequences before acting improves safety. Real-robot evaluation is hard to reproduce because of lighting, object placement, calibration and wear. A simulator can reset the starting state exactly, trading compute for efficiency and fairness. A real-time simulator also lets people teleoperate a virtual robot, and the corrected trajectories can go straight into training. Reinforcement learning in simulation could escape the limits of physical time, though he admits that is still far off. He rejects the idea that policies alone are enough, arguing that locally reliable feedback can already make a policy better.
ex: Teleoperation hardware is still needed; the savings are robots, space, resets and wear

root.d: No need to wait for a perfect simulator

items.d: Escape the limits of physical time

t165|700.c: Agent, policy and world model form a loop that improves itself once errors drop below a threshold.
t165|700.e: The three parts pass text, actions and video between them, which happen to be relatively mature, data-rich modalities. For now only simple tasks work, because each part's generalization errors stack up. Once errors fall below an acceptable threshold, the policy can go into new environments and collect data on its own. That data helps the world model learn physics and action control. A stronger policy then produces a narrower range of actions that is easier to simulate, creating a flywheel.
ex: The tipping point for simple tasks could come in 2026
World action models need about 2 to 3 years; a simulator boom about 5

items.d: Acts and collects data on its own
A stronger policy is easier to simulate

t165|700.c: Generalization is the top bottleneck. Trained only on expert data, a world model renders failures as successes.
t165|700.e: He ranks research priorities as generalization, long-horizon stability, then efficiency. Generalization covers both understanding physics and following actions. If a soft rag gets rendered as a rigid block, no image sharpness yields trustworthy feedback. Trained only on expert trajectories, the model has only seen success, so even a missed grasp gets rendered as a catch, and it can't tell good from bad. Ideally, a shaky action should produce shaky video. The fix is adding casual human motions from first-person video and actions the policy collects itself. Long-horizon stability will get a push from demand for film-quality video generation.
ex: A generative model may randomly decide whether an object shut in a cabinet still exists

items: Feedback can't tell good from bad

d.verdict: A world model must stay true to actions, not prettify results

t165|700.c: DeepMind has the most complete stack, though building strong foundation models first and adding robots later also works.
t165|700.e: He rates Google DeepMind highest. Genie 3 provides interactive worlds, SIMA acts as the policy, Veo is the video foundation model, and Gemini-type models plan and score, while game data isn't bound by physical time. NVIDIA's Cosmos sits at the foundation-model layer and needs post-training to take actions. He sees two paths to physical AGI: train on robot data now, or build strong multimodal foundation models first and then align them to robots. Both make sense, so Anthropic's quiet public profile doesn't mean it is absent.
ex: The Sora team was folded into robotics; he expects fierce competition in 2026
World models lack a shared benchmark, and action spaces are tied to each robot body

t166|423.c: Scientist founders are now mainstream. He wants a lasting, independent consumer brand, not a big company's research lab.
t166|423.e: He thinks the worry that scientists aren't fully committed is outdated. What's scarcest in the AI era is conviction in the technology and foresight, as with OpenAI's early insistence on piling up data. But he doesn't want Poke to be a big company's research arm. He wants an independent, long-term consumer brand for homes worldwide. Home robots have no agreed definition yet, so he follows Apple in having the company set the category, then borrows Xiaomi's user involvement to find the needs most people share. He won't build every component in-house and will focus on intelligence and product.
ex: He moved from game AI to robots for the bigger challenge and wider impact
Having never held a regular job, he can redesign workflows and evaluations from scratch

items: The company sets the product framework
Find the needs most people share

d.verdict: Home robots are undefined, so learn from both

t166|423.c: Being AI native means no single-task stunts, no narrow local data loops and no patchwork of small models.
t166|423.e: He sees AI as fundamentally an inducer that learns patterns from examples. So the variety of data matters more than piling up similar data in a closed setting, and diverse cases should be mixed from the start. That leads him to reject three approaches. One is classic robotics tackling single tasks like backflips or pouring wine, which can never all be listed. Another is the self-driving playbook of mastering one small area before expanding. The third is stitching small models into general intelligence, which he calls prehistoric deep learning. Small models suit doing one thing every day, not general intelligence.
ex: Counterexamples: backflips, balancing three spinning tops, robot-arm bands

root.d: AI generalizes from examples; variety first

items.d: Tasks can never all be listed
General intelligence needs one unified model

t166|423.c: Jagged AI earns trust by avoiding accidents over time, so the first product must rule things out.
t166|423.e: Large models are jagged: brilliant at some things, poor at others. He compares it to a veteran driver: go long enough without a serious accident and trust follows. So the product needs boundaries first. The first generation won't do services that touch the body, like sponge baths, turning someone over, lifting people or massage, and feeding comes last. It's like babysitting: ban dangerous behavior, and the worst case is a broken remote control. The first product may be a wheeled two-armed robot, with legged versions in parallel, aiming for about two hours of battery for homes worldwide.
ex: Wheels can't climb stairs, so multi-story homes may need one per floor
Weight, bringing batteries into homes, recharging and recovering crashed robots are all constraints

items.d: No bathing, massage or lifting for now
Worst case is a broken small item
Wheeled, two arms, about 2 hours of battery

t166|423.c: The industry underrates evaluation. Reinforcement learning must separate good data from bad, or robots get worse.
t166|423.e: Poke's model approach has three steps: the robot interacts with the world to produce data, evaluates which of it is good, mediocre or failed, and then makes good use of it. He thinks the industry mostly fixates on data volume and neglects evaluation. Feeding bad data into training indiscriminately can actually make the policy worse. Only a robot that explores, evaluates and uses data on its own can keep improving in an open environment like a home.

items.d: Interact with the world to make data

t166|423.c: Skip task-by-task fine-tuning. Better to be mediocre at everything early than to lose generalization.
t166|423.e: Post-training a model for one task gets quick results, but it erodes the generalization gained in pretraining. He insists on one unified model and wants post-training to generalize too. He accepts that every task will be just okay at first, expecting them all to improve together, rather than one task being great and the rest useless. The goal is for the model to transfer to homes it has never seen, the way multilingual models carry over across languages.
ex: In his view, 2025 produced no work on the level of the Transformer

items.d: Every task just okay at first

t166|423.c: Video becoming the main data source and models growing larger are certain. Architecture and robot form are not.
t166|423.e: He expects more data to come from video and to become accessible to everyone. Models will grow along with the data, and people will gradually accept robots as everyday devices. These are fairly certain. What's uncertain is the modeling path and what robot body people will end up accepting. Hardware is a solvable bottleneck. Robots need physical common sense, like the fact that things fall, so world models make a good backbone. But there's no need to build a world model or a vision-language model from scratch.
ex: He's bullish on the intelligence of PI, Generalist and Sunday
He doubts Figure, seeing marketing in its videos

marks.d: More of it, open to all

t166|423.c: Office demos in a year, homes in two, and yearly spending that will approach large-model labs.
t166|423.e: His goal is for the robot to show basic abilities in an office in about a year, and for real users to have it at home in about two. At current data volumes, pretraining plus post-training for a robot model costs roughly 100 to 200 million yuan a year. Once data volumes rise, that will approach what large-model labs spend. Big companies will only go all in once home robots become a core business, which gives startups a window.
ex: He estimates training costs about 100 to 200 million yuan a year

items.d: His rough guess for general intelligence

t166|423.c: China hasn't missed the robotics window, but needs patience and should track daily use, not shipments or stunts.
t166|423.e: He is sure China hasn't missed this window. His worry is missing the biggest prize. US teams are more strategically patient and better funded, while Chinese companies get pulled around by short-term shipments and demos. He opposes mindless mass production without disclosing how many robots are used daily, which he sees as the key metric. Competing on harder dance routines has little to do with intelligence. Selling data to competitors, especially to the US, is dangerous. Of the directions that might change society, he thinks embodied intelligence, AI that acts in the physical world, is the most certain.

t167|702.c: R&D is a fixed cost. Once paying city users cover it, rural schools get the same product free.
t167|702.e: Rural schools now have decent hardware. The gap is in how lessons are taught and how teachers and students interact. From day one, Onion set a rule: paying users and rural users get the same product, with no watered-down charity version. Product development is the biggest fixed cost, and paying city users can cover it. As scale grows, the cost of each extra user barely rises, and growth comes mainly from word of mouth. He rejects "make money first, do charity later", because once stakeholders lock you in you can't turn back. Social good should be the company's ballast.
ex: First full year of breaking even in 2022; NPS around 50-60
Its teaching-assistant program has supported about 60,000 rural teachers

t167|702.c: Kids who don't understand usually got a bad explanation. Self-directed learning grows from repeated small successes.
t167|702.e: He believes most school material can be understood. The problem is usually that it's taught in ways that ignore how people learn, not that kids are lazy or slow. Self-directed learning has four layers: willingness, ability, tools and belief. Belief is the goal, but all four depend on each other. When parents insist kids show initiative before they'll let go, the cycle stalls. Students need tools that lower the bar. When stuck, they should first hear "this is normal", then break the problem down and review it, so one question becomes practice in learning how to learn.
ex: He believes every struggling student secretly wants to be a top student

items.d: Can handle it alone next time

t167|702.c: Correct explanations aren't understanding. Each 5-8 minute unit must take students from learning to understanding to use.
t167|702.e: He draws on UBD (Understanding by Design), Bloom's taxonomy and the Feynman technique, writing a learning goal into every line of explanation. Checkable verbs like explain, give an example and compare show whether students understand. Without supervision, students are choosing between lessons and games or short videos, so every 5-8 minute unit must give them one complete experience of success. The "Onion flavor" uses a sense of purpose, empathy and relevance to manage students' tension. Math is the most abstract subject, so methods that work there transfer more easily to others.
ex: Plane geometry is unified around converting relationships between sides and angles
He rejects mnemonic tricks: for most students they only create fragmented memories

items.d: Students can explain, give examples, compare

t167|702.c: Teaching content has a quality threshold. Below it, spending produces nothing, so slowness is a price worth paying.
t167|702.e: A teacher's face can only convey so much, so abstract concepts need animation to be visible. One 5-8 minute interactive lesson costs about 100,000 yuan, two months and more than 20 production steps on average, with scripts debated again and again by the teaching team. His analogy: something made for 50 yuan is worth zero, and it only starts working at 80. After launch, second-by-second data on pauses, drop-offs and rewinds reveals problems, and the content gets fixed. That's why he believes the product keeps getting better.
ex: About 1,500 animations in the first five years, slower than Khan Academy
About 200 middle-school math lessons were made over two years before launch

marks.d: Past the threshold, it starts working

t167|702.c: Scaling with human teachers serves only those who can pay. Livestreams and dual-teacher classes decay into recordings.
t167|702.e: He thinks that as long as you scale with human teachers, good resources go only to those who can pay. Only standardized products built on human-computer interaction give rural and city students the same experience. Dual-teacher classes, a remote star teacher plus a local one, and livestreams often decay into pausable recordings local students can't keep up with. Years ago, rural students watching star teachers' recordings mostly couldn't take them in. Eye contact and feedback get lost on a small screen. Digital settings need digital-native ways of learning, not offline classes moved online. During the livestream boom, the company discussed it twice at most.
ex: Onion's content always follows the curriculum and school pace, so China's tutoring crackdown barely hurt it

items: Access goes to those who pay
Same product in city and village

d.verdict: Only standardized digital-native products can reach everyone

t167|702.c: Large models alone can't yet teach material that needs deep reasoning, so AI should fill gaps within courses.
t167|702.e: Large models learn from highly structured text and produce rigorous output, but schoolchildren are still building their mental frameworks. Models can't yet scaffold step by step for a kid starting from zero. They're fine as helpers, but as the main teacher most students fall behind. So Onion's AI tutor works within a defined course context and doesn't jump to material not yet covered or from other grades. When a student snaps a photo of a problem, it lays out the reasoning, finds weak spots and pushes make-up lessons. Duolingo-style gamification suits short practice loops, not K-12 subjects that need sustained reasoning.
ex: When Duolingo pushed a grammar module, retention dropped noticeably
He doesn't rule out models handling it after a big change in training methods

items.d: The main teaching line and pace
Spots sticking points, pushes make-up lessons
Encourage, then return to independent thinking

t167|702.c: "AI native" doesn't distinguish anyone. Education is a fragmented market of clashing philosophies, so giants are unlikely.
t167|702.e: He sees "AI native" as merely something every supplier shares. Approaches should be told apart by demand: standardizing teachers' workflows, standardizing the tasks around learning like assigning and grading problems, or, like Onion, focusing narrowly on the learning experience itself. Education isn't one market but many niches with mutually exclusive philosophies. A specialized product that scores 95 out of 100 will win families and schools. He isn't highly confident, but leans toward thinking no AI education giant will emerge. Even buying a thousand companies would hardly make them gel.
ex: He thinks even OpenAI, without structured content, would struggle to teach ordinary students today

items.d: E.g. firms rooted in large live classes

t167|702.c: Jobs ten years out are unpredictable, so education must teach how to learn. Knowledge carries ways of thinking.
t167|702.e: He thinks the fundamentals of education haven't changed. AI just makes the old system's problems impossible to ignore. Today's seventh graders will finish college in about ten years, in a job market no one can predict. So the goal is the ability to learn new things and put them to use. Math trains reasoning, which is hard to teach apart from specific knowledge, and rote memorization that keeps only conclusions cuts that link. If AI caters to laziness, it will widen gaps. Education should try not to leave the weakest behind. Schools will move toward classrooms of teacher, student and machine.
ex: Ten-year goal: make 5 to 10 million kids more eager to learn on their own
Serves more than 2,000 schools in depth each year

t168|710.c: Investing's hard part is gauging a good company's ceiling. The best signal: passion turned into years of focus.
t168|710.e: He thinks the VC challenge isn't telling good from bad but estimating how big a good company can become. The strongest early signal is a founder whose pure passion has turned into years of focus and then into core capability. Degrees, competitions and success templates are surface features. When Xingxing Wang built robot dogs in 2016, nobody knew what they were for, and that passion carried from robot dogs to humanoids. He believes the next Xingxing Wang will appear in every field where China isn't yet world number one. VC's social value is keeping diversity alive, not always picking right.
ex: Assembled founding teams aren't a sin; what counts is what they do with the money
Li Auto's vision was clear from day one

items.d: Turns into real ability to execute
What VCs really need to estimate

t168|710.c: Intuition is only a starting point. Conviction comes from six-plus months of repeated contact, judged case by case.
t168|710.e: He admits intuition comes from long training but treats it only as a starting point. Even if he likes a founder at the first meeting, he meets them monthly or more often, and with two founders he waited more than six months before investing. Each decision is judged on its own, neither held hostage by past wins nor scared off by failures. VC feedback is slow and outcomes are hard to attribute. That's why he left GGV for Kunlun, to test faster whether he could invest for the long haul.
ex: At GGV he wrote AR/VR reports in English running over 100 pages
He thinks technology is often overrated for two or three years and underrated for ten

items.d: Each case judged on its own

t168|710.c: A three-by-three grid finds crossover bets, and the more infrastructural large models become, the more cells they touch.
t168|710.e: Dragonball's tech map has three columns, AI, semiconductors and energy, and three rows, electric vehicles, robots and next-generation devices. The framework hasn't fundamentally changed since 2021. Only the weight of each cell shifts. Large models are infrastructure that covers almost every cell, and they will reshape semiconductors and energy in turn. Decisions are made by weighted votes, and no one has a veto. Meituan founder Wang Xing is just one equal partner. As he puts it, nobody is the sheriff.
ex: He doesn't see fund life as a hard limit; secondary funds and similar tools have matured

result.d: Large models run through nearly every cell

t168|710.c: Backing Moonshot AI was a bet on Zhilin Yang's technical vision. Afterward, help without getting in the way.
t168|710.e: In July 2023, Dragonball approved about $30 million for Moonshot AI, its only bet on a large-model startup. Rivals were already valued around $1.5 billion, Moonshot had no mature model yet, and there was internal pressure. He valued Zhilin Yang's technical vision, talent density and research organization, not any single paper. When Alibaba took a big stake, he fully supported it and left the board. He once urged the company to refocus on models rather than buying traffic, and thinks DeepSeek R1's shock worked better than any persuasion. He believes AGI has already arrived and ASI is next.
ex: Dragonball invested in Li Auto during its hard times in 2019

items.d: Model progress matters more than growth

t168|710.c: AI apps are investable but lack real winners. DAU is an old yardstick; watch tokens and delivered results.
t168|710.e: Dragonball only began systematically studying the app layer in mid-2024 and backed about ten companies in 2025, mostly at seed and Series A. He thinks no AI app company has truly succeeded yet. Daily active users are a yardstick from the last era and don't make his top three. Token usage, ARR and actual delivered results matter more. He notices this wave of founders was mostly born around 1997. The ideal profile is a "young veteran": young but with years in one field, or older yet open-minded.
ex: Xi Chen: born 1996, joined Douyin in 2018, about seven years of experience

d.verdict: AI apps need new metrics

t168|710.c: Locomotion has converged, so he backs only Unitree. Manipulation hasn't, so he bets on several approaches.
t168|710.e: At NeurIPS in late 2023, he saw robotics labs at Stanford, Berkeley, Harvard and MIT widely using Unitree's robot dogs. He judged its hardware would drive breakthroughs in AI capability, and Dragonball invested in 2024. Locomotion and whole-body control have converged, so there he backs only Unitree. Manipulation hasn't, so he covers different approaches to brains, data and use cases. He likens the real-versus-simulated-data debate to arguing over rocket fuel: reaching orbit is what counts. Key component makers could also become chain leaders, the way CATL did in batteries.
ex: Dragonball looked at more than 100 companies while studying embodied AI
In components it backed suppliers such as D-Robotics and Sharpe

root.d: Allocated by how settled each layer is

items.d: Unsettled; many brain and data approaches

t168|710.c: China underinvests in embodied AI. It should spend on the same scale and build products that beat rivals.
t168|710.e: He rejects treating all embodied AI companies as one kind of asset, and rejects equating high valuations with overinvestment. In his view, China is spending too little in this field, not too much. Building 50 to 80 percent of a rival's capability at 20 percent of the cost is the imitator's path. China should invest capital of the same order of magnitude, build products that surpass rivals and even lead with original work. He sees Xingxing Wang, DeepSeek's Liang Wenfeng and Xue Zhang as passion-driven, world-class attempts, not copycat businesses.

t168|710.c: The next robotics shakeout hinges on generalization, not sales, and a GPT-3.5 moment may come within two years.
t168|710.e: He thinks world models and data are nearing consensus. The next contest is who can push robots' generalization, handling situations they haven't seen, not who sells the most. The test the public can feel is a demo at normal 1x speed that still looks smooth, doing things humans do. In 2019 he invested in Pony.ai at about a $1.6 billion valuation, and only rode in a driverless product about six years later. But for a long-term fund, the gap between expectation and reality matters less than whether the core problem is being solved. Final demand is huge, but it won't be winner-take-all.
ex: He roughly estimates 8 billion people may need 24 billion robots
He estimates no more than 0.3% of people pay for advanced AI

items.d: Later than hoped, but problems being solved

t169|713.c: Cerebras challenges NVIDIA on specific workloads like inference. It isn't a full replacement.
t169|713.e: Cerebras's wafer-scale design puts compute, memory and communication on one piece of silicon as much as possible, cutting chip-to-chip traffic and trips to external HBM memory. That gives it an edge in inference, where bandwidth and latency are the limits. But NVIDIA's moat is the whole package: CUDA, its developer ecosystem, networking, systems software, customer trust and supply chain. It can't be reduced to a chip benchmark. Once a GPU training cluster is built, switching chips is a systemic risk, so Cerebras should compete for new inference demand instead.
ex: A decade ago, researchers estimated about 96% of GPU die area wasn't designed for deep learning
NVIDIA's acquisition of Groq is seen as a counterattack on inference

items: A whole wafer as the compute engine
Less data shuttling between chips and HBM

d.verdict: A challenger on inference, not a full replacement

t169|713.c: Cerebras's valuation jump reflects compute demand shifting from training to inference, not just market mood.
t169|713.e: Two or three years ago, the compute story was all about training. Nan Zhou now judges that more than half of GPU demand comes from inference, and coding and agents multiply token consumption. Inference latency, throughput and cost per token directly determine product experience and gross margin, so Cerebras's strengths have become fundamentals. If inference demand keeps growing, a $500 billion valuation wouldn't be surprising, but that's the optimistic ceiling. The floor depends on whether wafer-scale systems can keep scaling and deliver reliably.
ex: After its IPO its market value neared $100 billion; about $50 billion at recording
Customers remain concentrated in a few big buyers like G42

items.d: Over half of GPU demand is inference

t169|713.c: OpenAI's huge order aims to break the compute bottleneck and to diversify suppliers for independence.
t169|713.e: In January 2026, OpenAI signed a contract worth at least $20 billion. Nan Zhou thinks compute is now the main bottleneck to scaling models further, and frontier labs can't depend on a single supplier. He expects Anthropic and others to seek alternative or custom compute too. Sam Altman invested in Cerebras personally in 2016, showing he saw this early, and Zhou doesn't consider it a related-party deal. But nothing has been delivered yet. Delivery speed and long-term operating stability are the real test.
ex: Altman's personal investment came before Baidu's
Cerebras Cloud uses an API to make adoption easier

items.d: The main limit on further scaling
Frontier labs won't rely on one vendor
Not yet delivered; watch speed and stability

t169|713.c: Scaling laws were already emerging at Baidu's US lab, and slow training was the real pain point.
t169|713.e: Baidu researchers hadn't written the pattern down as a formula, but they saw that bigger models, more data, longer training and more compute kept improving results. The pain that followed was slow training: a language model of nearly 300 million parameters took over three months to train fully on GPUs, plus months more of tuning. Cerebras claimed a 1,000-fold training speedup, hitting that need squarely. By comparison, Graphcore wasn't disruptive enough, Wave was ruled out early over team issues, and ASICs looked more like inference solutions.
ex: Training, not inference, was the priority then
They also studied Graphcore, Wave Computing and several ASIC makers

items.d: Bigger models and more data keep improving

t169|713.c: Vetting hardware means pricing risks in time and money, then seeing if the founder can unpack each one.
t169|713.e: Nan Zhou doesn't require a system-chip CEO to design chips personally. He cares more about product definition, customer understanding and conviction. Andrew Feldman spent about two hours a day for four weeks working through yield, cooling, power, the compiler and customer adoption. On the technical side, Baidu ran large language models built on its PaddlePaddle framework on Cerebras's simulator. On manufacturing, Stanford professors and an autonomous-driving hardware team assessed the risks. One failed tape-out would cost about six extra months and $5-10 million, so they checked whether the company's cash could absorb it.
ex: A memo of a dozen-odd pages; the committee approved it in under two days
Baidu co-led the 2017 Series C at about a $700 million valuation
He forecast a $22 billion training-chip market for 2025, later admitting it was far too low

terms.d: Baidu's large model on the simulator
A failed tape-out costs about six months

result.d: Diligence done in about four weeks

t169|713.c: Nearly every worst case they modeled happened. Team resilience and a patient board got the company through.
t169|713.e: From 2017 to 2019, tape-outs, wafers and the compiler slipped one after another, putting the company a year or two behind plan. Top-tier VCs backed off, put off by an unclear market and wafer-scale risk. G42 was both investor and customer, which added single-customer risk. Nan Zhou thinks steady support for Feldman from early investors and the board was key to surviving a hardware cycle of nearly a decade. Some argue OpenAI would have trained on Cerebras if tape-out had come earlier. Zhou ultimately disagrees: the Transformer only appeared in 2017, and frontier labs wouldn't bet core training on an immature system.
ex: Later valuations rose from over $2 billion to over $4 billion, then over $8 billion

items.d: A contract of at least $20 billion

t169|713.c: Baidu's US lab got there early but missed out, mainly because of geopolitics rather than internal problems.
t169|713.e: At its peak, Baidu's US research lab had about 250 people, ample GPU budgets and research freedom. Its alumni went on to found or join early OpenAI, Anthropic, Inflection and Adept. Nan Zhou sees Baidu as an important stop in Dario Amodei's career. A growth fund Zhou helped plan had OpenAI, Databricks and Scale AI on its list, but limited partners pulled out one by one over geopolitics, and the fund never launched. He thinks the US is better at disruptive architectures and China at engineering catch-up and deployment, while admitting he knows the Chinese scene only partly.
ex: Around 2017-2018, OpenAI was also open to Baidu investment
In summer 2020, an ex-colleague said GPT-3 was nearly trained but still talked nonsense

t169|713.c: Early AI bets stay contrarian for only a month or two, so top funds pile into proven winners.
t169|713.e: In a private investment letter in February 2025, Nan Zhou listed general agents, video and multimodal models, Figure AI, physical AI and industry-specific AI. He found the gap between spotting an opportunity and consensus forming was often just a month or two. Top funds now write big follow-on checks into companies already breaking out. That's still a form of venture capital, but concentrated bets carry bigger single-point risk. Physical AI doesn't always need self-driving's roughly 99.9% accuracy, and model generalization could suddenly speed up progress. Low-power on-device chips, new CPUs for orchestrating agents and inference optimization still have room.
ex: AIG, founded by Song Han's students, was acquired by Nebius in March 2026
Infrastructure firms like Fireworks, fal.ai and Baseten have early flywheels

marks.d: Listed in a private investment letter
Top funds pile into breakout firms

t170|678.c: World models won't overthrow VLAs. They're being stitched into leading models, and the endgame is omni models.
t170|678.e: Last quarter, world models still looked like lab samples. This quarter, NVIDIA's Cosmos 3 is a deployable product in super, nano and edge versions, using a MoT architecture that lets autoregressive reasoning and diffusion generation share attention. NVIDIA's survey sorts them into video world models, action-conditioned world models and world action models. Even text instructions can count as actions, which itself hints at convergence. VLAs (models that map vision and language straight to actions) are fast but are basically behavior cloning, copying demonstrations. π0.7 already adds a lightweight world model to its VLA to predict images of subgoals.
ex: He sees Cosmos 3 as the first fully open-source omni model
The world-model funding boom is people who made money on large models reinvesting

t170|678.c: Figure's sorting livestream is a zero-to-one moment: soft parcels are exactly what the old tech stack couldn't handle.
t170|678.e: Figure's robot worked for over 100 hours straight and sorted about 130,000 parcels, roughly one every 3 seconds. Soft parcels deform, their barcodes get hidden, and they must be flipped and flattened. The vision-plus-industrial-arm approach of four or five years ago could only do simple pick-and-place, so it stayed stuck at the demo stage. Standard carton warehouses already have mature solutions, and the irregular e-commerce parcels left over suit embodied models well. Teleoperation isn't the issue. Every deployment needs long teleoperated data collection first, and remote takeover, as with robotaxis, is normal.
ex: Robotera's tests at China Post and SF Express already sort and flip parcels autonomously
Legs help with rare surprises like conveyors running too fast or items slipping

d.verdict: Irregular parcel logistics is a good fit for humanoids

t170|678.c: The robot marathon is like F1: extreme tests force system-level progress, and big companies' spending is paying off.
t170|678.e: The winning time at Beijing Yizhuang's humanoid marathon dropped from about 2 hours 40 minutes in the 2025 remote-controlled category to about 50 minutes for this year's top three in autonomous navigation. Hardware, control and autonomous navigation are all improving fast. Honor swept the top three, using custom motors and precision liquid cooling to beat overheating. It fielded ten teams and clearly outspent everyone else. Zhe Chen thinks many problems were solvable with existing designs; there just wasn't demand before. Big companies with high-end manufacturing experience and organizational strength are turning humanoids into a systems-engineering effort.
ex: Xiaomi, XPeng and Li Auto are already investing seriously in humanoids

t170|678.c: Whoever first supplies dexterous hands reliably and cheaply could become the de facto standard.
t170|678.e: At ICRA, Wuji's second-generation direct-drive hand had 20 degrees of freedom, better cooling and better back-drivability, at about half the size of Sharpa's. Most high-DOF hands are 1.5 to 2 times the size of a human hand, which makes it hard to learn human manipulation strategies. Zhe Chen calls Wuji the Unitree of dexterous hands: focused on turning cheap, reliable hardware into research infrastructure. Big companies following Tesla's tendon drive are mostly hedging organizationally. Hand data is tightly bound to hand shape and sensors, so third parties can't cover everything, and independent full direct-drive makers standardize more easily.
ex: Low-DOF hands ship tens of thousands a year, tracking humanoid sales
Top makers of high-DOF hands ship only thousands, mostly for research

items.d: Full direct drive, no forearm needed

t170|678.c: Big tech has about six months to enter. Robot brains will consolidate; models will split open versus closed.
t170|678.e: Zhe Chen sees training on ten thousand GPUs as today's compute ceiling for embodied research, not a big budget for OpenAI or Anthropic. OpenAI's robotics team comes from DALL·E and Sora, and he expects heavy spending on dexterous hands. Internet giants that don't start in 2026 will have no place in 2027 or 2028. Unitree's IPO approval gives leaders a valuation anchor. Bodies may not be winner-take-all, but brains could become an oligopoly, and a closed model that can't beat the best open one has no reason to exist. China wants full stacks but can't stand long stretches without revenue, so non-full-stack firms must lead a niche.
ex: Figure also lacks verified, concrete revenue from deployments
NVIDIA is the most valuable company but isn't full-stack

root.d: Where the next year or two leads

items.d: About six months, leaning to foundation models
Top open source versus top closed

t170|160.c: Honor's win signals big companies arriving. Robot startups that can't raise enough this year will be squeezed.
t170|160.e: Manqi Cheng thinks the marathon itself isn't market demand, but it has value as practice under pressure. Phone and car makers have more experience in mass manufacturing and product consistency. If startups building robot bodies can't raise enough this year, these big companies' robots could go straight to market in 2027.
ex: Honor swept the top three at the Yizhuang humanoid marathon

result.d: The race for robot bodies gets rewritten

t170|160.c: GEN-1's data curve suggests scaling may really work in embodied AI.
t170|160.e: GEN-1 trained an end-to-end model from scratch on about 500,000 hours of self-collected UMI-style data, gathered with handheld grippers, without relying on a pretrained base. It showed steady gains as data grew from 10,000 to 500,000 hours, and claims a 99% success rate on complex long-horizon tasks. Manqi Cheng takes this as a sign that scaling may work for embodied AI. She also notes how fast world models go from papers to new companies and rising valuations.
ex: By April, someone had already listed 49 world-model companies

t171|612.c: OpenAI used its rival's usage limits and price hikes to win back coders, but still trails on revenue.
t171|612.e: Anthropic's Claude 4.7 was poorly received. In May, Anthropic also began charging third-party harnesses (the programs that wrap a model so it can do work) full API prices. Users moved to OpenAI's Codex to save money, and Sam Altman offered companies two free months to switch. But Anthropic is growing revenue faster. Media reported its first profitable quarter, with its annual revenue forecast rising from about $47 billion to about $62 billion in just over a month. OpenAI's is about $40 billion. Henry thinks it matters little which one goes public first.
ex: Companies Henry invested in use Devin, Claude Code and Codex side by side
They kept Devin because it works well with Slack

t171|612.c: Quietly weakening a model without telling users breaks a basic rule of alignment, and top models are rationed.
t171|612.e: Fable and Mythos share the same base model and differ only in guardrails, the safety limits on what a model will answer. Fable's are so strict it refuses even cancer-related questions. Its system card also admits it may lower its abilities without telling users. Henry calls this an alignment mistake by definition, and within hours the company switched to telling users when it refuses. Three days after launch, a US government ban took Fable offline worldwide, and he thinks such rules may become normal. GPT-5.6 scores about 91.9% on Terminal Bench but is open to only about twenty approved organizations.
ex: OpenAI never published GPT-5.6's score on the SWE-bench Pro coding test

d.verdict: Each has strengths, but few people can actually use them

t171|612.c: Before AI can keep improving itself, it must first automate research, and its weak spot is research taste.
t171|612.e: Henry separates two ideas. Automated research means AI runs a whole research process on its own. RSI, recursive self-improvement, means a system keeps improving itself. He argues automation comes first. The ladder runs from hyperparameter search (auto-tuning training settings) to automated architecture search, to today's harness tuning, then training-recipe search, and finally optimizing the whole system. Anthropic says it is in a phase that is "not exponential, but compounding," with humans still the bottleneck. Anthropic has proposed slowing down on purpose, but Henry notes rivals may not slow down unless the whole world coordinates.
ex: Anthropic says Claude writes over 80% of its merged code
Each engineer now merges about 8 times as much code per day
One AI agent spent 800 hours completing a piece of safety research

t171|612.c: Firms with private data and clear evals will train their own models, but startups shouldn't rush into it.
t171|612.e: Harvey, the legal AI company, worked with Applied Compute to post-train Zhipu's open model GLM 5.1, further training it for their tasks. It beat Anthropic and OpenAI on Harvey's own legal-agent evals, and Harvey then trained another with Fireworks. There are three motives: closed models cost too much, a government ban could cut off access, and model makers might absorb the business and turn them into the next Cursor. Henry thinks open models plus private data could stay ahead long term. But this only suits companies with private data, clear evals and frequent, high-value work.
ex: Palo Alto Networks' CEO publicly called on Anthropic to cut Claude's prices
Chinese open models hit No. 1 four times in eight weeks; GLM 5.2 costs about one-sixth

root.d: Open model base plus private data

items.d: Closed frontier models cost too much
A ban could cut off access

t171|612.c: Top labs will keep trading the lead, unless one gets self-improving AI to speed up first.
t171|612.e: Models are now close in ability, so the contest is about product, go-to-market, keeping talent and how well models behave for users. Henry partly agrees with an OpenAI researcher who said the models are on par but the products are a mess. Even well-funded teams can no longer catch up through pretraining: xAI gave up training its own models and now rents compute, and Cohere was folded into SpaceX. The lead has always changed hands, and even GPT-4's lead in 2023 was caught. Unless one lab clearly speeds up self-improvement, the leaders will keep taking turns.
ex: SpaceX bought Cohere for about $60 billion
Google acquired the Windsurf team for a little over $2 billion
The best closed models still lead open ones by about six months

t171|160.c: Automated research and AI self-improvement are both partly happening, with humans doing less and less.
t171|160.e: On the debate over whether automation or self-improvement comes first, Manqi Cheng thinks both are already partly happening, just not fully automatic yet. That creates a dilemma: Anthropic argues for slowing down for humanity's sake while believing rivals won't slow down. Researchers' sense of achievement and worth is also taking a hit. She adds that almost nobody asks whether demand for intelligence and compute could ever be oversupplied. Top labs assume demand has no ceiling.
ex: AI is still in its "Tycho Brahe stage": lots of observation, little explanation

marks.d: Automation and self-improvement both partly happening

t171|160.c: Building on closed top models risks being cut off, and gains from training your own may not last.
t171|160.e: Fable was pulled by a ban three days after launch. Manqi Cheng points out that if the ban had come a month later, companies already building on it would have lost much more. That shows the risk of depending on closed frontier models. But on Harvey-style self-training, she notes that the fine-tuning gains of 2024 were eventually wiped out as base models improved. Whether this round lasts remains to be seen.

items.d: Fable gone three days after launch
The later the ban, the bigger the loss
Open model base plus private data
Better base models erased the last gains

t172|384.c: Outside driver-assist suppliers' window is nearly shut: two or three will remain in China, three or four globally.
t172|384.e: Cao stands by last year's call, based only on first-mover and scale advantages. Momenta and Huawei hold about 90% of city navigation-assist driving together, which gives them pricing power. Second-tier players have few customers and little revenue, and delivery work eats so much that little is left for core R&D. Carmakers pick suppliers based on whether they'll survive five years and whether the technology gap is shrinking or growing. As pricing shifts to subscriptions, brand and experience matter more, so the market will only concentrate. The third slot depends on chipmakers building their own systems. Tesla won't sell to others.
ex: Carmakers' in-house teams don't count; they're seen as internal suppliers
Tesla's FSD entering China will speed up the shakeout but won't change the outcome

items.d: All competing on city driving assist
Few customers, too little R&D money
Survival and the technology gap decide

t172|384.c: Driver assistance is like batteries: mostly good versus better, so suppliers consolidate, not car brands.
t172|384.e: About 80-90% of the driver-assist experience is a standardized contest of good versus better, and style accounts for only 10-20%. Industries like that reward first movers and scale, so there are few players. Cars, though, are like clothing or housing: tastes differ and many brands thrive. So Cao rejects the old prediction that car brands would shrink while suppliers fought price wars. Driver assistance is a paid option that many buyers take, helping carmakers sell more cars at higher prices, so suppliers add profit. Building in-house versus buying the best supplier is like making your own batteries versus using CATL.
ex: Momenta's gross margin rose from under 20% in 2023 to over 70% in 2025
BYD doing everything in-house is like leverage; what matters is a great car like the Han

d.verdict: Driver-assist suppliers are like batteries; car brands are like clothing

t172|384.c: If it gets ten times better each year, driver assistance becomes a must-have, not a bonus, by 2028.
t172|384.e: Two years ago driver assistance was a fun toy. It has just crossed the line into genuinely useful. If performance improves tenfold a year, then by 2028 even an ordinary L2++ car, which still needs a human watching, will drive at least as safely as a person. Cao disagrees that driver assistance isn't central to buying a car. It rarely beats price or looks, but in surveys it has climbed from last place to fourth. At carmakers, the person in charge of it has moved up from department head to president or chairman, making it a top-priority project.
ex: At road works, the newer R7 steers around earlier and more smoothly than R6

t172|384.c: R&D spending will keep doubling, mostly on training compute, but losses shouldn't keep growing.
t172|384.e: Momenta has spent somewhere between $1 billion-plus and just under $2 billion on self-driving R&D in total. To keep improving tenfold a year, most new money will go to training data centers, with spending on GPUs (the chips used to train AI) roughly doubling year after year. Cao believes that as a public company, piling up losses for years would hurt investors. So this year's planned loss keeps narrowing, with break-even in 2027 and profit in 2028. The main point of going public was brand and trust, not raising money.
ex: Cao rates Momenta as not very well known, but fairly well regarded

t172|384.c: Simple math says only mass-produced cars can supply enough data, a belief unchanged for a decade.
t172|384.e: Human drivers have about one major crash per 100 million km. To be ten times safer, a driverless car must go a billion km per crash. Proving that statistically takes about 100 such events, or 100 billion km of data. No company fleet can collect that, only mass-produced cars can, which is where Momenta's "one flywheel, two legs" strategy comes from. Cao thinks the key to success is simple: a data-driven architecture plus huge amounts of data. The culture is to build first and talk later. In 2020, when he talked about planning with deep learning, people called him a fraud, and explaining didn't help.
ex: The steps: deep-learning planning in 2023, end-to-end in 2024, reinforcement learning in 2025
The 2026 step is world models, AI that simulates how the real world changes

items.d: About one major crash per 100 million km

t172|384.c: One world-model foundation powers every robo business, and in robotaxis Momenta only supplies the AI driver.
t172|384.e: For the next five years, Robo One comes first, Robo Truck second and Robotaxi third. Robo Truck means bulk freight like coal and ore, where demand is strong and competition thin. Long-haul trucking is hardest and comes last. In robotaxis, Momenta only provides the AI driver for a revenue share, while platform partners own the fleets and the capital costs. It won't compete with Didi or Amap, or take on heavy assets. Mass-market cars and every robo business share one world model, an AI that simulates the real world, so a tenfold better base lifts them all.
ex: Fleet projection: from 30-some vehicles in late 2025 to over 100,000 by 2028
JD.com, Meituan and Hello entering is seen as driven by Waymo's high valuation

root.d: A tenfold better base lifts every application

items.d: Only the AI driver, for a revenue share

t172|384.c: Momenta will enter home robots in 2027, betting on a 2030 turning point and funding it with driving profits.
t172|384.e: World models make physical-world data truly usable, and he estimates over 80% of Momenta's self-driving data and training setup can be reused for robots. It's waiting through 2025 and 2026 to first upgrade its flywheel to L4 (fully driverless in set conditions) and the robo businesses, until the team has spare capacity. Otherwise it would be three pots with two lids. On-device compute can be solved by 2028, with self-driving leading the way, and robot hardware must drop to $10,000-20,000. Robot R&D will take at least $10 billion, paid from driver-assist profits rather than endless cash burn. Momenta designs robots but won't build the hardware.
ex: Generalist pretrained without a robot body, then post-trained on one; success rose from 50% to 90%
Cao estimates a home robot will cost about 100,000 yuan, with demand from an aging society

t172|384.c: Solve new problems with the main system first, then innovate inside it, instead of starting side projects.
t172|384.e: Cao believes too many separate silos would tear the company apart. So he set three rules: solve key problems in the simplest way, give low priority to methods that can't fit the shared architecture, and choose approaches that build up over time and pull the organization together.
