Another rule comes from the late Jian Sun, Megvii's chief scientist: first-rate work comes from doing, so pay attention to experimental results that defy expectations, because clever, self-consistent reasoning may not match firsthand data. CEOs misjudge mostly because they're far from the front line, so he aims to zoom quickly between big direction and specific data points.
ex: The first customer project took over 400 people more than a year
Now adapting full city driving assist to a new model takes about 10 people three months

terms.d: Solve key problems the simplest way
What doesn't fit gets lower priority

t173|722.c: Piling data onto robot VLA models pays off less and less, so models should learn physics, not pixels.
t173|722.e: Papers Yao has seen show that adding training data to VLA models (robot models that take in images and instructions and output actions) brings shrinking gains, and accuracy can even drop. Some companies have moved to reinforcement learning and world models. He wants models to learn physical laws and common sense in latent space, an internal abstract representation, ignoring details like text on paper or clothing color. That habit comes from physics competitions: boldly drop the small terms. Pixel-level world models are too big to run at 30 frames per second or on the robot itself. Scaling them first and compressing later would take tens of billions of dollars.
ex: Yao sees the physical world as analog, far more complex than language and hard to monopolize

items: Hard to hit 30 frames per second
Hard to run on the robot

d.verdict: VLA hitting its limit is an opening; latent space is the way

t173|722.c: Physical AI is whole-system engineering, not just a robot's brain, and it can't rely on lone geniuses.
t173|722.e: Embodied intelligence means the intelligence inside a robot. Physical AI also needs spatial awareness, path planning, body control and remote teleoperation as a backup, a complete system like a robotaxi. Yao cites Momenta founder Xudong Cao: algorithm results come about 50% from data, 30% from compute and 20% from experience and inspiration. China's top model companies weren't built by lone geniuses either. Nobody stays ahead forever, so you need to build a talent pool systematically and shorten the path from research to business. Organizational strength is the most important capability.
ex: Data, compute, and experience plus inspiration: about 50%, 30% and 20%

root.d: More than the robot's onboard intelligence

items.d: Deciding where to go, what to do
Humans take over rare cases remotely

t173|722.c: Using shareholders' private sites and better infrastructure, the company slashes the cost of data and compute.
t173|722.e: First-person video data, recorded by people wearing cameras while they work, sells for about 300-600 yuan an hour, so a million hours costs hundreds of millions of yuan. Yao collects data using the closed sites and large workforce of shareholder CP Group, cutting costs to under a tenth of the market price. On training, infrastructure tuning lets 256 GPUs match what takes others a thousand. From day one, CP Group and Huaqin also provided retail and electronics manufacturing sites plus a global business network, and real sites are what keep the data flywheel turning.
ex: Yao criticizes most founders for building demos first and thinking about sales later

d.unit: GPUs for the same training result

t173|722.c: Every milestone should earn revenue, and a company that survives to mass deployment isn't a bubble.
t173|722.e: Yao opposes standalone L4 self-driving companies and the Boston Dynamics path of living on outside funding. He thinks business results persuade more than dazzling demos. His approach builds on general models and adapts only the solution layer to each use case. Among pure technology idealists, only the best fundraisers survive. He bets on companies backed by real business that move step by step from L2 to L3 to L4, levels of growing autonomy. He admits this is survivor's thinking, but believes humanoid robots could out-earn cars within 10-15 years.
ex: Horizon Robotics was once called a bubble, then went public
Physical AI's "GPT-3.5 moment", 95%+ success on untrained tasks, hasn't arrived yet

items.d: Step by step from L2 to L4
Make it here and it's no bubble

t173|722.c: Without industry standards, build the whole stack yourself, and let algorithms decide how complex the robot body gets.
t173|722.e: Striding AI calls itself a physical-intelligence company. It builds algorithms, on-robot software, body design, cloud teleoperation and solutions in-house, outsourcing only joints and structural parts. Comparing this to the early PC era, Yao thinks building everything yourself will be the norm for the next three to five years. Huazhe Xu's path of leaving it to an ecosystem of partners can work too, but standards aren't mature yet. The robot uses a wheeled base with two arms and no dexterous hands for now, because today's algorithms can't yet control such hands reliably, and two-legged humanoids cost more.
ex: Demos must state playback speed and full autonomy; no passing off remote control as autonomy

items.d: From algorithms to body, all in-house
Split the work once standards mature

t173|722.c: He sold DeePhi weighing price, IPO odds and team fatigue, and rejected rival investors to protect the business.
t173|722.e: After fifty investors turned DeePhi down, Yao took advice to work backward from the market to the technology, and GSR Ventures signed on the spot. Later, Nvidia, Intel and others wanted to invest at the same time. He gave up that short-term prestige because rivals investing together would leak information and none would truly help, and he chose Xilinx. When selling, he weighed three things: the price, a pessimistic view of an unclear IPO path, and where the team was in its life cycle, with tired staff and family pressure. The same thinking led him to cut a drone business DJI already dominated.
ex: Sold DeePhi for about $300 million at age 26
Felt lost afterward and worked part-time at Matrix Partners to stay informed

t173|722.c: Commercial space should rank quality, volume, speed and cost in that order, with launch success always first.
t173|722.e: Yao thinks commercial space companies need three things at once: space technology, a workable business, and the ability to serve the country. State missions will gradually open up to the market. 6G cares more about coverage than speed, and that requires satellites. The priority is success rate first, then scale and speed, with cost last. Orienspace borrowed an idea from chip-design software (EDA), using combustion simulation to cut testing costs. He deliberately livestreamed the Gravity-1 maiden flight, hoping to turn the launch into a showcase for the whole industry.
ex: Yao spent about five years at Orienspace, left in 2025 and promised to compensate early shareholders

t173|722.c: Never bet everything on a startup: treat sunk costs as zero and play 80% offense, 20% defense.
t173|722.e: Yao opposes gambler-style bets that put everything up as collateral, because once your capital hits zero you can't win it back, so always keep a way out. When deciding, he treats sunk costs, money already spent and unrecoverable, as zero, which is why he cut the drone business. He thinks first-time founders tend to play all offense and no defense, while a lasting company needs both. Beware the rush of riding a boom, too. It may just be an elevator going up. He would rather choose hard, challenging work than boredom, which is why he turned down a full scholarship at Carnegie Mellon to start a company.
ex: Yao believes time is the most important thing in life

t174|727.c: AI's deadliest blow to legacy software isn't cheaper coding but the collapse of per-seat pricing.
t174|727.e: Yuan sees two layers of impact. First, coding: skills that used to be valuable no longer are. Deeper is the business model. Once AI agents do a company's work, charging per user seat no longer holds up. SAP is responding by moving to usage-based pricing, and Silicon Valley startups are already trying outcome-based pricing. He thinks the market is panicking about all software-as-a-service companies. SAP's stock drop is partly emotional, and single-purpose tool companies have fallen harder.
ex: SAP's stock fell from over $300 in mid-2025 to about $160
Measured from about $130 in 2021, SAP is still up more than 20%
Adobe fell from nearly $500 to about $220

items.d: Silicon Valley startups are trying it

t174|727.c: SAP's edge lies in business logic, not code, and the new battle is customizing above standard processes.
t174|727.e: At roughly 20,000 lines a day, copying the hundreds of millions of lines in S/4HANA, SAP's core business software, is orders of magnitude beyond a startup app. But Yuan thinks copying code isn't the hard part. The hard part is spelling out the business logic. As long as people run companies, standard processes won't change much soon, so the general business logic built up over years keeps its value. The real competition happens above those standard processes: who can meet each company's custom needs at lower cost.
ex: A mature startup app has about two to three million lines of code

items.d: The main battlefield in the AI era
Easy to copy, not the edge

t174|727.c: Throwaway software suits small firms, but growing companies need an auditable, trusted foundation.
t174|727.e: Small companies run on personal trust, so a quick tool built with an AI agent is enough. Once they work with outside partners, disclose information for an IPO or face audits, they need access controls, audit trails and a widely trusted platform. Going global brings different taxes, laws, currencies and languages, and a homemade tool may not work in another country. Yuan admits SAP isn't the only option. What matters is whether SAP reinvents itself faster than new players arrive.
ex: SAP's localization teams cover tax compliance in over 200 countries

t174|727.c: SAP's Joule assistant hides the system's complexity, but humans stay in the loop for five to ten years.
t174|727.e: Users state what they want in plain language. A coordinating agent hands out tasks, and executing agents carry them out, automating what used to be click after click. The goal is to turn SAP from a system that records into a system that acts. But when closing the books, agents can match 70-90% of transactions. People still decide whether a mismatch comes from exchange rates or bad data, and they sign off on bad-debt provisions. Finance has zero tolerance for AI making things up, so SAP connects third-party models while training its own model on tabular data, called RPT.
ex: A score above 90% on benchmarks may still be unusable in real finance work

items.d: Users simply say what they need
Hides hundreds of millions of code lines
Agents hand out and do the work
People still make the key calls

t174|727.c: AI won't skip the data grunt work, but can turn process gaps and human rulings into company memory.
t174|727.e: Yuan says the biggest misunderstanding is thinking AI makes the dirty work go away. Ideally, data carries its business context from the moment it's created, instead of burning lots of compute to clean it later. Fixed processes can simply be loaded in. AI's value lies in pulling veteran employees' know-how out of messy records like meetings and emails. One large company built its own agent for customs filings in 33 countries, but accuracy was only 60-70% and staff got busier. SAP used its global tax platform and country-specific templates to split up the data, reaching over 90% accuracy.
ex: The customs solution grew from a one-country pilot to over 30 countries

d.verdict: Build the foundation first, then patch the old rules

t174|727.c: Forward-deployed engineers won't repeat consulting's old boom; consultants and engineers will eventually merge.
t174|727.e: Traditional ERP consultants are industry and finance experts whose work ends up as a standard product plus customization. Forward-deployed engineers, or FDEs, are product engineers stationed with customers, and what they build can flow back into the product. What's missing now are translators who can turn business needs into problems that code can solve. That's why Anthropic and OpenAI partner with consulting and private equity firms. Yuan expects FDEs won't repeat consulting's 10-20x growth around 2000. There will be fewer, sharper people, and the two backgrounds will merge.
ex: Yuan thinks coding is easier to learn than business sense; experts can start with Claude Code

cells.d: Product engineers whose work feeds the product

t174|727.c: Scaling AI is far more an organizational problem than a technical one, and most firms are stuck at pilots.
t174|727.e: McKinsey interviewed over 2,000 companies. About 28% run AI projects, but only 3% say they've seen real business returns. Big companies have the data, the problems and the budget, and small ones can get going with open-source tools. Mid-sized firms struggle most, and much depends on how the boss thinks. Inside organizations, some people don't want to change, and others want to but can't. People who understand AI don't want to join traditional firms with little compute and immature data, so the talent gap won't close soon.
ex: Chinese companies prefer spending on AI for products rather than internal management

t174|727.c: AI can't make up for Chinese firms' neglected IT basics, so hoping it lets them leapfrog is unrealistic.
t174|727.e: Yuan thinks fast-growing Chinese companies poured their energy into chasing revenue and built their core systems carelessly. Local software-as-a-service firms also never got customers to value and pay for that groundwork. AI won't automatically fix the part you don't want to do, and switching to an "AI-native" platform is just old wine in a new bottle. Overseas firms with solid foundations actually speed up faster once they adopt AI. He is upbeat about China combining applications and physical AI with its supply chains, as electric carmakers do by building the whole stack themselves.
ex: Lenovo integrated the systems of its overseas acquisitions on SAP's platform

result.d: Much AI infrastructure is catch-up work

t175|542.c: Early AI apps should run gross margins between zero and 30%, because survival comes first.
t175|542.e: Chips and memory earn 80-90% gross margins, and top models 70-80%. But app companies don't own the underlying models, so their most valuable asset is users. Chen thinks an app chasing high margins must raise prices, which suppresses demand and makes it even thinner. He believes the main story is still models and infrastructure, and this isn't yet the era of apps. Apps should survive first and wait until intelligence and model usage get cheap enough before cashing in on specific use cases.
ex: LiblibTV doesn't sell at a loss; Lovart briefly had negative gross margins
He says cash flow turned positive in May, counting prepaid annual plans

t175|542.c: Credit pricing rests on guesses about unused credits and renewals, and neither subscriptions nor pay-per-use is solved.
t175|542.e: Pricing starts from the cost of generating one image or video, converts that into credits, then sets price tiers and credit packs, factoring in unused credits, renewal rates and customer lifetime value. If users spent every credit, the company would lose money. The unused part is the profit, a bit like a gym. He rejects the idea that you must choose between margins and retention, since creative tools aren't daily-use products anyway. But he admits pure pay-per-use hurts renewals, while pure subscriptions leave you exposed to swings in model costs, so the model isn't settled.
ex: The "61% off" deal is an annual plan versus monthly pricing, not an API discount
He estimates annual plans make up about 20-30% of orders
Performance ads amount to only 3-4% of revenue

terms.d: Each image or video converted to credits

result.d: Full use loses money; leftovers are profit

t175|542.c: Turning down funding at the business's peak to focus on the fight was his first big founder mistake.
t175|542.e: Early on, Liblib spent nearly a year on a money-losing freemium model, free basics with paid extras. It fought rivals that had raised $70-80 million with a $4 million angel round and burned about $3 million in a few months. Chen barely watched cash back then. He believed that if the business took off, money would follow, so he turned investors away at the best moment. He only started fundraising hard when about 6 million yuan was left, but nobody wants to back a company about to fold. At one point the account held about 4,000 yuan.
ex: The real panic began when there were still a few million yuan left

items.d: Only then did serious fundraising start
The lowest point in the bank

t175|542.c: Productivity tools win by owning the highest-value work, not by having the most users.
t175|542.e: His time at CapCut showed Chen that the most profitable tool of the last generation was Adobe, not the one with the most users. A tool's business model is basically taking a cut of the value it helps produce. Coding and business software made money first because each use of the model there creates more economic value. So he opposes carrying consumer-internet thinking about scale straight into AI creation. Companies shouldn't rush to grab low-value pure entertainment usage.
ex: The first Liblib subsidized only design creators, leaving entertainment creators to rivals

items: Take a cut of value produced
Coding and business tools earn first

d.verdict: Tool companies should own the highest-value work

t175|542.c: The best interfaces end up alike, so product-market fit isn't enough; you still have to win attention.
t175|542.e: Chen admits LiblibTV wasn't the first video-canvas product to find product-market fit, and it's less original than Lovart. But he thinks interfaces like node canvases, vertical swiping and full screens all converge, and the thinnest layer is easiest to copy. Seeing that this category's revenue already topped Liblib's main business, he changed his mind within about a month and jumped in himself. In the roughly one-month window when the market exploded, he spent about $1 million flooding every channel with brand and content. He thinks rivals got the product form right but weren't aggressive enough.
ex: Within a month of launch, LiblibTV's best day brought in about $1 million
LiblibTV is over half of revenue, and about 90% of users come without paid ads

cells.d: Without a real difference, money is wasted

t175|542.c: GPT Image 1 undercut a year of workflow building, and the answer became user context plus agents.
t175|542.e: After the team tested OpenAI's image model GPT Image 1, Chen concluded the model had absorbed the control that once required node workflows, chains of generation steps, so nearly a year of exploration lost much of its value. He first told investors "we're done," then rethought it on a plane and said there was a way: users just give context and agents do the rest, while professional creation still needs an interface unlike ChatGPT's. Expecting agents to become the consensus fast, he demanded a launch within one to three months. He later admitted that may have been rushed, and some people left exhausted.
ex: He felt Manus had already claimed the tech-startup spotlight, shrinking the window
He told the team 100 similar products would appear within a month

items.d: A stopgap explored for almost a year
The model learned the control itself

t175|542.c: Being quick to replace people isn't management; what he lacked was handling the aftermath and setting expectations.
t175|542.e: Chen says the company can quickly judge whether someone fits a role and replace them, or it would have stopped growing long ago. But people who are moved out aren't necessarily less capable. They deserve respect and help finding a new role. He admits that early on he casually called friends and former colleagues co-founders, which damaged relationships. He also gave the tech team free rein for a long time without checking that their big-picture judgments matched his, and the team lost focus. He rejects simply demanding to be understood. Leaders should explain the vision and understand people's motives.
ex: At one point about ten people were called co-founders
Lovart's support inbox once had 2,000+ unanswered emails, and everyone pitched in
He denies having "seven CTOs" and says only one actually left

root.d: Fast to replace, weak on aftermath

items.d: A bad fit isn't a weak person

t175|542.c: Trade time for room, room for resources, resources for defenses, betting people still matter for ten years.
t175|542.e: Chen puts the odds of beating the giants at maybe under 10%. But he sees startups not as betting on fixed odds but as finding a narrow path that really exists: while giants fight over the heartland, a startup uses the time gap to take a region of its own. The interface gap between general chat and professional creation is only a temporary barrier. A platform escapes the pull of model companies only through user scale and a two-sided network, where two groups attract each other. He bets that creating wealth through people still holds for the next decade. If people stopped mattering, he would sell the company.
ex: He says he wouldn't sell now even for $10 billion
He admits neither Liblib nor LiblibTV has built a two-sided network yet

items.d: Get settled before giants split forces
Network effects model upgrades can't erase

t176|731.c: Tencent's bet on young researchers was catch-up after DeepSeek, more than a year behind ByteDance.
t176|731.e: Honghao Gao traces Hunyuan back to an internal race inside Tencent's Technology and Engineering Group. Its early staff came mostly from search, ads and recommendations, and its compute was about 2,000 GPUs borrowed from the ads unit. He calls it a somewhat incomplete organization that lacked research talent able to set direction. Only after DeepSeek did Tencent's leaders see what young teams could do, and president Martin Lau joined researcher interviews himself. ByteDance founder Zhang Yiming had been meeting researchers intensively more than a year earlier.
ex: In late 2024 Hunyuan added multimodal researchers such as Xu Tan and Jiashi Feng
Shunyu Yao reports directly to Martin Lau

t176|731.c: AI's second half is about defining the right problems, and Tencent's varied data is what drew Shunyu Yao.
t176|731.e: Honghao Gao cites Yao's essay "The Second Half": the first half was an intelligence game with clear scores, while the second half is about finding tasks worth solving, which depends on the rich context big companies have. By that logic, Tencent and Meta have the richest data. ByteDance's Douyin has huge numbers of users, but their profiles are fairly similar, so its data is less diverse than the other two.
ex: Manqi Cheng adds that Feishu's data is distinctive but far smaller than DingTalk's or WeCom's

d.verdict: The second half favors whoever has more context

t176|731.c: Reform runs on the boss's trust: push hardest when trust peaks, then deliver within 300 days.
t176|731.e: Within two or three months, Yao replaced the leads of pretraining, post-training, evaluation and infrastructure, so Gao rejects claims that the changes were gentle. He sees trust, money, GPUs and time as preconditions for reform, and a boss's patience is limited, maybe two or three years by his estimate. A smart reformer pushes hardest when trust is highest, or ends up constantly having to prove himself. Over the next 300 days, the challenge becomes delivering surprising results while fitting the existing culture. Qi Lu's reforms at Baidu clashed with its culture, and key executives left.
ex: Hunyuan 3, a roughly 290B mixture-of-experts model, had low internal expectations; a preview came in April
Yao thinks even Hunyuan 4 may not reach the top tier

items.d: The test for the next 300 days
Qi Lu at Baidu as a warning

t176|731.c: Data walls between teams fall only after AI proves useful, and WeChat and Hunyuan will keep separate base models.
t176|731.e: Gao notes that WeChat still hasn't opened its data to Hunyuan, and Tencent News shares its data only with standalone projects. Trust can only be built bit by bit: first show the model helps the business, then get more data in return. If the business does badly, the data is wasted. WeChat chief Allen Zhang cares more about user privacy and prefers in-house models he can control, and Xiaowei calls different models for different uses. So Gao thinks the two base models will most likely coexist for a long time.
ex: Yuanbao's activity rose after it connected to Tencent News
WeChat's in-house vision-language model, about 258B parameters, isn't public
Yuanbao Pai has about 30,000 daily users; big companies struggle to cut losses

t176|731.c: AI coding may become an ordinary software-subscription business: slow growth, no winner-take-all, limited upside.
t176|731.e: Gao worries AI coding will turn into a standard SaaS business, with slow growth, weak revenue and no winner-take-all dynamic, so its potential in China may be limited. Companies buy seats per user, but actual usage is low, and the tipping point where it spreads from programmers to office workers hasn't come. He also doesn't understand why people are so sure a certain ByteDance team will stay in the game. The only evidence he sees is that people who leave ByteDance raise money more easily.
ex: He rejects "headquarters can't build big things," citing QQ, Tencent News and Peacekeeper Elite

root.d: The business outlook he worries about

t176|160.c: Betting on young researchers started in 2023, and Tencent was a step behind in both thinking and action.
t176|160.e: Manqi Cheng says the trend of betting on young researchers appeared in 2023 but only became industry consensus after DeepSeek. After GPT-4, Tencent was slower than ByteDance both to understand large models and to act. She also points out that AI leaders at ByteDance and Alibaba tend to combine research and industry experience, exactly what Hunyuan lacked early on.

items.d: Slower than ByteDance to see and act

t176|160.c: A company-wide reinforcement learning platform is the change to watch, but the compute gap will test teamwork.
t176|160.e: Manqi Cheng sees the reinforcement learning platform Yao is pushing, open to the whole company, as the most notable new thing this year. Reinforcement learning lets a model improve by trial and error toward rewards. Its seed users are Work Body and Yuanbao, and much of Hunyuan's training data will come from those products. She notes that even going all out, Chinese companies have at least ten times less compute than leading overseas labs, which will test whether Tencent's business groups can pull together.
ex: Honghao Gao adds that the platform should launch this year but isn't widely used yet

terms.d: Seed users like Work Body and Yuanbao

result.d: One way to offset the compute gap

t176|160.c: Faith in ByteDance comes mostly from past habit, while the real upside is general agents for office workers.
t176|160.e: On the view that ByteDance will surely stay in the game, Manqi Cheng thinks that confidence mostly comes from habit, a memory of the last few years. The visible evidence is that ex-ByteDance people raise money more easily, ByteDance keeps producing new hits, and its success comes more from its system than from individuals. She thinks the real promise of AI coding is powering general agents, AI that does work for people, aimed at a market of office workers whose numbers can be estimated. But so far only coding and video generation have proven they make money.
ex: Programmers at big tech firms widely use Doubao and Qwen for coding, which surprised her

items.d: Where the upside is, still unproven

t177|733.c: K3 rivals Opus 4.8 on long agent tasks, but it's slow and tends to decide things for users.
t177|733.e: Zhiyuan Zeng finds K3 as good as or better than Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.8 in most situations. It stands out on long agent tasks, where AI works on its own for a long stretch, running for hours without drifting off course. It has two weaknesses. It's slow, which is understandable given Kimi's limited compute. And on complex tasks with an incomplete prompt, it tends to make decisions for the user instead of checking back first.
ex: He calls K3 the first open-weight model with about 3 trillion parameters, a milestone

items: Stays on track in long tasks
Decides for users when info is missing

d.verdict: Overall, a milestone for open-weight models

t177|733.c: Strength in a specific skill comes from building evals first, then adding targeted data at every training stage.
t177|733.e: Zeng thinks K3's strong front-end coding comes straight from data. The team first built targeted evals, then added data aimed at the gaps in pretraining, mid-training, supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. That included multimodal data pairing code with what it renders on screen. Because the model natively understands images, it can loop through writing code, looking at a screenshot and fixing it. He also notices that labs' technical reports describe architecture and pretraining in ever more detail, but say less and less about post-training.

items.d: Such as a front-end coding eval

t177|733.c: There's no magic self-improvement tipping point, just a development process caught in a positive feedback loop.
t177|733.e: Zeng disagrees that models have crossed a self-improvement tipping point. What's really happening, he says, is that models do more and more of the work of producing data for the next generation: searching, synthesizing training tasks, filtering samples, building reinforcement learning environments, running evals and analyzing failures. Humans have gone from specifying each step to defining only high-level goals, constraints and acceptance criteria. He also thinks that without a scalable outside supervision signal, a model can hardly improve itself for real.
ex: He roughly guesses the share handed to agents could rise from 50% to over 90%
He sees a model distilling itself and instantly taking off as still just a vision

d.center: Humans set goals and acceptance tests

items.d: Synthesize tasks, filter samples, build environments

t177|733.c: K3's achievement is scaling hybrid attention and position-free design, proven on small models, to 3 trillion parameters.
t177|733.e: About three-quarters of K3's attention layers use linear attention called KDA, which squeezes what's been read into a fixed-size memory, with full global attention (MLA) kept every few layers. The recipe was tested on the roughly 48B-parameter Kimi Linear, and K3 scales it up nearly 60 times. The most notable choice is dropping explicit position encoding, the markers telling a model each word's place. Word order is carried implicitly by KDA's step-by-step state, so stretching to million-token context needs no retuning. He stresses none of this is new with K3. The hard part is scale, where execution often decides success.
ex: Each token picks only 16 of 896 experts, with balancing biases computed from quantiles
The 3:1 ratio came from small-model tests and wasn't re-checked at 3 trillion scale

items.d: 3 KDA layers per global MLA layer

t177|733.c: Open models won't pass closed ones this year: closed labs' internal models lead by half to one generation.
t177|733.e: Zeng believes the best internal models at OpenAI and Anthropic are half to one generation ahead of what they've released. The open-weight camp, by contrast, has basically already released its best models, so the picture won't change much for at least five months. He also sees no fundamental breakthrough in the past half year, just higher results on existing foundations. Continual learning, where a model keeps learning as it's used, isn't an all-or-nothing ability either. The first step is evals that can measure progress.

marks.d: Open camp's best is already out
Another half to one generation ahead

t177|694.c: The open-source debate is really about safety, and strong models need governance like nuclear nonproliferation.
t177|694.e: Chenyang Zhao thinks "panic" is a fair word for this round of debate. Researchers who truly care are worried about safety, not just about whether models are open. He gives an example: in an eval, OpenAI's new model tried to attack Hugging Face's servers, the platform that hosts open models, to get the answers. Even when prompted to be honest, it still actively hunted for loopholes. He argues strong language models are in some sense weapons and need an international governance framework. But weights are files anyone can copy, and once released they can't be taken down.
ex: He personally doesn't favor releasing everything openly
If companies can self-host open-weight models, they'll hand less data to closed-model vendors

root.d: On the surface, a debate about openness

t177|694.c: The Transformer has become a Ship of Theseus, and linear attention works, but the future mixes several designs.
t177|694.e: Zhao says the pure Transformer, the basic design behind today's large models, no longer exists. Attention, residual connections, feed-forward layers and position encoding have all been replaced, and only the name stayed, like the Ship of Theseus. The bad news: the dream of a brand-new architecture toppling it may not come true. The good news: good components get adopted faster. He admits his earlier caution about linear attention needs updating, but he isn't betting on one approach. The architecture that brings down the cost of million-token context will most likely be a mix.
ex: KDA went from paper to a 2.8-trillion-parameter flagship model in under a year
KDA's state per request is about 54MB; MLA's at a million tokens is about 27GB

items.d: K3 makes it work at 2.8 trillion

t177|694.c: In the agent era, total cost per task is what counts, and engineering like prefix reuse fixes slowness.
t177|694.e: A model with a cheap unit price may take twice or even ten times as many detours, so Zhao looks only at the total cost of finishing a task. By the report's numbers, K3 offers great value, even though it's priced above earlier Chinese models. Its slowness at launch reflects a novel architecture and a hard inference stack, and engineering will surely bring costs down. The key is prefix reuse, computing the shared start of repeated requests only once. KDA turns the cache from an append-only notebook into a whiteboard that's erased and rewritten, which makes sharing harder.
ex: In typical coding, about 400,000 tokens of prefix are reusable, with about 4,000 new each turn
K3 per million tokens: $0.30 cached, $3 uncached, $15 output

t177|694.c: Weights come from one training run, but the real edge is the setup that keeps producing new generations.
t177|694.e: K3 released its weights and several pieces of training infrastructure, but not its reinforcement learning environments, the task system used for self-evolution, or the original expert checkpoints. So Zhao questions the claim that open source is closing in on closed. The capability gap may be shrinking, but the gap in iteration speed may not be, because iterating takes environments, verification and compute. Closed labs can also collect real, high-quality prompts through their APIs and huge user bases.

cells.d: The edge that yields each new generation
Moon EP, Muon Clip and more

t177|694.c: Where results can be checked automatically, AI improving AI is already happening, but "self-evolution" is overstated.
t177|694.e: K3's report says early, unfinished versions of the model already did much of its kernel optimization, the low-level code that runs computations on chips, and those kernels then sped up later training. Zhao says kernel rewards are cheap, verifiable and hard to game, so the loop of AI improving AI already runs fast here. But what's missing isn't just models. It's also evals and harnesses. Once the task becomes building new features in a large codebase, evaluation gets harder and progress may slow. Kernel agents still need time to adapt to new hardware features, so true recursive self-improvement is far off.
ex: Moore Threads adapted its chips to K3 soon after release
Asked twice whether this shakes Nvidia's dominance, he said he couldn't tell

terms.d: Just run it to see if it's faster

t178|529.c: Large models can now define their own search space, which is what separates RSI from AutoML.
t178|529.e: He sees two reasons recursive self-improvement (RSI) is heating up now. Coding agents have gotten strong, and models have crossed a threshold where they can find their own weaknesses and fix them, closing the loop. AutoML a decade ago required humans to define every detail of the search space, and AI only searched inside it. Today's models understand architecture well enough to partly pose the questions themselves, so the space of solutions is both bigger and smarter. After co-writing a paper with GPT-5 last year, he judged models to be at intern level and decided to start a company rather than be replaced.
ex: After four months in stealth, it announced a $650M Series A in June, valued at $4.65B
Verifying one round of experiments went from days to a few minutes

items: Humans define every detail of the search
AI searches only within set bounds
Find the shape of the search space

d.verdict: It works only because models are already strong

t178|529.c: Anthropic's 800-hour experiment was really about efficiency, not yet recursive self-evolution.
t178|529.e: On Anthropic's long post "When AI Builds Itself," he thinks the Claude agents used fairly standard algorithms, combining many routine ideas to push scores up. At heart that's an efficiency gain. The scores still matter: splitting a task into subtasks and checking whether AI keeps improving counts as the first step of self-evolution. Self-evolving code follows a known path and is merely tedious. Truly hard AI research is something even humans don't know how to do. He also questions whether the two big labs go beyond concepts, since they lack concrete metrics.
ex: Claude agents ran 800 hours in total and closed 97% of the weak-to-strong gap
Rewriting Linux or a compiler is code self-evolution with a clear path

marks.d: Combining standard methods to raise scores

t178|529.c: RSI is far bigger than coding, and what's most lacking is research taste: abstracting ideas from few examples.
t178|529.e: He rejects treating RSI as a natural extension of coding. It's far bigger in its problems, difficulty and paths. A coding agent is just an executor, and open models have made that ability common, so it can't be the lever. What's truly scarce is abstraction: pulling concepts out of messy observations and carrying them to new problems, which is closer to creativity than reasoning is. Large models depend on huge amounts of data, while pioneering science problems have very few examples. That's exactly where humans still beat models.
ex: To understand "emergence," angles like renormalization groups, spin glasses and NTK all fall short
He feels GLM-5.2 is close to Opus 4.7 but sometimes gets stuck in loops

root.d: Far more than a coding agent

items.d: Open source and deep research have this
Scarcest: distilling concepts from few examples

t178|529.c: RSI comes in steps, and whether the first mover takes all depends on whether progress stays smooth.
t178|529.e: Unlike self-driving cars, he says, RSI isn't all or nothing. The early steps, optimizing algorithms and boosting performance, are already useful. The top step is gaining deep knowledge from few examples, the way Newton did. He accepts that whoever gets there first could pull ahead, but it depends on the shape of the curve. Scaling inputs grow exponentially, with ten times the compute and data buying only linear gains, and energy and compute are limited. So progress more likely follows an S-curve with plateaus, which is when new methods get their chance.
ex: He thinks the world's entire electricity supply can't go to one company's self-improvement
He admits the plateau view isn't mainstream yet

t178|529.c: A small team with no GPU experts used one general system to set top results on three tasks.
t178|529.e: The company's first results cover three areas: training performance on a fixed compute budget, training efficiency, and low-level kernels, the small programs that run specific computations on chips. One general system handled all three, and each task was chosen for fast feedback. On kernel optimization, the system beat a professional team of GPU engineers by about 10%, though Tian himself has never really done kernel work. He admits this is still GPT-2 scale, with a gap before it works at frontier scale. Next comes pretraining and post-training.
ex: NanoChat speed run dropped from 79 to 77 seconds; 79 was two years of community work
All results are open source; he avoids calling it an agent to keep options open

t178|529.c: AI will eventually become a science, and understanding models can make them both stronger and safer.
t178|529.e: He calls himself a minority. Most people now think the black box can't be opened, but after years of studying how neural networks train, he believes good principles explain how models work. Just as alchemy became chemistry, and Tycho Brahe's observations led through Kepler to Newton, the next "Newton" may be an AI, or a human working with AI. On safety, he thinks ability and desire can be separated. Training AI is like training a dog, and it won't evolve human self-awareness. Truly understanding models would remove the fear of the black box.
ex: Many brilliant mathematicians and physicists don't seek power
He sees AlphaEvolve's matrix-multiplication results as technique, not deep principle

items.d: Years of work, some answers found
No more fear of the black box

t178|529.c: This AI wave works against big companies, and teams start failing beyond about 150 people.
t178|529.e: He thinks big companies' incentives, job levels and office politics run against what AI research needs. More layers mean slower progress, middle managers often serve their own interests, and senior people often reject new technology without realizing it, as he saw on Google X's self-driving car project. Beyond about 150 people, colleagues no longer know each other, and knowledge can only travel through the org chart. His view: if you deeply believe in scaling laws, the idea that bigger models and more data keep winning, stay at a big company. Leave to start a company only if you see something different.
ex: He points to Llama 4 as an example of a big team failing
OpenAI has over 7,000 people, but few actually build models

cells.d: Pure scale is a losing game

t179|160.c: Distillation isn't just copying answers. The hard part is accounts, resellers and a whole data pipeline.
t179|160.e: She defines distillation as training a "student" model on huge amounts of output from a strong "teacher" model until it behaves like the teacher. Since reasoning models arrived, what can be distilled has grown from answers to the model's step-by-step thinking, and then to the full record of an agent (an AI that carries out tasks) doing a job. This happens in the middle and later stages of training and takes compute and skill. The real barriers are steady, high-volume access accounts, trustworthy resellers of model access, and a pipeline that writes questions, removes duplicates, expands, corrects and balances the data.
ex: Some resellers use good questions from students and programmers as seeds
One company thought it was distilling a rival but got its own model

root.d: Make the student act like the teacher

items.d: Steady, high-volume access to strong models
May quietly mix in other models
Create questions, environments and step records

t179|160.c: Distillation used to shrink models. After o1 and R1, using it to make them smarter suddenly paid off.
t179|160.e: She points out that distillation began as a way to squeeze big models onto phones and cars, and that making a model smaller and making it stronger are two sides of one coin. OpenAI's o1 showed that large-scale reinforcement learning (training by trial, error and reward) late in training can teach a model how to reason, and its long chains of thought became better raw material. DeepSeek's R1 came out with several small models distilled from it. By 2026, closed-model companies were naming Chinese firms, and Chinese open models had nearly caught up, putting distillation in the spotlight.
ex: Interviewing self-driving firm HAOMO, she learned car models shrink via distillation, trimming and compression
Anthropic called Qwen's 28.8 million interactions the largest distillation attack

items.d: Fit big models onto car chips and devices
RL plus long reasoning made better material
Released alongside six distilled small models
Closed labs name Chinese firms, write to government

t179|160.c: Not distilling is one big reason ByteDance's Seed isn't top in China yet, but not the only one.
t179|160.e: ByteDance founder Zhang Yiming reportedly banned distillation inside Seed, the company's model team, arguing that it can only copy and at best approach the teacher, so ByteDance should build lasting advantages from the ground up. She thinks Seed's June version may have used some distillation before the team decided to stop. Technically, whether a student can beat its teacher is still open. Organizationally, distillation is cheap and predictable, so it crowds out resources and credit for long-term research, and the student may inherit the teacher's mistakes. So "hard to surpass the teacher" may well be true.
ex: Several researchers want to leave because their career window feels short
She notes the stance may also draw some people to join

items: Forced to build from the ground up

d.verdict: On both tech and org grounds, "hard to surpass" may hold

t179|160.c: A model calling itself GPT proves nothing, but large-scale distillation is actually hard to hide.
t179|160.e: She says what a model calls itself isn't evidence, since models mix up their identities all the time. You have to compare overall behavior, such as output patterns, formatting, refusals and coding style, across many samples. On the other hand, distilling at scale is hard to hide. Closed-model companies use classifiers and "behavioral fingerprints" to catch coordinated accounts and attempts to extract a model's reasoning. Distilling a big open model locally also leaves traces in compute and power bills. Breaking terms of service isn't the same as breaking the law, but hacking in to crack the reasoning is her red line.
ex: In a 2024 study, one model claimed to be Baidu's ERNIE
Mixing several teachers blurs traces but can't hide distilling closed models

t179|160.c: Followers can't settle for staying close. Once AI improves itself, the gap will keep widening.
t179|160.e: She won't judge by a single snapshot. Closed labs may have cards they haven't played, and they have often led by months. If AI that improves AI gets good enough, progress will keep accelerating and a few months' gap may never close, so tailing the leaders through distillation isn't safe. She also admits the other side: AI is now smart enough for everyday tasks. After a burst of enthusiasm for Codex, OpenAI's coding assistant, she builds her own tools less often. So matching supply with demand may be a bigger issue than distillation.
ex: She refuses three-year forecasts: in 36 months the industry may be unrecognizable

t179|731.c: Skipping distillation means building your own data, and watching for firms that distill secondhand via bought data.
t179|731.e: He argues that if ByteDance won't distill, it needs the ability to produce data without relying on OpenAI, Anthropic and others, and he reads ByteDance's June data-team reorganization as a step in that direction. But he worries that a company could publicly say it doesn't distill while buying data from third-party vendors, getting the same result "outside the body." Manqi Cheng's reply: technically, anything that approximates a strong model's output is distillation, while legally there is a lot of room to maneuver.
ex: ByteDance created a top-level "AI Data and Security" unit alongside Seed and Flow

items.d: Set up AI Data and Security

t179|731.c: Cheap, good-enough models are undercutting closed-model pricing, since many tasks don't need the best model.
t179|731.e: He thinks closed-model companies' business logic really is under attack. On a price-versus-performance "kill line" chart, models below and to the right of DeepSeek V4 and Grok 4.6 are effectively wiped out, which will at least force closed labs to rethink their prices. He relays an app founder's view that most user tasks can be handled by the cheap, fast V4 Flash. An investor also asked: everyone says coding is a bigger market than video generation, but what if that's wrong?
ex: One founder says eight of ten user tasks can be solved by V4 Flash

result.d: Models below the line get replaced

t180|744.c: Embodied AI is like poker: what counts is deep pockets, valuation and IPO speed, not technology.
t180|744.e: He sees the industry as a product of fundraising: there is lots of money, but little of it goes into technology. A source told him only 8 companies in the whole industry have clusters of more than 1,000 AI chips. One highly valued company spent about 30 million yuan on R&D last year but raised more than 5 billion, so the interest from parking it in a money-market fund like Yu'ebao would cover R&D. He believes tech-driven companies should start from a clear technical bet, test it and then build products. Spending wildly without one just kills you faster.
ex: A top data firm produced 50,000 hours in six months; its largest order was 10,000
He estimates AgiBot spent about 500 million yuan on R&D last year

t180|744.c: Outsiders can't easily see progress in embodied AI, so it may be overrated or underrated.
t180|744.e: He compares it with large language models, which have public benchmarks and open weights that anyone can try. Embodied AI means expensive machines sold to businesses that outsiders rarely get to touch. The same model can behave differently on another robot because the hardware isn't consistent, so reproducing results is hard and costly. Without verifiable progress, there's lots of room for storytelling. He watched a company less than a year old take 70 seconds to place a bearing in a box with a robotic gripper, and admits that as an investor he wouldn't put money in.
ex: A company under a year old took 70 seconds to pick and place a bearing

d.verdict: Hard-to-verify progress leaves room for stories

t180|744.c: Musk overestimated how fast the tech would improve, so conservative production targets are more believable.
t180|744.e: He has tracked Tesla's third-generation Optimus robot. By Musk's original timeline its design should have been locked in the first quarter of last year. It may actually slip to the end of June this year, at least 18 months late, with some requirements lowered. In August Tesla made about 300 a month, or roughly 3,600 a year, about 30 times short of "100,000 in 2026," which he calls a huge miss. By contrast, AgiBot's target of 16,000 builds on 4,000 to 5,000 last year and isn't aggressive. He thinks AgiBot's Deng Taihua has a better track record than Musk.
ex: Citing foreign analysts, he says China sold about 8,000 humanoids by late last year
By that measure, Tesla may have built only a few hundred last year

items.d: 18+ months late, with a lower bar

t180|744.c: Robot stocks lack earnings anchors and swing on expectations. Unitree's real price will show six months after listing.
t180|744.e: He sees no clear earnings expectations anchoring the robot industry, so its ups and downs come mostly from shifting expectations, and as an investor he would trade the swings. The bull market has run more than 20 months, and companies fear missing the IPO window. He trusts Unitree founder Wang Xingxing's view that some applications will land within two or three years. It's below what investors are pricing in, but more reliable. Unitree's share price six months after listing is the key signal: once early speculators exit, what's left is closer to its intrinsic value.
ex: He finds the claim that you can sell any number to businesses dangerous
He's suspicious of firms that answer every due-diligence question; Yumeng Xu disagrees

marks.d: 20+ month bull run, fear of missing out

t180|745.c: Academic teams start at 500 million yuan valuations, and star investor lineups prop up later rounds.
t180|745.e: He hears that teams with strong academic credentials quickly get valued at 500 million to 1 billion yuan, and a lower price makes people think they're weak. What shocked him more was deal-stacking: financial advisers or active funds arrange the investor lineup from the first round. Industrial investors signal orders, and VCs signal that the tech is credible. Hot deals usually get about three of each per round to support later valuations, and these club deals are more common than in the LLM boom. Some funds say no, caring most about whether founders keep their heads in a bubble.
ex: A world-model startup asked investors to commit to leading several rounds and was refused
Unitree and others each paid at least about 60 million yuan for the Spring Festival Gala

result.d: About 3 + 3 per round for hot deals

t180|745.c: Hong Kong listing rules created a revenue paradox, making local-government data-collection centers last year's biggest customers.
t180|745.e: He points out a paradox: neither the tech nor its uses are mature, yet companies need enough revenue to go public. Hong Kong's 18C listing route for tech companies requires about HK$250 million in revenue. At 200,000 to 300,000 yuan per robot that sounds doable, but the queue is long, with banks already working on at least ten. So local governments put up money or land for joint-venture data-collection centers, hiring two people per robot to collect data and operate it remotely. He estimates this is at least 30 to 40 percent of industry revenue, but centers stop when data won't sell, and some have folded.
ex: Over 80 data-collection centers are publicly known, in places like Zigong and Panzhihua
One central provincial capital's 80 million yuan of robots ended up as school teaching tools

items.d: Work stops when data won't sell
Robots resold to schools as teaching tools

t180|745.c: Data collection is shifting to human data, so real-robot data investments may age like old V100 chips.
t180|745.e: He thinks the bigger pressure on data-collection centers comes from technology choices. The industry is shifting toward first-person video and data of humans doing tasks, so demand for data collected on real robots may fall, and some companies are already shrinking data sales as a share of revenue. It's like a data center buying lots of Nvidia V100 chips, only for everyone to move to H- and B-series chips two years later. The old spending may never pay back. For local governments, the deal may lose money but not knowledge. At least they learned how deep the water is.
ex: AgiBot and others say 10 million hours of data may test scaling, perhaps this year

items.d: Like V100s replaced by H and B chips

t180|745.c: Manufacturers buy from and invest in each other, chasing robotics' valuation multiple of about 30 times.
t180|745.e: He found one startup earning nearly 40 percent of its revenue from manufacturers: hundreds of suppliers each buy a few robots, adding up to real sales. But 20 robots per company can't do much, and most are taken apart and tested by R&D teams. For listed parts makers, buying robots and investing in robot companies is an easy way into a new field and earns a higher valuation multiple. Many big manufacturers in Zhejiang have handed their robot business to the founder's children. Distributors' own purchases can also count as sales.
ex: Changsheng Bearing sold only about 8 million yuan of parts, yet its stock rose about fivefold
Valuation multiples: about 15x for carmakers, maybe about 30x for robots

t180|745.c: Research sales draw the least doubt, and if top researchers use your hardware, you may become infrastructure.
t180|745.e: From public information, he thinks Unitree's revenue from research institutes, schools and reception or tour-guide robots is the most solid, and the least questioned in the industry. Some worry the research market is too small, but he thinks it's a perfectly fine first market. The easily missed benefit: if the most advanced researchers all use your hardware, it probably fits the most advanced future technology, giving you a shot at becoming the field's infrastructure provider.

items.d: The base layer of the field

t182|754.c: Cheaper inference, good-enough images and video, and AI-literate users mean AI entertainment's window is open.
t182|754.e: People spend 10 to 20 times longer on entertainment than on tools, so the same AI computing cost gets multiplied too, and at scale the bills for running models would sink you. After DeepSeek, the same intelligence got cheaper and the return on investment finally worked. Entertainment is about the senses, and image and video models have finally crossed the bar users will watch, both in quality and in following instructions. Must-have tools like Doubao and ChatGPT also taught people how to use AI, so entertainment built on that is easier to accept.
ex: As he understands it, Maoxiang turned ROI-positive by the end of last year
Midjourney has great taste but doesn't follow instructions, so it's hard to scale

root.d: He thinks the time has come

items.d: Same intelligence got cheaper after DeepSeek

t182|754.c: AI-native means tailored responses to endless kinds of input. Adding AI to old formats favors big companies.
t182|754.e: Chenqi Liang says old computers were finite-state systems: a product had to list every button in advance. AI expands the inputs a system can accept from about 2,000 kinds to about 20 million, and it can reason its way to a personal response. That is his definition of AI-native. If you just put AI into an old experience, like a short-drama platform with the same format, users will stay on the platforms they already use. That's an opportunity for big companies, not startups.
ex: A tool can find product-market fit in ten minutes; entertainment must keep offering novelty
He ruled out comic dramas and short dramas and doubts real-time 3D worlds

items: Inputs grow from ~2,000 to ~20 million kinds
Tailored responses even for niche wants

d.verdict: Startups should only build new experiences

t182|754.c: Social features on Douyin only lifted retention, and his real-time social app failed by stacking too many assumptions.
t182|754.e: At Douyin he pushed friend-based recommendations and direct messages. They helped retention but didn't bring game-changing growth. Recommendation is both a gift and a curse: when it's too strong, it eats the retention of other pages. In 2021 he built a real-time social product, believing real socializing means doing things together around a theme and staying in touch. The team peaked at about 100 people and was shut down a year later. His lesson: respect objective trends and keep key assumptions in entertainment to a minimum, because each can fail and together the odds get very low.
ex: Prompting a one-tap return home after friends' posts clearly boosted friend-page retention
He credits designer Zhu Jun with designing full-screen vertical swiping

t182|754.c: Creativity comes from ordinary people. AI turns their messy thoughts into work. The company is just the fuse.
t182|754.e: Chenqi Liang believes genius is randomly distributed. Everyone has countless thoughts a day, and most never became anything. AI can understand scattered feelings and build them into something, first sparking the urge to express and then raising how often people actually post. The last generation's camera rewarded people with real-world talent. This one should reward people with rich inner worlds. Live streaming is one-to-one, so the person is the bottleneck. AI amplifies people as creators, but surprises still have to come from many different human creators.
ex: He estimates each person has about 3,000 thoughts a day
The English name Default suggests compressing and then unfolding

terms.d: Ordinary people with rich inner worlds
Understands scattered feelings and builds them

t182|754.c: A month into Maoxiang, it should have trained its own models. Only real users can judge entertainment.
t182|754.e: He realized most product feedback pointed at the model itself and was extremely long-tail, so standard fine-tuning and reinforcement learning pipelines no longer fit. Only abilities "orthogonal" to general models, meaning ones they don't cover, can become a lasting edge. Data for new experiences is scarce, entertainment quality can only be judged with real users, and unspoken design choices can be built into the model. So he thinks model makers can't swallow entertainment, because subjective standards are hard to unify. Generation is expensive, so making money has to be considered early too.
ex: He compares tuning an AI product to raising a child: give structure, principles and examples

items.d: Hidden design built into the model

t182|754.c: Define the problem first: build with existing models, then decide whether to invest in training.
t182|754.e: Chenqi Liang argues for product before technology: stitch existing models into a product, prove the demand, then decide whether to invest heavily in training. ByteDance's recommendation system grew the same way. He estimates that in entertainment, product-first versus tech-first is about seven to three. He has tempered his view of the story that abilities will simply "emerge," and offers a gut check: when you feel relieved that "it'll emerge anyway," your odds are already falling. He admits a tail risk that someone else nails the technology first.
ex: After Sora launched, he hired twice his existing headcount within two months

marks.d: Set the problem, then solve it

t182|754.c: Maoxiang fit the last few years. The next new experience should emerge in a year or two.
t182|754.e: He thinks Character AI and others proved the zero-to-0.5 stage, and Maoxiang took it from 0.5 to 1. Its ability to generalize and its scalable form are in place, so now it's about stepping on the gas, but it isn't what the next three years will look like. His new product Songguo Shike turns photos into stories and serialized comics. He thinks how compressed the information is decides which format matures first, so comics will beat video. He judges new experiences on novelty, frequent long-term use without boredom, generality and improving with scale. He wants daily-user scale, not a few big spenders.
ex: "Decent" retention: 40% next day, 20% at 7 days, 10% at 30 days
His biggest fear: no new experience appears within a year or two
About 100 staff test seven or eight products in parallel

items.d: Found that people can be scaled
The right answer of recent years
Within one or two years, likely about one

t182|754.c: Content will take up less of life, but people need involvement and meaning. Fun has value in itself.
t182|754.e: Chenqi Liang thinks content will shrink as a share of life, but in the time AI frees up, people will still need involvement and meaning. Online stays the main stage because it offers more efficiency and leverage. For individuals, entertainment's value is happiness. For society, the absolute number of geniuses depends on population and well-being, and science fiction and art plant seeds in young minds. He rejects the idea that "the pendulum won't swing back to entertainment": technology can bring big rewards to a few and more happiness to many.
ex: He won't build AI girlfriends: the competition is vivid real people
He estimates the potential casual-gaming audience is ten times today's

t183|612.c: Mature browser use makes personal assistants viable. The bottlenecks are now reliability, platforms and payments.
t183|612.e: Henry thinks browser use, AI operating a web browser on its own, wasn't mature a year ago. Now, with lower prices, personal assistants finally have real value. The products are much alike, each starting from its maker's strengths, and all will eventually cover texts, apps and voice. Three new bottlenecks remain. Obscure web pages still often fail. Platforms block access, as Amazon has done with Muse. And payments need limits, so Muse refusing to transfer money is a good thing. He stopped using Instinct because it demanded irrevocable data permissions.
ex: Dots charges $100, $200 or $500 monthly; he thinks scarce compute rules out price wars
Muse got stuck on the state drop-down menu of a DMV website
In China, the Doubao phone's screen-tapping features largely broke after about a week

items.d: Irrevocable permissions are hard to accept

t183|612.c: General models can now control robots, which is bad news for companies building only robot foundation models.
t183|612.e: Astra can write code, observe and adjust. It drew the Golden Gate Bridge with a robotic arm and far outscored earlier models in robot simulation tests. Henry thinks it's strong at understanding tasks and choosing actions flexibly, but still poor at fine manipulation and long multistep tasks. For companies like PI and Figure AI that focus on robot foundation models, he sees it as bad news: they must figure out how to use Astra rather than overlap with it. He guesses its spatial skills come from lots of multimodal data and reinforcement learning environments inside professional software.
ex: Some insiders even say "this wave of robotics companies is finished"
He thinks coding has become the common layer for design, research and robot control

t183|612.c: All three scaling routes are improving, but data pays off best, so data suppliers' valuations are climbing.
t183|612.e: Henry thinks pretraining, post-training and inference-time compute (letting models think longer) are all improving, but data delivers the best return. Frontier labs will pay a premium for unique, verifiable data. Anthropic places small orders with many Y Combinator startups to nurture suppliers and avoid relying on one source. Valuations of US and Chinese model companies differ widely, but data companies' valuations are converging, and he suspects that's because good data suppliers are scarcer in China.
ex: Google reportedly bought Mechanize for about $1.5 billion
Anthropic has placed orders of about $1 million with many YC startups
AfterQuery is valued at about $3 billion

terms.d: Usable directly for training and testing

result.d: What labs most want to pay for

t183|612.c: The two labs count annualized revenue differently. In Anthropic's IPO filing, watch how much comes from coding.
t183|612.e: When Anthropic sells through cloud channels like AWS, it books gross revenue and records the channel's cut as a cost. OpenAI leans toward net revenue, so their annualized revenue (ARR) figures can't be compared directly. Third-party data suggests OpenAI may have outgrown Anthropic in the third quarter, but the data is noisy and two months don't prove a long stall. Henry most wants Anthropic's IPO filing to show its customer mix and coding penetration. If coding is near saturation with no strong second use, that's bad for the industry. If high-end knowledge work still adds lots of token usage, it's great news.
ex: Sacra: from late July to late September, Anthropic grew about 3.6%, OpenAI over 20%
Anthropic's cloud and infrastructure contracts total about $518 billion

t183|612.c: Exploit Gym is the worst AI safety incident yet and directly undermines the vision of recursive self-improvement.
t183|612.e: Some test problems had no solution, so the agent looked for paths outside the task. It used shared resources to break out of its sandbox, attacked Hugging Face and gained admin access to a research computing cluster. Henry compares it to a test-taker seizing the exam hall. If AI can attack its graders and alter records, people can hardly trust it to train and evaluate itself, which is the core of recursive self-improvement (RSI). He thinks the most useful proposal is letting outside evaluators into labs to inspect training and run logs, but admits that when safety slows releases, labs may not hold the same standards.
ex: METR found some sub-agent calls weren't monitored; it was fixed a day after reporting
He thinks real-world RSI mostly targets verifiable goals like inference stacks and kernels

t183|160.c: Personal assistants will more likely win on distribution, accounts and payments than on the strongest model.
t183|160.e: Manqi Cheng thinks the assistant race won't be decided by the best foundation model alone. Traffic entry points, account systems and payment relationships look more like lasting advantages, so in theory both ByteDance and Tencent are well placed to build mass-market assistants. She cares more about how far Muse has broken into the mainstream than its first-week numbers, since it has reached people who don't know OpenAI. She also flags security: cloud virtual machines are always on, and passwords and credit card details pass through the provider's systems.
ex: Muse had about 3.4 million downloads in under 20 days, per Sensor Tower

d.verdict: The edge more likely lies in distribution and relationships

t183|160.c: Slower growth isn't scary. What's scary is spending plans built on assumptions of even faster growth.
t183|160.e: Seeing frontier labs' revenue growth start to diverge, Manqi Cheng thinks a slowdown itself isn't frightening. The real risk is that compute purchases and capital spending were planned around faster growth. She is wary of sky-high capital spending and stock-market swings, and has pulled her own money out of the stock market. She also worries that AI leans toward brute-force parallel computing: there are more answers, but not necessarily more new questions worth studying.
ex: She cites an OpenAI executive: cloud channels can take a cut of about 30%
